q: Why does the dependency lock file record cryptographic hashes for each selected provider, not just version numbers?
options: So state files can be encrypted with the same hashes
So the registry can bill the team per provider download
So providers can be decrypted before Core loads them
So init can verify that the package it downloads is exactly the build that was originally selected, untampered and unchanged
explain: Hashes make selections tamper-evident: if a mirror or download delivers a different build than the locked one, checksum verification fails instead of silently running unknown code. Providers are not encrypted with these hashes, and they play no role in billing or state encryption.

q: Which argument in a module block tells Terraform where to load the child module's code from?
options: source
count
depends_on
providers
explain: The source argument is the address Terraform loads the module from, such as a registry address or local path. The providers argument (A) passes provider configurations, count (B) repeats the module, and depends_on (C) only orders operations.

q: A developer adds a new registry module block to the configuration on Friday. On Monday, terraform plan fails with an error that the module is not installed and the working directory must be initialized. What is the correct remedy?
options: Re-run terraform init, because adding a module is one of the changes that requires initialization to download and record the new module before plan can proceed
Delete the module block and inline its resources by hand
Run terraform fmt so the module reference is registered
Run terraform validate, which installs any missing modules as a side effect
explain: New module sources are fetched at initialization time; after adding a module block, only a fresh init installs it into .terraform/modules so plan can evaluate it. Removing the module (A) abandons the design, fmt (B) only reformats text, and validate (C) consumes what init installed rather than installing anything itself.

q: A configuration reads 'data "aws_region" "current" {}' and uses its name attribute to build resource names. If the team runs the same configuration against a different region, what should they expect?
options: The region data source creates a new region
Terraform errors because a data source may only be read once ever
The names change to reflect the newly read region, because the data source returns information about the environment it actually runs against
The names stay identical because data results are fixed at authoring time
explain: Data sources query the live provider environment, so the same configuration can produce different results in different regions. Results are not frozen at authoring time (A), reads can repeat every run (B is false), and a read never creates a region (D).

q: A variable `instance_type` has `default = "t3.micro"`. It is also set in `terraform.tfvars` to `t3.small`, and the engineer runs `terraform apply -var="instance_type=t3.large"`. Which value wins?
options: t3.micro — defaults always win
The apply fails — setting a variable three ways is an error
t3.small — tfvars files override the command line
t3.large — `-var` flags have the highest precedence
explain: EXAM TRAP — the precedence ladder: environment variables < terraform.tfvars < *.auto.tfvars < -var-file < -var. The command line always wins. A and B invert the ladder. D is false; multiple sources are normal and resolve by precedence.

q: A configuration declares required_providers with the AWS provider at ~> 5.0 but a teammate edits the lock file by hand to record 6.1.0 and commits it. What happens at the next init?
options: Nothing; hand edits to the lock file are the supported upgrade path
Init installs 6.1.0, because the lock file overrides constraints
Init silently rewrites the constraint in required_providers to match
Init fails, because the locked version does not satisfy the configuration's constraint and the lock must be regenerated legitimately
explain: Constraints are authoritative: a lock entry outside them is an inconsistency init reports rather than obeys, and the fix is to change the constraint deliberately and re-lock. The lock file never overrides configuration, and hand-editing it is unsupported precisely because it creates this failure.

q: A nightly CI job runs terraform init in a job that has no human attached. The job is configured so that if initialization unexpectedly needs a decision, it should fail immediately rather than wait forever for input nobody will type. Which flag provides that behavior?
options: -diff, because unattended runs must show their changes
-backend=false, because prompts only ever come from the backend
-get=false, because unattended jobs cannot download anything
-input=false, because it disables interactive prompts and makes Terraform error out when required input is missing
explain: -input=false is the automation flag: Terraform will not prompt, and errors instead when a prompt would have been required, so CI fails fast instead of hanging. Prompts can arise outside the backend (A), downloads work fine unattended (B), and -diff (D) belongs to fmt, not init.

q: An engineer tests an expression in terraform console: `zipmap(["a", "b", "c"], [1, 2, 3])`. What is displayed?
explain: zipmap() pairs keys with values positionally: the first key takes the first value, and so on.

q: Which two scenarios are correct uses of HCP Terraform cross-workspace features? (Choose two.)
options: Remote state sharing lets an authorized workspace read another workspace's outputs to consume shared infrastructure values
A run trigger queues a run in a dependent workspace after a successful apply in the workspace it depends on
A run trigger copies the source workspace's state file into the downstream workspace, replacing its state
Remote state sharing grants the consuming workspace permission to apply changes in the source workspace
explain: Run triggers automate downstream runs after successful upstream applies, and remote state sharing provides read access to outputs for authorized consumers. Neither feature copies or replaces state, and sharing outputs grants no write or apply rights in the source workspace.

q: Which two adjustments will terraform fmt actually make to a configuration file? (Choose two.)
options: Aligning consecutive single-line argument assignments so their equals signs line up
Converting count-based resources to for_each for better stability
Inserting a missing closing brace so the file parses correctly
Normalizing indentation to the canonical two-space style
explain: Alignment of adjacent assignments (A) and two-space indentation (B) are textbook fmt operations, purely presentational. Converting count to for_each (C) is a semantic refactor only a human should make, and fmt cannot repair broken syntax such as a missing brace (D); a file that does not parse is an error to fix, not something fmt silently mends.

q: An engineer runs terraform state rm aws_instance.old and then terraform apply. What happens to the real EC2 instance?
options: It is stopped but not terminated
Nothing — the instance keeps running; it was only removed from Terraform's tracking
It is terminated, because apply reconciles state with reality
It is moved to a backup state file automatically
explain: state rm forgets the object without touching reality — the classic trap versus terraform destroy, which deletes real infrastructure. A describes destroy. B and D are invented.

q: A team is standardizing how it manages values across two hundred HCP Terraform workspaces. Which two practices match the platform's variable model? (Choose two.)
options: Marking credential values sensitive knowing they become write-only and cannot be read back from the UI later
Putting shared values in variable sets and applying those sets to many workspaces and projects instead of duplicating entries
Making sensitive values readable to any workspace member so they are easy to rotate
Storing shared values in a text file inside every repository and deleting all workspace variables
explain: Variable sets exist to share values across workspaces and projects from one definition, and sensitive marking intentionally makes values write-only for safety. Duplicating files per repository abandons the model, and sensitive values are deliberately never readable in the UI, regardless of convenience.

q: Someone modified a security group in the cloud console. You want to see what drifted and update state to match reality, without proposing any configuration changes yet. Which command?
options: terraform import the security group again
terraform plan -refresh-only
terraform apply -auto-approve
terraform state rm on the security group
explain: Refresh-only mode syncs state to reality and reports drift while proposing zero changes. A is for unmanaged resources, not drifted ones. B would revert the drift immediately without review. C would stop managing the group.

q: In a mature workspace, an engineer runs terraform state list with a module address as an argument. What does that form of the command do?
options: It shows the full attributes of every resource in the module
It validates that the module's configuration matches its state entries
It lists only the state addresses under that module path, filtering the full inventory
It moves every resource in the module to the root module
explain: state list accepts address arguments that filter its output, which is handy for inventorying one module inside a large state. It never moves resources, it prints addresses rather than full attributes, which is state show's job, and it performs no configuration validation.

q: While debugging a configuration, an engineer evaluates `concat(["web"], ["db", "web-2"])` in the console. What is displayed?
options: ["web-2", "db", "web"]
["web", "db", "web-2"]
["web", "db"]
explain: concat() appends the elements of each later list to the earlier ones in order, producing a single combined list.

q: Which of these can a local value reference? (Choose two.)
options: Other local values, allowing layered expressions built from simpler locals
Caller-supplied module arguments that override the local
Input variables, such as building a name from var.project
Values passed in with -var flags targeted directly at the local's name
explain: Locals are built from configuration expressions, so they routinely consume variables and other locals. They cannot be targeted by -var (that mechanism assigns variables) and cannot be overridden by module callers; both of those describe input variables, not locals.

q: Why do teams prefer remote state over emailing terraform.tfstate files between engineers?
options: A remote backend provides a single shared, lockable, access-controlled home for state that the whole team uses consistently
Local files cannot be read by Terraform when received by email
Remote state eliminates the need for state entirely
Emailing state is faster and versioned better than any backend
explain: Sharing through a remote backend solves the collaboration problems of local files: one authoritative copy, locking, access control, and no manual file passing. Emailing copies creates divergent lineages and serial conflicts almost immediately.

TF_LOG_PROVIDER and TF_LOG_CORE are independent component controls, so raising the provider to DEBUG while holding core at WARN isolates the misbehaving provider. A global TRACE floods the file with core noise, the reversed split silences the evidence needed, and TF_VAR_ only sets an input variable, not logging.
options: Set TF_LOG=TRACE with no component variables, so core and provider logs are both at maximum verbosity
Set TF_LOG_PROVIDER=DEBUG and TF_LOG_CORE=WARN, so provider detail is high while core stays quiet
Set TF_VAR_provider_debug=true, which enables provider debugging through a variable
Set TF_LOG_CORE=DEBUG and TF_LOG_PROVIDER=OFF, so only core workflow messages are captured
q: In a production incident only the AWS provider is returning malformed responses while Terraform core behaves normally. Which logging setup captures detailed provider evidence without flooding the capture with core messages?

A CI pipeline runs terraform plan with the -detailed-exitcode flag. In this run, the configuration matches the existing infrastructure exactly and the output says 'No changes.'. What exit code does the pipeline see?
explain: With -detailed-exitcode: 0 = success with no changes, 1 = error, 2 = success with pending changes. Here Exit code 0 means the plan succeeded and found nothing to do.

q: A team is deciding what belongs in a child module's outputs.tf. Which two values are appropriate outputs? (Choose two.)
options: The AWS secret access key from the module's provider block
The ID of the VPC the module creates, so callers can place resources in it
The ARN of the IAM role the module creates, so callers can attach policies
The module's internal local value used to build a resource name
explain: Outputs should expose identifiers callers genuinely need, like resource IDs and ARNs produced inside the module. Internal naming locals (A) are implementation details that stay private, and credentials (C) must never be module outputs (provider blocks do not belong in shared child modules either).

q: A migration spans AWS, Azure, and GCP objects. Why can't the team use one shared ID format in all their import blocks?
options: Import ID syntax is defined per provider and per resource type, ranging from short names to full Azure resource ID paths and GCP project-qualified paths
HashiCorp requires each cloud's imports to run on different days
Import IDs must always be the object's IP address regardless of provider
Only AWS supports import, so the Azure and GCP objects cannot be adopted at all
explain: Every provider documents its own identifier format for each resource type, and those formats differ dramatically across clouds, from a bucket name to a long Azure resource path. There is no scheduling rule, IP addresses are rarely the identifier, and all three clouds' providers support importing their resources.

q: After a security incident, an auditor asks: `Who changed the production firewall rules last month, when, and was it approved?` The team manages firewalls in Terraform with every change merged through pull requests. Which IaC advantage answers the auditor?
options: Automation and speed — changes deploy in minutes
Version control — every change is a timestamped, peer-reviewed, reversible commit
Cost control — `terraform plan` shows changes before they happen
Consistency — every environment looks identical
explain: Version-controlled infrastructure gives a complete audit trail: who, when, what, and the review record. Speed (A) and cost visibility (C) are real IaC advantages but don't answer an audit question. Consistency (D) is about environments matching, not about change history.

q: A plan lists these actions: aws_instance.web will be created, aws_security_group.app will be updated in place, aws_s3_bucket.old will be destroyed, and data.aws_ami.ubuntu will be read. Which summary line matches this list?
options: Plan: 0 to add, 0 to change, 0 to destroy — reads cancel out the other actions
Plan: 1 to add, 1 to change, 1 to destroy — the data source read is not counted in the summary
Plan: 1 to add, 1 to change, 2 to destroy — the data read counts as a destroy
Plan: 2 to add, 1 to change, 1 to destroy — the data read counts as an add
explain: Creates count as adds, in-place updates as changes, and destroys as destroys, while data source reads (<=) never appear in the three summary numbers. Counting the read in any column produces the wrong line.

q: A CI pipeline runs terraform plan with the -detailed-exitcode flag. In this run, the configuration differs from the infrastructure and two resources would be created. What exit code does the pipeline see?
explain: With -detailed-exitcode: 0 = success with no changes, 1 = error, 2 = success with pending changes. Here Exit code 2 means the plan succeeded and differences were found.

q: An engineer wants one canonical definition of an application's name used in tags, DNS, and bucket names across the configuration. Which construct fits, given the name should be derived from the project and environment inputs?
options: A data source that creates the name
A separate hardcoded copy of the name inside each resource
An output, because outputs feed values back into resources
A local that builds the name from var.project and var.environment, referenced everywhere the name is needed
explain: A derived, reused value referenced in many places is the textbook locals use case, keeping every consumer consistent from one definition. Hardcoded copies drift (B), outputs publish results outward rather than feeding resources (C), and data sources read external systems rather than composing names (D).

q: A configuration declares required_version = "~> 1.11.0". A laptop runs Terraform 1.12.0. What happens when any command runs against this configuration?
options: Only apply is blocked; plan and validate still run
Terraform silently downgrades itself to 1.11 for this project
Terraform runs fine, because required_version uses provider-style ranges loosely
Terraform errors out, because ~> 1.11.0 admits Core 1.11.x only and 1.12.0 falls outside it
explain: Core version constraints use the same operators as provider constraints, so ~> 1.11.0 means >= 1.11.0 and < 1.12.0, and Core 1.12.0 is rejected at startup for every command. Terraform never downgrades its own binary to satisfy a configuration.

q: Right after terraform init finishes in a brand-new working directory, a developer lists hidden items to see what was created. Which directory did init create to hold the downloaded provider plugins and module copies?
options: .providers
.git
.modules-cache
.terraform
explain: Init creates the .terraform directory, which holds provider plugins under .terraform/providers and downloaded modules under .terraform/modules. The other names are invented distractors; .git belongs to Git, not Terraform, and no .providers or .modules-cache directory is part of the working directory layout.

q: A company must run the Terraform platform entirely inside its own data center, behind its firewall, with no dependency on HashiCorp's hosted service. Which offering fits?
options: Terraform Registry private modules
The open-source CLI with a local backend
HCP Terraform, which offers an optional on-premises installer
Terraform Enterprise, the self-hosted distribution of the platform
explain: Terraform Enterprise is the self-hosted edition installed in the customer's own environment. HCP Terraform is hosted by HashiCorp with no on-premises option, and the open-source CLI alone lacks the platform's workspace, policy, and collaboration features.

q: A configuration contains the expression `coalesce(null, "", "prod", "dr")`. What does Terraform return?
options: dr
prod
null
explain: coalesce() returns the first argument that is neither null nor an empty string, so null and "" are skipped and "prod" wins.

q: Which two statements about drift detection and health assessments in HCP Terraform are accurate? (Choose two.)
options: Drift detection automatically applies a corrective run whenever drift is found
Health assessments can surface more than drift, including the results of other workspace health checks
Health assessments require a developer to keep the workspace open in a browser tab
Drift detection can run on a schedule and notify the team when real infrastructure diverges from state
explain: Assessments run on schedule without human initiation, notify on divergence, and aggregate health signals beyond drift alone. Detection is deliberately non-destructive, since it never auto-applies corrections, and no browser session is involved in a server-side scheduled check.

q: A junior engineer confuses .terraform.lock.hcl with state locking during an incident. Which correction is accurate?
options: Both files are the same mechanism viewed from different commands
State locking writes its holder information into .terraform.lock.hcl
.terraform.lock.hcl is the file that holds the state lock ID during an apply
.terraform.lock.hcl pins provider versions and checksums; state locking is a backend mechanism that prevents concurrent state writes — they are unrelated
explain: The similar names hide different jobs: the dependency lock file ensures reproducible provider selection, while state locking coordinates writers through the backend. Looking for a state lock ID in the dependency lock file will not help resolve a stuck lock.

q: A networking team publishes the ID of a shared transit gateway outside Terraform. A workload configuration needs to attach to it. What is the cleanest Terraform-native way to consume that ID?
options: Paste the ID as a literal string in every attachment resource
Declare a data block that looks the gateway up by its ID or tags and reference the data attributes in the attachment
Create the gateway again in this configuration and ignore the shared one
Declare a resource block for the transit gateway so Terraform adopts it on first apply
explain: A data lookup by ID or tags reads the shared, externally owned object without taking over its lifecycle. A resource block would attempt to manage or recreate it (A and D), and scattering literal IDs (B) is brittle compared with a single named lookup.

q: A module outputs the value of `sort([18, 9, 29])`. What value does it produce?
explain: sort() orders the elements ascending: 9, 18, 29. The original written order is not preserved.

q: A module is sourced from a local path: `source = "./modules/networking"`. Which statements are true about this module?
options: It must be published to a registry before init will accept it
Local modules cannot accept input variables
It is referenced by filesystem path, has no versioning, and is read directly — no download step needed
It supports the `version` argument for pinning releases
explain: Local-path modules are just directories on disk: no registry, no versions, no download. A is wrong — version is registry-only. C is false. D is false — local modules take inputs/outputs like any module.

q: Which two statements describe how Terraform supports hybrid cloud estates? (Choose two.)
options: Hybrid support requires a separate Terraform binary for each data center
Providers exist for on-premises platforms such as VMware alongside public cloud providers
The same plan and apply workflow can target on-premises and cloud resources
On-premises resources must first be migrated to a public cloud before Terraform can manage them
explain: Hybrid support comes from providers for on-premises platforms combined with the single workflow that targets them alongside clouds. No migration is required first, and one Terraform CLI works with all providers rather than needing a binary per site.

q: A tech lead asks terraform fmt to also standardize the codebase by renaming aws_instance.WebServer to snake_case, moving variable blocks above resource blocks, and dropping an unused argument. What should the team expect fmt to do with that request?
options: Fmt removes the unused argument but leaves names untouched
Fmt renames the resource but refuses to reorder blocks
Fmt performs all three, because naming and ordering are part of canonical style
Fmt does none of it: it adjusts style only, such as whitespace, indentation, and alignment, and never renames objects, reorders blocks for logic, or changes what the configuration means
explain: Fmt is deliberately cosmetic: identical semantics in and out, with only presentation normalized. Renaming (A, B) would change resource addresses and state mappings, and deleting arguments (A, C) would change behavior, so both are far outside a formatter's mandate; semantic cleanup is human work, checked by validate rather than performed by fmt.

q: An engineer expects a data block to support 'lifecycle { prevent_destroy = true }' to protect the underlying VPC. Why will this not work as intended?
options: Because prevent_destroy only works on output blocks
Because lifecycle blocks are only allowed in the terraform settings block
Because data sources do not manage the underlying object, so there is no Terraform-managed destruction for a lifecycle rule to prevent
Because the VPC provider does not support any lifecycle rules anywhere
explain: Lifecycle meta-arguments govern managed resources; a data source owns nothing, so there is nothing for prevent_destroy to guard. The distractors misplace where lifecycle is allowed (A and B) or overstate a provider limitation (D) that is not the reason.

q: How does moving a resource between two different state files differ fundamentally from terraform state mv within a single state?
options: Moving between states destroys and recreates the real resource, while moving within a state does not
Moving within a state requires pushing two state files, while moving between states requires none

Within one state, mv is a single rename in one snapshot; between states, the entry must be removed from one snapshot and added to another, typically via pull, mv with -state/-state-out, and pushing both states, which is riskier and not atomic
There is no difference; both operations are a single atomic rename in one backend
explain: A same-state mv rewrites one address in one snapshot in a single operation. A cross-state move spans two snapshots and two backends, with manual pull and push steps and no atomicity, though done correctly it still never destroys or recreates the real resource.

q: A declarative import completed last week and the imported server has applied cleanly several times since. What may the team safely do with the import block?
options: Keep it forever, because deleting it will destroy the server
Move it into terraform.tfvars so it stays hidden
Convert it to a data block so the server stays imported
Remove it from configuration, because the import has already happened and the resource is now managed normally
explain: Import blocks are needed only to perform the adoption, so once apply has imported the object they can be removed without affecting the resource in state. Keeping one is harmless but unnecessary, and removing it never destroys the now-managed resource.

q: After Core is upgraded, init for one project succeeds for most providers but fails for one, reporting it was built for a provider protocol version Core no longer supports, while another project's newer release of the same provider works. What is the precise fix for the failing project?
options: Reinstall the identical provider version from the registry to refresh its protocol
Downgrade every other provider to the same protocol generation
Delete only the failing provider's hashes from the lock file so Core skips it
Raise that provider's constraint to a release built on a supported protocol, run init -upgrade, and commit the regenerated lock file
explain: Protocol support is a property of the provider build itself, so only moving that one provider to a newer compatible release, re-resolving with init -upgrade, and committing the new lock fixes it. Reinstalling the same build changes nothing, removing hashes breaks verification without changing the binary, and unrelated providers are unaffected.

q: A security review asks why the backend block cannot simply read its bucket name from an input variable like the rest of the configuration. Which explanation about initialization order is correct?
options: Variables work in backend blocks, but only when they have default values
Variables are loaded only after the first apply, so the backend block would always see empty values
Backend blocks reject variables purely as a licensing restriction in the open-source CLI

The backend is initialized before the configuration is fully evaluated, so variables and references do not exist yet at that point; that is why partial configuration is completed with -backend-config at init time instead
explain: Backend initialization happens first, before variable evaluation, which is the architectural reason backend blocks accept only literal values plus -backend-config completions. Variables are in fact loaded at plan time, not after apply (A), there is no licensing restriction (C), and defaults do not rescue the pattern (D) because evaluation order, not value availability, is the blocker.

q: While reading a plan, an engineer wants to preview how state and configuration will be reconciled across the whole workspace before approving anything. Which statement best describes terraform plan in that role?
options: Plan is a read-only reconciliation preview: refresh updates its picture of reality, then it reports creates, updates, and destroys without executing them
Plan applies small changes immediately and only previews large ones
Plan skips refresh by default, so its preview never reflects console changes
Plan writes its reconciliation decisions directly into the state file
explain: Plan's inspection value comes from refreshing against reality and diffing against configuration while changing nothing, making it the safe preview for reconciliation decisions. It never applies partially, refresh is on by default rather than skipped, and state writes happen during apply, not plan.

q: A team models a fleet as list(object({ name = string, cpus = number })). What does this type constraint guarantee?
options: A map keyed by server name with numeric values
An ordered sequence of objects, each with a string name attribute and a numeric cpus attribute
A single object whose attributes are lists of names and CPU counts
A set of objects that Terraform will sort by name automatically
explain: Complex types compose: list(object({...})) means an ordered collection where every element is an object matching the inner schema. It is not a map (no keys are declared), not a set (order and duplicates follow list rules), and not a single transposed object.

q: A module author wants a variable that accepts either a single CIDR string or a list of CIDR strings from different callers without forcing every caller into one shape. Which statement is most accurate?
options: type = any accepts both shapes, but the module must then normalize the value itself, for example with flatten and conditionals, because no schema is enforced
Setting type = string makes Terraform wrap single values into lists automatically
Terraform type constraints support a native union type written as string | list(string)
object() automatically unions a string and a list into one type
explain: Terraform has no union type syntax and no automatic string-to-list wrapping; the pragmatic pattern is type = any (or no constraint) plus explicit normalization logic in locals. That trades early validation for flexibility, which the author must handle deliberately.

q: A constraint combines several operators: version = ">= 4.10.0, < 5.0.0, != 4.12.0". The registry offers 4.11.0, 4.12.0, and 4.13.0. Which is the newest version init may select?
options: 4.12.0, because != only excludes it when no alternative exists
4.11.0, because any != in a constraint caps selection below it
4.13.0, because it clears the floor and ceiling and is not the excluded build
None; mixing != with a range makes the constraint unsatisfiable
explain: All comma-separated parts must hold at once: 4.13.0 is >= 4.10.0, < 5.0.0, and not equal to 4.12.0, so it wins. The != operator removes exactly the one named build rather than capping the range below it.

q: A migration must adopt forty existing DNS records whose IDs are held in a map variable. Which import block capability, added in Terraform 1.7, avoids writing forty separate blocks?
options: count inside an import block, which imports objects in numeric order
for_each inside a single import block, iterating the map and importing each record to its matching resource instance
A dynamic import block generated by terraform fmt
Import blocks cannot be repeated, so forty CLI commands are the only option
explain: Terraform 1.7 added for_each support to import blocks precisely for bulk adoption, pairing each map entry's ID with the corresponding for_each resource instance. Count is not supported in import blocks, fmt generates nothing, and the CLI fallback ignores the feature built for this case.

q: A configuration declares 'variable "tags" { type = map(string); default = {} }'. What does the default of {} accomplish?
options: It forbids callers from supplying tags
It makes tags optional: callers who assign nothing get an empty map instead of an error, while callers may still supply their own map
It makes the variable required
It converts all tags to sensitive values
explain: An empty-map default is the standard way to make a collection input optional while keeping its type. It does the opposite of making the variable required (A), callers can still override it (C), and defaults have no effect on sensitivity (D).

q: In required_providers, an entry reads source = "hashicorp/random". How are the two parts of this address interpreted?
options: hashicorp is the account name and random is the workspace
hashicorp is the version channel and random is the module name
hashicorp is the namespace (publisher) and random is the provider type
hashicorp is the hostname and random is the region
explain: A source address is namespace/type, with the hostname implied when omitted: hashicorp publishes the provider whose type is random. Hostnames, regions, versions, and workspaces are separate concepts that never appear in these two positions.

q: Why is restricting access to the remote backend effectively equivalent to restricting access to the infrastructure secrets?
options: Anyone who can read state can read the sensitive attribute values stored in it in plaintext
Reading state automatically grants provider API credentials
State access is unrelated to secrets because values are hashed in state
State contains the cloud account root password in a dedicated field
explain: State is a snapshot of attribute values, including passwords, keys, and tokens that providers returned, stored without hashing. So backend read access must be treated like secret access, even if CLI output normally redacts sensitive values.

q: Why does terraform state push warn and require extra care before overwriting remote state?
options: Pushing an older or edited state can overwrite newer state, causing Terraform to lose track of resources created since that snapshot
Push converts the state file to HCL and breaks future plans
Push is safe because Terraform always merges pushed state with remote state
Push automatically destroys any resource missing from the pushed file
explain: state push replaces remote state with the file you supply; if that file is stale, work done after it was taken disappears from Terraform's record even though the real resources still exist. Terraform does not merge the two snapshots, which is why push is dangerous.

q: A configuration change deletes a resource block, adds no removed block, and the plan shows that resource will be destroyed. A teammate expected it to be preserved. What explains the plan?
options: Deleting a block by itself is a destroy instruction; preservation requires an explicit removed block with lifecycle destroy = false (Terraform 1.7+) or a state rm workflow
Terraform preserves deleted-block resources by default and the plan display is a bug
Destroy in the plan means the object is removed from state but kept running
The resource is preserved only when the backend is remote, regardless of blocks
explain: Plain block deletion means 'this should no longer exist,' so Terraform plans destruction. Preservation is the exception that must be declared explicitly with a removed block and destroy = false, not the default for deleted blocks.

q: An engineer runs terraform import aws_instance.web i-0abc123 with no resource block for aws_instance.web anywhere in the configuration. What happens?
options: Terraform creates a resource block automatically and imports successfully
The import fails because the CLI import requires a matching resource block to already exist in configuration
Terraform imports the instance into a temporary holding state
The import succeeds but the instance is marked as a data source
explain: The CLI import maps a real object to an existing configuration address, so the resource block must be written first, even if it starts out minimal. Terraform does not author the block for you during a CLI import, hold objects temporarily, or convert them to data sources.

q: An engineer wants a quick inventory of every resource address currently tracked in state. Which command lists them?
options: `terraform state list`
`terraform output`
`terraform providers`
`terraform show -json`
explain: `state list` prints every tracked resource address — the state inventory. B dumps full state as JSON (verbose, not an address list). C lists required providers. D shows output values, not resources.

q: After refresh, a plan shows drift on several managed resources following a weekend of manual console work. Which two responses are legitimate ways to reconcile the drift? (Choose two.)
options: Apply the unchanged configuration to revert console changes the team does not want to keep
Edit terraform.tfstate directly in a text editor until it matches the console
Delete the state file so the next run stops reporting differences
Update the configuration to match any console changes the team wants to keep, then apply
explain: Drift is reconciled in exactly two directions: codify the change you want by editing configuration, or revert it by applying the configuration you already have. Hand-editing state corrupts Terraform's record-keeping, and deleting state orphans every managed resource instead of reconciling anything.

q: A compliance team requires that a shared module be fetched over a channel where the exact archive contents are integrity-checked on every machine. Comparing Git with ?ref=<full commit SHA> versus an HTTP URL serving a zip, which statement is most accurate?
options: The commit SHA pin is content-addressed by Git history and effectively immutable, while a zip at a plain HTTP URL can be silently replaced server-side, so the Git pin gives stronger reproducibility guarantees
HTTP sources support the version argument, making them more reproducible
SHA pins are weaker because branches can be renamed
Both are equally reproducible because URLs never change
explain: A full commit SHA identifies one immutable tree in Git's content-addressed history, whereas whoever controls the web server can swap a zip behind a stable URL without any visible change. HTTP module sources do not take version arguments (A), and branch renaming concerns branch refs, not SHAs (D).

List, show, then plan moves from inventory to detail to comparison, and all three steps are read-only, so the workspace and infrastructure stay untouched while understanding grows. Apply, import, and state mv all mutate state or infrastructure and would corrupt the very baseline the engineer is trying to learn.
options: terraform apply to synchronize everything, then terraform state list to see what changed
terraform state list to inventory addresses, then terraform state show on key resources to see recorded attributes, then terraform plan to see how configuration compares with reality
terraform import for every cloud object in the account, then terraform state list to confirm adoption
terraform state mv to group resources logically, then terraform plan to validate the new names
q: You are handed an unfamiliar workspace with no documentation. Which sequence builds a mental model in the safest order, changing nothing along the way?
An init run after a backend change offers three conceptual choices. Which choice matches 'keep managing the same infrastructure, just store its record elsewhere'?
options: Accept the migration so existing state is copied to the new backend
Choose reconfigure and discard the old state entirely
Destroy the infrastructure and rebuild it in the new backend
Delete the new backend and return to local state permanently
explain: Copying state during init preserves the existing management relationship while changing only where state is stored. Reconfigure without migration breaks continuity, and rebuilding infrastructure is unnecessary for a storage move.

q: Which two facts about saved plan files are correct? (Choose two.)
options: A saved plan can become unusable if the underlying state changes before it is applied, producing a stale plan error
terraform apply of a saved plan file does not ask for interactive approval, because approval happened when the plan was reviewed
Applying a saved plan re-runs refresh to make sure nothing drifted
A saved plan file can be edited in a text editor to tweak values before applying
explain: The saved-plan contract is review once, apply the identical artifact without a prompt, and only while state still matches the plan's basis. Plan files are binary and not hand-editable, and apply of a saved plan does not re-refresh or re-plan.

q: An air-gapped build runner already contains every module the configuration uses, copied in ahead of time, and network access is disabled. The team wants init to skip the module-download step entirely. Which flag does that?
options: -backend=false, because module downloads are part of backend setup
-input=false, because downloads would otherwise prompt for confirmation
-reconfigure, because pre-copied modules count as a reconfiguration
-get=false, because it disables downloading and installing modules during init
explain: The -get flag controls module retrieval: -get=false tells init to use modules already present instead of downloading them. -backend=false (A) skips backend setup, not module fetching; -input=false (B) only suppresses prompts; and -reconfigure (C) concerns saved backend configuration, not module installation.

q: An engineer runs 'terraform output -json' in a directory with existing state. What does she get?
options: A JSON copy of the entire configuration
A new apply performed in JSON mode
An error, because outputs are text-only
A JSON document mapping each output name to its value and type information, suitable for scripts and other tools to consume
explain: terraform output -json renders the root module's outputs as machine-readable JSON, which is why automation uses it to hand values to other systems. It is not a dump of the configuration (B), JSON output is fully supported (C), and the command reads state without applying anything (D).

q: In what exceptional situation does terraform state push reject an upload unless -force is used?
options: When any resource in the file has sensitive attributes
When the pushed state has a lower serial or a different lineage than the current remote state
When the state file is larger than 1 MB
When the backend is S3 rather than a local file
explain: The serial and lineage checks protect against overwriting a newer or unrelated state; -force bypasses those safeguards. That bypass is exactly why force push should be rare and deliberate, not a routine recovery shortcut.

q: A developer has the plan permission level on a workspace. She queues a plan and reviews its output, then tries to confirm the resulting apply but is blocked. Why?
options: Her plan expired because plans are valid for only sixty seconds
Only organization owners can ever confirm an apply in any workspace
Applies are disabled for everyone during business hours by default
Plan permission allows queueing and viewing plans but does not include applying runs, which requires write permission
explain: The permission ladder is read, plan, write, admin: plan lets users start and inspect plans, while confirming applies requires write. There is no business-hours lockout or sixty-second plan expiry, and workspace write access, not just ownership, permits applies.

q: A firm runs some workloads on AWS and some in a private data center because of data residency rules. They want the same engineers and process for both. Which term and tool fit?
options: Single-cloud with ARM templates for both sites
Hybrid cloud with Terraform, using providers for AWS and for on-premises platforms in one workflow
Multi-cloud with CloudFormation for both sites
Imperative migration with manual runbooks for both sites
explain: Cloud plus private data center is hybrid cloud, and Terraform's providers span both worlds under one workflow. CloudFormation and ARM are single public-cloud tools and cannot manage the data center side.

q: Two engineers argue about plan refresh: one says plan never changes state, the other says refresh writes to state during plan. For Terraform 1.12 behavior on a normal plan, which nuance is correct?
options: State is never read during plan; the diff uses provider caches from init
Refresh happens only during init, never during plan
Plan permanently rewrites the state file on every run, even if the plan is discarded
A normal plan refreshes its in-memory view of state to compute the diff, but the refreshed values are only persisted to the state file when an apply (including apply -refresh-only) runs
explain: Plan refresh affects the plan calculation and the proposed state shown in output, but discarding the plan does not persist refreshed values; persistence happens on apply. The distractor claiming every plan rewrites state overstates it, and refresh is a plan/apply phase, not an init phase.

q: Which two capabilities become available to a CLI user once a configuration is connected to HCP Terraform through the cloud block? (Choose two.)
options: Running terraform plan and apply as remote runs in the connected workspace when its execution mode is remote
Editing cloud provider resources directly in the HCP Terraform web console without Terraform
Automatically converting all local modules into public registry modules
Viewing run status, logs, and state information for the workspace from the CLI workflow
explain: The cloud block ties CLI commands to the workspace, enabling remote runs and visibility into run and state activity. HCP Terraform offers no direct console editing of resources bypassing Terraform, and it never publishes local modules to the public registry automatically.

q: During terraform apply, Terraform reports that a resource argument changed in a way that cannot be modified on the existing object. No -replace flag was passed. What will Terraform do for that resource?
options: Fail the entire apply and change nothing
Destroy the old object and create a new one as part of the apply, shown in the plan as -/+ replacement
Silently keep the old object and mark the run successful
Update the object in place anyway and log a warning
explain: When a changed argument is marked by the provider schema as forcing new resource creation, Terraform replaces the object automatically and shows -/+ in the plan; -replace is only needed to force replacement when the diff would not. Apply does not fail or silently skip such changes.

q: Before letting fmt touch anything, a developer wants to see the exact line-by-line differences it proposes for a messy file. Which flag shows those differences?
options: terraform fmt -write=false alone, which converts fmt into a diff viewer
terraform fmt -check, because check mode always prints full diffs
terraform fmt -list=false, because suppressed listings are replaced by diffs
terraform fmt -diff, which displays the formatting changes as diffs
explain: -diff is the flag that renders proposed formatting changes as a diff. -check (A) reports which files fail and signals via exit code without printing diffs, -list=false (B) suppresses file names rather than showing changes, and -write=false (D) merely prevents writing; paired with -diff it previews safely, but alone it shows nothing.

q: A skeptical manager asks for one concrete difference between Terraform and a configuration management tool that installs software. Which answer is most precise?
options: Terraform declares cloud and platform resources such as networks and load balancers through providers; configuration tools mainly enforce desired package and file state inside operating systems
Configuration tools are always declarative and Terraform is always imperative
There is no difference the exam recognizes
Terraform cannot run on Linux while configuration tools can
explain: Precision matters: Terraform provisions platform-level resources via provider APIs, while Ansible, Chef, and Puppet center on in-guest configuration. The OS claim is false, the declarative labels are oversimplified, and the exam explicitly recognizes the distinction.

q: While debugging a configuration, an engineer evaluates `pow(2, 8)` in the console. What value does it produce?
explain: pow() raises the first number to the power of the second: 2^8 = 256. The distractor values come from applying the wrong operation or rounding the wrong way.

q: With HCP Terraform remote operations, a developer runs `terraform plan` on their laptop. Where does the plan actually execute, and what is the security benefit?
options: On the laptop, as always — remote operations only affect `apply`
In the Git repository's CI system
On HCP Terraform's runners — cloud credentials stay server-side, so developers never need sensitive keys on their machines
On the cloud provider's API servers directly
explain: Remote operations move execution to HCP Terraform: plans and applies run there, credentials live server-side, laptops hold no secrets. A denies the feature. q: An engineer proposes managing an on-premises VMware cluster and an AWS VPC with the same Terraform workflow. What is this pattern called?
options: Hybrid cloud management, because one workflow spans on-premises and public cloud
Single-cloud provisioning, because both use virtualization
Imperative scripting, because VMware requires manual steps
Configuration drift, because the two environments will differ
explain: Hybrid cloud means combining on-premises infrastructure with public cloud under one management approach, which Terraform supports through providers for both. It is not single-cloud, it is still declarative, and differing environments are not automatically drift.

q: During backend migration, terraform init detects the backend changed and asks whether to copy the existing state to the new backend. What happens if the operator answers yes?
options: Terraform merges the new backend state with a random other workspace
Terraform copies state to the new backend so the same resources remain managed and are not recreated
Terraform destroys the infrastructure and rebuilds it under the new backend
Terraform deletes the old state without copying anything
explain: Answering yes to the migration prompt copies the existing state snapshot to the new backend, preserving the mapping to real resources. That is the point of migration: change where state lives without changing what is managed or recreating it.

q: A developer removes an aws_sqs_queue block from the configuration entirely and runs terraform plan, expecting the queue to survive because its block is gone. What does the plan actually propose?
options: Creation of a replacement queue with default settings
An in-place update setting the queue's attributes to empty
Destruction of the queue, because a resource in state but absent from the configuration is planned for destroy — removing the block is how you tell Terraform to delete a resource
No action, because deleted blocks are ignored completely
explain: Configuration is the desired state: a tracked resource with no block is undesired, so plan proposes its destruction. This is the normal way to delete individual resources, distinct from terraform destroy which targets everything in state.

q: A configuration contains 'data "aws_caller_identity" "current" {}'. What does Terraform do with this block during a run?
options: It creates a new AWS account identity and stores it in state as a managed object
It queries AWS for information about the caller and makes the returned attributes available to the configuration, creating nothing
It imports an existing IAM user into management
It deletes any IAM identity that is not referenced elsewhere
explain: A data block only reads information from a provider and exposes attributes such as account_id for use elsewhere; it creates and manages nothing. A resource block, not a data block, is what creates objects (A and B), and Terraform never deletes unmanaged identities (D).

q: A security review asks why developers using remote execution mode do not need cloud access keys on their workstations. Which answer is correct?
options: Because keys are stored in the Git repository and checked out automatically during runs
Because terraform login converts a user's laptop password into cloud credentials
Because the run executes in HCP Terraform, which supplies credentials from workspace variables or dynamic credentials on the server side
Because HCP Terraform disables all provider authentication for remote runs
explain: Remote runs execute server-side, so credentials configured in the workspace, or minted dynamically per run, never need to live on developer laptops. Authentication is not disabled, keys must never sit in Git, and terraform login authenticates to HCP Terraform, not to cloud providers.

q: An engineer proposes extracting a one-time data migration bucket, used by a single script next week and then deleted forever, into a shared reusable child module. What is the best call?
options: Extract it, but only after publishing it to the registry first
Keep it inline in the root configuration, because a resource used once with no prospect of reuse gains nothing from a module interface and only adds indirection
Extract it so the bucket can avoid appearing in state
Extract it, because every resource group should live in a module
explain: A module pays off through reuse and encapsulation of a repeated pattern; a throwaway one-off resource gains neither, so the inputs, outputs, and maintenance overhead are pure cost. A states a rule HashiCorp does not give, publishing first (B) adds even more ceremony to a disposable resource, and module resources still appear in state, ruling out D.

for_each in an import block, available from Terraform 1.7, pairs each element of a map or set with a distinct real object ID and a distinct resource instance, enabling bulk adoption from one block. It does not duplicate one object, delete unmanaged objects, or schedule repeated runs, which are common misreadings of the feature.
options: Run the import repeatedly on a schedule until every object succeeds
Delete many unmanaged objects in one plan without writing resource blocks
Import the same cloud object into many addresses at once for redundancy
Import many distinct existing objects in one declaration by iterating a collection of their provider IDs
q: In Terraform 1.7 and later, what does adding for_each to a single import block let a team do in plain terms?

explain: The implicit default only covers hashicorp/<type> on registry.terraform.io, a legacy convenience for official providers. A vendor provider lives under a different namespace, so without an explicit source Terraform looks in the wrong place. The distractor about version constraints is wrong; constraints work fine, they were just applied to the wrong implied address.
options: When source is omitted, Terraform assumes the hashicorp namespace on the public registry; a provider published under any other namespace is only found when its full source address is declared
Omitting source makes Terraform build the provider from source code, which fails for vendor providers
Version constraints are ignored unless a source is also present in the same block
Third-party providers must be installed with a separate terraform providers install command
q: A team adopts a monitoring provider published by a small vendor under that vendor's own registry namespace. A junior engineer omits the source from required_providers, keeping only a version constraint, and init installs nothing useful. Why is the explicit source mandatory here?
An incident review requires both granular core and granular provider diagnostics from a single terraform run. Which two settings belong in that run's environment? (Choose two.)
options: TF_LOG_PATH alone, which raises both core and provider verbosity automatically
TF_LOG_PROVIDER=TRACE to capture the most detailed provider plugin logging
TF_VAR_log_level=TRACE to set a configuration variable named log_level
TF_LOG_CORE=DEBUG to capture detailed core workflow logging
explain: TF_LOG_CORE and TF_LOG_PROVIDER independently set each component's level, so DEBUG core plus TRACE provider output can be captured together for the review. TF_VAR_ only feeds input variables, and TF_LOG_PATH selects a destination file without changing any verbosity by itself.

q: A destroy preview ends with: Plan: 0 to add, 0 to change, 9 to destroy. A teammate asks whether running the corresponding apply of this destroy plan would leave any managed resources standing in this workspace. What is the answer?
options: No resources will be destroyed because a plan with 0 adds is invalid
Yes; 9 destroys in a preview means only the 9 oldest resources are removed and newer ones stay
The 9 resources will be updated in place instead of destroyed
No; all 9 state-tracked resources will be destroyed and nothing is added or changed, so the workspace will manage zero resources afterward
explain: A plan of 0/0/9 is a complete teardown of everything in state: nine destructions and no compensating creates. It is a valid plan shape (exactly what plan -destroy produces), and destroys in the summary mean real terminations, not updates.

q: A configuration contains the expression `length(["api", "cache", "db"])`. What is the result?
explain: length() of a list counts its elements: the list has 3 elements.

q: An engineer tests an expression in terraform console: `merge({ Name = "web", Env = "dev" }, { Env = "qa", Team = "ops" })`. What value does it produce?
options: { Env = "qa", Name = "web", Team = "ops" }
{ Env = "dev", Name = "web", Team = "ops" }
{ Env = "qa", Team = "ops" }
{ Env = "dev", Name = "web" }
explain: merge() combines maps left to right and later maps win key conflicts, so Env is overwritten with "qa" while Name survives and Team is added.

q: An organization has 40 workspaces that all need the same AWS credentials and region variables. What is the DRY way to manage this in HCP Terraform?
options: Variable sets only work for a single workspace, so this is impossible
Variable sets — define the shared variables once and attach the set to all 40 workspaces (or their project)
Store them in `terraform.tfvars` in each workspace's repo
Copy the variables into each workspace by hand
explain: Variable sets are shared variable collections attached across workspaces or projects — define once, inherit everywhere. A is the manual anti-pattern. C works for CLI runs but misses HCP's native mechanism. D is false; multi-workspace attachment is the point.

q: When is a local value a better choice than a variable?
options: When the value is derived inside the configuration from other data and should not be set independently from outside, such as a standardized resource name built from the environment variable
When the value must appear in terraform output automatically
When each environment must supply its own value at deploy time
When the value is a password that must be prompted for
explain: Derived, internally consistent values are the locals sweet spot: the formula lives in the configuration and callers cannot set it inconsistently. Prompted secrets (A) and per-environment inputs (C) are variable use cases, and locals do not surface in output unless an output references them (D).

Provider installation methods are a per-machine CLI configuration concern: a provider_installation block with filesystem_mirror (and direct excluded) makes init resolve providers from the local mirror only. The distractor about source addresses is wrong because source identifies which provider to get, never the local directory to get it from.
options: Copy the provider binaries into each project's .terraform directory by hand before running init
Configure the backend with the file share path; backends control where providers are downloaded from
Set each provider's source in required_providers to the file share path
Add a provider_installation block to the CLI configuration file with a filesystem_mirror pointing at the staging directory, and exclude direct registry installation
q: A regulated site has no internet access, and provider packages are staged in a directory on an internal file share. How do engineers configure their workstations so terraform init installs providers only from that local staging area?
Which statements correctly describe local values? (Choose two.)
options: A local value is referenced from other expressions as local.<name>
A local can be overridden at run time by passing -var with the local's name
A local can be derived from input variables combined with fixed text, such as building a standardized resource name
Every local is automatically printed to the console after terraform apply
explain: Locals are named internal expressions referenced with the local. prefix, and deriving standardized names from variables is their classic use. They cannot be assigned with -var, which only targets declared variables, and they are not printed after apply unless an output explicitly exposes them.

q: A configuration references a provider that was just added to `required_providers`. `terraform validate` now fails with `Missing or incomplete provider configuration`. What is the most likely cause?
options: The provider's credentials are missing
validate cannot be used with more than one provider
init has not been re-run since the provider was added, so provider schemas are unavailable to validate
The configuration has a syntax error
explain: validate needs provider schemas, which only exist after init downloads the provider. Adding a provider without re-running init is the classic cause. A is possible but the error message points at the provider, not syntax. C is false. D is wrong — validate never needs credentials.

q: A team splits backend settings: the backend block in code names only the type, and environment-specific bucket and key values are supplied at initialization. Which mechanism are they using?
options: A moved block that redirects the backend address
Workspace overrides stored in terraform.tfvars
Variable interpolation inside the backend block
Partial backend configuration, completed at init with -backend-config files or flags
explain: Partial configuration leaves some backend arguments out of the block and supplies them during terraform init via -backend-config=<file> or key=value flags. This exists precisely because backend blocks cannot use variables or references.

q: A platform team keeps all Terraform configuration in Git and routes every infrastructure change through a branch and a pull request instead of editing files directly on a shared server. What is the main workflow benefit of this arrangement?
options: Every change is peer-reviewed, timestamped, and reversible, and the repository becomes the single source of truth for what infrastructure should exist
Pull requests guarantee that every apply completes with zero downtime
Provider plugins download faster when configuration is hosted in Git
Git automatically supplies cloud credentials to Terraform at apply time
explain: Version control gives the team review, history, and rollback for infrastructure exactly as for application code, which is the core team-workflow benefit. Git does not speed up provider downloads (A), inject cloud credentials (C), or promise zero-downtime applies (B); those depend on providers, authentication setup, and resource design.

q: Which two controls best reduce the risk of secrets exposed through Terraform state? (Choose two.)
options: Print the full state file in CI logs on every run
Restrict backend access to only the people and automation that need it
Store state in a remote backend with encryption at rest enabled
Commit terraform.tfstate to a public repository for transparency
explain: Encryption at rest plus tight backend access control directly limit who can obtain plaintext values from state and how they are stored. Publishing state or logging it does the opposite, expanding the audience for embedded secrets.

q: A database password variable is declared with 'sensitive = true'. What does that change about how Terraform handles the value?
options: The password is never sent to the provider
The password value is redacted from Terraform's CLI plan and apply output, though it is still stored in state
The password is encrypted inside the state file
The password variable cannot have a default value
explain: Marking a variable sensitive hides its value in terminal output; the value still reaches the provider and still lands in state, which is why state itself must be protected. It does not encrypt state (A), block provider use (C), or forbid defaults (B).

q: After running `terraform plan -refresh-only` and confirming the drift is legitimate (an approved out-of-band change), what is the correct next step to make Terraform's record match reality permanently?
options: Run `terraform destroy` and re-apply
Nothing — refresh-only already updated the state file, so Terraform now agrees with reality
Delete the state file so the next plan starts clean
Run `terraform apply -refresh-only` to write the refreshed values into state
explain: Subtle but tested: `plan -refresh-only` only previews the refresh; `apply -refresh-only` actually writes the synced state. A confuses the preview with the write. C is wildly destructive. D discards all tracking — the opposite of fixing drift.

q: A manager opens the HCP Terraform health view and sees one workspace flagged for drift and another flagged for a failed health assessment related to policy outcomes. What is the purpose of these assessments?
options: To automatically fix every problem they find without human involvement
To continuously evaluate workspace health, including drift between state and real infrastructure and other checks, so problems are noticed between runs
To rank workspaces by cost so the most expensive can be deleted
To replace the need for plans before applies
explain: Health assessments give ongoing visibility into workspace condition, prominently including drift detection, so divergence is caught even when nobody is running Terraform. They notify rather than auto-fix, they are not cost rankings, and they never substitute for the plan-before-apply workflow.

q: A CI pipeline runs terraform plan with the -detailed-exitcode flag. In this run, the configuration contains an invalid reference and planning stops with an error. What exit code does the pipeline see?
explain: With -detailed-exitcode: 0 = success with no changes, 1 = error, 2 = success with pending changes. Here Exit code 1 means an error occurred.

q: An operator runs terraform state pull | jq -r '.outputs.api_endpoint.value' against a remote backend and gets a single URL printed. What just happened?
options: jq edited the remote state and replaced the api_endpoint output with the printed URL
The command unlocked the state so the output could be read
Terraform queried the cloud API live and registered a new DNS record for the endpoint
state pull downloaded the current state as JSON and jq extracted the recorded value of the api_endpoint root output from that snapshot
explain: state pull emits the current state snapshot as JSON on stdout, and piping it to jq is a read-only inspection pattern for values stored in state, here a root output's recorded value. Nothing is written back to the backend and no cloud resources are queried or changed by jq itself.

q: A module author wants CI to check a child module's configuration in a repository where no backend credentials exist and no state should be touched. Which init invocation prepares the working directory while skipping backend setup?
options: terraform init -migrate-state
terraform init -upgrade
terraform init -backend=false
terraform init -get=false
explain: The -backend=false flag tells init to skip backend initialization entirely, which is the documented pattern for validating child modules or working without backend access. -upgrade (A) only re-resolves versions, -get=false (B) skips module downloads rather than the backend, and -migrate-state (D) does the opposite of avoiding state: it copies state between backends.

q: A service consumes another configuration via terraform_remote_state and a plan suddenly fails because the source configuration renamed its outputs. What lesson does this illustrate?
options: The failure proves terraform_remote_state also writes to the source state
Consumers should read source resource attributes directly to avoid output interfaces
Remote state consumption couples configurations through the source's outputs, so output names and meaning are an interface that must be changed carefully
Remote state failures always mean the backend bucket was deleted
explain: Outputs are the published contract between configurations; renaming them breaks consumers just like renaming an API field. Reading internal attributes increases coupling rather than reducing it, and a read data source does not write source state.

q: A file named `prod.auto.tfvars` sits in the working directory. When are its variable values loaded?
options: Never — `.auto.tfvars` is not a recognized extension
Only during `terraform init`
Only when passed explicitly with `-var-file=prod.auto.tfvars`
Automatically, on every plan and apply — `*.auto.tfvars` files load without flags, after `terraform.tfvars`
explain: `*.auto.tfvars` (and `*.auto.tfvars.json`) are auto-loaded in lexical order, sitting above terraform.tfvars in precedence. A describes -var-file behavior. C is wrong — values load at plan/apply. D denies a real, heavily used feature.

q: An auditor asks how to protect state at rest when using a remote backend. Which answer is most accurate?
options: Encryption is impossible for state files in any backend
Move state into the Git repository and protect the branch instead
Enable the backend's encryption-at-rest features and restrict who can access the backend, because state holds plaintext sensitive values
Mark every variable sensitive and state will be encrypted automatically
explain: Remote backends and their underlying storage offer encryption at rest, and access to the backend becomes the control point for who can read secrets in state. Sensitive marking only redacts display, and committing state to Git widens exposure instead of protecting it.

q: A root configuration needs the private subnet IDs a networking child module created. The child exposes output "private_subnets". Which reference is correct in the root?
options: aws_subnet.networking.private_subnets
module.networking.private_subnets
networking.private_subnets
data.module.networking.private_subnets
explain: Child outputs are read as module.<MODULE NAME>.<OUTPUT NAME> from the caller. Bare names (A) do not resolve, modules are not data sources (C), and the root cannot address resources inside the child directly by their resource address (D).

q: What is the most accurate way to describe the relationship between Terraform and configuration management tools such as Chef and Puppet?
options: Terraform cannot be used in the same pipeline as Chef or Puppet
They overlap, but Terraform focuses on provisioning infrastructure while Chef and Puppet focus on maintaining software configuration on machines
Chef and Puppet provision cloud APIs better than Terraform in all cases
They are identical categories with no meaningful difference
explain: The exam expects the provisioning versus configuration management distinction while acknowledging overlap. Terraform commonly creates the machines that Chef or Puppet then configure, so they are complementary rather than identical or mutually exclusive.

q: A registry module upgrade from 5.0.0 to 6.0.0 renames its output subnet_ids to private_subnet_ids. A caller's plan fails after bumping the version constraint and running init -upgrade. What kind of change broke the caller, and what does it illustrate?
options: A provider breaking change; module outputs are unrelated to versions
A state corruption caused by init -upgrade
A licensing change in the registry terms
A breaking change to the module's interface: outputs are a module's public API, so renaming one breaks callers and justifies the major version bump under semantic versioning
explain: A module's inputs and outputs are its contract; renaming an output breaks every consumer, which is exactly what a major version increment signals. The failure is in the caller's references to the old output name, not the provider (B), state (C), or licensing (D).

q: Which statements about output blocks are true? (Choose two.)
options: An output in the root module is displayed to the operator after a successful apply
An output creates the infrastructure whose attribute it references
An output can include a description documenting what the value represents
An output must always be marked sensitive
explain: Descriptions document outputs just as they document variables, and root outputs are the standard post-apply report to the operator. Outputs never create infrastructure (that is a resource's job) and sensitivity is optional, used only when the value warrants redaction.

q: A team composes a large system as an application module that itself calls database, networking, and caching child modules. What is this pattern called?
options: Module flattening
Provider inheritance
State sharding
Module composition — nesting modules inside modules to build larger systems from small, focused pieces
explain: Composition (nesting) lets small single-purpose modules combine into larger assemblies, and a module can call other modules to any depth. Flattening (A) would mean inlining everything into one level, and provider inheritance (B) and state sharding (D) are not module patterns.

q: The variable "region" receives values from several places: TF_VAR_ is set in the shell environment sets it to "eu-west-1"; the variable block declares default = "ap-northeast-1"; a value in terraform.tfvars.json sets it to "eu-central-1". No other sources set it. Which value does Terraform use?
options: eu-central-1
eu-west-1
ap-northeast-1
ca-central-1
explain: Variable precedence, lowest to highest: default < TF_VAR_ environment < terraform.tfvars < terraform.tfvars.json < *.auto.tfvars < -var-file < -var. The highest source present here is terraform.tfvars.json, so its value "eu-central-1" wins.

q: A variable set defines region as eu-west-1 for a group of workspaces, but one workspace in the group defines region as eu-central-1 at the workspace level because its data must stay in Germany. Which value does that workspace's run use, and why?
options: eu-west-1, because variable sets always override workspace values
The run fails, because duplicate keys across a set and a workspace are an error
Both values alternate between runs depending on load
eu-central-1, because workspace-level values take precedence over variable set values for the same key
explain: Precedence favors the more specific scope: a workspace-level value beats a variable set value for the same key, which is how exceptions like the German residency requirement are implemented. Sets do not override workspaces, duplicates are an intended override pattern rather than an error, and values never alternate.

q: What happens to data source values when 'terraform plan -refresh=false' style workflows or a deferred read are involved, conceptually?
options: Data sources return compile-time constants
Data sources are converted into variables
Data results depend on when the read actually occurs; if the read is deferred or based on stale information, the values used can reflect that timing rather than the newest external state
Data sources ignore refresh settings and always write to state
explain: The key concept is timing: a data result is only as current as the read that produced it, and deferred reads resolve later than plan-time reads. Data sources do not write managed state (A), are not constants (B), and are not variables (D).

q: Inside a resource using count, an argument sets 'name = "server-${count.index}"'. What is count.index here?
options: The total number of resources in the whole configuration
The instance number of the current resource instance being configured, starting at 0
A function that counts characters in a string
A reference to a variable named count
explain: Within a counted resource, count.index is the index of the instance currently being evaluated, which is how per-instance names and tags are made unique. It is not a variable (A), not a global total (B), and not a string function (D).

q: A workstation disk failure destroys the only local terraform.tfstate for a production network, but every VPC, instance, and bucket it managed is still running in the cloud. Which recovery approach restores Terraform management of that infrastructure?
options: Restore management by copying another environment's state file and editing the resource IDs by hand
Use terraform import or import blocks to bind each existing cloud object to its resource address, rebuilding the state mapping, then verify a plan shows no unexpected changes
Delete the cloud resources and rebuild them from configuration so a clean state is created
Re-run terraform apply immediately so Terraform recreates the state file from the configuration alone
explain: Importing re-creates the address-to-object mapping Terraform lost, so the existing infrastructure becomes managed again without recreation. Simply applying with empty state would try to create duplicates of everything that already exists, and destroying production to rebuild it is unnecessary when the objects are healthy.

q: A long-lived server has received hundreds of in-place patches, config edits, and hotfixes over three years. Which model does it exemplify and what risk does it carry?
options: Hybrid model with risk only from the cloud provider
Mutable model with drift risk because its history cannot be reproduced from a single definition
Declarative model with no risk because patches were documented
Immutable model with low risk because it is frequently updated
explain: Continuously modifying a running server is mutable infrastructure, and years of unrecorded changes create drift and reproducibility risk. It is not immutable, documentation alone does not make it declarative, and the risk comes from its own history, not the provider.

q: An application team wants to read a shared services workspace's outputs, but the shared workspace's owner has not authorized their workspace. What happens when the application workspace plans?
options: It reads the outputs anyway, because all workspaces in an organization share state by default
It automatically receives admin permission on the shared workspace
It cannot access the state; remote state sharing is opt-in per consumer workspace, so the read fails until the owner authorizes it
It falls back to reading the shared workspace's Git repository for the values
explain: State sharing is explicit and least-privilege: the owning workspace must authorize each consumer, and unauthorized access fails. Organization membership alone grants no state access, no permissions are auto-granted, and repositories are not a fallback source for state outputs.
