q: A contractor initializes the root configuration successfully, then creates a brand-new subdirectory containing a separate standalone configuration and runs terraform plan inside it, which fails with an initialization error. What explains the failure?
options: Initialization is per working directory: the subdirectory is its own working directory and needs its own terraform init before plan can run there
Standalone configurations in subdirectories are forbidden; everything must live in the root
The lock file from the parent directory blocks all child directories
Plan is limited to one directory per machine per day
explain: Each directory containing configuration that you run commands against is an independent working directory with its own .terraform, backend setup, and lock file, so each needs init. There is no daily plan quota (A), a parent's lock file does not block children (B), and multi-directory layouts are normal (D); child modules are simply initialized as part of the root that calls them, unlike standalone configs.

q: A developer runs terraform fmt with no flags inside a configuration directory. What does the command do by default?
options: It prints a formatting report but never modifies any file
It rewrites the .tf files in that directory in place to canonical style, using two-space indentation and aligning consecutive argument assignments
It formats files and also corrects any invalid argument names it finds
It formats every directory on the machine that contains Terraform files
explain: Bare fmt rewrites files in place, but only in the current directory, normalizing indentation, alignment, and spacing. It is not report-only by default (B), it never corrects argument validity, which is validate's domain (C), and recursion into subdirectories requires the explicit -recursive flag (D).

q: Which two apply behaviors are guaranteed by Terraform's design? (Choose two.)
options: Apply prompts for approval even when a saved plan file is supplied as an argument
Apply always runs every resource operation in the exact order the blocks appear in the configuration files
Apply updates state as individual resources complete, so progress before a mid-run error is not lost
Apply acquires a state lock (on supporting backends) while writing state so two applies cannot interleave
explain: Locking and incremental state writes are core apply guarantees that make concurrent and failed runs safe. Operation order comes from the dependency graph, not file order, and a saved-plan apply deliberately skips the prompt.

q: Which statement correctly contrasts a resource block with a data block?
options: Resources declare objects Terraform manages through their lifecycle, while data sources fetch read-only information about objects Terraform does not manage
Data sources support lifecycle blocks that control creation order, while resources do not
Data sources appear in state as managed resources, while resources do not
Resources are read during refresh, while data sources are created during apply
explain: Managed resources are created, updated, and destroyed by Terraform and tracked in state; data sources are a read-only lookup whose results feed other expressions. The roles in A are reversed, data results are not managed objects in state (B), and lifecycle meta-arguments belong to resources, not data sources (D).

q: A reviewer asks how a pending import declared in an import block will first become visible to the team. Which answer is correct?
options: It appears only in the state file after someone runs the CLI import command
It appears only after the resource is destroyed and recreated
It appears as an import action in terraform plan output before any apply runs
It appears in terraform fmt output as a formatting suggestion
explain: Because import blocks are declarative, plan evaluates them and shows the resource as being imported, giving reviewers a preview before apply performs the adoption. No separate CLI import is involved, formatting tools do not report imports, and recreation is never part of the flow.

q: A mandatory post-plan run task returns a failed result because the plan contains a publicly exposed storage bucket. What is the effect on the run?
options: The run is blocked and cannot proceed to apply until the issue is resolved or the run is handled according to the task's mandatory setting
The run task is uninstalled from the workspace automatically
The bucket is created but immediately quarantined by HCP Terraform
The run continues, because run task results are always informational
explain: A run task marked mandatory blocks progression when it fails, gating the apply on the external check. Advisory tasks are the informational kind, HCP Terraform never quarantines created resources on a task failure, and failed tasks are not auto-uninstalled.

q: A team wants every production change reviewed as a plan file before anything is applied, with a guarantee that apply executes exactly what was reviewed. Which workflow achieves this?
options: terraform apply -auto-approve for speed, then review the logs afterward
terraform validate followed immediately by terraform apply
terraform plan -refresh-only, then terraform destroy
terraform plan -out=tfplan, review it, then terraform apply tfplan
explain: Saved plan files decouple review from execution: the reviewed artifact is exactly what gets applied. B skips review entirely. C never previews changes. D is nonsense — refresh-only proposes nothing and destroy tears everything down.

q: A hiring manager wants engineers who understand why teams adopt IaC. Which two statements are accurate advantages to listen for? (Choose two.)
options: The same configuration can rebuild an environment after it is destroyed
Manual console changes become easier to track than code changes
Infrastructure changes no longer need any testing or review
Changes can be peer reviewed before they are applied
explain: Peer review before apply and rebuildability after destruction are core IaC advantages grounded in code review and reproducibility. IaC does not remove the need for testing, and manual console changes are harder, not easier, to track than code changes.

q: A module outputs the value of `floor(39.7)`. What value does it produce?
explain: floor() rounds down to the whole number below, so 39.7 becomes 39. The distractor values come from applying the wrong operation or rounding the wrong way.

q: A configuration contains an import block for a legacy queue. Which two pieces of information must that block provide at a minimum?
options: count, naming how many objects, and id, naming their shared identifier
to, naming the resource address to import into, and id, naming the provider-specific identifier of the real object
from, naming the old address, and to, naming the new address
source, naming the provider, and version, naming its release
explain: An import block needs to say where the object lands in configuration, the to address, and which real object it is, the id in the provider's format. The other pairings describe moved blocks, provider requirements, or count behavior, not declarative import.

q: While debugging a configuration, an engineer evaluates `element(["ap-northeast-1", "eu-west-1", "ap-south-1", "eu-central-1"], 1)` in the console. What value does it produce?
options: ap-south-1
eu-central-1
eu-west-1
ap-northeast-1
explain: element() selects by index modulo the list length: index 1 mod 4 = 1, which is "eu-west-1". It never errors on an out-of-range index — it wraps around, unlike direct indexing.

q: The plan output ends with: Plan: 6 to add, 0 to change, 6 to destroy, and every affected resource in the detail is marked -/+ . What is really happening in this apply?
options: Six existing resources are each being replaced — destroyed and recreated — likely from a change to an argument that forces new resources across the set
Six resources are created first and the same six are then destroyed in the same run as a test
Nothing is replaced; equal adds and destroys always indicate a no-op move
Twelve unrelated resources are affected: six brand-new and six retired
explain: When every line is -/+, equal add and destroy counts are the signature of mass replacement of the same objects, a high-risk pattern reviewers should interrogate. It is not twelve unrelated resources, not a create-then-destroy test, and never a no-op.

q: An operator force-pushes a week-old state file over current remote state. Which two consequences follow? (Choose two.)
options: A later plan may propose creating duplicate replacements for those still-running resources
Resources created during the week become orphaned because Terraform no longer records them, even though they still exist
The push immediately deletes the newer cloud resources when the file is uploaded
Terraform automatically rediscovers the missing week of resources at the next refresh
explain: A stale forced push replaces the authoritative record with an older snapshot, so newer objects vanish from Terraform's view while still running, leading to duplicate-create proposals. Push itself never deletes cloud resources, and refresh cannot rediscover unmanaged objects.

q: A module output is marked sensitive. A parent resource uses that output value in one of its arguments. What should the team expect?
options: The value becomes unusable anywhere outside the module
The output cannot be referenced from the parent at all
Sensitivity propagates: Terraform tracks the value as sensitive in the parent so it is redacted from CLI output where it appears
The parent resource is automatically destroyed
explain: Sensitive values stay usable in expressions, but Terraform propagates the sensitive marking so plans and applies redact them downstream. Sensitivity does not block use (A and B) and has no destructive side effect (C).

q: During a code review, a teammate asks what `try(element([], 0), "fallback")` evaluates to. What is the result?
options: error: index out of range
fallback
null
explain: try() evaluates its arguments in order and returns the first that succeeds; element() on an empty list errors, so try() falls through to "fallback".

q: A solo developer prototypes on a laptop using default settings and loses the laptop before migrating anything. Which local-state risk has materialized?
options: Automatic deletion of all cloud resources when state disappears
Loss of the only copy of state, leaving the real infrastructure orphaned with no mapping back to the configuration
Expiration of the state lock after 24 hours
Corruption of the provider registry entry for that configuration
explain: With local state the file on that machine may be the only authoritative copy; losing it orphans the infrastructure because Terraform no longer knows which real objects it manages. The cloud resources themselves keep running, they are just no longer tracked.

q: A team builds servers by patching a running golden server and cloning it, so no one knows which patches the clone includes. A consultant recommends codifying the build and rebuilding from code each release. Which problem is being addressed?
options: Excessive use of modules in the repository
Opaque, unreproducible builds caused by manual mutation of a live system
Lack of a private module registry
Provider version locking across environments
explain: Cloning a mutated live server bakes in an unknown history; codifying and rebuilding makes each release reproducible and inspectable. Lock files, modules, and registries are unrelated to the unknown-patch problem described.

q: A new hire asks what an HCP Terraform workspace actually is. Which definition is correct?
options: A Git branch that HCP Terraform watches
A dashboard folder for billing reports
A local directory containing `.tf` files
One managed unit: a Terraform configuration plus its state file, variables, and run history — with remote execution on HCP Terraform
explain: An HCP workspace binds config + state + variables + run history into one managed unit with remote runs. A describes a CLI working directory (related but not a workspace). C confuses VCS integration with the workspace itself. D is billing, not infrastructure.

q: An output exposes a generated admin password. The team sets 'sensitive = true' on the output. What changes?
options: The password is removed from state
Terraform hides the value in CLI output, requiring terraform output -json (by an authorized reader of state) to reveal it deliberately, instead of printing it in plain view after apply
The password output is deleted at the end of apply
The output can no longer be referenced by a parent module
explain: Sensitive outputs are redacted in normal CLI display so secrets are not printed by default, while remaining stored in state and retrievable by anyone with state access. The value is not removed from state (A), not deleted (C), and parent modules can still consume it, with sensitivity propagating (B).

q: A team wants operators to see a friendly message combining an instance ID and region after apply. Which output definition does this?
options: locals "summary" { value = aws_instance.web.id }
output "summary" { value = "Instance ${aws_instance.web.id} in ${var.region}" }, interpolating references into a string
output "summary" { value = aws_instance.web.id + var.region }, adding the strings with a plus operator
variable "summary" { value = aws_instance.web.id }
explain: String interpolation inside an output value is the idiomatic way to compose a message from references. HCL does not use + to concatenate strings (B), and neither locals (C) nor variable blocks (D) publish post-apply messages to the operator.

q: A root module contains module "worker" { source = "./modules/worker"; count = 3 }. Another resource needs the id output of only the first worker instance. Which reference is correct?
options: module.worker[0].id, because count makes the module a tuple of instances addressed by numeric index
module.worker["0"].id, because count indexes are map keys written as strings
module.worker.first.id, because count instances are named after their position words
module.worker.id[0], because the index applies to the output after it is read
explain: Module instances created with count form a tuple, so a single instance's outputs are read as module.worker[0].id with a numeric index on the module itself. String keys belong to for_each instances (D), position words are not an addressing form (B), and indexing the output after reading it (C) fails because the unindexed module reference no longer resolves to one instance.

q: One pull request changes three things at once: it adds a brand-new provider, calls a new external module, and moves the backend from local files to a remote backend. A reviewer asks which single step prepares the working directory for all three changes, and what decision that step will surface. Which answer is correct?
options: terraform fmt prepares all three, and it surfaces a prompt listing files whose formatting changed
terraform validate prepares all three, and it surfaces a prompt asking which provider version to trust
terraform apply prepares all three, and it surfaces a prompt asking whether to copy the configuration to the new backend

terraform init prepares all three by installing the provider, downloading the module, and configuring the new backend, and because the backend changed it surfaces the state-handling decision between migrating the existing state with -migrate-state and starting fresh with -reconfigure
explain: Init is the one preparation step for providers, modules, and backend alike, and a backend change is precisely the case where it forces the migrate-versus-reconfigure decision before proceeding. Validate installs nothing, apply cannot run before initialization, and fmt only restyles text, so none of the distractors can prepare a working directory for all three changes at once.

q: A platform lead creates an HCP Terraform organization for a company, then invites three product teams. Which statement correctly describes what the organization owns and contains?
options: An organization is a billing label only and holds no technical resources
An organization contains one workspace only, and each team needs its own organization
An organization contains workspaces, projects, teams, variable sets, and policy sets for that tenant
An organization is the same thing as a project with a different display name
explain: An organization is the top-level HCP Terraform tenant: it holds workspaces organized into projects, plus teams, variable sets, policy sets, and registry content. It is not limited to one workspace, is far more than a billing label, and is distinct from a project, which sits inside it.

q: A team debating module granularity asks when a group of resources deserves to become its own module. Which guideline best matches HashiCorp's guidance?
options: Modules must contain at least ten resources to be valid
Extract a module when a cohesive set of resources is used together repeatedly or forms a logical unit with a clear purpose, while avoiding over-nesting tiny modules that add interface overhead
Every single resource should be its own module
Granularity is irrelevant because Terraform flattens modules at init
explain: Good modules package a meaningful, reusable logical unit; wrapping single resources adds indirection without benefit and deep nesting raises maintenance cost. There is no minimum resource count (C), single-resource modules are legal but usually poor design (A as a rule), and modules are not flattened away at init (B).

q: Which comparison of mutable and immutable infrastructure is correct at a basic level?
options: Mutable servers are replaced for each change; immutable servers are patched in place
Immutable infrastructure means infrastructure that can never be deleted
Both models require manual SSH changes to be safe
Mutable servers are updated in place over their lifetime, risking drift; immutable servers are replaced with new builds, keeping each build reproducible
explain: Mutable means in-place updates over time with drift risk; immutable means replacement with fresh, code-built instances. The first option reverses the definitions, manual SSH fits neither model well, and immutable servers are routinely deleted when replaced.

q: A cost-estimation run task is configured as advisory. It fails during a run because the estimation service times out. What happens to the run?
options: The plan is discarded and the run restarts from the beginning
The workspace switches to local execution mode automatically
The run fails, because any run task failure fails the run
The run can continue toward apply; the failed advisory result is recorded and shown but does not block
explain: Advisory run tasks report results without gating the run, so a timeout is surfaced but the run may proceed. Only mandatory tasks block, and a task failure never changes execution mode or restarts the run automatically.

q: An S3 bucket resource and a separate bucket in a second account are in one configuration. The second bucket's resource sets provider = aws.backup. What does this meta-argument guarantee?
options: The bucket is copied to the backup account after creation by the storage service
The resource is excluded from state as a backup copy
That resource is managed using the aliased aws.backup provider configuration, while resources without the meta-argument use the default configuration
The default provider is disabled for the whole run
explain: The provider meta-argument on a resource selects which configuration of that provider type manages it, here the aliased backup-account configuration. It triggers no copying by the cloud service, the resource is fully state-tracked, and the default configuration still serves every other resource of that type.

q: A nuanced exam item states a team uses Terraform to provision servers and Ansible to configure them, then asks which statement is still true despite the overlap between modern tools. Which is correct?
options: Ansible can provision some cloud resources and Terraform can run provisioners, but their primary design centers remain provisioning for Terraform and in-guest configuration for Ansible
Terraform's provisioners are its recommended main feature for software configuration
The overlap means the provisioning versus configuration distinction no longer exists
Using both tools together is an anti-pattern the exam discourages
explain: This is the edge case: overlap is real, yet the exam still tests primary design centers, and Terraform provisioners are documented as a last resort, not a main feature. The distinction has not vanished, and combining the tools is a common recommended pattern.

q: During a code review, a teammate asks what `values({ "b-team" = "ops", "a-team" = "dev", "c-team" = "sec" })` evaluates to. What does Terraform return?
options: ["ops", "dev", "sec"]
["a-team", "b-team", "c-team"]
["dev", "ops", "sec"]
["sec", "ops", "dev"]
explain: values() returns values in the order of the sorted keys (a-team, b-team, c-team), so the values come out as dev, ops, sec.

q: An engineer tests an expression in terraform console: `cidrhost("10.1.2.0/24", 1)`. What value does it produce?
explain: cidrhost() returns the address at host number 1 within the prefix, counting from the network address 10.1.2.0, which gives 10.1.2.1.

q: During a code review, a teammate asks what `merge({ Name = "web", Env = "dev" }, { Env = "dr", Team = "ops" })` evaluates to. What does Terraform return?
options: { Env = "dev", Name = "web", Team = "ops" }
{ Env = "dev", Name = "web" }
{ Env = "dr", Team = "ops" }
{ Env = "dr", Name = "web", Team = "ops" }
explain: merge() combines maps left to right and later maps win key conflicts, so Env is overwritten with "dr" while Name survives and Team is added.

q: A manager worries that importing a production VPC will rebuild it and cause an outage. Which reassurance is accurate?
options: Import rebuilds the object once, but during a maintenance window Terraform chooses automatically
Import converts the object to a data source that can never be changed
Import pauses the object until the next destroy run
Import only records the existing object in state so Terraform can manage it; it does not destroy or recreate the object
explain: The entire purpose of import is adoption without recreation: the real object keeps running while Terraform adds it to state. A rebuild, a pause, or conversion to a read-only data source would defeat that purpose and none of them describe how import behaves.

q: During a long apply, a second engineer starts another apply against a backend that supports locking and gets an error instead of running concurrently. What has happened?
options: The second engineer lacks the provider plugin installed locally
The backend has run out of storage space for a second state file
The first run holds the state lock, so the second run is blocked to prevent concurrent writes that could corrupt state
Terraform always blocks a second plan even when no apply is running
explain: Locking is held while Terraform performs operations that could write state, so a competing run fails with a lock error rather than interleaving writes. This is intentional protection, not a storage or plugin problem.

q: The plan output ends with: Plan: 1 to add, 0 to change, 1 to destroy, and the detail shows a single aws_db_instance marked -/+ . How should a reviewer describe this plan in one sentence?
options: The database will be updated in place and also backed up once
Two unrelated resources are affected: one new resource created and one old resource deleted
Nothing changes, because the add and destroy cancel each other out
One existing database will be replaced: destroyed and recreated as a single replacement action, not two unrelated resources
explain: A -/+ replacement contributes exactly one add and one destroy to the summary while affecting a single resource. Describing it as two unrelated resources misses the downtime and data implications that make replacements the most important lines in a review.

q: Three identical workers were created with count, and only the second worker, index 1, exists already and needs importing. Which command performs that import?
options: terraform import aws_instance.worker i-0abc123, which imports all three indexes at once
terraform import aws_instance.worker[1] i-0abc123, targeting exactly that count instance address
terraform import count.aws_instance.worker[1] i-0abc123, prefixed with the count keyword
terraform import aws_instance.worker.1 i-0abc123, using the legacy dot-index syntax
explain: Count instances are addressed with square-bracket indexes, so [1] selects exactly the second instance for import. Importing the bare resource address does not adopt every index, the dot form is not valid modern addressing, and count is never part of a resource address.

q: A root module instantiates a child module four times with count, and needs a single flat list of every instance's generated ID. Which root-side expression pattern collects them?
options: data.module.worker[*].id
Concatenating the four outputs as literal strings
module.worker.id, read once
A for expression over module.worker, such as [for inst in module.worker : inst.id], since count makes the module a tuple of instances
explain: With count, module.worker is a tuple of instance objects, and a for expression (or splat) gathers each instance's id output into one list. The bare single reference (A) no longer resolves, modules are not data sources (B), and hand-listing strings (D) discards the values Terraform computed.

q: A module outputs the value of `can(cidrhost("10.0.0.0/33", 1))`. What is displayed?
options: null
true
false
"yes"
explain: can() returns true if its expression evaluates without error and false otherwise; /33 is not a valid IPv4 prefix, so the result is false — can() itself never errors.

q: A saved plan was created against state serial 41. Before it is applied, a colleague applies a different change, advancing state to serial 42. What happens when someone runs terraform apply on the older saved plan?
options: Terraform prompts the user to confirm overriding the newer state
Terraform merges the two plans automatically
Terraform refuses with a stale plan error because the state lineage or serial no longer matches what the plan was created against
Terraform applies the old plan anyway and rolls state back to serial 41
explain: Saved plans are bound to the state they were planned against; if state has moved on (different serial or lineage), apply fails as stale rather than corrupting newer work. Terraform never rolls state backward or merges plans, and there is no override prompt for staleness.

q: A module block includes providers = { aws = aws.west }. What does this accomplish?
options: It renames the child module to west
It passes the caller's aliased aws provider configuration into the child module, so the child's resources use that configuration
It forces the child module to declare its own provider block named west
It installs the AWS provider version named west
explain: The providers map in a module block hands specific provider configurations from the caller into the child, which is how one module call targets a different region or account. It has nothing to do with installing versions (B) or renaming modules (C), and the child must not declare its own provider configurations to receive passed ones (D).

q: A variable marked sensitive = true feeds a database password. The CLI hides it, but a teammate with backend read access finds it anyway. Where did they find it?
options: In the provider plugin cache under .terraform/providers
In the plan binary only, because state never stores passwords
In the state file, because sensitive controls display redaction, not storage encryption
In the .terraform.lock.hcl file, which stores all variable values
explain: Sensitive values are still persisted in state so Terraform can manage the resource; sensitive only affects what Terraform prints. The lock file records provider versions and hashes, not variable values or passwords.

q: The same networking configuration must be rolled out to development, staging, and production, which differ only in names, sizes, and CIDR ranges. How does the core workflow support this promotion pattern?
options: The identical code is written once, then planned and applied separately per environment with environment-specific variable values, with the plan reviewed in each environment before its apply
The configuration is copied into three unrelated repositories so each environment can drift independently
Terraform automatically promotes a successful development apply to production after a waiting period
State files are copied between environments so all three share one record of resources
explain: Promotion works because the workflow is repeatable: same code, per-environment inputs, and a plan review gate in every environment. Copying code into drifting repositories (A) defeats reuse, sharing one state file across environments (B) would make environments fight over the same record, and automatic promotion (D) does not exist.

q: A read-only terraform plan that needs no state changes is run while another engineer applies. Why might the plan still encounter locking in some backends?
options: The plan locks the provider registry, not the state
Plans always write a new state file even when nothing changes
Plans never interact with locking under any circumstance
Some operations that read and potentially update state acquire a lock to ensure a consistent snapshot, depending on the backend and command
explain: Certain Terraform operations acquire a lock around state access to prevent races while reading or writing state. It is not about the provider registry, and while not every read locks in every backend, locking is tied to state access rather than to apply alone.

q: A registry module is pinned with `version = "~> 5.0"`. A new 5.9.0 release appears and the team wants it. Which command upgrades the installed module?
options: `terraform module upgrade vpc`
Edit the lock file by hand to 5.9.0
`terraform init -upgrade` — re-resolves modules (and providers) to the newest allowed versions
`terraform apply -upgrade`
explain: init -upgrade re-resolves both providers and modules within their constraints. A and D are not real commands. C is wrong — hand-editing the lock file bypasses checksum verification; the lock file is managed by init.

q: An expression reads: var.environment == "prod" ? 3 : 1. The variable is set to "dev". What does the expression return and what is the construct called?
options: It returns 3 and is called a for expression
It returns true because the comparison itself is the result
It returns 1 and is a conditional expression that selects between two results based on a boolean condition
It returns an error because both branches must be evaluated
explain: The ternary form condition ? true_result : false_result is Terraform's conditional expression; with a false condition it yields the second branch, 1. Only the selected branch's value is used, and the construct is distinct from for expressions, which build collections.

q: A pull request updates a provider constraint from ~> 5.0 to ~> 6.0 and also updates .terraform.lock.hcl, but CI running plain terraform init still fails with a locked-version error. What did the author forget?
options: CI must run terraform apply before init when majors change
Major provider upgrades require deleting .terraform on every developer machine first
The lock file in the pull request was not regenerated with init -upgrade (or providers lock) under the new constraint, so it still records a 5.x selection the new constraint rejects
The state file must be migrated before providers can change majors
explain: Changing a constraint does not rewrite existing lock entries; the lock must be deliberately regenerated with init -upgrade so it records a selection the new constraint admits, then committed. Apply order and state migration are unrelated, and deleting .terraform does not fix a stale committed lock entry.

q: A team wants three layers of defense: (1) reject invalid variable values as early as possible, (2) fail a run if a resource's assumptions are violated around its create/update, (3) continuously warn after apply if infrastructure drifts out of policy without ever failing runs. Which trio implements this?
options: Input variable `validation` blocks, `precondition`/`postcondition` blocks, and `check` blocks
`check` blocks, `precondition` blocks, and variable `validation` blocks, in that order
`sensitive = true`, `prevent_destroy`, and `ignore_changes`
Three `terraform validate` runs with different flags
explain: EXAM TRAP — the 004 custom-conditions trio: validation rejects bad input early; pre/postconditions assert around actions and fail the run; check blocks assert continuously post-apply and only warn. B scrambles the mapping. C invents validate flags. D lists unrelated lifecycle/sensitivity features.

q: A team moves their state from local files to an S3 backend by updating the `backend` block. What must they run next, and what does it do?
options: `terraform init -migrate-state` — it copies the existing state to the new backend so nothing is recreated
`terraform state push` — it uploads the configuration files
`terraform apply` — it recreates all infrastructure in the new backend
Nothing — Terraform detects the backend change automatically on the next plan
explain: Changing backends requires init -migrate-state, which moves the state file to the new home; resources are adopted, not recreated. A would be catastrophic and wrong. C uploads state but does not reconfigure the backend. D is false — Terraform prompts for migration via init.

q: A parent configuration calls a child module that creates a database. Which statements about getting the database endpoint back to the parent are true? (Choose two.)
options: The parent can reference the child's database resource directly by its resource address
The endpoint automatically becomes an input variable of the parent after apply
The parent references the value as module.<module_name>.<output_name>
The child module must declare an output that exposes the endpoint for the parent to consume
explain: Modules are encapsulated: values cross the boundary only through declared outputs, addressed from the caller as module.<name>.<output>. The parent has no direct line to the child's internal resources, and outputs do not turn into parent variables; the two directions of data flow use different mechanisms.

q: A CI pipeline should fail a pull request if any `.tf` file is not in canonical format, without modifying the files. Which command implements this gate?
options: terraform validate -check
terraform fmt -write=false
terraform fmt -check — exits non-zero when files need formatting, changing nothing
terraform plan -detailed-exitcode
explain: `fmt -check` is the CI formatting gate: it reports unformatted files via its exit code and rewrites nothing. There is no validate -check (B). C is a real flag but tests for plan diffs, not formatting. D is not a real flag combination.

q: Which two facts about required_version in a terraform block are true? (Choose two.)
options: It selects which provider versions init downloads
If the running Core binary falls outside the constraint, Terraform refuses to run the configuration
Terraform automatically upgrades or downgrades Core to satisfy it
It constrains the version of Terraform Core itself, not any provider
explain: required_version is a gate on the Core binary: a mismatch stops the run before work begins. Provider selection is governed by required_providers constraints and the lock file, and Terraform never modifies its own binary to meet a configuration's demand.

q: Which two statements about using multiple configurations of the same provider are true? (Choose two.)
options: A resource selects an aliased configuration with the provider meta-argument, such as provider = aws.eu
Aliases are declared inside required_providers next to the version constraint
A configuration may declare two default (unaliased) blocks for one provider if their regions differ
The configuration without an alias is the default and serves resources that do not specify a provider
explain: Multi-configuration setups rest on one unaliased default plus aliased extras chosen per resource through the provider meta-argument. Aliases live in provider blocks rather than required_providers, and two unaliased blocks for the same provider are a duplicate-configuration error regardless of their arguments.

The terraform block is where Core's own requirements and behavior live: required_version, required_providers, backend, and cloud configuration. The main distractor misplaces the backend inside a provider block; backends are configured by Core before providers run, so they cannot be provider settings.
options: The cloud block replaces required_version, so the two can never appear in the same terraform block
All of these are settings for Terraform itself and belong in the terraform block, including backend and cloud; provider connection settings and resource arguments belong in their own blocks, not here
required_providers belongs inside each resource block so every resource pins its own provider
The backend block belongs inside the provider block for the cloud it stores state in
q: A single terraform block in a configuration contains required_version, a required_providers block, and a backend block, and a teammate asks whether a cloud block could live there too. Which statement about this block is correct?
An engineer runs terraform apply with no saved plan and no flags in a terminal. After reviewing the displayed plan, the engineer types yes. What did Terraform do between the command and the prompt?
options: It ran destroy first to guarantee the plan started from empty infrastructure
It executed changes immediately and the prompt was only asking whether to save logs
It applied the most recent saved plan file found in the directory
It refreshed state, generated a fresh plan from the current configuration, and displayed that plan for interactive approval before making any changes
explain: A bare apply is plan-plus-prompt-plus-execute in one command: the plan is generated fresh at that moment, shown, and only executed after the yes. It never hunts for saved plan files and never destroys first.

q: A perfectly formatted configuration is run through terraform fmt a second time, and a teammate worries the file will keep shifting on every run. What actually happens?
options: Fmt refuses to run on a file it has already formatted once
Nothing changes: canonical formatting is deterministic, so a file already in canonical form is left as-is and repeated fmt runs are stable
The file is rewritten with a fresh timestamp header on every run
Each run alternates between two equally canonical layouts
explain: Canonical style is a fixed point: once a file matches it, fmt has nothing to change, so repeated runs converge instead of oscillating. There are not two alternating layouts (A), fmt adds no headers or timestamps (B), and it imposes no once-only restriction (D).

q: A module's callers complain they cannot change a hardcoded region suffix defined in the module's locals. What is the correct design response?
options: Tell callers to edit the module source in their own checkout
Explain that locals are intentionally internal; to make the value caller-controlled, the author should expose it as an input variable instead
Add a second locals block with the same name to override the first
Tell callers to set it with -var using the local's name
explain: If a value must be controlled from outside, it belongs in a variable; locals are deliberately not part of a module's external interface. -var cannot target locals (B), editing consumed module source is not a supported workflow (C), and duplicate local names conflict rather than override (D).

q: An engineer runs terraform workspace new staging in a CLI workspace setup, then asks why staging does not appear as a separate workspace in the HCP Terraform UI with its own variables and permissions. What explains this?
options: CLI workspaces are alternate states sharing one backend and configuration, while HCP Terraform workspaces are separate managed environments with their own state, variables, and access controls
CLI workspaces were removed in Terraform 1.12, so the command silently did nothing
CLI workspaces appear in the UI only after the first destroy run completes
The HCP Terraform UI only refreshes workspace lists once per day
explain: This is the classic trap: CLI workspaces partition state inside a single backend and configuration, whereas HCP Terraform workspaces are independent environments with their own state, variables, run history, and permissions. CLI workspaces still exist, the UI is not on a daily refresh, and no destroy is involved.

q: An internal provider is addressed as builds.corp.example.net/platform-team/network in required_providers, and a second entry uses the short form hashicorp/aws. Which statement about resolution is correct?
options: Both resolve on the public registry; custom hostnames are treated as namespaces
The first is invalid because provider addresses may never contain a hostname
The second is invalid because all addresses must spell out the hostname

The first resolves against the registry at builds.corp.example.net in the platform-team namespace for the network provider type, while the second uses the implied public registry hostname registry.terraform.io
explain: Provider addresses are hostname/namespace/type: supplying a hostname targets that registry, and omitting it implies registry.terraform.io, which is why hashicorp/aws is valid shorthand. Three-part addresses with private hostnames are fully supported and central to private registry workflows.

q: Which two outcomes are direct benefits of storing Terraform configuration in version control? (Choose two.)
options: State files no longer need protection or access control
Changes carry an author, timestamp, and review history
Cloud resources become immune to provider outages
Any past version of the infrastructure definition can be restored by checking out that commit
explain: Version control provides rollback to known-good definitions and a full attribution and review history. It does not protect against provider outages, and state still contains sensitive data that needs protection regardless of where configuration is stored.

q: A company keeps expensive GPU instances running in a dev environment `just in case`, because tearing them down manually takes a full day to rebuild. How does IaC change this cost picture?
options: IaC moves the workloads to cheaper regions automatically
IaC automatically pauses billing on unused instances
IaC makes cloud providers discount idle instances
IaC lets the team destroy the environment when idle and recreate it identically in minutes with `terraform apply`
explain: Because the environment is code, destroying it is safe — it can be recreated identically on demand. That turns always-on dev infrastructure into an on/off cost switch. A, C, and D describe billing magic Terraform does not perform; the savings come from confident teardown and fast recreation.

q: What is the practical difference between terraform init -migrate-state and terraform init -reconfigure? (Choose two.)
options: -reconfigure destroys and recreates the state lineage in the cloud
-migrate-state deletes all managed resources before copying state
-migrate-state copies existing state from the old backend to the new backend
-reconfigure reconfigures the backend without copying state from the old backend
explain: Migration preserves continuity by copying state, while reconfigure abandons the old backend's state as the source and uses the new backend as-is. Neither flag destroys managed infrastructure; they differ only in whether state is carried over.

q: Two configurations both need a company's standard security group that is maintained centrally outside their state. Each configuration references it. What keeps Terraform from trying to own it in both states?
options: The group is marked sensitive in both configurations
Both configurations use data blocks to read it, so neither state claims management of the group
Both configurations declare resource blocks with the same name
Terraform automatically shares one state entry between the configurations
explain: Reading through data sources is precisely how multiple configurations can consume a shared object without competing to manage it. Duplicate resource blocks would create conflicting ownership (B), states are not auto-shared (C), and sensitivity only affects display (A).

q: After a teammate edits a module block and changes its source from a local path to a registry address, terraform plan complains the module is not installed. What is the fix?
options: Re-run terraform init so it installs the module from the new source before planning
Run terraform validate with the -upgrade flag
Run terraform apply once to fetch the new source
Delete the state file so plan rebuilds the module cache
explain: Any source change requires re-running init (or terraform get) to install modules from the new address into .terraform/modules. Apply (B) does not install modules, deleting state (C) destroys resource tracking without fetching code, and validate has no -upgrade flag (D).

q: Terraform crashes with an internal panic during a plan and the terminal output mentions a log file. Which file should the engineer preserve for the bug report?
options: terraform.tfstate, renamed automatically after a crash
crash.log, written in the working directory when Terraform itself panics
.terraform.lock.hcl, which stores crash diagnostics
plan.out, which always contains panic stack traces
explain: When Terraform panics, it writes crash.log containing the stack trace and diagnostic details needed by maintainers. State, plan files, and the lock file serve other purposes and do not capture the panic record Terraform directs users to share.

q: A team is documenting why Terraform replaced its manual build process. Which two statements belong in that justification? (Choose two.)
options: Desired state is declared once and Terraform reconciles reality toward it
Pull requests give infrastructure changes a review and approval record
Destroying an environment is risky because it can never be faithfully recreated
Every rebuild depends on the same engineer remembering the manual steps
explain: Declarative reconciliation and reviewable pull request history are direct replacements for memory-based manual builds. The other statements describe the old manual weaknesses: dependence on one person's memory and fear of recreation, which IaC removes rather than preserves.

q: A security group needs one ingress rule per port in var.ports, and the number of ports varies per environment. Which construct generates the repeated nested blocks cleanly?
options: A dynamic block with for_each over var.ports
A data source for each port
Multiple provider aliases, one per port
A count meta-argument on the security group resource
explain: Dynamic blocks generate repeated nested blocks from a collection — exactly this use case. A duplicates whole resources, not nested blocks. B and C are unrelated to the problem.

q: A configuration contains the expression `tostring(42)`. What is displayed?
explain: tostring() converts the number to its string representation, so the result is the string "42", not the number 42.

q: During a code review, a teammate asks what `cidrsubnet("10.0.0.0/16", 8, 255)` evaluates to. What is displayed?
explain: cidrsubnet() adds 8 bits and picks subnet number 255: starting from 10.0.0.0/16, subnet 255 of the /24 series is 10.0.255.0/24.

q: An engineer adds 'data "aws_subnet" "selected" { id = var.subnet_id }' and then deletes the data block a week later. What happens to the actual subnet in AWS on the next apply?
options: Terraform prompts to convert the subnet into a managed resource
Nothing happens to the subnet; removing a data block only removes the lookup, since Terraform never managed the subnet
The subnet is removed from state and orphaned with an error
The subnet is destroyed because its block was removed
explain: Data sources are not managed, so removing one has no effect on the real infrastructure; only the read disappears. Destruction on block removal (A and B) applies to managed resources tracked in state, and no conversion prompt (D) exists for data blocks.

q: Documentation refers to the `root module`. What is it?
options: The module with the highest version number in the dependency tree
The backend configuration block
A special module published by HashiCorp that every configuration must call
The top-level configuration itself — the `.tf` files in the working directory where you run Terraform
explain: The root module is simply your working directory's configuration — every Terraform run has one, and it calls child modules. A invents a mandatory HashiCorp module. C confuses versioning with hierarchy. D confuses state storage with module structure.

q: Why do experienced teams avoid putting provider blocks inside shared child modules even though Terraform permits it in legacy cases?
options: Embedded provider configurations prevent callers from passing their own configurations, block count/for_each usage cleanly, and tie the module to one region or account, destroying reusability
The registry refuses modules containing variables
Provider blocks double the size of the state file
Provider blocks inside modules are a syntax error in current Terraform
explain: A child module with its own provider configuration is locked to that configuration and cannot be freely instantiated per region or account with passed providers, which is why modern practice passes configurations in. It is discouraged rather than a syntax error (B), state size is unaffected (C), and variables in modules are normal and expected (D).

q: A CI pipeline needs a fast, credential-free check that a pull request's Terraform configuration is syntactically valid and internally consistent, without contacting any cloud APIs. Which command fits?
options: terraform validate
terraform plan, because it never contacts APIs
terraform apply -refresh-only
terraform fmt -check
explain: validate checks syntax and internal consistency without API access or credentials. B is wrong — plan refreshes state via APIs by default. C contacts APIs to refresh. D only checks formatting, not correctness.

q: Which edge case best tests understanding of declarative IaC: a configuration declares a security group rule that already exists exactly as declared, created earlier by Terraform itself. What should the next plan show?
options: The rule should be recreated because declarative tools always rebuild
A manual approval step for each matching attribute
No action for that rule, because actual state already matches desired state
An error, because declarative tools cannot handle pre-existing resources they created
explain: Declarative reconciliation means matching desired and actual state yields no action, even across runs. Always rebuilding, erroring on its own resources, or per-attribute approvals contradict the convergence model Terraform is built on.

q: A module outputs the value of `replace("prod-web-01", "prod", "dev")`. What does Terraform return?
options: dev-web-01
dev-web
prod-web-01
prod-dev-01
explain: replace() substitutes every occurrence of the search substring, so only the leading prod segment changes to dev.

q: An account contains an old storage bucket that no Terraform configuration has ever managed. A teammate runs terraform destroy in an unrelated workspace and asks whether the bucket is at risk. What is the correct answer?
options: No, but only because destroy requires the bucket owner's approval first
Yes, destroy scans the whole account and removes anything it finds
Yes, but only if the bucket is in the same region as the workspace
No, objects that were never imported or created by Terraform are invisible to it and are not destroyed
explain: Terraform only acts on objects recorded in its state, so an unmanaged, never-imported bucket is completely outside its view and survives any destroy. Destroy performs no account-wide scan, and region or owner approval do not factor into that invisibility.

q: What is the primary purpose of a locals block in a Terraform configuration?
options: To expose results to other modules
To define named values computed once inside the configuration — such as a common name prefix or merged tags — and reuse them across many resources
To store provider credentials securely
To accept values from the person running Terraform
explain: Locals give a single name to a reusable expression so it is defined once and referenced as local.<name> throughout the configuration. Accepting outside values is the variable's role (A), exposing results is the output's role (C), and locals offer no special secret storage (D).

q: A networking workspace owns a VPC, and an application workspace reads the VPC ID and subnet IDs from the networking workspace's outputs rather than hard-coding them. Which HCP Terraform feature makes those outputs available across workspaces?
options: Speculative plans, which publish outputs to all workspaces in the organization
Variable sets, which copy output values between workspaces nightly
Remote state sharing, where the networking workspace authorizes specific consumer workspaces to read its state outputs
Run tasks, which pass outputs between runs as attachments
explain: Cross-workspace data flow uses remote state sharing, often consumed through terraform_remote_state, and the owning workspace controls which workspaces are authorized. Variable sets share input values not state outputs, and neither run tasks nor speculative plans distribute outputs.

q: Developers currently keep long-lived cloud API keys on their laptops to run Terraform locally. Which HCP Terraform feature eliminates these static credentials?
options: Remote state sharing between workspaces
terraform login, which stores cloud keys in the CLI config
Dynamic provider credentials — short-lived, workload-identity-based credentials minted per run
The private module registry
explain: Dynamic credentials mint short-lived tokens per run via workload identity — no static keys to rotate or leak. A is the trap: terraform login authenticates the CLI to HCP Terraform, not to cloud providers. C and D are unrelated to credentials.

q: Contrast removing a resource block from configuration with running terraform state rm on its address. What is the key difference?
options: Neither action affects the real object in any scenario
Both actions destroy the real object, just at different times
Removing the block plans destruction of the real object; state rm forgets it in state while the real object keeps running
Removing the block forgets the object; state rm destroys the real object
explain: Configuration is desired state, so deleting a block tells Terraform the object should no longer exist and it plans a destroy. State rm is a state-only operation that orphans the object intentionally, leaving it running unmanaged.

q: Which two version statements can both be true of one healthy project at the same time, given required_providers pins the AWS provider to ~> 5.0 and required_version is >= 1.9?
options: Core and the provider must always share the same version number
The provider constraint ~> 5.0 also constrains Core to 5.x
Core 1.11 runs the configuration while the AWS provider stays at 5.40.0, because Core and provider versions advance independently
Upgrading Core to 1.11 automatically upgrades the provider to 5.11.0
explain: Core and providers are separate binaries with independent version lines: Core 1.11 fully satisfies >= 1.9 while the provider independently sits at 5.40.0 under its own constraint. Neither binary's version ever implies or changes the other's.

q: A team wants to import an existing application server that will live inside a child module named app. Which address should the import target?
options: app.aws_instance.web, using the module's folder name instead of its block label
aws_instance.web, because modules are ignored during import
module.app, because importing the module imports everything in it at once
module.app.aws_instance.web, using the full module path plus the resource address inside that module
explain: Resources inside modules are addressed through their full path, so an import targets module.app.aws_instance.web, matching how state addresses are written. The bare address would point at the root module, a module itself is not an importable object, and the block label, not the folder name, forms the path.

q: A module block reads: module "db" { source = "../shared/database" }. What kind of source is this, and how does Terraform obtain it?
options: A registry source; init downloads the newest release
A Git source; init clones the repository at the default branch
A private registry source; init authenticates with an HCP token
A local path source; Terraform reads the directory directly relative to the calling module, with nothing to download
explain: Paths starting with ./ or ../ are local path sources read straight from the filesystem, so there is no download or version selection. Registry sources (A) use the NAMESPACE/NAME/PROVIDER format, Git sources (C) carry a git:: prefix or host pattern, and private registry sources (D) include a hostname.

q: A legacy database was brought under Terraform management for a migration, which is now complete. The team wants Terraform to stop managing it, but the database must keep running untouched. Which approach does this safely?
options: Add a `removed` block with `lifecycle { destroy = false }` — Terraform drops it from state without destroying the real object
Delete the resource block — Terraform will leave the database alone
Run `terraform destroy -target=aws_db_instance.legacy`
Run `terraform state push` to overwrite the state
explain: The removed block is the controlled decommission: with destroy = false, Terraform forgets the resource and the real database keeps running. A is the trap — deleting the block plans destruction. C destroys it outright. D uploads state and changes nothing about management.

q: A team declares import blocks for three legacy buckets and wants draft configuration for all three in one pass. Which command sequence accomplishes this?
options: Run terraform plan -generate-config-out=generated.tf with the import blocks present, then review and move the generated blocks into the real configuration
Run terraform validate -generate-config-out=generated.tf before declaring any import blocks
Run terraform import three times, then terraform state show to print configuration files
Run terraform apply -generate-config-out, which generates blocks instead of importing
explain: Generated configuration is produced during a plan that includes import blocks, and the output file is a draft to review, split up, and refine rather than finished code. Repeating the CLI import generates no HCL, the flag belongs to plan rather than apply, and validate never generates configuration.

q: A team decommissions a staging environment but wants to keep one shared NAT gateway that other environments also reference through the same workspace state. A colleague proposes terraform destroy. What is the flaw in that proposal?
options: There is no flaw; destroy asks about each resource individually so the gateway can be spared at the prompt

terraform destroy removes everything in state including the shared gateway; keeping one resource calls for removing the other resources' blocks and applying, or a carefully scoped targeted destroy — not a full destroy
The gateway would survive because destroy only removes the most recently created resources
Destroy automatically preserves any resource described as shared in its tags
explain: Destroy is all-of-state with a single approval, not a per-resource checklist, and tags confer no protection. Preserving one resource means using the surgical paths — block removal plus apply, or an exceptional targeted destroy — instead of the total teardown.

q: A module outputs the value of `reverse(["proxy", "db", "worker"])`. What does Terraform return?
options: ["db", "worker", "proxy"]
["worker", "db", "proxy"]
["proxy", "db", "worker"]
["worker", "proxy", "db"]
explain: reverse() returns the list with the elements in the opposite order; it does not sort them.

q: An emergency console fix raised a managed database's storage from 100 to 200 GB, and the team decides the larger size should stay permanently. How should this be reconciled?
options: Run terraform apply unchanged so Terraform raises the size a second time
Add the database to an import block so plan adopts the new size
Edit the configuration to declare 200 GB so it matches reality, after which plan shows no change for the database
Delete the database from state and import it again with the same block
explain: Keeping an out-of-band change means codifying it: update the declared value to the real one and the drift disappears legitimately. Applying unchanged configuration would try to shrink storage back, and removing or re-importing the resource does nothing to change the declared size causing the diff.

q: Every pull request should show the infrastructure impact of the change before merge, without applying anything. Which HCP Terraform capability does this?
options: Run triggers
Dynamic provider credentials
Drift detection
Speculative plans on pull requests
explain: Speculative plans run automatically on PRs and show the plan output as a check. B chains workspaces after applies. C finds drift on a schedule. D mints short-lived credentials — unrelated to PR review.

q: After a successful import of a legacy server, what should you do immediately, and why?
options: Delete the state file to start fresh
Nothing — imports are always perfectly aligned with configuration
Run `terraform destroy` to verify the import worked
Run `terraform plan` to see what Terraform wants to change to reconcile your resource block with the imported real object
explain: Because import does not generate configuration, the immediate plan reveals the gap between your declared block and reality — reconcile it before it surprises you later. A destroys what you just adopted. C discards the adoption. D assumes a perfection imports do not provide.

q: A legacy queue must be adopted into a queueing module rather than the root module. How is that expressed declaratively?
options: CLI import is the only way to import into modules, so the block approach cannot do it
A moved block pointing from the queue's cloud ID to the module
A module block with an import = true argument
An import block whose to address is the full module path, such as module.queueing.aws_sqs_queue.legacy
explain: Import blocks target any valid resource address, including module-qualified ones, so to = module.queueing.aws_sqs_queue.legacy performs the adoption declaratively. Moved blocks rename addresses already in state, modules have no import argument, and module imports are not a CLI-only capability.

q: A team moves a resource into a module and also renames it at the same time. Can a single moved block describe that change?
options: No, moved blocks only work within the same module level
No, any rename combined with a module move always requires destroy and recreate
Yes, but only if the resource uses count and not for_each
Yes, a moved block's from and to can be full addresses that differ in both module path and resource name
explain: A moved block maps one full address to another, so crossing module boundaries and renaming in the same mapping is exactly its use case, such as root aws_instance.web to module.servers.aws_instance.frontend. The instance model does not limit this.

q: A required_providers block sets version = "5.12.1" for the AWS provider. Which of these versions can terraform init select?
explain: The constraint 5.12.1 admits exactly one of the listed versions: 5.12.1. The others fall outside the range the constraint defines (recall ~> lets only the rightmost written component increase).

q: A CI pipeline needs a fast check that a pull request's Terraform configuration is syntactically valid and internally consistent. The check must not require cloud credentials and must not contact any cloud APIs. Which command fits?
options: terraform plan, because plans are always credential-free
terraform validate — it checks syntax and consistency using provider schemas, with no API calls
terraform fmt -check
terraform apply -refresh-only
explain: validate is the credential-free correctness gate: it checks block types, attribute names, and references without touching APIs. A is wrong — plan refreshes state via APIs by default. C contacts APIs to refresh. D only checks formatting, not correctness.

q: Which statement best describes the declarative approach Terraform uses?
options: You write shell scripts that Terraform runs top to bottom
You describe the desired end state and Terraform determines the steps to achieve it
You write the exact sequence of API calls Terraform must execute in order
You manually approve each individual API request during the apply
explain: Declarative = declare what you want; the tool computes how. B and D describe imperative approaches. C is wrong — you approve the plan as a whole, not individual API calls.

q: Over the weekend a teammate created a brand-new reporting bucket in the console for a project that Terraform otherwise manages, and leadership wants it under Terraform without recreation. How does this differ from ordinary drift, and what is the fix?
options: It is drift that refresh fixes alone, because refresh adds new account objects to state
It cannot be adopted, because Terraform only manages objects created after the workspace's first apply
It is ordinary drift, so applying the existing configuration will absorb the new bucket automatically
It is not drift on a managed resource but an entirely unmanaged object, so the team writes a resource block plus an import block or CLI import to adopt it
explain: Drift means a managed object changed; a wholly new console object has no state entry or block, so nothing in a normal apply touches it until an explicit import adopts it. Refresh never enrolls unknown objects, and adoption has no restriction based on when the workspace began.

q: What performance and collaboration benefit do teams cite when a state file grows to thousands of resources and plans are run from CI?
options: A large state file eliminates the need for a dependency graph
Local state automatically shards itself across CI runners for speed
Remote state lets CI fetch the single current state on demand and state caching reduces repeated provider queries for known attributes
Remote state makes plans skip refresh and validation entirely
explain: Central remote state means any authorized runner works from the same current snapshot, and recorded attributes reduce how much must be re-queried. Plans still refresh, validate, and build a graph; remote storage does not shard a local file.

Plan on pull request is a preview gate: the proposed creates, updates, and destroys are visible for human review before merge. It does not apply anything, it makes review more informed rather than unnecessary, and the code still has to be written by developers.
options: Reviewers can see exactly what will change, including cost and risk, before any infrastructure is touched
Review becomes unnecessary because the pipeline generated the plan
The pull request itself creates production resources faster
Developers no longer need to write Terraform code
q: A fintech team wires Terraform into its pipeline so every pull request automatically runs a plan and posts the result for reviewers, with no apply at that stage. What is the main purpose of that design?
On a freshly cloned repository, an engineer runs terraform validate before anything else and gets an error that provider schemas are not available. What is the root cause?
options: Validate only works after a successful plan has generated a schema cache
Validate requires cloud credentials, which have not been configured yet
The configuration must contain at least one resource before validate can run
Validate requires terraform init to have run first, because it checks the configuration against provider schemas that only init downloads
explain: Validate is schema-driven: it verifies argument names and types against each provider's schema, and those schemas arrive with the provider plugins at init. Credentials are never needed for validate (B), empty configurations validate fine (C), and no plan-generated cache exists (D); init is the one prerequisite.

q: An attribute a resource needs is computed by its provider and is not set anywhere in the configuration, such as an instance's private IP. When can another resource reliably reference it?
options: Only if the value is also declared as a variable
Never; only arguments written in the configuration can be referenced
Immediately at parse time, before any provider calls
After the referenced resource has been created (or read from state on later runs), because computed attributes are unknown until the provider returns them
explain: Computed attributes become known when the provider creates or reads the object, and references to them resolve at that point, showing as unknown in an initial plan. They do not need variable declarations (A), configuration-written arguments are not the only referenceable attributes (B), and parse time precedes any provider data (D).

q: A Sentinel policy with advisory enforcement fails during a run because a resource is missing a recommended tag. What happens to the run?
options: The policy is deleted from the policy set after its first failure
The run fails immediately and the workspace is locked
The run is converted into a speculative plan automatically
The policy failure is recorded and shown, but the run is allowed to continue toward apply
explain: Advisory enforcement is informational: failures are surfaced and logged while the run proceeds. The run is not failed or locked, it is not downgraded to a speculative plan, and failing policies are never auto-deleted.

q: A team runs terraform init and it succeeds, but a developer claims providers were also upgraded because the registry published new releases that morning. How do you settle it?
options: Check terraform.tfstate: provider versions are recorded there after init
Ask the registry: it tracks which versions each workstation installed
Check .terraform.lock.hcl: a plain init keeps the locked versions, so unchanged entries prove no upgrade happened
Re-run apply: only apply can change provider versions
explain: The lock file is the record of provider selections, and plain init is deliberately reproducible: it installs the locked builds rather than chasing the registry. State records infrastructure, not provider selections, and applies never change which provider build is installed.

q: A team manages AWS infrastructure with Terraform and also needs to manage GitHub repositories, Datadog monitors, and PagerDuty schedules. What does this illustrate about Terraform?
options: Terraform only works with cloud compute resources
Terraform is service-agnostic: providers exist for any API-backed resource, not just clouds
GitHub and Datadog must be managed with the `null` provider
Terraform requires a separate binary for non-cloud providers
explain: Terraform is service-agnostic — the provider ecosystem covers SaaS APIs like GitHub, Datadog, and PagerDuty alongside clouds. That's a 004 objective (1c). A is false. C is false; providers are plugins of the same CLI. D is wrong; the null provider is for throwaway test resources, not real integrations.

q: A security team requires that no security group open to `0.0.0.0/0` can ever be applied, and that every resource carry a `cost-center` tag. Which HCP Terraform feature enforces these rules on every plan?
options: Drift detection
Policy enforcement with policy sets (OPA/Rego) — policies evaluate each plan and can warn or block the run
Speculative plans
Run triggers
explain: Policy-as-code (Sentinel/OPA policy sets) evaluates every plan against governance rules and can block violations. A detects drift after the fact. C previews changes but enforces nothing. D chains workspace runs — unrelated to policy.

q: A private HCP Terraform registry module has source app.terraform.io/acme/billing/aws, while a public one has source terraform-aws-modules/vpc/aws. What distinguishes the private address?
options: Private addresses must end in .git
Private addresses use four segments because the first segment is the registry hostname, followed by organization, name, and provider
Private addresses are the only ones allowed a version argument
Private addresses cannot be pinned
explain: Hostname-prefixed addresses target a specific registry: hostname/organization/name/provider. Version arguments work for both public and private registry modules (B is false), .git suffixes belong to Git sources (C), and pinning is standard practice for private modules too (A).

q: Which scenario is the WRONG tool choice?
options: Using a data source to find an existing S3 bucket owned by a logging team
Using a resource block to declare a bucket this configuration should create and own
Using a data source to declare a brand-new bucket that only this configuration will ever use, expecting Terraform to create it
Using a data source to read the current AWS account ID
explain: Expecting a data block to create a bucket is the misuse: data sources only read, so the bucket would never be created. The other choices match each block type to its purpose: reading shared or environmental facts, and managing owned infrastructure.

q: Logs from a one-off debugging session scroll past in the terminal and are lost when it closes. Which setting would have kept them for later review?
options: A lifecycle block with a log_path argument on each resource
TF_LOG_PATH pointing at a file, which persists Terraform log output to that path
TF_LOG=ERROR, which automatically archives logs for thirty days
terraform apply -out=logs, which saves logs inside the plan file
explain: TF_LOG_PATH redirects log output to a file so it survives the terminal session and can be attached to a support case. Changing the level alone does not archive anything, plan files do not embed logs, and resources have no log_path lifecycle argument.

q: A module will be reused by many teams, and its author wants a sensible instance type when callers say nothing, while still letting callers override it. Which declaration achieves this?
options: locals { instance_type = "t3.micro" }, because locals are overridable defaults
variable "instance_type" { type = string; default = "t3.micro" }, so the default applies unless a caller supplies a value
output "instance_type" { value = "t3.micro" }
variable "instance_type" { type = string }, which forces the default t3.micro
explain: A default in the variable block is exactly the overridable fallback mechanism; callers who assign a value replace it, callers who do not get the default. Omitting the default makes the variable required instead (B), locals cannot be overridden by callers (C), and outputs expose values rather than accept them (D).

q: On the public Terraform Registry, what does the verified badge on a module indicate?
options: HashiCorp has reviewed the module and its publisher as a trusted, verified provider or partner
The module is guaranteed to work in every Terraform version
The module passed an automated virus scan only
The module has the most downloads in its category
explain: Verified modules come from publishers HashiCorp has vetted, signaling maintained, trusted content. Download counts (A) do not confer verification, no badge guarantees universal version compatibility (C), and verification is a publisher review process, not merely a malware scan (D).

terraform workspace new both creates the workspace and switches to it, and a fresh workspace has empty state, so planning the unchanged configuration proposes creating everything for that environment. It does not clone prod state, leave the previous workspace selected, or require init, and treating it as a state copy, the main distractor, would wrongly suggest staging already exists.
options: The new workspace inherits a copy of the prod state, so the plan proposes no changes
The new workspace is created and automatically selected, its state starts empty, so the plan proposes creating the full configuration for staging
The command fails because new workspaces can only be created during terraform init
The command only creates the workspace but leaves prod selected, so the plan still targets prod
q: A team that already uses the default and prod workspaces needs to run the same workflow against a brand-new staging environment that should start with no tracked resources. The operator runs terraform workspace new staging and then immediately runs terraform plan. What should the operator expect?
A plan output shows `<=` next to a `data "aws_ami" "ubuntu"` block. What does this symbol mean?
options: The data source has a syntax error
The data source will be read during the plan/apply
The data source will be destroyed
The data source is being imported into state as a managed resource
explain: `<=` marks a read: data sources are fetched, not managed. They are never destroyed (A) or imported as managed resources (D). C is wrong — a syntax error would fail validate long before plan.

q: A team wants to pick up the newest provider versions allowed by their version constraints. Which command does this, and what else changes as a result?
options: `terraform providers upgrade`, which edits `required_providers` automatically
Delete `.terraform/` and run `terraform plan`; plan upgrades providers by default
`terraform apply -upgrade`, which upgrades providers during the apply
`terraform init -upgrade`, which selects the newest allowed provider versions and rewrites the lock file
explain: init -upgrade re-resolves providers to the newest versions within constraints and rewrites the lock file. There is no apply -upgrade (B) or providers upgrade command (C). D is wrong — a plain plan reuses the locked versions; only -upgrade re-resolves.

q: An architect must split a growing monolith workspace handling networking, databases, and three applications. Applying the one-state-per-workspace rule, what is the strongest reason to split it into several workspaces?
options: Workspaces cannot contain more than one provider, so the split is forced by the tool
Smaller workspaces limit blast radius, let each component carry its own variables, permissions, and run cadence, and keep state operations fast and focused
Splitting is required because a workspace stops working after one hundred resources
Each new workspace increases the organization's run concurrency for free
explain: Decomposing by component gives each part isolated state, tailored variables and access, and independent runs, so a failure or lock affects one component instead of everything. Splits are not about free concurrency, there is no hundred-resource limit, and a workspace can use many providers.

q: Which two actions require generating a new saved plan rather than reusing the existing one? (Choose two.)
options: The plan file is copied from the CI agent to a different CI agent for applying
The reviewer wants to see the plan output a second time before approving
