Another apply has modified the workspace state since the plan was created
A variable value used by the deployment needs to change from what the plan was created with
explain: Any input change (such as a variable value) and any intervening state change both invalidate reuse: the first needs a new plan by design, the second makes the old plan stale. Copying the file between machines is fine, and re-displaying a plan for review never invalidates it.

q: While debugging a configuration, an engineer evaluates `cidrsubnet("10.0.0.0/16", 8, 255)` in the console. What is displayed?
explain: cidrsubnet() adds 8 bits and picks subnet number 255: starting from 10.0.0.0/16, subnet 255 of the /24 series is 10.0.255.0/24.

q: A cloud engineer changes an instance's tags in the console on Friday. On Monday the plan proposes changing the tags back. How should this sequence be described?
options: The console change caused drift, and plan's refresh compared live values against configuration and proposed correcting the difference
The plan is corrupted because tags can never change outside Terraform
The state lock expired, so Terraform forgot the original tags
Terraform imported the console change as a new resource automatically
explain: Drift is any divergence between real infrastructure and what Terraform expects; refresh during plan reads the live tags, so the diff proposes restoring the configured values. The state itself is not corrupted by an out-of-band tag change.

q: A variable has no type constraint and is assigned values of different shapes in different workspaces. Which statement about the any type is correct?
options: The any type performs full schema validation against the first value ever assigned
Leaving type unset forces the value to string in every workspace
The any type is only available for output values, never for variables
Leaving type unset is identical to type = any, and Terraform infers a concrete type from each assigned value
explain: With type = any (the implicit default when no constraint is written), Terraform accepts the value as-is and infers its concrete type, deferring checks to where the value is used. It neither coerces everything to string nor validates against an earlier assignment.

q: In a monorepo, the networking configuration lives in /networking and the application configuration lives in /apps/api, each tied to its own workspace. Which workspace setting makes each VCS-triggered run operate on the correct code?
options: The workspace Terraform version setting, matched to the folder name
The workspace name, which must equal the folder path character for character
The workspace working directory setting, pointed at each configuration's subdirectory
The auto-apply setting, enabled for both workspaces
explain: The working directory setting tells HCP Terraform which subdirectory of the repository contains the configuration for that workspace. Terraform version, auto-apply, and workspace naming do not steer runs to a folder.

q: A team keeps a golden image updated by hand and cannot explain why two images built a month apart behave differently. Which IaC principle, applied to the image build, fixes the root cause?
options: Building from a versioned, declarative definition so every image is reproducible and its contents are reviewable
Storing finished images in more regions for redundancy
Building images more frequently by hand to reduce the gap
Naming images with the builder's initials for accountability
explain: The root cause is an unrecorded manual process; a versioned declarative build definition makes contents explicit, reviewable, and reproducible. Frequency, naming, and extra copies do not reveal or control what is inside the image.

q: Which input method requires no file in the working directory and no change to the configuration, and is set in the shell before Terraform runs?
options: Editing the variable block's default
Adding a locals block
Setting a TF_VAR_-prefixed environment variable matching the variable's name
Running terraform fmt
explain: TF_VAR_ environment variables are the file-free, configuration-free assignment channel recognized automatically at run time. Editing a default changes the configuration (B), locals are internal values rather than inputs (C), and fmt only formats code (D).

q: A junior engineer leaves TF_LOG=TRACE enabled on a shared CI runner for a week. Which two risks does this create? (Choose two.)
options: TRACE logging changes planned infrastructure to match provider defaults
Enormous log volume can slow runs and consume significant disk space
TRACE logging automatically rotates state backups to a public location
Log output can expose sensitive values such as credentials or tokens that providers handle during runs
explain: Verbose logs are a known secret-leak channel because providers may log request details containing sensitive values, and TRACE volume is large enough to hurt performance and storage. Logging never publishes state backups and never alters what the plan proposes, since it only observes the run.

q: During a plan review, a database password attribute displays as (sensitive value) instead of the actual password. A junior engineer files a bug saying the value is missing. What is the correct explanation?
options: Sensitive values are excluded from the plan and must be re-entered at apply
The password is stored encrypted and Terraform cannot read it during plan
The value is present and will be used, but Terraform redacts sensitive values in plan and apply output so secrets are not exposed in logs or terminals
The variable was never set, so Terraform substituted a placeholder
explain: Sensitive values are masked in CLI output as (sensitive value) for safety, but the real value is still in the plan and used at apply. It does not mean the variable is unset; an unset required variable errors instead of showing this marker.

q: You rename a resource from aws_instance.web to aws_instance.frontend in configuration. Without any other change, what will terraform plan propose, and which block avoids it?
options: It proposes destroy + create; a moved block maps the old address to the new one so state updates in place
It proposes nothing; renames are detected automatically
It proposes an in-place update; a lifecycle block with ignore_changes avoids it
It fails; renames require terraform state push
explain: Terraform sees a deleted address and a new address = destroy + recreate. A moved { from, to } block tells it the object is identical, so state is rewritten with no recreation. A is false. B misapplies ignore_changes. D invents a requirement.

q: A manager asks what HCP Terraform adds on top of the CLI workflow for a distributed team. Which answer is exam-accurate?
options: A rewritten provider protocol that makes applies twice as fast
Hosted remote state, remote plan and apply runs, and workspace-based collaboration managed by HashiCorp
Local-only execution with an optional cloud backup of state
Free private provider binaries for every public provider
explain: HCP Terraform is the hosted platform layer: remote state, runs executed in HashiCorp's environment, and workspaces for team collaboration. It does not change the provider protocol or apply speed, execution is remote rather than local-only, and it does not redistribute provider binaries.

q: A consultancy is formalizing how a five-person team should work with Terraform day to day. Which two practices belong to a sound team workflow around the write, plan, apply loop? (Choose two.)
options: Review the plan output for a change before approving the apply that executes it
Store the cloud account root password in the repository so every teammate can apply
Edit the state file directly in a pull request when a quick fix is needed
Commit configuration to version control and review infrastructure changes through pull requests before they are applied
explain: Version-controlled, peer-reviewed configuration (A) and reviewing the plan before apply (C) are the two pillars of the team workflow: one governs the code, the other governs the execution. Hand-editing state (B) bypasses Terraform's tracking and corrupts its record, and committing root credentials (D) is a serious security failure no workflow endorses.

q: A root module calls a database child module that outputs endpoint and port, and an app child module that declares inputs db_host and db_port. Which wiring gives the app its database connection values?
options: Reference the database resources inside the app module block using their full resource addresses
Have the app module read the database module's state file directly
Set db_host and db_port in the app block from environment variables the database module exports at apply time
Set db_host = module.database.endpoint and db_port = module.database.port as arguments in the app module block, letting Terraform order the two modules from those references
explain: Cross-module data flow is always explicit at the parent level: the root reads the database module's outputs and passes them as the app module's input arguments, which also creates the correct dependency ordering. Modules cannot read each other's state files (B) or reach inside each other for resource addresses (C), and Terraform modules do not export shell environment variables to one another (A).

q: Why would a team choose Terraform over writing a detailed runbook and following it carefully for every deployment?
options: Runbooks cannot be stored in version control while Terraform can
A runbook guarantees the same result if everyone reads it carefully
Terraform removes the need for anyone to understand the infrastructure
Terraform executes the definition automatically and checks current state before acting, reducing human variance
explain: Even a careful runbook depends on humans executing every step identically; Terraform compares desired state to actual state and executes consistently. Runbooks can be versioned too, and IaC increases rather than removes the need to understand the systems being automated.

q: Mid-refactor, a flat configuration hardcodes cidr_block = "10.20.0.0/16" inside the networking resources being extracted into a child module. Staging needs a different CIDR later, but production must keep 10.20.0.0/16 exactly. What should the extraction do?
options: Delete the CIDR and let the provider choose one at apply time
Leave the CIDR hardcoded in the child and fork the module when staging is built
Store the CIDR in the child module's outputs so callers can read it back after creation
Turn the CIDR into an input variable of the child module and have the production root pass "10.20.0.0/16" as the argument, preserving current behavior while making the value caller-controlled
explain: Parameterizing environment-specific values as inputs is the core move of a good extraction: today's caller passes the existing value so nothing changes, and tomorrow's caller passes its own. Forking the module for staging (A) recreates the duplication modules exist to remove, providers do not invent CIDR allocations (B), and an output reports a value rather than controlling it (D).

q: An SRE needs to inspect what Terraform currently tracks before a maintenance window. Which two commands give direct, read-only views of recorded state? (Choose two.)
options: terraform state push to display state by uploading it
terraform state show aws_instance.web to view one resource's recorded attributes
terraform destroy to list resources by deleting them
terraform state list to enumerate every resource address in state
explain: state list inventories addresses and state show displays one resource's recorded attributes, both without changing infrastructure. destroy deletes resources rather than inspecting them, and state push uploads a state file, which is a risky write operation, not a read-only view.

terraform providers schema -json emits the full provider, resource, and data source schemas as JSON, and it needs init to have installed those providers first. The main distractor, terraform providers, only lists which providers a configuration requires; it contains no attribute or block schema detail.
options: terraform version -json, which reports Core and provider versions only
terraform show -json, which describes state and configuration values rather than provider schemas
terraform providers schema -json, run after terraform init has installed the providers whose schemas it prints
terraform providers, which prints the provider requirement tree but no schemas
q: A developer needs a machine-readable dump of every resource and data source schema a provider exposes, including nested block and attribute types, to feed into a code generator. Which command produces it, and what is required first?
A junior engineer deletes terraform.tfstate to 'start fresh' while the infrastructure is still running. What does Terraform believe on the next plan?
options: That all resources were destroyed outside Terraform and should be imported
That no managed resources exist, so it proposes creating everything again
That the configuration is empty and nothing needs to happen
That the state was archived and it should restore it automatically
explain: Without state Terraform has no record linking configuration to real objects, so it treats every resource as new and proposes creation. It does not auto-import existing objects or restore a deleted file, which is why losing state orphans real infrastructure.

q: A lock error message shows a specific lock ID, who acquired it, and when. A teammate suggests running force-unlock without copying that ID. Why will that not work as suggested?
options: force-unlock only needs the resource address that was being applied
terraform force-unlock requires the exact lock ID from the lock error as its argument
The lock ID is only needed when using the local backend
force-unlock derives the ID automatically from the workspace name
explain: force-unlock is invoked as terraform force-unlock <LOCK_ID> using the ID shown in the error output. Guessing or omitting it cannot target the stuck lock, and the local backend does not provide this locking mechanism in the first place.

q: After an out-of-band console change, an engineer runs terraform plan -refresh-only and sees a note that state would be updated to match reality, with no resource changes proposed. What has this mode done differently from a normal plan?
options: It refreshed state from the real infrastructure but proposed no configuration changes, even if the configuration disagrees with the refreshed values
It deleted the drifted resource from state
It saved a plan file that must be applied within one hour
It applied the configuration changes needed to undo the console edit
explain: Refresh-only mode stops after syncing state to reality and reporting drift; it never proposes creates, updates, or destroys from the configuration. A normal plan would go on to propose reverting the console change, which is exactly what refresh-only withholds.

q: A team manages AWS with CloudFormation and is adding a GCP data pipeline. Leadership wants to avoid splitting the team into two tooling specialties. What should they evaluate?
options: Adopting Terraform so both clouds share HCL, state practices, and the plan and apply workflow
Extending CloudFormation to GCP with custom scripts
Using Deployment Manager for AWS as well as GCP
Training each engineer on both native tools and accepting separate workflows
explain: Terraform's multi-cloud workflow is designed for exactly this: one language and process instead of separate CloudFormation and Deployment Manager specialties. CloudFormation and Deployment Manager are each single-cloud, and keeping two native workflows preserves the split leadership wants to avoid.

q: Which statement about terraform state show and sensitive attributes is most accurate for an operator inspecting state?
options: Sensitive attributes are omitted from state entirely, so show displays nothing for them
State stores the actual values, so inspecting state can reveal sensitive attribute values even though normal plan output redacts them
Only the backend administrator can ever see any attribute through state show
State show always replaces every sensitive value with a permanent hash that cannot be recovered
explain: Because state is the record of real attribute values, tools that read state expose the underlying values; redaction is a presentation behavior of plan and apply output, not a property of the stored data. That is why state access itself must be controlled.

q: A published module v2 declares configuration_aliases for aws and aws.dr, requires Terraform >= 1.3, and its caller on Terraform 1.12 passes only the default aws configuration. Plan fails even though every resource could use the default. Why, and what are the caller's options?
options: The caller should add a provider block inside the child module
Terraform 1.12 dropped support for provider passing

Declaring configuration_aliases makes those configurations part of the module's required interface: the caller must pass every declared alias in the providers map (even if several aliases point at the same underlying configuration), or use a module version that does not declare the extra alias
Aliased configurations are optional decorations, so the failure must be a bug
explain: Once a module declares configuration_aliases, callers are obligated to supply each one; pointing both aliases at one real configuration satisfies the interface when a second region is not actually needed. It is specified behavior, not a bug (A), embedding provider blocks in the child contradicts the passing model (B), and provider passing is fully supported in 1.12 (D).

q: A console hotfix changed a managed security group's rules, the change was never approved, and the configuration is considered the source of truth. What is the correct reconciliation?
options: Remove the security group from state so Terraform stops noticing the difference
Approve the hotfix retroactively by deleting the resource block
Edit the state file by hand to copy the console rules into Terraform
Run terraform apply with the unchanged configuration so the plan's proposed update reverts the console edit
explain: When configuration is authoritative, the ordinary plan and apply cycle is the reconciliation tool: refresh surfaces the drift and apply restores the declared rules. Hand-editing state is dangerous and unsupported, and forgetting the resource or deleting its block abandons management instead of restoring the intended rules.

q: Which statement correctly describes the open-source Terraform CLI on its own?
options: It is a free, locally run binary that can plan and apply configurations without any HashiCorp hosted account
It requires an HCP Terraform organization before the first plan
It can only run terraform validate; applies need the paid platform
It stops working after a 14-day trial unless licensed
explain: The CLI is fully functional open-source software: write, init, plan, and apply all run locally with no account or license. HCP Terraform and Enterprise add collaboration and governance around the same workflow rather than unlocking apply.

q: A team stores a shared module in a Git repository subdirectory: the repo root holds several modules and the networking one sits in modules/net. Which source address reaches it?
options: git::https://example.com/infra.git/modules/net with a single slash
The subdirectory cannot be addressed; the whole repo must be one module
../infra/modules/net, because Git sources resolve like local paths
git::https://example.com/infra.git//modules/net with a double slash separating the subdirectory
explain: For package-style sources, a double slash // separates the repository address from the subdirectory inside it. B single slash (A) would be treated as part of the repository path itself, C is false since subdirectory addressing exists precisely for monorepos, and D mixes local and Git addressing.

q: A configuration will use HCP Terraform with the remote backend, storing state in a single named workspace called prod-network belonging to the organization acme-infra. Which backend configuration expresses this?
options: backend "remote" with only a hostname argument, because workspaces are selected in terraform.tfvars
backend "remote" with a resource_group_name and storage_account_name for acme-infra
backend "remote" with an organization argument set to acme-infra and a workspaces block with name = "prod-network"
backend "remote" with bucket = "acme-infra" and key = "prod-network" arguments
explain: The remote backend identifies the HCP Terraform organization and then selects the workspace, using workspaces { name = ... } for a single workspace. Bucket and key belong to the S3 backend, resource groups belong to azurerm, and workspace selection is backend configuration, not a variable value.

q: After a successful apply with no configuration edits, the engineer immediately runs terraform plan again and the output ends with: Plan: 0 to add, 0 to change, 0 to destroy. What does this confirm?
options: A destroy is scheduled to run next
The state file was lost during apply and Terraform sees an empty world
The infrastructure has converged: real-world state now matches the configuration, so there is nothing left to do
The plan command is broken and must be reinstalled
explain: An empty plan right after apply is the expected sign of convergence — desired and actual state agree. If state had been lost, plan would propose recreating everything as adds, which is the opposite of an all-zero summary.

q: A hard-mandatory Sentinel policy requires encryption on every storage resource. A run's plan creates an unencrypted bucket, and a senior engineer offers to override the failure as she did for a tagging policy last week. What happens?
options: The policy converts itself to soft-mandatory after the first override attempt
The run applies everything except the bucket and reports partial success
The run cannot proceed until the plan complies; hard-mandatory failures cannot be overridden by anyone
She can override it because senior engineers can override any policy
explain: Hard-mandatory is absolute: no user, regardless of seniority, can override it, so the configuration must be fixed and replanned. The tagging policy she overrode must have been soft-mandatory. Policies do not downgrade themselves, and blocked runs do not partially apply.

q: Which of these is a valid reason to prefer a data source over passing the same value in as an input variable? (Choose two.)
options: The value must be stored permanently in state as a managed object
The value must be different for every person who runs the configuration interactively
The value should be looked up fresh from the provider on each run so external changes are picked up automatically
The value describes infrastructure owned by another team that this configuration must never create or destroy
explain: Fresh lookups and referencing other teams' unmanaged infrastructure are the two classic data source motivations. Sensitivity is handled by marking values sensitive rather than by choosing a data source, and per-runner interactive variation is what variables, not data sources, provide.

q: A team importing fifty hand-built resources dreads writing every resource block from scratch. Which Terraform feature can draft that configuration for them?
options: terraform plan -generate-config-out, which writes generated HCL for imported resources into the named file
terraform fmt -recursive, which expands empty blocks into full configuration
terraform init -upgrade, which scaffolds blocks for existing infrastructure
terraform console, which prints a complete configuration when given an address
explain: Used together with import blocks, plan -generate-config-out produces a starting HCL file for the imported objects that the team can review and refine. fmt only formats, console evaluates expressions, and init installs dependencies, none of which draft resource configuration.

q: A log file contains only messages about failed provider calls and nothing about routine run progress. Which TF_LOG level most likely produced that narrow output?
options: DEBUG, which is documented as the errors-only level
ERROR, which records only error messages and suppresses informational detail
TRACE, which records only errors while hiding internal detail
OFF, which still prints errors while hiding everything else
explain: ERROR sits near the quiet end of the verbosity ladder, emitting failures without INFO or DEBUG chatter, which matches a failures-only log. TRACE and DEBUG are the most detailed levels, and OFF suppresses log output rather than printing errors selectively.

q: A team uses an S3 backend with encryption enabled on the bucket and a classic DynamoDB lock table. Which concern does the DynamoDB table address, and which does bucket encryption address?
options: Both address locking, and neither addresses encryption
DynamoDB addresses locking against concurrent writes; bucket encryption addresses confidentiality of state at rest
DynamoDB encrypts state; bucket encryption provides the state lock
Both address state versioning, and neither addresses locking
explain: In the classic S3 setup the roles are distinct: DynamoDB holds the lock so writers do not collide, while server-side encryption protects the stored state object at rest. Versioning is a separate bucket feature for recovery history.

q: A module declares `version = "~> 1.4"` for a provider. Which provider versions satisfy this constraint?
options: Any version >= 1.4, including 3.x
1.4.0 only
explain: EXAM TRAP: the pessimistic operator `~>` allows only the rightmost specified component to increment. With two components specified (`~> 1.4`), the minor version may rise but the major is locked: >= 1.4, < 2.0. (With three components, `~> 1.4.0` would mean >= 1.4.0, < 1.5.0.) A describes `= 1.4.0`. D describes `>= 1.4`.

q: A pipeline runs terraform plan -detailed-exitcode and the step exits with code 2. What should the pipeline conclude?
options: The plan succeeded and changes are present, so there is a non-empty diff to review or apply
Terraform is prompting for approval and waiting for input
The plan succeeded with no changes and the infrastructure already matches the configuration
The plan failed with an error and must be fixed
explain: With -detailed-exitcode, 2 means success with a present diff, 0 means success with an empty diff, and 1 means an error. The pipeline should treat 2 as changes pending, not as a failure like code 1.

q: A module outputs the value of `zipmap(["a", "b", "c"], [1, 2, 3])`. What value does it produce?
explain: zipmap() pairs keys with values positionally: the first key takes the first value, and so on.

q: A provider constraint reads version = "~> 5.0". Which two versions satisfy it? (Choose two.)
explain: ~> 5.0 means >= 5.0.0 and < 6.0.0, so both 5.0.0 and 5.7.3 qualify; 4.9.9 is below the floor and 6.0.0 crosses the major boundary the pessimistic operator forbids.

q: During a code review, a teammate asks what `coalesce(null, "", "dr", "test")` evaluates to. What is the result?
options: test
dr
null
explain: coalesce() returns the first argument that is neither null nor an empty string, so null and "" are skipped and "dr" wins.

q: A production database must never be destroyed by any Terraform run, even if someone removes its block from the configuration. Which safeguard enforces this?
options: Marking the resource `sensitive = true`
`lifecycle { create_before_destroy = true }`
Storing the state file in a private S3 bucket
`lifecycle { prevent_destroy = true }` — any plan that would destroy the resource fails with an error
explain: prevent_destroy is the safety rail: plans proposing destruction fail loudly instead of executing. B changes replacement ordering, not permission. C only redacts CLI output. D protects state access but does not stop a legitimate apply from destroying.

q: An engineer removes the only reference between a security group and an instance, then wonders why Terraform no longer guarantees the group exists before the instance. What changed?
options: Nothing; Terraform remembers old dependencies forever
The security group was deleted from state automatically
The implicit dependency came from that reference; without any reference (or an explicit depends_on), Terraform sees the two resources as independent and may order them freely
The instance now uses a data source instead
explain: Implicit dependencies exist only while references exist; removing the last reference removes the graph edge and the ordering guarantee that came with it. Terraform does not retain historical edges (A), state is not altered by editing expressions (C), and no data source is created by removing a reference (B).

q: A referencing resource needs an attribute that the referenced resource will only have after a provider-side update in place. On the next plan after that update, the referencing resource shows a change. Why?
options: Because the referencing resource lost its state entry
Because references are live expressions: when the referenced attribute's known value changes, expressions built on it re-evaluate and can produce a new planned value downstream
Because Terraform duplicates resources whenever an attribute changes
Because outputs force all resources to update together
explain: References are not one-time copies; they are expressions re-evaluated against current known values each run, so upstream changes flow downstream through the graph. No duplication (B), state loss (C), or output coupling (D) is involved in ordinary reference propagation.

q: A configuration contains the expression `lower("Production")`. What is the result?
options: production
PRODUCTION
pRODUCTION
Production
explain: lower() converts every cased character in the string to lowercase.

q: An engineer passes the same variable twice: terraform plan -var-file=base.tfvars -var="replicas=3" , and base.tfvars sets replicas to 5. Which value does the plan use, and why?
options: 3, because a -var flag has higher precedence than any -var-file value
The plan errors because a variable may only be set once
Whichever source Terraform reads last alphabetically
5, because files always beat command-line flags
explain: Variable precedence puts individual -var assignments above all -var-file sources, so replicas is 3. Setting a variable in multiple places is normal and resolved by precedence rather than erroring, and file values never outrank the command line.

q: An apply is interrupted by closing the terminal halfway through a long creation. The cloud console shows the resource actually finished creating a minute later. What should the engineer expect from the next terraform plan?
options: The state file is permanently unusable after any interrupted apply
The engineer must delete the resource in the console before Terraform can run again
Terraform assumes every resource in the configuration was destroyed
The next plan refreshes from the real infrastructure and reconciles, typically proposing to adopt or correct the resource rather than assuming the interrupted apply recorded nothing accurately
explain: Because plan refreshes against reality and state is written as operations complete, the next plan shows the true gap between configuration, state, and reality, and the engineer converges from there. An interruption is recoverable; it does not brick state or force manual deletion as the only path.

q: Inside a child module, an engineer writes region = var.aws_region but the caller passed the value as region in the module block while the child declares variable "aws_region". What went wrong?
options: Nothing; module arguments are matched by position, not name
Terraform renames caller arguments to match child variables automatically
The caller's argument name must exactly match the child's declared variable name, aws_region; mismatched names are an error
The child should read the caller's variable through the root namespace instead
explain: Module arguments bind to input variables by exact name, so passing region when the child declares aws_region fails as an unsupported argument. Binding is never positional (B) or auto-renamed (D), and children have no backdoor into root variables (C).

q: Which combination correctly wires a complete small configuration together?
options: A variable reads an existing AMI, a resource supplies the instance type, an output builds the instance, and a local publishes its ID
An output reads an existing AMI, a data source supplies the instance type, a local builds the instance, and a resource publishes its ID
A local reads an existing AMI, an output supplies the instance type, a data source builds the instance, and a variable publishes its ID
A data source reads an existing AMI, a variable supplies the instance type, a resource builds the instance from both, and an output publishes its ID
explain: Each block plays its own role: data sources read, variables input, resources manage, outputs publish. Every other option rotates those roles onto constructs that cannot perform them, which is exactly the confusion this domain tests.

q: An engineer writes `for_each = var.availability_zones` where the variable is a list of strings. Terraform errors out. What is the fix, and why?
options: Change it to `count = length(var.availability_zones)` — for_each cannot iterate variables
Add `depends_on` to the resource
Lists work fine; the error must be from something else
Wrap it with `toset()`: `for_each` accepts maps and sets of strings, not lists — lists have no stable keys
explain: for_each needs keys: it accepts maps or sets of strings. A list must be converted with toset() first. B dodges the question by switching to count (losing keyed identity). C is irrelevant. D denies a real, frequently tested error.

q: A locals block defines a value with the expression `zipmap(["a", "b", "c"], [1, 2, 3])`. What is displayed?
explain: zipmap() pairs keys with values positionally: the first key takes the first value, and so on.

q: A configuration contains the expression `trimsuffix("state.tfstate", ".tfstate")`. What is the result?
options: .tfstate
state.
state.tfstate
state
explain: trimsuffix() removes the suffix only when the string ends with it, leaving "state".

q: A module block passes providers = { aws = aws.a, aws.replica = aws.b }. The child module was written expecting aliases named aws and aws.dr. What happens?
options: The child silently falls back to the default provider for both
The map keys rename the caller's provider configurations
Terraform matches provider configurations by position, so it works
The run errors, because the keys in the providers map must match the configuration aliases the child module declares it expects
explain: The providers map keys are the alias names inside the child module's world, and they must correspond to configuration_aliases the child declares; mismatches are errors, not silent fallbacks. Matching is by declared alias name, never positional (A), and the map passes configurations rather than renaming the caller's (D).

q: A module block sourced from the public registry sets version = "~> 5.0". Which is the NEWEST module version terraform init can download?
explain: The constraint ~> 5.0 allows 5.0.0, 5.2.1; the newest of these is 5.2.1. Versions outside the range are rejected — ~> never allows crossing into the next increment of the component to its left.

q: A workspace uses remote execution mode. An engineer runs terraform plan from a laptop on a slow hotel network, yet the plan finishes quickly and the output appears line by line in the terminal. How is this possible?
options: The plan was cached from the last CI run and no new plan actually executed
The laptop delegates the plan to the nearest teammate machine that is online
The plan executes on HCP Terraform runners close to the cloud APIs, and the CLI only streams the remote output back for display
The CLI compresses the configuration and runs the plan locally in a sandbox
explain: With remote operations the run executes on HCP Terraform infrastructure while the local CLI displays streamed logs and results. Nothing executes in a local sandbox, on a teammate machine, or from a cache; a fresh remote plan is what produced the output.

q: A junior engineer proposes storing the development and production states inside a single HCP Terraform workspace to save time, separating them only by resource naming prefixes. Why is this design rejected?
options: Because production resources cannot be created from a workspace that also created development resources
Because HCP Terraform charges per resource prefix, making the design expensive
Because an HCP Terraform workspace holds exactly one state, so both environments would share one state and one variable set
Because naming prefixes are not allowed in HCP Terraform workspaces
explain: One workspace equals one state, one set of variables, and one run history for a configuration, so mixing environments in it destroys isolation. Prefixes are allowed and are not priced, and nothing technically blocks mixed creation, which is exactly why the design is dangerous rather than impossible.

q: A data source that reads an existing Azure resource group must come from the secondary subscription managed by an aliased provider. How is that arranged?
options: Rename the data source with the alias as a prefix
Set provider = azurerm.secondary in the data block, the same meta-argument resources use
Declare the alias inside the data block with an alias argument
Data sources cannot use aliased providers and always use the default
explain: Data blocks accept the same provider meta-argument as resource blocks, so provider = azurerm.secondary routes the read through the aliased configuration. Aliases are declared in provider blocks, never inside data blocks, and name prefixes have no routing effect.

q: Which two statements about an organization's private registry in HCP Terraform are accurate? (Choose two.)
options: Modules published privately are visible only to members of that organization, not to the public internet
Private registry modules can only be consumed by the single workspace that published them
Private registry modules are versioned, allowing consuming configurations to pin specific releases
Publishing a module privately also publishes it to the public Terraform Registry after a delay
explain: Private registry content is scoped to the organization and carries versions that consumers pin or constrain. Private content never leaks to the public registry, and any workspace whose users have access can consume published modules, not just a publishing workspace.

q: Why would an author choose map(string) instead of object() for a variable holding environment labels such as team, cost_center, and owner?
options: Because map(string) preserves insertion order and object() does not
Because map(string) allows each key to hold a different type of value
Because object() cannot be used in variables at all
Because map(string) requires every value to share one type and allows any keys, while object() fixes named attributes each with its own type
explain: A map is a collection of arbitrary keys whose values must all conform to a single element type, which fits open-ended label sets. An object fixes a named attribute schema where each attribute may have a different type, which is stricter than this use case needs.

q: An operator runs terraform plan -refresh=false for speed during an outage review. What trade-off are they accepting?
options: Refresh will happen twice to compensate for the flag
The plan may be based on stale state and miss drift that happened outside Terraform
The plan will destroy resources faster than a refreshed plan
Configuration files will be ignored for this run only
explain: Skipping refresh avoids provider reads but means Terraform trusts the last recorded state, so recent console or other out-of-band changes are invisible to that plan. It is a speed-for-accuracy trade-off, not a faster destroy mechanism.

q: An auditor wants the binary plan file from last night's deployment kept with the change ticket. Which command in the pipeline produced a file suitable for that, and what is inside it?
options: terraform validate produced it automatically; it contains syntax results
terraform plan without flags produced it in the .terraform directory by default
terraform fmt -out=change.plan produced it; it contains only formatting diffs
terraform plan -out=change.plan produced it; the file contains the planned actions, the configuration and variable values used, and the state snapshot it was based on
explain: Only plan -out writes a plan file, and it embeds the actions plus the inputs and prior state needed to execute exactly that plan later. A plain plan prints to the terminal and saves nothing, and fmt and validate produce no plan artifacts.

A soft-mandatory policy failure holds the run at the policy stage awaiting a human decision: an authorized user must override the check or discard the run, and it will wait indefinitely until then. State locks belong to apply operations in a single workspace, this workspace is not agent-based in the scenario, and provider rate limits surface as plan or apply errors, not as a policy-stage hold.
options: The provider API is rate-limiting the run, and HCP Terraform retries it silently for up to 24 hours
The soft-mandatory failure pauses the run by design until a user with override permission reviews the failure and overrides it, or the run is discarded
The workspace's agent has gone offline, and the run resumes when the agent reconnects
The state is locked by another workspace, and the run proceeds automatically when that workspace finishes
q: A production run has sat in the policy evaluation stage for 45 minutes. Its plan completed successfully, and the run page shows a failed soft-mandatory policy check awaiting action. Nothing else about the run is abnormal. What is actually happening, and what unblocks it?

An engineer wants to bootstrap a project from a published example: copy a remote module's configuration files into an empty directory and initialize the result in one step, rather than calling the module from a separate root. Which init feature does this?
options: terraform init -from-module=SOURCE, which copies the source module's configuration into the current directory and then initializes it
terraform init -reconfigure, which re-roots the module as a standalone configuration
terraform init -backend-config pointing at the module's repository
terraform init -get=false, because the module is treated as pre-downloaded
explain: The -from-module flag exists for this scaffolding case: it copies the referenced module's files into the working directory and proceeds with initialization. -backend-config (A) only completes backend settings, -get=false (B) skips downloads rather than copying a starting point, and -reconfigure (C) only revisits backend setup.

q: An apply against a large workspace is slow because resources are created a few at a time. What is Terraform's default concurrency, and which flag raises it?
options: Terraform has unlimited parallelism by default and -parallelism only lowers it for safety
Terraform creates one resource at a time by default, adjustable with -serial=true
Parallelism is fixed at 100 and cannot be changed without editing the backend
Terraform walks the dependency graph with a default parallelism of 10, adjustable with -parallelism=N on apply
explain: Apply (and plan and destroy) walk the graph with 10 concurrent operations by default, and -parallelism overrides that number. Concurrency is still bounded by the dependency graph itself, so independent resources parallelize while dependent ones wait their turn.

q: A team needs to launch instances in a VPC that was created years ago by another department and is not in any Terraform configuration. How should the configuration reference that VPC's ID?
options: With a `resource "aws_vpc"` block — Terraform will adopt the existing VPC automatically
By hardcoding the VPC ID as a string literal everywhere
It cannot be referenced; Terraform only works with infrastructure it created
With a `data` block (data source) that reads the existing VPC — Terraform reads it without managing it
explain: Data sources read existing infrastructure Terraform does not manage — exactly the case for a pre-existing VPC. A is wrong: a resource block would make Terraform try to create (or fight over) the VPC. C works but is brittle and untestable. D is false; data sources exist precisely for this.

q: During an incident, an engineer needs to know exactly which change introduced a bad route. With Terraform in Git, what is the fastest reliable source?
options: The cloud provider's marketing changelog
The memory of whoever was on call that week
A fresh terraform destroy of the networking stack
The Git history and blame for the route resource, showing the commit, author, and pull request discussion
explain: Version control gives a precise, searchable history of each line of infrastructure code, including who changed it and in what review context. Memory is unreliable, provider changelogs are unrelated, and destroying the stack would worsen the incident.

q: A data platform workspace must refresh its plan whenever the upstream warehouse workspace completes a successful apply, because its configuration consumes the warehouse outputs. A run trigger is configured from warehouse to data platform. A warehouse run is discarded before applying. Does the downstream run queue, and why?
options: Yes, because run triggers fire on any finished run regardless of outcome
Yes, but only as a speculative plan that the team must convert manually
No, because run triggers only work in the upstream direction from consumer to producer
No, because run triggers fire on successful applies; a discarded run applies nothing, so downstream workspaces are not triggered
explain: Run triggers chain on successful applies in the source workspace, so discarded or failed runs queue nothing downstream. They do not fire on any outcome, do not create speculative plans, and the direction is producer to consumer, exactly as configured here.

q: You need the ID of an existing VPC (created by another team, not in your configuration) to place subnets into it. What should you use?
options: A variable hardcoded with the VPC ID copied from the console
An import block, because the VPC must be recreated under your management
A data source block that reads the existing VPC
A resource block for the VPC, since Terraform will adopt it automatically
explain: Data sources read infrastructure Terraform doesn't manage. A would try to create a new VPC. C is for bringing objects under management, which isn't asked for. D works but is brittle and manual — the exam prefers data sources for this.

q: A teammate runs `terraform state pull > backup.tfstate` before a risky state operation. What did they capture, and what is the complementary command?
options: They exported the plan file; the complement is `terraform apply`
They downloaded the remote state to stdout; `terraform state push` uploads a state file (dangerous — it can overwrite remote state)
They listed all resources; the complement is `terraform state show` Domain 7: Maintaining Infrastructure with Terraform — 8 questions
They backed up the configuration files; the complement is `terraform state restore`
explain: `state pull` downloads remote state; `state push` uploads a local state file — powerful and dangerous since it can clobber the shared state. B invents a restore command. C confuses state with plans. D confuses pull with list.

q: A run in HCP Terraform shows a plan waiting for a human to confirm before apply proceeds. Which platform behavior does this illustrate?
options: The lock file is waiting for a second signature
Providers require manual approval for every API call
The CLI has uploaded the state and stopped working permanently
Remote runs execute plan and apply in HCP Terraform with an approval step in the workspace workflow, unlike a local CLI run that prompts in the terminal
explain: In HCP Terraform, runs are remote: the plan is produced in the hosted environment and a user confirms it in the workspace before apply continues. Nothing about providers, lock files, or the CLI involves per-call approvals or signatures; the confirmation is a platform workflow step.

q: A configuration's state contains a resource that no longer exists in the real cloud account because someone deleted it in the console. What does the next plan propose?
options: Automatic removal of the resource block from configuration
Nothing, because state still lists the resource so Terraform assumes it exists
An error that can only be fixed by deleting the whole state file
Creation of the resource again, because refresh finds it missing and configuration still wants it
explain: Refresh discovers the object is gone, updates the recorded state accordingly, and the diff then proposes recreating what configuration still declares. Terraform does not edit configuration to match a console deletion.

q: Terraform's architecture is described as plugin-based. What does this mean in practice?
options: The Terraform core binary contains all provider logic; plugins are optional UI themes
All infrastructure logic ships as separate provider plugins downloaded at init, keeping the core binary small and provider-agnostic
Each `.tf` file is compiled into a plugin at plan time
Provider plugins must be written in HCL
explain: Terraform core is a small engine; every provider is a separate plugin binary fetched during init. That is why init is required before plan, and why one CLI manages hundreds of providers. A inverts the design. C confuses configuration with compiled code. D is false — providers are typically Go binaries.

q: A monorepo pipeline must reject unformatted files anywhere in the tree, and reviewers want to see the exact pending changes for nested module directories as well as the root. Which single command serves as that gate?
options: terraform fmt -check -diff -recursive, which walks subdirectories, writes nothing, exits non-zero on unformatted files, and shows the diffs
terraform fmt -recursive on its own, because rewriting files counts as failing the build
terraform fmt -check in the root, because it covers subdirectories automatically
terraform validate -recursive, which reports formatting nested inside modules
explain: The three flags compose: -recursive reaches nested directories, -check converts the run into a non-writing gate with a failing exit code, and -diff exposes the exact changes. Root-only -check (A) silently misses nested files, plain -recursive (B) fixes files instead of gating on them, and validate -recursive (D) is not a formatting tool at all.

q: A teammate says: `Just run terraform fmt — it will fix the broken variable reference in main.tf.` What is wrong with this advice?
options: fmt cannot run on files with errors; it deletes them instead
Nothing — fmt fixes both formatting and broken references
fmt only works on `.tfvars` files, not `.tf` files
fmt only rewrites formatting (indentation, alignment); it never changes what the configuration does or fixes logic errors — that is validate's job to catch
explain: The classic fmt-vs-validate trap: fmt is cosmetic only; validate checks correctness. A attributes magic to fmt. C is false — fmt happily reformats files that have logic errors. D reverses the file types.

q: A resource block contains 'user_data = aws_instance.web.private_ip' inside the aws_instance.web block itself. What happens?
options: The value silently becomes an empty string
Terraform resolves it to the instance's own IP after creation
Terraform treats it as a reference to a different instance with the same name
Terraform reports an error for a self-reference, because a resource cannot use its own attributes to configure itself
explain: Self-references are invalid: a resource's own attributes are not available while that same resource is being configured, so Terraform errors. It cannot resolve after creation within its own arguments (A), does not redirect to another object (B), and does not silently empty the value (D).

Generated configuration dumps the live object's attributes verbatim, including computed and defaulted values that should not be declared explicitly, which is why cleanup is part of the workflow. It is readable HCL with full arguments, the opposite of empty blocks, and it is neither encrypted nor JSON by default.
options: The generated file is encrypted and must be decrypted with the state file first
The generated file contains only empty resource blocks with no arguments at all
The generated file is written in JSON and must be translated by hand into HCL
The generated file populates every attribute the provider returned, including values best left to provider defaults, so it is a verbose first draft to trim, not finished configuration
q: A team runs terraform plan -generate-config-out=generated.tf for a set of imported servers and opens the file. Why should they expect to edit the file heavily before using it?
Before a risky refactor, an engineer runs terraform state pull | jq '[.resources[] | select(.mode=="managed")] | length' and gets 148. What has the engineer learned, and what has NOT changed?
options: The engineer learned the live cloud account contains 148 resources, and the remote state was updated to match
The engineer learned 148 resources will be destroyed by the refactor, and the state lock was released
The engineer counted 148 managed resource entries recorded in the current state snapshot; the backend state itself was not modified by this read-only inspection
The engineer validated that all 148 resources match the configuration exactly, with no drift
explain: The count comes from the state snapshot state pull downloaded, not from a live inventory of the cloud account, and pull plus jq never writes state. It also says nothing about drift, because no provider refresh or configuration comparison happened in that pipeline.

q: During a code review, a teammate asks what `format("%s-%s", "web", "dev")` evaluates to. What is displayed?
options: dev-web
%s-%s
web-dev
webdev
explain: format() substitutes the arguments into the format string in order, so the first %s takes the first argument.

q: A data source is configured with a filter that matches no existing objects. What is the expected behavior?
options: The plan fails with an error reporting that no matching result was found, because a data read expects a result
Terraform silently substitutes an empty string and continues
The data source is skipped and treated as a managed resource
Terraform creates a matching object to satisfy the query
explain: A data source read that finds nothing to return is an error at read time; Terraform does not invent a result. It never creates infrastructure to satisfy a read (A), does not silently substitute empties for a failed lookup (B), and does not reclassify the block (D).

q: Which two statements describe foundational facts about Terraform state? (Choose two.)
options: It replaces version control as the canonical copy of the configuration
It maps configuration resource addresses to the real-world objects Terraform manages
It stores the provider plugin binaries downloaded during init
It records metadata such as dependencies and attribute values used when planning changes
explain: State's foundational roles are binding configuration addresses to real objects and holding the metadata, attributes, and dependencies that planning depends on. Provider binaries live in .terraform/providers, and configuration source belongs in version control, not in state.

q: A configuration looks up `var.instance_types["prod"]` but the key might not exist. Which function safely returns a fallback instead of erroring?
options: `coalesce(var.instance_types)`
Direct indexing is safe — missing keys return null automatically
`element(var.instance_types, "prod")`
`lookup(var.instance_types, "prod", "t3.micro")` — returns the default when the key is absent
explain: lookup(map, key, default) is the safe-access function with a fallback. element() is for list indexes. coalesce() returns the first non-empty of its arguments — wrong tool. D is false; missing keys error without lookup or try().

q: An object-typed variable value is read in two places as var.server.name and var.server["name"]. What is true of these two accesses?
options: The bracket form returns the attribute's type rather than its value
The dot form works only after the object has been converted with tomap()
Only the dot form is valid for objects; bracket form works only on maps
Both forms access the same object attribute; the dot form is simply the idiomatic shorthand
explain: Object attributes can be accessed with either dot notation or bracket indexing, and both return the attribute value. Bracket form is often used when the attribute name comes from an expression; no tomap() conversion is needed first.

q: Drift detection reports that a production database's instance size in the cloud no longer matches the workspace state. The change was an emergency scaling action the team wants to keep. What is the correct follow-through?
options: Delete the workspace state so the drift flag disappears
Update the configuration to match the new size and run a plan and apply so code, state, and reality agree again
Ignore the flag forever, because drift flags cannot be cleared
Disable drift detection for the production workspace permanently
explain: Keeping an intentional change means codifying it: update the configuration to the new reality and run normally so all three sources agree and the drift clears. Ignoring leaves permanent noise, deleting state loses management of the database, and disabling detection hides future real problems.

q: Which capability set is associated with Terraform Enterprise rather than with HCP Terraform?
options: HashiCorp-managed hosting on a shared multi-tenant service
A free tier for small teams managed at app.terraform.io
Automatic upgrades performed by HashiCorp on a fixed schedule
Self-hosted installation in the customer's own infrastructure, with the organization controlling upgrades, networking, and data residency
explain: Enterprise is the self-hosted distribution, so the customer runs and controls the platform, including where data lives. HCP Terraform is the HashiCorp-managed multi-tenant service with HashiCorp-controlled upgrades, which is exactly what Enterprise customers opt out of.

q: A root module composes three child modules: network, compute, and database. The compute module declares an input variable subnet_id, and the network module exposes an output private_subnet_id. How should the root wire the network result into compute?
options: Pass subnet_id = aws_subnet.private.id in the compute block, using the subnet resource address from inside the network module
Leave subnet_id unset in compute and let Terraform match the two modules by variable name automatically
Copy the subnet ID into a shared locals block that both child modules can read directly
Set subnet_id = module.network.private_subnet_id in the compute module block, so the value flows root-side from one module's output into the other module's input
explain: The root wires modules together by feeding one module's outputs into another module's inputs, here module.network.private_subnet_id into compute's subnet_id argument. Option A fails because the subnet resource is encapsulated inside the network module and unreachable from the root, C invents automatic name matching that does not exist, and D is wrong because locals never cross a module boundary.

q: Two teams argue about sharing a database module: one wants to copy the module folder into every repository, the other wants to publish it to the private registry. Which advantage decides the argument for the registry?
options: The registry converts the module into a provider automatically
Registry modules do not require input variables, unlike copied modules
Copies automatically update themselves whenever the original changes
A single published, versioned source means fixes and standards ship once, consumers upgrade by version, and usage is discoverable across the organization
explain: Central publishing gives one governed, versioned source of truth with discoverable consumers and deliberate upgrades. Copied folders drift independently, modules never become providers by being published, and registry modules use variables exactly like any other module.

q: An engineer attempts to import a resource type whose provider documentation lists no import support and provides no importer. What should they expect?
options: The import succeeds but produces an empty state entry
Terraform falls back to managing the object through its data source form
The import fails, because a resource type can only be imported if its provider implements importing for it
The CLI automatically writes a custom importer for the resource type
explain: Import is a provider-implemented capability, so resource types without an importer cannot be adopted this way and the attempt errors out. There is no empty-entry success, no data-source fallback for management, and Terraform never generates provider importer code on the fly.

q: Two engineers each keep a private copy of the production configuration on their laptops and apply from whichever copy is newest in their memory. Outages follow when the copies diverge. Which workflow practice fixes the root problem?
options: Keeping one version-controlled repository as the shared source of truth, with changes pulled, branched, reviewed, and merged before anyone applies
Running terraform fmt on both laptops so the files at least look identical
Giving both engineers the cloud account root credentials so either can fix anything
Emailing the state file to each other after every apply
explain: Divergent private copies are a source-control problem: one shared, reviewed repository makes divergence visible and mergeable. Formatting (A) only aligns whitespace and cannot reconcile different content, root credentials (B) widen risk without fixing divergence, and passing state files around by email (C) is fragile and unsafe compared with a proper shared workflow and backend.

q: A module outputs the value of `substr("terraform", 0, 5)`. What is displayed?
options: terraform
form
terra
terr
explain: substr() takes characters starting at offset 0 for a length of 5, giving "terra".

q: A variable is declared as type = set(string) and is assigned the value toset(["web", "api", "web", "db"]). How many elements does the resulting set contain, and why?
options: Two, because a set also discards any value that appears out of alphabetical order
Four, because a set preserves every assigned value including duplicates
Three, because a set stores only unique values and silently discards the duplicate
It errors, because duplicate values in a set assignment are rejected
explain: A set stores unique values only, so the second "web" is discarded and three elements remain. A list, by contrast, preserves duplicates and order; sets are unordered collections of distinct values by definition.

q: During a code review, a teammate asks what `join("-", ["staging", "qa"])` evaluates to. What does Terraform return?
options: staging,qa
staging/qa
stagingqa
staging-qa
explain: join() concatenates the list elements with the given separator between them.

q: A team is about to run terraform plan -generate-config-out for imported resources. Which two statements describe the generated file accurately? (Choose two.)
options: It automatically deletes the import blocks once generation succeeds
It is a starting point that should be reviewed and cleaned up, since generated blocks can include attributes best left unset
It contains HCL resource blocks drafted from the real objects referenced by import blocks
It replaces the state file as Terraform's record of the imported objects
explain: Generated configuration drafts real HCL for imported objects, which saves manual authoring, but HashiCorp positions it as a starting point needing review because it can surface every settable attribute verbatim. Generation never replaces state and never removes import blocks on its own.

q: A team migrates a workload from AWS to Azure by rewriting the resource blocks for Azure providers. They ask what carries over unchanged from everything they learned. Which answer is correct?
options: Nothing carries over, because each cloud has its own Terraform workflow and CLI
The core workflow carries over intact: write HCL, plan to preview, apply to execute, using the same CLI, with only the provider configuration and resource types changing
Only the provider binaries carry over; the workflow must be relearned per cloud
The state file carries over, so Azure resources are adopted automatically from AWS state
explain: Terraform's provider-agnostic design means the write, plan, apply loop and CLI are identical across clouds; that consistency is a central exam theme. Separate workflows per cloud (A) and reusable cross-cloud state (B) are both false, and provider binaries are cloud-specific downloads, not the transferable part (C).

q: A team stores its lock file in version control, and a pull request shows the lock file changed after a routine init on a developer's machine with no constraint edits. What is the most likely legitimate explanation?
options: The state file leaked into the lock file and must be purged
A provider was silently upgraded to a new major version by plain init
The lock file is corrupted and the pull request should be closed
Init added hashes for the developer's platform or recorded a provider newly added to the configuration, both normal lock updates to review and commit
explain: Lock files legitimately evolve when platforms or provider requirements change, and those updates belong in review like any dependency change. Plain init never upgrades across constraints, the lock file contains no state data, and a changed lock file is evidence to review, not automatic corruption.

q: A configuration needs an AWS provider for us-east-1 and another for eu-west-1 in the same run. How is this declared?
options: Declare one provider block with both regions listed
Use two provider blocks with distinct alias arguments, and reference the non-default one via the provider meta-argument
Write two provider "aws" blocks, one per region — Terraform merges them automatically
Run terraform init twice, once per region
explain: Multiple configurations of the same provider require alias arguments; resources select one with provider = aws.west. A is invalid — duplicate unaliased blocks are an error. B is not valid syntax. D misunderstands init entirely.

q: Which two statements about the version argument in a module block are true? (Choose two.)
options: It is required for local path modules
It is supported for modules sourced from generic Git repositories
It is supported for modules sourced from the Terraform Registry
It accepts constraint expressions such as ~> 5.0, not only exact versions
explain: Only registry sources (public or private) accept the version argument, and it takes full constraint syntax like providers. Git sources pin with ?ref= and error on version (B is false), and local path modules have no versions at all (C is false).

q: Which reference correctly pulls the first IP from a counted instance fleet into a monitoring resource, assuming aws_instance.node uses count?
options: aws_instance.node[0].private_ip, selecting instance index 0 and its private_ip attribute
aws_instance.node[*].id with no further selection, which returns exactly one IP
aws_instance.node.private_ip[0], placing the index after the attribute
data.aws_instance.node[0].private_ip, because counted resources are read as data
explain: For counted resources the index belongs to the instance address, before the attribute: type.name[index].attribute. Indexing after the attribute (B) addresses the wrong thing, a splat returns a collection rather than one IP (C), and managed counted resources are not data sources (D).

q: Which version constraint for a registry module allows 3.2.0 and 3.7.1 but rejects 4.0.0?
options: version = "~> 3.2"
version = "< 3.0"
version = "3.2.0"
version = ">= 3.0"
explain: The pessimistic constraint ~> 3.2 permits the rightmost component to grow, so any 3.x at or above 3.2 qualifies while 4.0.0 is excluded. The >= 3.0 constraint (A) would also accept 4.0.0, the bare 3.2.0 (C) pins exactly one release, and D excludes everything listed.

q: While debugging a configuration, an engineer evaluates `merge({ Name = "web", Env = "dev" }, { Env = "test", Team = "ops" })` in the console. What is the result?
options: { Env = "dev", Name = "web" }
{ Env = "dev", Name = "web", Team = "ops" }
{ Env = "test", Team = "ops" }
{ Env = "test", Name = "web", Team = "ops" }
explain: merge() combines maps left to right and later maps win key conflicts, so Env is overwritten with "test" while Name survives and Team is added.

Sentinel is the policy-as-code framework built into HCP Terraform and Enterprise, where policy sets attach to workspaces and mandatory policies can halt a run. The main distractor, validate, only checks configuration syntax and schema consistency locally; it has no policy sets, no enforcement levels, and no central governance.
options: The plain CLI, using lifecycle prevent_destroy rules on every bucket resource
Any S3-compatible backend, which enforces Sentinel policies during state writes
HCP Terraform or Terraform Enterprise, using Sentinel policy sets with defined enforcement levels applied to workspaces
The plain CLI, using terraform validate with stricter settings enabled
q: An organization wants guardrails such as 'no public storage buckets' enforced centrally on infrastructure runs, with some policies mandatory and able to block a run before apply. Which platform and feature does this require?
A team supports developers on Windows and Linux plus CI on ARM, and wants one committed lock file that lets init succeed on all three. What is the right preparation?
options: Commit three separate lock files and rename the right one before each run
Delete the lock file so each platform generates its own without verification
Pin providers with = constraints; exact pins remove the need for platform hashes
Record hashes for every needed platform in the lock file, for example with terraform providers lock -platform flags for each platform, then commit it
explain: Provider builds differ per platform, so the lock file must contain the checksum for each platform in use, which terraform providers lock -platform adds in one file. Terraform reads only the single standard lock filename, deleting it sacrifices verification, and exact pins still need per-platform hashes.

q: A resource created with for_each is addressed as aws_subnet.all["prod"]. What does the ["prod"] part select?
options: The provider alias named prod
A variable named prod
The third subnet alphabetically
The instance of aws_subnet.all whose for_each key is the string prod
explain: Instances of a for_each resource are addressed by their key, so the bracket selects the instance created for the prod entry. It is not a positional or alphabetical selector (A), and neither a variable nor a provider alias is being referenced (C and B).

q: During a code review, a teammate asks what `trimsuffix("state.tfstate", ".tfstate")` evaluates to. What is the result?
options: .tfstate
state.
state.tfstate
state
explain: trimsuffix() removes the suffix only when the string ends with it, leaving "state".

q: A platform team rebuilds a training environment every Monday from Terraform in about 15 minutes, whereas the manual build used to take two days. Which IaC advantage is most visible here?
options: Immutable infrastructure enforced by the cloud provider
Version control reverting the environment to last week
Configuration management of packages inside the VMs
Automation and speed from executing code instead of manual steps
explain: The time collapse from days to minutes comes from automation: code executes the build repeatably without human clicking. Version control helps manage the code, but it does not by itself explain the speed, and no detail suggests image-based immutability.

q: The security team requires that no security group in any workspace allows 0.0.0.0/0 ingress, enforced automatically on every run. Which HCP Terraform feature implements this?
options: Workspace naming conventions documented in a wiki
Refresh-only mode on a nightly schedule
Variable sets with a banned_cidrs variable
Policy enforcement with policy sets (OPA) that evaluate each plan and can block runs
explain: Policy-as-code sets evaluate plans against rules and can fail or block runs — the governance answer. A just shares variables; nothing enforces them. B is documentation, not enforcement. C detects drift; it doesn't gate changes.

q: In a plan output, a new aws_s3_bucket resource is prefixed with a single plus sign (+). What action will apply take for this bucket?
options: Destroy the bucket and then recreate it
Read the bucket as a data source only
Update the bucket in place without recreating it
Create the bucket because it does not exist in state yet
explain: The + symbol means create: the resource is in the configuration but not in state, so apply creates it. The main distractor is update in place, which is shown with ~ instead. Destroy-and-recreate is -/+, and a data read is <=.

q: A repository has Terraform configurations in the root directory and in `./modules/*` subdirectories. Which command formats every `.tf` file in the whole tree?
options: terraform fmt (run in the root — it always recurses)
terraform fmt -recursive
terraform fmt -all
terraform validate -recursive
explain: Plain `fmt` formats only the current directory; `-recursive` walks subdirectories. A is the trap — root-only is the default. C and D are not real flag combinations.

q: Which of these is a valid reason to extract repeated resources into a child module, per module best practice?
options: To hide resources from the state file
To make terraform plan run without a backend
To avoid declaring provider versions
To encapsulate a related group of resources behind a small set of inputs and outputs so it can be maintained and reused as one unit
explain: Modules encapsulate a cohesive set of resources behind a narrow interface, reducing duplication and letting owners change internals without breaking callers. Module resources still live in state (A), backends are still required (C), and provider requirements still apply inside modules (D).

q: A virtual machine's guest agent is corrupted so in-place updates keep failing, and the team decides the instance must be recreated. Which flag forces that replacement on the next apply?
options: -replace=aws_instance.web passed to terraform apply, which plans that one resource for destruction and recreation
-target=aws_instance.web passed alone, which always recreates the targeted resource
-destroy passed to terraform plan, which recreates everything it removes
-refresh-only passed to terraform apply, which rebuilds resources that fail health checks
explain: The -replace flag tells Terraform to treat the named object as tainted for that run, so the plan shows it destroyed and recreated while other resources are untouched. Refresh-only only syncs state, targeting alone does not force recreation, and a destroy plan removes rather than rebuilds.

q: The variable "instance_type" receives values from several places: a value passed with -var on the command line sets it to "t3.large"; a value in settings.auto.tfvars sets it to "t3.micro"; the variable block declares default = "m5.xlarge"; TF_VAR_ is set in the shell environment sets it to "m5.large". No other sources set it. Which value does Terraform use?
options: t3.large
m5.large
m5.xlarge
t3.micro
explain: Variable precedence, lowest to highest: default < TF_VAR_ environment < terraform.tfvars < terraform.tfvars.json < *.auto.tfvars < -var-file < -var. The highest source present here is a -var flag, so its value "t3.large" wins.

q: One terraform block contains both required_version = ">= 1.6" and a required_providers entry pinning the AWS provider. What does each setting constrain?
options: Both constrain provider plugins at different stages of init
Both are alternative spellings of the same Core constraint
required_version constrains the AWS provider; required_providers constrains Core
required_version constrains the Terraform Core binary; required_providers constrains the provider plugins the configuration uses
explain: The two settings guard different binaries: required_version gates the terraform executable itself, while each required_providers entry gates one provider plugin. Swapping them is a common exam trap, since a Core upgrade never satisfies a provider constraint and vice versa.

q: Which two statements about moved blocks are accurate? (Choose two.)
options: Its from and to addresses can cross module boundaries, such as moving a resource into a module while renaming it
A moved block must be run with terraform state mv before it can work
A moved block is declared in configuration and takes effect during plan and apply, not as a standalone CLI command
A moved block destroys the old real object and creates a new one at the new address
explain: Moved blocks are declarative configuration evaluated in a normal run, and they can map full addresses across modules while preserving the same real object. They exist specifically to avoid destroy and recreate, and they are not executed via state mv.

q: A configuration contains the expression `lookup({ dev = "t3.micro", staging = "t3.small", prod = "m5.large", qa = "t3.medium" }, "qa")`. What value does it produce?
options: t3.medium
t3.small
t3.micro
m5.large
explain: lookup() returns the value stored under the key "qa", which is "t3.medium". Without a third argument, lookup() would error if the key were absent.

q: An external tagging tool manages the `tags` on instances, and every `terraform plan` wants to revert its changes. How do you make Terraform leave the tags alone?
options: Run every plan with `-refresh=false`
`lifecycle { ignore_changes = [tags] }` — Terraform stops tracking drift on those attributes
Remove the `tags` argument from the configuration entirely
`lifecycle { prevent_destroy = true }`
explain: ignore_changes tells Terraform to accept external modifications to listed attributes instead of reverting them. B does not help — Terraform would still manage tags as empty. C blocks destruction, unrelated to attribute drift. D disables refresh globally, hiding all drift — dangerous and wrong.

q: What is a snowflake server in IaC discussions?
options: A server that uses immutable images for every deployment
A uniquely hand-tuned server that cannot be reproduced from code
A server built from a high-availability cluster template
A server that is automatically rebuilt nightly from configuration
explain: A snowflake is a one-off, manually drifted server whose exact state exists nowhere in code, so it cannot be recreated reliably. The other choices describe templated, immutable, or automated servers, which are the opposite problem.

q: Two engineers run `terraform apply` at the same time against a configuration using the default local backend. The state file becomes corrupted. What is the root cause?
options: The state file was too large for concurrent writes
One engineer forgot to run `terraform init`
