The `local` backend provides no state locking — locking is a backend feature, and concurrent applies raced on the same file
Terraform core has a bug with parallel applies
explain: EXAM TRAP: locking is a backend feature, not a core feature. The local backend does not lock, so concurrent runs corrupt state. The fix is a remote backend with locking (HCP Terraform, S3, azurerm, etc.). A blames file size. C blames the core. D is unrelated to corruption.

q: A provider constraint reads version = "~> 4.2, != 4.5.0, < 4.8.0". The registry offers 4.5.0, 4.7.9, 4.8.0, and 4.9.1. Which version does init select?
options: 4.7.9, the newest build that is >= 4.2, < 4.8.0, and not the excluded 4.5.0
4.8.0, because < bounds are inclusive when combined with ~>
4.5.0, because != is overridden by the pessimistic operator
4.9.1, because ~> 4.2 has no upper bound once an explicit < is present
explain: Every clause must hold simultaneously: ~> 4.2 sets >= 4.2.0 and < 5.0.0, the explicit < 4.8.0 tightens the ceiling, and != removes 4.5.0, leaving 4.7.9 as the newest valid build. Bounds never become inclusive or disappear when operators are combined.

q: A team currently starts every run by typing terraform apply in a terminal against HCP Terraform, but wants merges themselves to start runs so laptops are out of the deployment path. Which change moves them to the VCS-driven workflow?
options: Remove the cloud block so runs default to the VCS integration
Instruct everyone to use terraform apply -auto-approve from their terminals instead
Enable drift detection so merges are noticed on the next health check
Connect each workspace to its repository and branch in workspace settings so pushes queue runs automatically
explain: Switching workflows means connecting workspaces to a VCS provider, repository, and branch so pushes queue runs without CLI involvement. Terminal auto-approve keeps the CLI-driven model, removing the cloud block does not create a VCS link, and drift detection observes infrastructure rather than triggering deployments.

q: A workspace has scheduled drift detection enabled. Overnight, someone changes a managed security group rule directly in the cloud console. No Terraform run occurs. What does HCP Terraform do?
options: It deletes the security group to restore consistency
Nothing, because drift can only be found when a user runs a plan
It automatically reverts the console change within minutes
The scheduled check compares real infrastructure against the workspace state, detects the divergence, and flags the workspace as drifted with a notification
explain: Scheduled drift detection periodically refreshes and compares reality to state, surfacing drifted workspaces and notifying the team without any user-initiated run. It reports drift rather than reverting or deleting anything, since remediation is a human decision executed through a normal run.

q: Which statement about Terraform and single-cloud native tools is most accurate for the exam?
options: Native tools cannot be used alongside Terraform in any architecture
Terraform cannot manage AWS as deeply as any other tool can
Terraform trades deep single-cloud focus for a provider model that spans clouds, on-premises, and SaaS APIs
CloudFormation, ARM, and Deployment Manager each manage multiple clouds through providers
explain: Native tools are single-cloud by design, while Terraform's provider model spans many platforms and service types. The other choices invert the facts: native tools are not multi-cloud, they can coexist with Terraform, and Terraform manages AWS extensively through its provider.

q: A team member proposes committing the .terraform directory to Git so new hires never need to run init for providers. Why is this the wrong solution to a real onboarding need?
options: Because init is optional once any provider exists on the machine
Because .terraform contains the state file, which must never be committed

The .terraform directory is a local, platform-specific working cache rebuilt by init; the reproducible path is committing the lock file and running init, which installs the exact locked providers on each platform
Because Git cannot store binary files of any kind
explain: Provider binaries are platform-specific build artifacts, and .terraform is disposable working state that init recreates; committing it bloats the repo and still gives other platforms the wrong binaries. The lock file plus init is the designed reproducibility mechanism, state lives outside .terraform, and Git handles binaries fine, just not as a package manager.

q: Why would an author add 'depends_on' inside an output block?
options: To encrypt the output value
To declare an explicit dependency so Terraform understands the output relies on a resource completing, for example when a value is produced by an external process tied to that resource
To prevent the output from being stored in state
To make the output print in a specific color
explain: Output depends_on exists for the rare case where the output's real dependency is not visible from its value expression — typically values created by side effects — ensuring correct ordering and handling. It has nothing to do with display color (A), encryption (C), or state storage (B).

q: A new engineer asks for the standard Terraform workflow in order. Which sequence is correct?
options: Validate -> Destroy -> Init
Apply -> Plan -> Write
Write -> Plan -> Apply (with init first in a new working directory)
Fmt -> Import -> Push
explain: The core loop is Write -> Plan -> Apply, and a fresh working directory needs `terraform init` before anything else. A reverses the loop. C and D string together unrelated commands — destroy tears everything down and is not part of the normal loop.

Console evaluates expressions against state, so it depends on the same initialization as plan: init configures the backend and installs providers so state can be read and schemas are known. Console does not need a saved plan file or a prior apply, and it is not a paid feature, which makes the plan-file distractor wrong about what init actually supplies.
options: Console only runs after a successful apply has populated the provider cache
Console requires a saved plan file, and only init can create plan files
Console is a paid HCP Terraform feature that must be unlocked during init
Console needs an initialized working directory so it can load the backend, read the current state, and evaluate expressions against real recorded values
q: On a freshly cloned repository, a developer runs terraform console before running any other Terraform command and gets an error that the working directory is not initialized. Why does console have this prerequisite?
Which expression correctly uses the public IP of an instance named api inside a DNS record resource?
options: value = var.aws_instance.api.public_ip
value = "aws_instance.api.public_ip" in quotes, so Terraform treats it as a reference
value = aws_instance.api.public_ip, placing the reference where the record's value argument belongs
value = data.aws_instance.api.public_ip, because all reads use data blocks
explain: An unquoted reference expression resolves to the attribute's value; quoting it (B) turns it into a literal string of characters. The instance is a managed resource in this configuration, so neither the data. form (C) nor the var. form (D) addresses it.

q: After terraform plan -out=db.plan succeeds, a developer edits a resource argument in the configuration but does not touch state. The team then runs terraform apply db.plan . What does apply execute?
options: Nothing; apply detects the edit and demands the file be deleted
The edit is merged into the saved plan automatically at apply time
A fresh plan reflecting the developer's edit, because apply always re-reads configuration
The saved plan exactly as originally generated, because apply of a plan file does not re-read the edited configuration to recompute actions
explain: The saved plan is self-contained: apply executes its recorded actions and does not recompute them from the now-edited configuration. This is precisely why process discipline matters — the edit only takes effect in a newly generated plan.

q: Before Terraform computes a plan diff, what does it do by default on every normal terraform plan run?
options: It locks the configuration files so no one can edit them during planning
It destroys any resource that has drifted from the configuration
It writes a saved plan file to disk automatically
It contacts each provider to refresh state with current real-world attribute values, then diffs configuration against that refreshed state
explain: By default plan refreshes first: providers read live objects and state is updated in memory so the diff reflects reality and exposes drift. Plan never destroys drifted resources (that would be apply), and a saved file is only written when -out is used.

q: A team renames a provider's source address in required_providers but runs a plan before migrating state. The plan errors out referencing the provider recorded in state. What is the correct interpretation and next step?
options: The state still points at the old provider address while configuration now requires the new one; run terraform state replace-provider to align state with configuration, then plan again
The error means the new provider is not installed, and deleting .terraform.lock.hcl alone will fix it
The resources must be destroyed, because a provider rename always forces recreation
The backend must be migrated with init -reconfigure before any plan can run
explain: The mismatch is between the provider address stored in state and the one configuration now declares; replace-provider exists precisely to rewrite that stored address without touching real resources. Recreation is not required, and neither the dependency lock file nor the backend configuration is the cause.

Local state and CLI workspaces are core open-source CLI features. Sentinel policies, run tasks, and private registry hosting are HCP Terraform / Enterprise platform features layered on top of runs, so the distractors all require the paid platform the engineer does not have.
options: A private registry for internal providers and modules
Sentinel policy sets enforced on every run
Run tasks that call external services during a run
Local state files used with CLI workspaces
q: A solo engineer runs everything locally with the open-source Terraform CLI and no paid platform. Which capability is available to them without HCP Terraform or Terraform Enterprise?
A configuration defines three identical web servers. One server is later patched by hand to a different version, causing errors only on that node. Which term describes what the hand patch created?
options: A provider alias conflict
Convergence toward the desired state
An immutable deployment that needs no rollback
A snowflake server that diverged from the common configuration
explain: Hand-patching one node makes it a unique snowflake that no longer matches the code, which is exactly the inconsistency IaC aims to prevent. Convergence would mean bringing it back to the declared state, not diverging from it.

q: A reviewer sees this line in a plan for a data lookup: <= data.aws_ami.latest . The apply completes minutes later. What role did that data source play?
options: It locked the state while the AMI was being built
It was imported and converted into a managed resource
It was destroyed and recreated to fetch fresh values
It was read to supply values such as an AMI ID to managed resources; it was not created, updated, or destroyed as infrastructure
explain: <= marks a read: data sources fetch external or existing values for the configuration and are not lifecycle-managed objects. They are never imported by a read, never destroyed, and have nothing to do with state locking.

q: A script needs apply to proceed without any interactive prompt, and the team has already reviewed a plain terraform plan (not a saved file) in a previous step. The script runs terraform apply -auto-approve . What risk remains compared with applying a saved plan?
options: The apply generates a new plan at execution time, so drift or edits between the earlier review and this run can change what gets applied, unlike a saved plan which freezes the reviewed actions
The risk is that -auto-approve skips refreshing state entirely
There is no risk; -auto-approve guarantees the earlier reviewed plan is the one executed
The risk is that -auto-approve deletes the state lock permanently
explain: -auto-approve only skips the prompt; without a saved plan file the apply re-plans live, so the executed changes can differ from what was reviewed earlier. The saved-plan pattern exists to close exactly this gap between review and execution.

q: A workspace's state was built only from resources Terraform created itself, yet the account also holds a forgotten analytics cluster nobody ever imported. During a cost review, why does no Terraform plan or destroy in this workspace ever mention the cluster?
options: Terraform hides resources that have not been modified in over a year
It is an orphan relative to this configuration: with no state entry and no resource block, Terraform has no knowledge of it at all
The cluster is being managed by the workspace's backend lock
Plans suppress unmanaged resources to keep output readable
explain: Terraform's universe is state plus configuration, and the cluster is in neither, making it completely invisible until someone writes a block and imports it. Age-based hiding, backend locks, and output suppression are invented behaviors that distract from the state-based model.

q: A legacy team hosts module code in Mercurial. Which prefix forces Terraform to treat the address as a Mercurial repository?
options: No prefix exists; Mercurial is unsupported
mc::
hg::
git:: with a Mercurial compatibility flag
explain: Generic VCS sources use a forced prefix, hg:: for Mercurial just as git:: is for Git. There is no mc:: prefix (B), Git tooling cannot clone Mercurial repositories with a flag (C), and Mercurial is a documented supported source (A is false).

q: A regulated enterprise needs workspace collaboration, policy enforcement, and a private registry, but its security board forbids any control plane hosted outside its own network. Which choice satisfies every requirement?
options: The open-source CLI plus a shared network drive for state files
Terraform Enterprise, self-hosted inside the enterprise network, providing the platform features under the customer's own control
HCP Terraform with a dedicated single-tenant add-on hosted by HashiCorp
HCP Terraform, because its data residency options move hosting into customer data centers
explain: Only Terraform Enterprise is installed and operated inside the customer's own infrastructure while still delivering workspaces, Sentinel policies, and a private registry. HCP Terraform remains HashiCorp-hosted regardless of tier, and shared-drive state with the bare CLI provides none of the platform governance features.

q: A vendor claims their imperative automation framework is identical to Terraform because both can create a VM. What is the most exam-accurate rebuttal?
options: Terraform creates VMs without using any provider APIs
Creating a VM is the only capability that matters, so the claim is correct
Imperative frameworks cannot create VMs at all
Terraform also declares and continuously reconciles desired state using its state file, while a step-based framework executes instructions without a desired-state model
explain: The distinction is the desired-state and state-tracking model, not the single act of creating a VM. Imperative tools can create VMs, and Terraform absolutely uses provider APIs, so the rebuttal must rest on reconciliation and state.

q: A platform team builds a hardened VPC module and wants only teams inside its HCP Terraform organization to discover and consume it, with the same registry experience as public modules. Where should they publish it?
options: In the public Terraform Registry under a misleading name so outsiders ignore it
On a public wiki page as a zip download
In the organization's private module registry in HCP Terraform
Inside a single workspace's state file
explain: The private module registry lets an organization publish modules for internal discovery and consumption with registry versioning and access control. Wiki zips lose versioning and integration, publishing publicly under any name exposes the module, and state files are not a distribution mechanism.

q: A backend migration finishes, but the old local terraform.tfstate file is still sitting in the working directory. A teammate assumes it remains the active state. What should they understand?
options: The local file and remote backend stay synchronized after migration automatically
The migration failed unless the local file was manually uploaded a second time
Terraform merges local and remote state on every plan from then on
After a successful migration and re-init, the configured remote backend is authoritative; the leftover local file is not the live state
explain: Migration copies state to the new backend and init records that backend as the source of truth. Terraform does not continuously sync or merge a leftover local file, which is why stale local copies should be handled carefully and not trusted.

q: Beyond downloading providers and modules, which backend-related job does terraform init perform on every successful run?
options: It migrates the state file to the newest Terraform format version
It configures the backend declared in the configuration, setting up access to the state storage the working directory will use
It backs up the previous state snapshot into the .terraform directory
It verifies that every resource in state still exists by calling each cloud API
explain: Backend configuration is one of init's core duties alongside installing providers and modules: it prepares state access for all later commands. Init does not migrate state format on every run (A), keep state backups in .terraform (B), or call cloud APIs to verify resources (D), which is refresh behavior during plan.

q: You need the full recorded attributes of one specific resource, aws_s3_bucket.logs, exactly as stored in state. Which command shows them?
options: terraform show -plan aws_s3_bucket.logs
terraform state list aws_s3_bucket.logs
terraform output aws_s3_bucket.logs
terraform state show aws_s3_bucket.logs
explain: terraform state show <address> displays the attributes of a single resource instance as recorded in state. List only prints addresses, output shows root module outputs, and terraform show without the state subcommand is for plans or general state views.

q: A fleet of six instances built with for_each includes two with corrupted boot volumes and four healthy ones. Which two actions correctly force recreation of only the broken instances? (Choose two.)
options: terraform plan -replace with a broken instance's keyed address to preview its recreation before applying
Deleting the state file so every instance is recreated from scratch
terraform apply -replace with the eu instance's keyed address, repeated for the other broken instance
terraform destroy followed by a full apply to rebuild the entire fleet
explain: -replace accepts a specific instance address, including a for_each keyed address, so each broken instance can be recreated individually, and running it through plan first previews the change safely. Destroying the fleet or deleting state sacrifices four healthy instances and all tracking to fix two objects.

q: An engineer wants to set the variable `region` from a shell environment variable without touching any files or command flags. Which environment variable name will Terraform pick up automatically?
options: REGION_TF_VAR
TERRAFORM_region
TF_region
TF_VAR_region
explain: The convention is `TF_VAR_` — Terraform automatically maps TF_VAR_region to variable "region". The other names are invented; only the TF_VAR_ prefix is recognized.

q: An engineer tests an expression in terraform console: `can(cidrhost("10.0.0.0/33", 1))`. What is displayed?
options: false
null
"yes"
true
explain: can() returns true if its expression evaluates without error and false otherwise; /33 is not a valid IPv4 prefix, so the result is false — can() itself never errors.

q: A team adds != 5.4.0 to a provider constraint of >= 5.0 after that release proves buggy. What does the != operator do here?
options: It downgrades the installed provider to the release before 5.4.0
It blocks every version from 5.4.0 upward
It marks 5.4.0 as deprecated in the registry for all users
It excludes exactly version 5.4.0 while still allowing other versions that satisfy >= 5.0
explain: The != operator excludes a single named version from an otherwise valid range, so 5.4.1 or 5.3.0 can still be selected. It performs no downgrade by itself and does not block later releases or change the registry.

q: Using the remote backend, a team wants local workspaces dev, staging, and prod to map automatically to HCP Terraform workspaces named app-dev, app-staging, and app-prod. Which configuration achieves this?
options: Setting the TF_WORKSPACE environment variable to app- in every shell
Three separate backend blocks, one per environment, inside the terraform block
A workspaces block with name = "app-" in the backend configuration
A workspaces block with prefix = "app-" in the backend configuration, so each local workspace name is prefixed when resolving the remote workspace
explain: The remote backend's workspaces prefix option maps each CLI workspace to a remote workspace of prefix plus local name, which is how one configuration serves many HCP Terraform workspaces. A single name pins exactly one workspace, only one backend block is allowed, and the environment variable selects a workspace rather than adding a prefix.

q: A locals block defines a value with the expression `keys({ "b-team" = "ops", "a-team" = "dev", "c-team" = "sec" })`. What is the result?
options: ["ops", "dev", "sec"]
["a-team", "c-team", "b-team"]
["b-team", "a-team", "c-team"]
["a-team", "b-team", "c-team"]
explain: keys() returns the map's keys as a sorted list — alphabetical here — not in the order they were written.

q: A plan shows aws_launch_template.app marked -/+ and the summary reads: Plan: 2 to add, 1 to change, 1 to destroy. Another resource in the detail is a plain create. Reconcile the numbers.
options: The destroy belongs to the in-place change, which always deletes first
The summary is inconsistent and the plan should be discarded
The replacement counts as the 1 change, and the 2 adds are both plain creates
The replacement accounts for 1 add and 1 destroy, the plain create accounts for the second add, and the remaining resource is the 1 in-place change
explain: Tallying the detail: -/+ gives one add and one destroy, a separate + gives the second add, and a ~ gives the one change — the summary reconciles exactly. In-place changes never destroy, and replacements never count as changes.

q: Which tool is primarily focused on provisioning infrastructure rather than configuring software inside already-running servers?
options: Puppet, which enforces packages and files on agents
Ansible configuration tasks applied to existing hosts
Chef, which runs recipes on nodes
Terraform, which creates networks, instances, and managed services through provider APIs
explain: Terraform's core job is provisioning: creating the infrastructure itself via provider APIs. Chef, Puppet, and Ansible configuration tasks mainly manage the software state inside hosts that already exist, though the tool categories do overlap at the edges.

q: A junior engineer is about to run terraform init -reconfigure after a backend change that affects live production state, assuming it is just a stronger form of migration. What risk should the reviewer flag before the run proceeds?
options: -reconfigure upgrades all providers to their newest versions as a side effect
Terraform will initialize against the new backend without copying the existing state, so the previously managed resources will appear unmanaged and a subsequent plan will propose creating them again
-reconfigure locks the backend so no other engineer can ever initialize the directory
-reconfigure permanently deletes the old state file from the previous backend
explain: The danger of -reconfigure is orphaned state: initialization succeeds against the new backend, but the existing state never arrives there, so Terraform sees an empty world and plans fresh creates. It does not upgrade providers (A), delete the old state where it lives (C), or lock anyone out permanently (D); the loss is one of continuity, not destruction.

q: An engineer stores subnet IDs in a set(string) and then tries to read the first one with var.subnet_ids[0]. Why does this fail?
options: Sets are 0-indexed, so the engineer should use index 1 instead
The index works, but only inside a count meta-argument
Sets can only be indexed after the first terraform apply has run
Sets are unordered and have no index positions, so elements cannot be addressed by numeric index at all
explain: Sets are unordered collections of unique values, so there is no first element and no positional indexing; iteration happens through for expressions or for_each. Sets have no 1-based indexing variant either, and neither apply state nor count changes how set values are addressed.

q: During a code review, a teammate asks what `lower("Live")` evaluates to. What is the result?
options: lIVE
live
Live
LIVE
explain: lower() converts every cased character in the string to lowercase.

q: A module outputs the value of `length(["batch", "db", "web"])`. What is the result?
explain: length() of a list counts its elements: the list has 3 elements.

q: Which command must be run in a freshly cloned Terraform working directory before terraform plan will work?
options: terraform validate
terraform init
terraform output
terraform fmt
explain: init downloads providers and modules and configures the backend — plan refuses to run without it. A only reformats. B also requires init to have run first. D reads state from an existing setup.

q: The AWS provider ships a critical bug fix in a new release while Terraform Core itself has not changed in months. Why is this release pattern possible?
options: HashiCorp must release a new Core version for every provider fix
Provider fixes are delivered by editing the lock file by hand
Core auto-updates its embedded AWS code every night
Providers are versioned and released independently of Core, so a provider can be upgraded without a Core release
explain: Independent versioning is a core benefit of the plugin architecture: each provider has its own release cadence, and teams adopt a fix by relaxing or upgrading that provider's constraint and re-running init. Core contains no embedded provider code to update.

q: What does backend "remote" connect Terraform to, at a concept level?
options: A generic SFTP server for uploading terraform.tfstate
A Git remote used to commit state files after each apply
The local backend running on a remote desktop session
HCP Terraform / Terraform Enterprise workspaces, where runs and state are managed remotely
explain: The remote backend delegates state and, depending on configuration, runs to HCP Terraform or Terraform Enterprise workspaces. It is not an SFTP or Git mechanism for shipping a local tfstate file around.

q: During a code review, a teammate asks what `sort([7, 28, 8])` evaluates to. What does Terraform return?
explain: sort() orders the elements ascending: 7, 8, 28. The original written order is not preserved.

q: A team manages servers by SSHing into each machine and running setup commands by hand. After an outage, nobody can reconstruct exactly what was configured on the failed server. Which statement best describes the Infrastructure as Code practice that would have prevented this?
options: A backup script that snapshots each server's disk nightly
Hiring a dedicated engineer to run all setup commands from a single laptop
A shared wiki page documenting every manual step the team performs on each server
Infrastructure defined declaratively in version-controlled, machine-readable files that are provisioned automatically
explain: IaC means infrastructure lives as declarative, version-controlled code — so every server is reproducible and every change is a reviewable commit. A wiki (B) documents but does not enforce; snapshots (C) preserve a mess without explaining it; centralizing manual work (D) keeps the same unrepeatable process. Only A makes the environment reconstructable.

q: A new team member asks where reusable modules and input variables fit in the day-to-day loop, since the workflow diagram only shows three boxes. Which explanation is accurate?
options: Modules are applied separately before the root configuration is written
Variables are defined during the plan step by answering prompts Terraform invents
Modules and variables are created automatically by init whenever the configuration runs short of them
They are part of the Write step: authors compose resources, variables, and module calls into configuration first, and only then does the loop plan and apply that configuration
explain: Authoring is broader than typing resource blocks: composing module calls and declaring variables is Write-step work that produces the configuration the later steps consume. Init (A) only downloads modules already referenced, modules are not applied before the root exists (C), and variables are declared in code, not invented by prompts (B).

q: Drift is detected on a load balancer listener that an external automation intentionally manages. The team accepts the external values and does not want plans to keep proposing reverts. What is the Terraform-side concept that addresses attribute-level acceptance?
options: Using lifecycle ignore_changes for the externally managed attributes so Terraform stops proposing to revert them
Marking the listener output as sensitive so drift is hidden
Running terraform state push after every external change
Deleting the listener from state every morning before planning
explain: ignore_changes tells Terraform to accept out-of-band values for listed attributes instead of fighting the external system on every plan. Repeated state surgery or hiding outputs does not create a stable, reviewed acceptance of that drift.

q: While debugging a configuration, an engineer evaluates `index(["ap-northeast-1", "ap-south-1", "eu-central-1"], "eu-central-1")` in the console. What does Terraform return?
explain: index() returns the zero-based position of the value: "eu-central-1" is the third element, index 2.

q: A provider was forked and the team must switch state records from the old provider address to a new provider address without recreating resources. Which command is built for this?
options: terraform state replace-provider
terraform init -replace-provider
terraform providers replace -state
terraform state mv -provider
explain: terraform state replace-provider rewrites the provider address recorded for resources in state, which is needed after a provider move or fork. It changes bookkeeping, not the real resources, and is distinct from state mv for resource addresses.

Migration centralizes state in the workspace with managed locking and a visible, attributable run history, and remote execution moves plan and apply work off laptops onto HCP Terraform infrastructure. State is never again merged by hand from private copies, and remote runs record the initiating user rather than being anonymous.
options: Teammates can no longer see who ran an apply, because remote runs are anonymous by design
Plans and applies execute remotely in HCP Terraform while the local CLI only sends the configuration and streams the output back
Each engineer keeps a private copy of the state file and merges conflicts by hand at the end of the week
State is stored and locked in the workspace, and the team gains a shared run history instead of a state file on one laptop
q: A four-person team moves from local state and laptop runs to HCP Terraform with remote execution. Which two changes describe their new working reality after migration? (Choose two.)
A developer finds a registry module and wants to know the exact inputs it accepts before calling it. Where does the registry surface that information?
options: On the module's registry page, which renders the module's README plus its inputs, outputs, and resources from its repository
In the .terraform.lock.hcl file once the module is pinned
Nowhere; inputs can only be learned by reading the source code after init
Only inside the provider's own documentation site
explain: Each registry module page documents inputs, outputs, dependencies, and resources generated from the published repository, alongside usage examples. The lock file (D) records providers, not module interfaces, and the information is available before downloading anything, ruling out C.

q: A CI job fails builds on unformatted files but the logs are cluttered with long file lists, and the team wants only the pass or fail signal from fmt. Which invocation keeps the formatting gate while suppressing the list of file names?
options: terraform fmt -check -list=false
terraform fmt -write=false -recursive
terraform fmt -diff -list=true
terraform fmt -check -get=false
explain: Adding -list=false to -check keeps the non-zero exit behavior while stopping fmt from printing each offending file name, which is the quiet-gate pattern. -write=false with -recursive (B) never fails a build on formatting, -diff with -list=true (C) increases output instead of reducing it, and -get=false (D) is an init flag that fmt does not accept.

q: A CI script runs terraform validate under set -e and treats its exit status as the pipeline gate. The pull request contains an invalid configuration. What behavior should the pipeline author expect?
options: Validate exits zero but writes the errors into the state file for plan to find later
Validate prompts interactively for corrections, hanging the job until timeout
Validate prints diagnostics describing the problems and exits with a non-zero status, which fails the step and stops the pipeline
Validate prints warnings but always exits zero, so the gate must parse its text output
explain: An invalid configuration makes validate exit non-zero with diagnostics, which is exactly what shell gates and CI steps rely on. It does not always exit zero (A), never writes findings into state (C), and is a non-interactive check that reports rather than asks for fixes (B).

q: An engineer tests an expression in terraform console: `formatdate("DD MMM YYYY", "2026-10-23T12:00:00Z")`. What value does it produce?
options: 23 Oct 26
explain: formatdate() renders the timestamp with the given specifiers: DD is the day, MMM the abbreviated month name, and YYYY the four-digit year.

q: What is the exact name of the dependency lock file Terraform maintains for provider selections?
options: terraform.lock, stored next to the terraform binary
.terraform/providers.lock, stored inside the backend
providers.lock.json, stored inside the state file
.terraform.lock.hcl, stored in the root of the configuration
explain: The dependency lock file is .terraform.lock.hcl in the configuration root, written by init. The other names are invented; state files and backends hold infrastructure data, not the provider version and hash record.

q: While reviewing a pull request, you spot a resource argument spelled instnace_type, which no provider defines. Which command will flag this misspelled argument against the provider's schema without calling any cloud API?
options: terraform validate
terraform fmt -diff
terraform output, which lists every argument a resource accepts
terraform plan -refresh=false run offline, which never checks argument names
explain: Validate checks argument names and value types against the installed provider schemas, entirely locally, so a misspelled argument fails fast. fmt (B) only restyles whitespace and never inspects argument validity, plan is unnecessary and heavier for this check (C), and output (D) reads state values rather than auditing configuration.

q: A module outputs the value of `lookup({ dev = "t3.micro", staging = "t3.small", prod = "m5.large", qa = "t3.medium" }, "staging")`. What does Terraform return?
options: t3.medium
t3.small
m5.large
t3.micro
explain: lookup() returns the value stored under the key "staging", which is "t3.small". Without a third argument, lookup() would error if the key were absent.

q: An engineer tests an expression in terraform console: `flatten([["a", "b"], ["c"], ["d", "e"]])`. What is displayed?
explain: flatten() takes nested lists and produces one flat list with every element in order.

q: After editing the backend block to point at a different bucket, an engineer runs terraform plan without re-initializing and gets an error telling them to run init. Why?
options: Plan cannot run more than once after a backend was first configured
The new bucket must be created by an apply before plan can read it
Backend changes require re-initialization so Terraform can set up the new backend and, if chosen, migrate state to it
Editing any .tf file always requires a full destroy first
explain: Init is what configures the backend; changing the backend block makes the recorded backend configuration stale until init runs again. During that init Terraform can migrate or reconfigure, rather than silently using the old location during plan.

q: A directory contains main.tf, terraform.tfvars, terraform.tfstate, and .terraform.lock.hcl. A developer runs terraform fmt there. Which files are candidates for reformatting?
options: All four files, because fmt normalizes every file Terraform produces
main.tf and terraform.tfvars, because fmt formats configuration files and variable definition files, while state and the lock file are not source files it rewrites
Only terraform.tfvars, because .tf files are formatted by validate instead
Only main.tf, because fmt ignores variable definition files
explain: Fmt's scope is authored source: .tf configuration files and .tfvars variable files (including their JSON variants). State (terraform.tfstate) is generated data and the lock file is init's record; fmt rewrites neither, so C overstates its reach, A wrongly excludes tfvars, and D swaps fmt's and validate's jobs.

q: A team changes its backend block from local to an S3 backend, but the existing local state describes an environment they intend to abandon and rebuild, so the state must NOT be copied into S3. When init notices the backend change, which flag gives them a clean start against the new backend?
options: -reconfigure, because it reinitializes the backend from the new configuration and disregards the previously saved backend setup without copying state
-migrate-state, because it moves state wherever the backend points
-get=false, because abandoned state is treated as an undownloaded module
-upgrade, because a new backend requires new provider versions
explain: -reconfigure reinitializes the working directory against the new backend configuration and ignores the old one, without migrating state, which matches the abandon-and-rebuild intent. -migrate-state (A) is the exact opposite choice: it copies existing state into the new backend. -get=false (C) and -upgrade (D) address modules and versions, not backend reinitialization.

q: A module block declares `source = "git::https://example.com/vpc.git"` and `version = "1.2.0"`. What will `terraform init` do?
options: Fail — the `version` argument is only valid for registry sources; Git modules are pinned with `?ref=` instead
Install version 1.2.0 of the module from Git
Convert the Git URL into a registry address automatically
Ignore the version and install the latest commit
explain: EXAM TRAP: version is registry-only. On Git sources it is invalid — pin with `source = "git::https://example.com/vpc.git?ref=v1.2.0"`. A assumes version works everywhere. C and D invent lenient behaviors; init errors on the invalid argument.

q: Which backend is Terraform using when a configuration contains no backend block at all?
options: The http backend
The remote backend
The local backend
No backend, so state is kept only in memory during the run
explain: Omitting the backend block selects the default local backend, which stores state in terraform.tfstate in the working directory. State is not memory-only, and remote or http backends must be explicitly configured.

q: A security review finds a module sourced as git::https://example.com/platform.git?ref=main. Why will auditors flag this for a production root module?
options: Because ref=main floats: every init can fetch a different commit as main advances, making builds non-reproducible and letting unreviewed code enter production; pinning to a tag or full commit SHA fixes it
Because the git:: prefix disables provider locking
Because branch names longer than three characters are invalid refs
Because HTTPS Git sources are forbidden in production
explain: Pinning to a moving branch defeats reproducibility and change control; tags and especially commit SHAs are immutable references. HTTPS Git sources are legitimate (B), provider locking is independent of module sourcing (C), and ref names have no such length rule (D).

q: Resources for regional caches use for_each with string keys, and the eu cache already exists with ID cache-991. Which import target correctly adopts it?
options: aws_instance.cache[1], using the position of eu in the variable list
aws_instance.cache.eu, using dot notation for the key
aws_instance.cache, because for_each keys are ignored during import
aws_instance.cache["eu"], using the quoted string key in the instance address
explain: for_each instances are addressed by their key, and string keys appear in brackets with quotes, so the eu instance is aws_instance.cache["eu"]. Numeric indexes belong to count, dot notation is not instance addressing, and dropping the key would target an address that does not exist.

q: A module author wants callers to supply a subnet ID explicitly instead of the module looking one up. Which mechanism matches that intent, and what does it say about data sources?
options: A local, because locals accept caller overrides
An input variable, because the author deliberately chose caller-supplied values over an internal data lookup
An output, because outputs are the module's inputs
A data source, because data sources are how callers pass values in
explain: Passing values in is the job of input variables; a data source is an internal lookup the module performs itself, not a caller interface. Outputs move data out of a module, not in (C), and locals cannot be overridden by callers at all (A).

q: An author documents a variable with a clear description, gives it a type, but no default, and the module's README lists it as required. A caller who supplies the value in module arguments succeeds. What made the caller's assignment possible?
options: Callers can assign locals the same way, so the mechanism is identical
The description argument unlocks caller assignment
The type argument converts the variable into an output
The module block can set any declared variable of the child as an argument, which is how callers supply required inputs
explain: Passing values into a module means setting its declared variables as arguments in the module block; required variables are simply the ones with no default to fall back on. Description (B) and type (C) do not create that channel, and locals explicitly cannot be assigned by callers at all (D).

q: A variable named enable_logging has 'type = bool'. Which assignments are valid for it? (Choose two.)
options: true, assigned in a tfvars file
false, assigned with -var="enable_logging=false"
"yes", assigned in a tfvars file, because any non-empty string counts as true
1, because bool accepts all numbers as truthy
explain: A bool variable accepts true and false, whether they arrive from a tfvars file or a -var flag. Terraform's bool type does not treat an arbitrary string such as yes or the number 1 as a boolean; the assigned value must actually be true or false.

q: A team restructures code by moving aws_instance.web from the root module into module.compute, keeping the same server. They run terraform state mv aws_instance.web module.compute.aws_instance.web. What happens to the server?
options: Nothing in the real world; only its address in state changes to match the new module location
The server is imported fresh and its old state entry remains as a duplicate
The server is terminated and a replacement is launched inside the module
The module code is rewritten automatically to match the old address
explain: state mv renames an address in state, including moving resources into or between modules, without touching the real object. If the configuration address matches the new state address, the next plan shows no recreation.

q: What is the primary purpose of the Terraform state file?
options: To store a backup copy of your .tf configuration files
To cache provider plugins for faster initialization
To map resource addresses in configuration to real-world objects and track metadata
To log every API call made during apply for auditing
explain: State is the mapping between config and reality plus dependency metadata — that's what makes plan diffs possible. A is wrong (configs live in .tf files). B is wrong; state is not an audit log. C describes .terraform/, not state.

q: An engineer switches to a Git branch whose configuration declares a different backend than the branch they were just working on, then immediately runs terraform plan in the same working directory and hits a backend initialization error. What must happen first?
options: Run terraform fmt -recursive to realign the branch with the backend
The branch must be renamed to match the backend name
Delete terraform.tfstate so plan stops noticing the mismatch
Re-run terraform init, because the working directory's initialized backend no longer matches the configuration on this branch and init is what reconfigures it
explain: Initialization is per working directory and per configuration: when the backend declaration changes, including by switching branches, init must run again to set up the working directory for the new backend. Renaming branches (A) is irrelevant, deleting state (C) destroys tracking without fixing initialization, and fmt (D) never touches backend setup.

q: A company is moving from manual builds to Terraform. Which two changes should leadership expect in how the team works? (Choose two.)
options: Environments will be describable and rebuildable from the repository
Engineers will stop needing a process for approving production changes
All infrastructure decisions will be made by the cloud provider automatically
Infrastructure changes will be proposed and reviewed as code changes
explain: The working shift is toward code review for infrastructure and rebuildable, repository-defined environments. Providers do not make architecture decisions, and approval processes become more structured through review, not unnecessary.

q: A child module declares an output named vpc_id. How does the parent configuration reference that value?
options: As data.module.vpc_id
As aws_vpc.main.id, because module outputs are inlined into the parent namespace
As module.<module_name>.vpc_id, using the module block's name and the child's output name
As var.vpc_id in the parent, automatically
explain: Values leave a child module only through its outputs, addressed from the caller as module.<name>.<output>. The child's internal resource addresses are not visible to the parent (B), outputs do not become parent variables (C), and there is no data.module address form (D).

q: During a code review, a teammate asks what `lookup({ dev = "t3.micro", staging = "t3.small", prod = "m5.large", qa = "t3.medium" }, "prod")` evaluates to. What value does it produce?
options: t3.micro
m5.large
t3.small
t3.medium
explain: lookup() returns the value stored under the key "prod", which is "m5.large". Without a third argument, lookup() would error if the key were absent.

q: Which phrase best completes this definition: Infrastructure as Code treats infrastructure definitions the same way teams treat application code, meaning they are stored, versioned, and reviewed in what?
options: A version control system such as Git
A cloud provider billing dashboard
A ticketing system with manual approval comments
A local folder on one engineer's laptop
explain: IaC borrows software practices, so definitions live in version control where history, branching, and review are possible. Tickets, billing views, and a single laptop folder provide none of that shared, auditable history.

q: Which statement about refresh during a normal terraform plan is correct?
options: Plan never refreshes; only the deprecated terraform refresh command does
Refresh happens only during apply, never during plan
Refresh rewrites the configuration files to match the console
By default plan refreshes state from real infrastructure before computing the diff, unless refresh is disabled
explain: Modern Terraform refreshes as the first phase of plan (and apply) so the diff is against reality. The standalone refresh command is the older, deprecated way, and refresh updates state records, not .tf configuration files.

q: A `check` block asserting `aws_s3_bucket.logs` has versioning enabled starts failing after someone disables versioning in the console. What happens on the next `terraform plan`?
options: The check block is deleted from the configuration
Terraform emits a warning but the plan and apply continue normally — check blocks never fail runs
Terraform automatically re-enables versioning
The plan fails with an error and cannot proceed
explain: Check blocks are non-blocking health assertions: failures warn, never fail. That distinguishes them from preconditions/postconditions, which do fail runs. A describes precondition behavior. C and D invent automatic remediation.

q: While debugging a configuration, an engineer evaluates `split(",", "api,batch,web")` in the console. What is the result?
options: ["api,batch,web"]
"api,batch,web"
["api", "batch", "web"]
["api", "batch", "web", ""]
explain: split() divides the string at each comma and returns a list of the three resulting names.

q: What does convergence mean when discussing Terraform's behavior over multiple runs?
options: Repeated runs move actual infrastructure toward the declared state until no further changes are needed
Terraform converts all resources to a single cloud region over time
Runs converge on the cheapest possible configuration automatically
Each run adds a small random variation to keep infrastructure diverse
explain: Convergence is the process by which repeated applies bring reality in line with the declaration and then stop changing anything. It does not introduce variation, force a region, or optimize cost on its own.

q: An engineer tries to import a data source lookup for an existing AMI so Terraform will manage the image going forward. Why will this not work?
options: The AMI must first be destroyed before it can be imported
Data sources can only be imported on weekends when the registry allows it
Terraform imports data sources only through the console, never the CLI or blocks
Data sources are read-only lookups that are never managed or stored as managed resources, so there is nothing to import into
explain: Import applies to managed resources whose lifecycle Terraform controls; a data source merely reads an external object at plan time and owns nothing. Timing, prior destruction, and console-only rules are invented and miss the managed-versus-read distinction the exam tests.

q: An engineer tries terraform apply release.plan -var="image_id=ami-123" to swap one value at the last minute. What does Terraform do?
options: It ignores the -var flag silently and applies the original plan
It errors, because variable values cannot be overridden when applying a saved plan file; a new plan must be created for different values
It converts the saved plan into an interactive apply with the new value
It applies the saved plan but substitutes the new image ID
explain: A saved plan is a fixed artifact: apply of a plan file rejects -var and -var-file overrides because the decisions were already made at plan time. To change any value, the team must generate and review a new plan rather than patching the old one.

q: A company organizes its HCP Terraform estate so the payments project contains six workspaces, the identity project contains four, and project membership controls which teams can even see each group. What problem does this project structure primarily solve?
options: It reduces the number of state files the organization must store
It groups related workspaces for organization and team access, creating a clear governance boundary around each product area
It removes the need for workspace-level permissions anywhere in the organization
It allows all ten workspaces to share a single state file safely
explain: Projects group related workspaces so access and governance can be managed at a product or team boundary. They do not reduce state count, never merge states, and complement rather than replace workspace-level permissions.

q: An output references 'aws_lb.main.dns_name'. During a later plan where nothing about the load balancer changes, what value does the output show?
options: A newly generated DNS name each run
Unknown, because outputs are recomputed from scratch every run and never stored
An error, because outputs may only reference variables
The DNS name recorded in state from the existing load balancer, because outputs are evaluated from known attribute values
explain: For existing infrastructure, attribute values are known from state and refresh, so dependent outputs evaluate to the recorded value. Outputs are stored in state rather than never stored (A), provider DNS names are stable rather than regenerated (C), and outputs commonly reference resource attributes (D).

q: During 'terraform plan', the output shows a data source result changing even though the configuration did not change. What is the most likely explanation?
options: Data sources are only read once, at init time
Terraform randomly regenerates data source values on each plan
Data sources are re-read on refresh/plan, so if the underlying existing infrastructure changed, the returned attributes change with it
Data source results are cached forever, so this indicates state corruption
explain: A data read happens during refresh and plan, so its result reflects the current real-world object; a changed external object yields a changed result. That rules out permanent caching (A and D) and random regeneration (B), neither of which describes how reads work.

q: (Choose TWO) A team wants builds to be reproducible: the same commit must always use the same provider and module versions. Which two practices together achieve this?
options: Delete the .terraform directory before each run ANSWER: A and B EXPL: Version constraints bound what can be selected; the lock file records exactly what was selected so every run is identical. C does the opposite — it upgrades. D only clears the plugin cache; it doesn't pin anything. Q16. A database password must be passed to a provider during apply but must never be written to the state file. Which Terraform 1.10+ feature addresses this? A. Marking the variable sensitive = true B. Storing the password in terraform.tfvars with restricted file permissions C. Ephemeral resources and write-only attributes, whose values are never persisted to state D. Using terraform state push to overwrite the state after apply
Run terraform init -upgrade on every build
Pin provider and module versions with constraints like ~> 5.0
Commit the .terraform.lock.hcl file to version control
explain: Ephemeral values exist only during the run and are never written to state or plans. A only redacts CLI display — the value still lands in state plaintext, the exam's favorite trap. B still ends up in state. D is dangerous and unrelated.

q: A junior engineer tries to set the AWS provider version by writing version = "5.0.0" inside a provider "aws" block. Why does modern Terraform reject this?
options: Provider blocks reject all arguments except region
Provider versions belong in required_providers in the terraform block; the version argument inside provider configuration blocks was removed
The version must be written in terraform.tfvars instead
Version arguments are only allowed in aliased provider blocks
explain: Since Terraform 0.13, version selection is centralized in required_providers so requirements are declared once per provider; the legacy in-block version argument is an error. It is not an alias-only feature, tfvars assign variables, and provider blocks accept many configuration arguments.

q: A provider constraint reads version = ">= 5.0, < 6.0, != 5.4.0". Which two offered versions satisfy every part of it? (Choose two.)
explain: Versions 5.3.9 and 5.9.1 both clear the 5.0 floor, stay below the 6.0 ceiling, and are not the excluded build. Version 5.4.0 is removed by the != clause and 6.0.0 breaches the strict < 6.0 ceiling, so neither can ever be selected under this constraint.

q: Which outcome is the textbook example of idempotency in Terraform?
options: Running apply creates resources faster the second time because of caching
Running destroy removes only resources that have drifted from configuration
Running plan deletes and recreates every resource to keep it fresh
Running apply once creates resources and running it again with unchanged configuration proposes no changes
explain: Idempotency, or convergence, means repeated application of the same configuration settles on the same result with no further changes. Faster caching is not the definition, and recreating everything on each run would be the opposite of convergence.

Init can only select from versions its installation sources actually offer, and none on the mirror satisfies >= 5.50, so the constraint and the available supply must be reconciled. Deleting the lock file (the main distractor) never makes an out-of-range version satisfy a constraint; it only removes pinning.
options: Terraform Core is too old; upgrading the terraform binary adds newer provider versions to the mirror
The provider binary is damaged; re-running init repeatedly will eventually download a 5.50 build from the 5.40 mirror
The lock file checksum is corrupt; delete .terraform.lock.hcl and init will accept version 5.40 against a >= 5.50 constraint
No source Terraform can reach offers a version satisfying the constraint; either publish a matching version to the mirror or deliberately relax the constraint, then re-run init
q: terraform init fails with an error that no suitable version is available for a provider. The configuration requires that provider at version >= 5.50, but the internal mirror the team installs from only carries versions up to 5.40. What is the correct diagnosis and fix?
Two teams, networking and applications, both need to propose changes to a shared environment without overwriting each other's work. How does IaC help most?
options: Both teams work in the same repository with branches and pull requests, reviewing each other's changes before merge
Each team keeps its own private copy of the configuration with no merging
The environment is rebuilt from memory whenever the teams disagree
One team is given exclusive console access and the other submits requests by email
explain: Shared version-controlled code with branching and review is the collaborative model IaC enables. Console exclusivity, rebuilding from memory, and unmerged private copies all recreate silos and conflicts instead of resolving them.

q: A startup runs production on AWS, analytics on GCP, and DNS through Cloudflare. The platform team is tired of maintaining three different native toolchains (CloudFormation, Deployment Manager, and API scripts). Which Terraform characteristic directly solves their problem?
options: Terraform automatically converts CloudFormation templates into working HCL
Terraform is free, while native tools charge per deployment
Terraform's provider-agnostic workflow: one language, one CLI, and one plan/apply loop across all providers
Terraform provisions infrastructure faster than any native tool
explain: Terraform's strategic pitch — and a 004 objective — is the provider-agnostic, multi-cloud workflow: one HCL language and one workflow across hundreds of providers. A is an unprovable speed claim the exam never makes. C is false (native tools are generally free; clouds charge for resources). D is false; Terraform does not translate CloudFormation.

q: A plan finishes with: Plan: 5 to add, 4 to change, 2 to destroy. When the engineer runs terraform apply and confirms, how many brand-new resources will exist afterwards that did not exist before?
explain: Only the 5 "to add" entries create new resources. In-place changes modify existing resources, and destructions remove resources rather than creating them.

q: The platform team runs terraform plan and the output ends with: Plan: 4 to add, 1 to change, 3 to destroy. How many resource actions will terraform apply perform in total?
explain: Every planned action runs at apply: 4 additions + 1 updates + 3 destructions = 8 actions. Counting only two of the three categories understates the work apply will do.

q: Two sibling child modules both need the same database password value that only exists in the root configuration. How does each child receive it?
options: The root passes the value as an argument in each module block, into an input variable each child declares
The children share values automatically because they sit in the same configuration
Both children read the root variable directly by name
One child outputs it and the other reads it through the root variable namespace
explain: Values move between modules only through explicit channels: the root passes arguments into each child's declared inputs. Children cannot reach root variables directly (A), siblings share nothing implicitly (C), and sibling-to-sibling flows must go through the root's wiring (B describes the mechanism backwards).

q: During a code review, a teammate asks what `reverse(["cache", "db", "proxy"])` evaluates to. What does Terraform return?
options: ["db", "proxy", "cache"]
["cache", "db", "proxy"]
["proxy", "db", "cache"]
["proxy", "cache", "db"]
explain: reverse() returns the list with the elements in the opposite order; it does not sort them.

q: Which statements about sensitive values in variables and outputs are true? (Choose two.)
options: Marking a value sensitive encrypts it inside the state file
A variable marked sensitive has its value redacted from Terraform's normal CLI plan and apply output
Marking a variable sensitive prevents Terraform from sending the value to the provider
An output marked sensitive hides its value in normal display, so revealing it is a deliberate act by someone with state access
explain: Sensitivity is a display and handling control: values are redacted from CLI output and must be revealed deliberately, but they still live in state in plain form and are still sent to providers that need them. That is why encryption claims and provider-blocking claims are both wrong, and why state access must be controlled separately.

q: An enterprise evaluates Terraform Enterprise over HCP Terraform specifically for centralized identity and deeper compliance evidence. Which capabilities are characteristic reasons organizations choose the self-hosted offering?
options: A completely different configuration language that replaces HCL
Built-in video conferencing for run approvals and automatic code generation
Removal of workspaces in favor of managing state on each administrator's laptop
Enterprise additions such as SAML SSO integration and detailed audit logging, on top of the same workflow model as HCP Terraform
explain: Terraform Enterprise keeps the HCP Terraform workflow model and adds enterprise controls, notably SAML-based SSO and richer audit logging, for organizations that need them in a self-hosted deployment. It does not change the language, remove workspaces, or add unrelated collaboration gimmicks.

q: A registry module's page lists a Inputs table showing a variable named azs with type list(string) and no default. What does a caller know from that?
options: azs is a required input: the module block must supply a list of strings for it or the run errors
azs is an output the module produces
azs is optional and will default to an empty list
azs can only be set through an environment variable
explain: A listed input with no default is required, and its documented type tells the caller what shape to pass. It is not optional (A), inputs are distinct from the outputs section (C), and module inputs are supplied as module block arguments, not environment variables (B).

q: A configuration references 'aws_s3_bucket.logs.arn' in three different resources. What is true about those references? (Choose two.)
options: All three resources will receive the same ARN value once the bucket exists
Each referencing resource gains an implicit dependency on the bucket
Each reference causes Terraform to plan a separate replacement bucket
Terraform requires depends_on to be added manually in all three resources
explain: A shared reference gives every referrer the same attribute value and its own implicit dependency edge to the bucket. References never duplicate the referenced object, and implicit dependencies make manual depends_on unnecessary for reference-based ordering.

q: A module block for a registry module omits the version argument entirely. What does terraform init install?
options: The latest available version of the module at the time init runs
Init fails; version is required for registry modules
The oldest stable version, for safety
Whatever version is recorded in the provider lock file
explain: The version argument is optional for registry modules, and omitting it selects the newest release, which is convenient but makes builds non-reproducible. Init does not fail (A), never prefers the oldest release (B), and the lock file (D) pins providers, not modules.

q: Two engineers run terraform apply at the same time from their laptops against the default backend, and the state file ends up corrupted. What is the root cause and fix?
options: Root cause: apply is not thread-safe; fix: run applies sequentially by team policy
Root cause: provider version mismatch; fix: pin provider versions
Root cause: the local backend provides no state locking; fix: use a remote backend with locking
Root cause: missing lock file; fix: commit .terraform.lock.hcl
explain: Locking is a backend feature and the default local backend doesn't lock — concurrent writes corrupt state. A is a workaround, not the fix the exam wants. C confuses the dependency lock file (provider versions) with state locking. D is unrelated.

terraform output and terraform state show only read recorded state and display values, so they cannot alter infrastructure or state during the window. State mv rewrites state addresses and apply -replace destroys and recreates a resource, so both are state-changing and need change approval.
options: terraform state show for a resource address, which displays its recorded attributes
terraform apply -replace, which recreates a named resource
terraform state mv, which renames an address in state
terraform output, which reads output values recorded in state
q: During a tightly controlled maintenance window, an operator may run only read-only diagnostics. Which two commands qualify as read-only? (Choose two.)
A platform team groups its dev, staging, and prod workspaces under a `payments-team` container with shared governance boundaries. What is this container in HCP Terraform?
options: A run trigger
A project — it organizes related workspaces with shared governance (variable sets, permissions) boundaries
A policy set
An organization — teams cannot subdivide an organization
explain: Projects group related workspaces and set governance boundaries: who can see and change which environments. B chains runs. C enforces policy. D is wrong — organizations absolutely subdivide into projects and teams.

q: Which two statements describe an errored terraform apply correctly? (Choose two.)
options: Resources that were successfully created or updated before the error are recorded in state and will not be recreated on the next run
The operator should fix the underlying problem and run plan or apply again to converge on the full configuration
An errored apply corrupts the state file so it must be restored from backup before any further work
Terraform automatically destroys everything it created during the failed run to restore the prior state
explain: Errored applies are resumable by design: completed work is in state, and re-running after a fix converges the rest. Terraform performs no automatic rollback destruction, and a normal provider error does not corrupt state or force a restore.

q: Which practice best describes using outputs in an automated pipeline that provisions a network and then configures servers in a second step?
options: The first configuration emails its outputs to the second step
The first configuration exposes needed IDs and addresses as outputs, and the pipeline reads them with terraform output -json to feed the second step
Outputs are ignored because pipelines cannot read them
The second step guesses resource IDs from naming conventions in screenshots of the apply output
explain: Outputs are the designed hand-off surface between a Terraform run and anything downstream, and -json makes them machine-consumable. Guessing IDs (B) discards that contract, pipelines read outputs routinely (C is false), and Terraform has no email hand-off (D).

q: A company publishes internal modules to its HCP Terraform private registry. What does a module source address for the private registry look like?
options: `terraform-aws-modules/vpc/aws` — private modules use the same address as public ones
Private registry modules cannot be sourced; they must be copied locally Domain 6: Terraform State Management — 11 questions
`app.terraform.io/my-org/vpc/aws` — the organization's hostname, org name, module name, and provider
`github.com/my-org/vpc` — the private registry is just a GitHub alias
explain: Private registry addresses include the hostname and organization: app.terraform.io///. B is the public registry form. C is a Git source, a different mechanism. D is false — the private registry exists precisely for governed sharing.

q: An organization standardizes on Terraform specifically so a acquisition's Azure estate and its own AWS estate can be run by one platform team. Which objective does this standardization serve?
options: Forcing both estates onto a single cloud within a year
One provider-agnostic workflow, language, and skill set across multiple clouds
Eliminating the need for cloud-specific provider configuration entirely
Making CloudFormation and ARM templates interoperable
explain: The point of standardizing on Terraform after an acquisition is operational unification: one workflow and skill set across clouds. It does not force a cloud migration, provider configuration remains cloud-specific in details, and native template formats do not become interoperable.

q: A terraform.tfvars file in the project has inconsistent spacing and misaligned equals signs, and a teammate claims fmt only cares about .tf files so the tfvars file must be cleaned by hand. Is the claim correct?
options: No, fmt also formats .tfvars variable definition files when run in the directory, normalizing their spacing and alignment like any configuration file
No, but only because validate reformats tfvars files during validation
Yes, because tfvars files are considered state and are therefore read-only to fmt
Yes, fmt's scope is .tf files only, and tfvars files are never touched
explain: The claim is wrong: fmt formats variable definition files (.tfvars and .tfvars.json) as well as .tf files, since both are authored source. A restates the misconception, C misclassifies tfvars as state, and D credits validate with a formatting role it does not have; validate checks correctness and rewrites nothing.

q: A support engineer needs provider TRACE logs for one failing apply, but the runner's combined log is hundreds of megabytes and the relevant lines cannot be found afterward. Which combined setup would have prevented both problems?
options: Set TF_LOG_PROVIDER=TRACE with TF_LOG_PATH to a dedicated file for that run, then disable verbose logging once the case is captured
Leave TF_LOG=TRACE on permanently so the failing run is guaranteed to be included somewhere
Set TF_LOG=INFO globally, which captures the same detail as provider TRACE
Pipe all output to the state file where it can be searched later
explain: Scoping TRACE to the provider component, persisting it to a named file, and turning it off after the incident keeps the evidence complete but bounded and searchable. Permanent TRACE guarantees the volume problem, logs never belong inside state, and INFO omits the detailed provider exchanges support asked for.

q: A configuration contains the expression `cidrsubnet("10.0.0.0/16", 8, 255)`. What is the result?
explain: cidrsubnet() adds 8 bits and picks subnet number 255: starting from 10.0.0.0/16, subnet 255 of the /24 series is 10.0.255.0/24.

q: A variable is declared as 'variable "admin_cidr" { type = string }' with no default, and no value is supplied by any file, environment variable, or flag. What happens when the team runs terraform plan?
options: Terraform skips every resource that uses the variable
Terraform errors (or prompts interactively) asking for a value, because a variable with no default is required and has no value
Terraform generates a random CIDR block
Terraform uses an empty string automatically
explain: A variable without a default is a required input: with no value from any source, Terraform prompts in interactive runs and errors in non-interactive runs. It never invents an empty or random value (A and B), and it does not silently skip dependent resources (C).

q: A database must leave Terraform management during a handover to another team, but must not be interrupted. The handover uses configuration, not CLI state edits. Which construct fits?
options: A terraform state push of an empty state file
A lifecycle prevent_destroy block left in place after deleting the resource
A removed block for the database address with lifecycle destroy = false
A moved block pointing the database to a null resource
explain: As a declarative handover, removed with destroy = false tells Terraform to drop the database from state while leaving it running for the next team. prevent_destroy would block a destroy plan rather than complete a clean unmanaged handover.

q: Which of these are recognized ways to assign a value to a declared input variable for a run? (Choose two.)
options: Passing it with a -var flag on the terraform plan or apply command line
Redefining a local value with the same name inside a locals block
Assigning it in a terraform.tfvars file in the working directory
Adding the value to an output block with a matching name
explain: Variable values arrive through input channels: auto-loaded tfvars files and command-line -var assignments are both standard sources. A locals block defines internal values under the local. namespace and cannot assign a variable, and an output publishes a result rather than accepting an input.

q: An engineer runs terraform plan -target=aws_instance.web to preview a fix for one broken server in a 200-resource workspace. What caveat must the team accept about this approach?
options: Targeting limits the plan to the specified resource and its dependencies, so the resulting plan may be incomplete and is intended for exceptional recovery situations, not routine workflow
Targeting is the recommended way to deploy changes one resource at a time in production
Targeting permanently removes all other resources from state
Targeting requires the workspace to be destroyed first
explain: -target is an escape hatch for exceptional cases such as recovering from errors: it plans only the target and what it depends on, so other pending changes are hidden and the plan is not a complete picture. It does not touch state by itself and HashiCorp advises against routine targeted applies.

q: An engineer tests an expression in terraform console: `substr("terraform", 0, 5)`. What is the result?
options: form
terra
terraform
terr
explain: substr() takes characters starting at offset 0 for a length of 5, giving "terra".

q: During a review, a manager asks why dev, staging, and prod keep drifting apart. The team adopts Terraform modules reused across all three. Which advantage are they mainly pursuing?
options: Consistency, because the same module produces the same pattern in every environment
Elimination of all variables between environments
Lower cloud list prices negotiated through Terraform
Automatic application debugging inside each environment
explain: Reusing the same module is a consistency play: environments differ only by explicit inputs, not by hand-built quirks. Terraform does not negotiate prices or debug applications, and variables remain necessary because environments legitimately differ in size and naming.

Environments of the same application share ownership and standards, so one project lets project-level variable sets and team access cover all three coherently while each workspace still isolates its own state and variables. Projects never merge state, never auto-promote applies between environments, and complement rather than replace workspace permissions.
options: A single state file shared safely by dev, stage, and prod
Automatic promotion of a successful dev apply into stage and then prod with no further runs
Exemption from workspace-level permissions, because projects replace them entirely
One shared governance and access boundary for the application, with project-scoped variable sets and team grants covering all three environments while each workspace keeps its own state
q: A company models one application as three workspaces named app-dev, app-stage, and app-prod, all inside a single project, instead of creating three separate projects. What does the single-project choice give them that three projects would fragment?
A module outputs the value of `upper("dev")`. What is displayed?
options: Dev
DEV
dev
ved
explain: upper() converts every cased character in the string to uppercase.

q: An engineer tests an expression in terraform console: `values({ "b-team" = "ops", "a-team" = "dev", "c-team" = "sec" })`. What is displayed?
options: ["dev", "ops", "sec"]
["sec", "ops", "dev"]
["a-team", "b-team", "c-team"]
["ops", "dev", "sec"]
explain: values() returns values in the order of the sorted keys (a-team, b-team, c-team), so the values come out as dev, ops, sec.

q: A CI job runs terraform init -backend-config=base.hcl -backend-config="key=eu/prod.tfstate", where base.hcl already sets bucket, region, and a default key. How are the two sources combined?
options: The key=value pair is written back into base.hcl for future runs
The values are merged, with the later -backend-config argument overriding the key from base.hcl while bucket and region from the file still apply
The file is ignored entirely whenever any key=value pair is also given
The command fails, because only one -backend-config may be passed to init
