IaC makes infrastructure consistent, reviewable, versioned, and automatically deployable — the configuration becomes executable documentation
IaC guarantees zero downtime during every deployment
explain: The exam's IaC advantages: consistency/idempotency, automation, version control, collaboration via review, and configuration-as-documentation. A is false (you still need provider accounts). C overpromises — IaC enables safer deploys but guarantees nothing. D invents a compliance mandate.

q: A module outputs the value of `upper("prod")`. What value does it produce?
options: dorp
Prod
prod
PROD
explain: upper() converts every cased character in the string to uppercase.

q: After a refactor, `terraform plan` wants to recreate a resource whose address changed in state but whose real-world object is fine. You prefer the CLI over a `moved` block. Which command fixes the state address?
options: `terraform refresh`
`terraform state mv ` — renames the resource in state without touching the real object
`terraform fmt`
`terraform state rm` followed by `terraform import`
explain: `state mv` is the CLI equivalent of a moved block: it renames within state, so the next plan shows no changes. B is a clumsy two-step that risks recreation. C is deprecated in favor of refresh-only and does not rename. D formats files — unrelated.

q: A repository's committed lock file pins the AWS provider to an exact 5.x build. A new hire initializes a fresh checkout without any special flags and is surprised the newest 5.x release was NOT installed. Why did init behave that way?
options: Init honors the existing lock file by default, installing exactly the recorded versions and verifying their checksums; only -upgrade re-resolves to newer selections
The Terraform Registry serves stale binaries to new machines for 24 hours
Provider downloads are disabled until the first apply completes
Init always installs the oldest provider version that satisfies the constraints
explain: By default init respects .terraform.lock.hcl, which is the reproducibility mechanism: every machine installs the pinned builds. Re-resolution to newer versions happens only with -upgrade. Init does not prefer the oldest versions (A), the registry is not time-delayed (C), and downloads are init's own job, long before any apply (D).

q: An engineer is explaining Terraform to a team that only knows imperative scripts. Which two contrasts are correct? (Choose two.)
options: Terraform requires scripts to run in alphabetical order
Terraform tracks state to know what already exists; a plain script typically does not
A script automatically converges when rerun after a partial failure
Terraform declares desired state; a script lists steps to execute
explain: Desired-state declaration and state tracking are the two defining contrasts with imperative scripts. Alphabetical ordering is invented, and plain scripts generally lack convergence, often duplicating work or failing when rerun after a partial failure.

q: A module author is preparing a v2.0.0 release. Which two changes justify the major version bump under semantic versioning? (Choose two.)
options: Renaming an existing output that callers reference
Adding a new optional input variable with a default value
Fixing a typo in the README
Removing an input variable that callers currently pass
explain: Breaking interface changes — renaming outputs or removing inputs — force callers to change their code, which is what a major bump signals. Adding an optional input (C) is backward compatible (a minor bump), and a README typo fix (D) is patch-level at most.

q: A team lead needs to change a workspace's execution mode, update its VCS connection, and delete an obsolete workspace entirely. Which workspace permission level does the lead need?
options: Any level, because workspace settings are controlled only by the VCS provider
Read, because settings are visible to all team members
Plan, because execution mode affects future plans
Admin, because workspace settings, connections, and deletion are administrative actions
explain: Admin is the workspace level that controls settings such as execution mode and VCS connection and permits destructive actions like deletion. Read and plan are progressively view and plan oriented, and the VCS provider controls the repository, not HCP Terraform workspace settings.

q: You clone a Terraform repository and run `terraform init`. Which of the following does init do? (Select the best answer.)
options: It creates all infrastructure defined in the configuration
It validates the configuration syntax without contacting any APIs
It downloads provider plugins into `.terraform/`, downloads modules, configures the backend, and writes the dependency lock file
It formats all `.tf` files to canonical HCL style
explain: init prepares the working directory: provider plugins into .terraform/, child modules into .terraform/modules/, backend setup, and the lock file. Creating infrastructure (A) is apply's job. Validation without APIs (C) is validate. Formatting (D) is fmt.

q: During a code review, a teammate asks what `contains(["eu-west-1", "eu-central-1", "ap-south-1"], "sa-east-1")` evaluates to. What is displayed?
options: error: value not found
true
null
false
explain: contains() returns true only when the exact value is an element of the list; "sa-east-1" is not in the list, and contains() returns false rather than erroring when it is absent.

q: During a code review, a teammate asks what `flatten([["a", "b"], ["c"], ["d", "e"]])` evaluates to. What is the result?
explain: flatten() takes nested lists and produces one flat list with every element in order.

q: An engineer runs `terraform login` on their laptop. What did this accomplish?
options: It initialized the backend for the current directory
It logged into the AWS console in the browser
It authenticated the Terraform CLI to HCP Terraform, storing a token for API access
It stored cloud provider credentials (AWS keys) for Terraform to use
explain: EXAM TRAP: `terraform login` authenticates the CLI to HCP Terraform (token in ~/.terraform.d/credentials.tfrc.json) — it has nothing to do with cloud provider credentials, which are a separate layer. A and C confuse the two auth layers. D is init's job.

q: Which two statements about the terraform_remote_state data source are accurate? (Choose two.)
options: It merges the two configurations into a single shared state file
It grants the consuming configuration write access to the source state
Consumers should preferably rely on the source configuration's published outputs rather than its internal resource attributes
It reads another configuration's state through that configuration's backend configuration
explain: terraform_remote_state is a read-only lookup of another configuration's state via its backend, and outputs are the stable interface consumers should depend on. It never writes to the source state and never merges two states into one.

q: A team notices that every manually built server gets slightly different logging agents depending on who built it. Which IaC practice eliminates this class of error?
options: Defining the server build once in code and applying that same definition for every server
Adding a post-build inspection meeting every week
Asking builders to be more careful and double-check their work
Rotating builders so each person builds fewer servers
explain: Codifying the build removes per-builder variance because the machine executes one definition every time. Exhortations, rotation, and inspection meetings may catch some errors but still rely on human consistency, which is the failure mode described.

q: A configuration calls the same networking module three times for three environments instead of copy-pasting its resources three times. Which benefit of modules is the team mainly using?
options: Encryption of variable values at rest
State locking across the three environments
Automatic provider version upgrades
Reuse — one maintained definition instantiated many times with different inputs
explain: Calling one module repeatedly with different inputs is reuse, the headline reason modules exist. State locking (A) is a backend feature, provider upgrades (C) come from init -upgrade, and modules do not encrypt values (D).

q: State bucket versioning is enabled, and a bad state push overwrites the current state. How does versioning help here?
options: Versioning locks state so pushes require two operators
Versioning prevents any push from ever overwriting state
Versioning automatically merges the bad push with the correct state
Earlier versions of the state object can be retrieved to recover the pre-push snapshot, because versioning retains prior object versions
explain: Versioning is a recovery aid: it keeps prior state object versions so a known-good snapshot can be restored after a bad overwrite. It does not block pushes or merge states, and restoring still requires care with serial and lineage.

q: A configuration needs its runs to execute in the organization's HCP Terraform `prod-network` workspace. Which block connects the configuration to it?
options: A `provider "hcp"` block with the workspace name
A `cloud` block with `organization = "my-org"` and `workspaces { name = "prod-network" }`
A `workspace "prod-network"` block at the root
A `backend "s3"` block pointing at the workspace name
explain: The cloud block (or equivalently backend "remote") links a configuration to an HCP Terraform organization and workspace. A points at S3, not HCP. C invents a provider-based link. D invents a block type.

q: A consultant hand-edited a state file to fix a corrupted attribute and now wants to upload it, knowing it will be rejected by the normal safety checks. Which command reflects that deliberate override?
options: terraform apply -force-state edited.tfstate
terraform state push -force edited.tfstate
terraform init -push-force edited.tfstate
terraform state pull -force edited.tfstate
explain: state push -force uploads a local state file while overriding serial/lineage protection. Pull downloads state, and the apply/init forms shown are not real flags for uploading a hand-edited state.

Source addresses are exact registry coordinates, and hashicorp/awss is a nonexistent provider, so init correctly finds nothing. The main distractor blames registry availability, but a healthy registry still has no provider at a mistyped address; only fixing the source string helps.
options: The version constraint is too strict; removing it lets Terraform guess the intended provider
The registry is temporarily down; retrying init will succeed once it recovers
The AWS provider was renamed upstream; the team must switch to a community fork
The source address points at a namespace/type that does not exist; correcting it to hashicorp/aws and re-running init resolves the real provider
q: After a copy-paste edit, required_providers contains source = "hashicorp/awss" for the AWS provider. terraform init now fails, reporting that the requested provider could not be found in any registry. What happened and what fixes it?
A root module reads a child module's output inside its own output block to show users the final load balancer DNS name. Which expression in the root output is valid?
options: value = module.alb.dns_name
value = module.alb.output.dns_name
value = output.alb.dns_name
value = aws_lb.main.dns_name, referencing the child's resource directly
explain: Root outputs commonly re-export child outputs, and the reference is module.<name>.<output>. The child's aws_lb resource is encapsulated and unreachable from the root (A), and outputs are not referenced through an output namespace (C) or a nested output attribute (B).

q: A configuration contains the expression `flatten([["a", "b"], ["c"], ["d", "e"]])`. What is displayed?
explain: flatten() takes nested lists and produces one flat list with every element in order.

q: Which two conditions must hold for a removed block with destroy = false to leave an object running unmanaged? (Choose two.)
options: The object must first be destroyed in the console so state can forget it
The removed block must name the resource's address in its from argument matching its state address
The backend must be the local backend for the lifecycle setting to work
The configuration must run on Terraform 1.7 or later so removed blocks are understood
explain: Removed blocks need a CLI that supports them (1.7+) and a from address that matches the state entry being forgotten. Destroying the object first defeats the preservation purpose, and the feature is not limited to the local backend.

q: A team is refactoring a 900-line flat root configuration into modules. What is the safest way to sequence the work?
options: Delete the state file first so the new module structure starts clean
Rename every resource to its final name before moving anything

Extract one cohesive group, such as networking, into a child module, wire the root to call it with the same values, and run terraform plan to confirm the move produces no unintended destroys before extracting the next group
Rewrite the entire configuration into modules in one change and apply it the same day
explain: Incremental extraction with a plan check after each group proves every step is behavior-preserving and isolates any addressing problem to the group just moved. A big-bang rewrite (A) makes failures impossible to localize, deleting state (B) orphans real infrastructure, and renaming resources first (C) adds a second disruptive change on top of the move.

q: A team wants the same Terraform workflow on AWS and Azure. Which native tool would NOT cover both clouds?
options: Terraform with the AWS and AzureRM providers
A single Terraform root module using aliased providers
HCP Terraform with workspaces for each cloud
CloudFormation, which manages AWS resources only
explain: CloudFormation is AWS-native and cannot provision Azure resources, which is why Terraform's multi-cloud workflow is the alternative. The other choices all describe Terraform itself, which works across providers with one workflow.

q: Someone terminates a Terraform-managed database instance directly in the provider console, and the resource block remains in configuration. What does the next plan show?
options: A create action to replace the missing instance, because refresh finds the object gone while configuration still declares it
An update action that repairs the terminated instance in place
A destroy action for an instance that no longer exists
No changes, because Terraform cannot detect deletions made outside its workflow
explain: When refresh discovers a state-tracked object has vanished, Terraform treats it as needing creation, so plan proposes recreating it from configuration. A terminated object cannot be updated in place, deletions are exactly what refresh detects, and there is nothing left to destroy.

q: What is a Terraform module, in the simplest terms?
options: A single provider plugin binary downloaded from the registry
A saved plan file that can be applied repeatedly
A container for multiple resources defined together in a set of .tf files, packaged so the group can be reused
A remote backend that stores state for a team
explain: A module is a directory of .tf files grouping related resources into one reusable unit. A provider plugin (B) is an executable that talks to an API, not a configuration package. Saved plans (C) and backends (D) are unrelated workflow pieces.

q: A plan shows an aws_launch_template resource marked -/+ . The engineer planned only a small edit and is surprised. What does -/+ tell the reviewer?
options: The resource is a data source that will be read twice
The resource will be destroyed and then recreated because a changed argument forces replacement
The resource will be updated in place with no downtime
The resource will be destroyed and never recreated
explain: -/+ means destroy and recreate: some attribute (such as an AMI or user data on certain resources) cannot change in place, so Terraform replaces the object. It is not an in-place update (~), not a pure destroy (-), and not a data read (<=).

q: What does a terraform_remote_state data source actually return access to?
options: The outputs (and, if relied upon, attributes) recorded in another configuration's state, read from that configuration's backend
A merged state file combining both configurations into one
A live SSH session into resources managed by the other configuration
Write access to modify the other configuration's state directly
explain: remote state is a read mechanism: the consuming configuration reads the other state's stored values, typically its root outputs, via the same backend type. It does not grant write access or merge the two states into one file.

q: A module outputs the value of `split(",", "batch,queue,proxy")`. What is the result?
options: ["batch", "queue", "proxy"]
["batch", "queue", "proxy", ""]
"batch,queue,proxy"
["batch,queue,proxy"]
explain: split() divides the string at each comma and returns a list of the three resulting names.

q: A company uses Ansible to install packages and harden operating systems on servers that Terraform creates. How should the division of labor be described?
options: Terraform and Ansible are interchangeable, so using both is redundant
Terraform provisions the infrastructure and Ansible handles configuration management inside the instances, a common complementary pairing
Ansible provisions the cloud networks and Terraform configures the packages
Only one tool may be used per environment by HashiCorp policy
explain: The classic pairing is provisioning with Terraform and configuration management with Ansible, Chef, or Puppet after instances exist. The tools overlap somewhat, but describing them as fully interchangeable or reversing their primary roles misses the exam distinction.

q: A data block and a resource block share the same type name in one configuration, such as data "aws_ami" and resource "aws_instance" patterns aside — what distinguishes their addresses?
options: The address is decided by whichever block appears first in the file
Data sources are addressed with the data. prefix (data.aws_ami.ubuntu) while managed resources use the bare type and name (aws_instance.web)
Nothing; the blocks are interchangeable
Resources are addressed with the data. prefix
explain: The data. prefix is part of a data source's address and is how expressions and the dependency graph tell a read from a managed object. The two block kinds are not interchangeable (A), the prefix belongs to data sources rather than resources (C), and file order does not define addressing (D).

q: A configuration contains the expression `parseint("ff", 16)`. What is displayed?
explain: parseint() interprets the string in the given base: ff in hexadecimal is 15×16 + 15 = 255.

q: A child VPC module declares `output "vpc_id"`. The root module needs that ID for an instance's `subnet_id`. How does the root access it?
options: As `data.module.vpc.vpc_id`
As `module.vpc.vpc_id` — child outputs are exposed on the module object in the calling configuration
As `vpc.vpc_id` directly, since outputs are global
Outputs cannot cross module boundaries; the value must be hardcoded
explain: Module outputs are addressed `module..` in the calling module — the standard data-out channel. B drops the required module. prefix. C invents a data. lookup. D denies the core module composition pattern.

q: An engineer tests an expression in terraform console: `format("%s-%s", "proxy", "dr")`. What is the result?
options: proxydr
%s-%s
dr-proxy
proxy-dr
explain: format() substitutes the arguments into the format string in order, so the first %s takes the first argument.

q: A consultant adds a cloud block naming an organization and a single workspace to a configuration that previously used local state, then runs terraform init. What does init do in response to the cloud block?
options: It uploads the configuration files so other users can edit them in a web editor
It converts the cloud block into an S3 backend block for future runs
It connects the working directory to that HCP Terraform workspace and offers to migrate the existing local state into it
It creates a new organization and a new cloud provider account with those names
explain: Adding a cloud block and re-running init reconfigures the backend to HCP Terraform and can migrate existing state into the named workspace. It does not create organizations or provider accounts, provide a web editor, or translate the block into a different backend type.

q: After reading 'data "aws_vpc" "main"', a configuration needs that VPC's CIDR block. Which expression retrieves it?
options: aws_vpc.main.cidr_block, the same form used for a managed resource
data.aws_vpc.main.cidr_block, using the data. prefix plus the block's type, name, and attribute
var.aws_vpc.main.cidr_block
module.aws_vpc.main.cidr_block
explain: Data source attributes are addressed as data.<type>.<name>.<attribute>, so the leading data. segment is required. Dropping it (B) addresses a managed resource instead, and the var. and module. prefixes (C and A) address entirely different kinds of objects.

q: Which two practices help callers use a published registry module safely? (Choose two.)
options: Always edit the module code inside .terraform/modules to match local needs
Pin the module with a version constraint instead of always taking the latest release
Depend on the module's internal resource addresses from the root configuration
Read the module's documented inputs and outputs on its registry page before wiring it in
explain: Version pinning keeps builds reproducible, and the registry page is the authoritative interface documentation. Editing the downloaded copy (A) is lost on the next init and is never a supported workflow, and callers must depend only on outputs, never internal resource addresses (B).

q: An engineer runs terraform destroy -target=aws_instance.legacy to remove one forgotten instance. What caveat applies to this targeted destroy?
options: It also deletes every resource the target depends on, including shared networks

Like targeted plans, it is an exceptional-case tool: it destroys the target (and anything depending on it as required) while leaving the rest of the workspace in place, and it should not become the routine way to delete resources
It is the recommended routine method for deleting individual resources
It removes the instance from state but leaves it running in the cloud
explain: destroy -target narrows teardown to one address for exceptional cleanup; the routine way to retire a resource is removing its block and applying. Targeted destroy really terminates the object (unlike state rm), and it does not wipe out the shared dependencies the target relies on.

q: After an engineer repairs a broken configuration, terraform validate finally completes without diagnostics. What exactly does Terraform print to confirm the result?
options: Success! The configuration is valid.
No formatting changes required
Configuration applied successfully
Plan: 0 to add, 0 to change, 0 to destroy
explain: On success validate prints the confirmation 'Success! The configuration is valid.' A (A) is apply's territory, the plan summary line (C) comes from plan output, and the formatting message (D) resembles fmt -check behavior. Knowing validate's success line also helps scripts and humans distinguish a pass from a silent command.

q: Which two statements about applying a saved plan file are accurate? (Choose two.)
options: A confirmation prompt still appears at apply time whenever the saved plan contains any destroys
Skipping the confirmation prompt is by design for saved plans, because the plan file itself was the reviewed and approved decision
The plan file must be named with a .plan extension or apply will prompt as a fallback
The safeguard for a saved-plan apply is reviewing the exact plan file beforehand, since no prompt will appear at apply time
explain: Apply of an explicit plan file never prompts, whatever the file is named and whatever it contains, including destroys. The control point is the earlier review of that exact file, which is why pipelines gate on plan approval rather than on an apply-time prompt.

q: A team wants different variable values for dev and prod but the same configuration files. Which pattern fits best?
options: Hardcode both environments' values and toggle them with comments
Keep one configuration and supply per-environment values through separate .tfvars files selected with -var-file, or separate auto-loaded files per working directory
Maintain two copies of the whole configuration and edit each by hand
Use two different Terraform versions, one per environment
explain: Variable files exist precisely to separate environment values from shared configuration, with -var-file selecting the set for a run. Duplicated configurations drift (A), comment toggling is error-prone manual work (C), and the Terraform version has nothing to do with environment values (B).

q: A networking configuration needs the VPC ID and subnet IDs that a separate platform configuration manages. The platform team does not want to share its full state details. What is the recommended pattern?
options: Both teams share one configuration and one backend for all resources forever
The platform configuration exposes only the needed values as outputs, and the networking configuration reads them with a terraform_remote_state data source
The networking team copies the platform terraform.tfstate into their own directory
The networking configuration guesses the VPC ID from the AWS console each run
explain: terraform_remote_state reads another configuration's state, and best practice is to consume only its published outputs rather than depending on internal resource attributes. Copying state files is fragile and exposes far more than the needed IDs.

q: A constraint reads version = "> 5.0.0" and the only registry builds are 5.0.0 and 5.0.1. Which build can init install?
options: Both, because > and >= behave identically
5.0.0 only, because > means at least that version
5.0.1 only, because > excludes the named version itself
Neither, because single-operator ranges are invalid
explain: The > operator is strictly greater than, so 5.0.0 does not satisfy > 5.0.0 while 5.0.1 does. Treating > as >= is the classic trap; inclusive minimums are written with the >= operator instead.

q: A team wants to reuse a community VPC module in their root configuration. Which block calls it, and what does the `source` argument look like for the public registry?
options: A `data` block with `source = "registry/vpc"`
A `module "vpc"` block with `source = "terraform-aws-modules/vpc/aws"` — registry address format is `//`
A `resource` block with `source = "terraform-aws-modules/vpc/aws"`
An `import` block with the registry URL
explain: Child modules are called with module blocks; public registry sources use namespace/name/provider form. A confuses modules with resources. C is for importing existing infrastructure. D confuses modules with data sources.

q: A database password is marked `sensitive = true` in its variable and output. It no longer appears in CLI output. A teammate claims the password is now encrypted in the state file. Is this correct?
options: No — sensitive values are never written to state at all
Yes, but only when using the S3 backend
No — `sensitive = true` only redacts CLI output; the value still sits in the state file in plaintext
Yes — sensitive values are encrypted at rest in state
explain: EXAM TRAP: sensitive is display-only. State still contains the plaintext value — real protection means encryption at rest, access control, Vault, or ephemeral values. A is the exact misconception the exam hunts. C invents backend-specific encryption. D describes ephemeral values, not sensitive.

At the workflow level the sequence is list to see what exists and which is current, select to switch the active workspace, and show to confirm the one now selected, which here is dev. Show does not list all workspaces, dump state JSON, or stay pinned to the starting workspace, which is why the prod distractor is wrong once select has succeeded.
options: The full state contents of the dev workspace in JSON format
dev, because show reports the currently selected workspace, which select just switched to dev
A list of every workspace in the working directory with their state serial numbers
prod, because show always reports the workspace that was active when the pipeline started
q: An operator manages separate dev and prod environments from one configuration using workspaces. The operator runs terraform workspace list and sees an asterisk next to prod, then runs terraform workspace select dev, and then runs terraform workspace show. What does terraform workspace show display after those commands?
A manager asks whether adopting Terraform means abandoning Ansible entirely. What is the best answer?
options: No, teams commonly provision with Terraform and then configure operating systems and applications with Ansible
Yes, HashiCorp requires removing configuration management tools
Yes, because Ansible cannot run after Terraform under any circumstances
No, because Terraform's main role is installing packages inside servers
explain: Terraform and Ansible are frequently combined: Terraform provisions, Ansible configures. Nothing requires removing Ansible, it can run after provisioning, and package installation inside servers is Ansible's typical role rather than Terraform's main one.

q: A configuration declares two `provider "aws"` blocks — one for us-east-1 and one aliased `west` for us-west-2. A resource block has no `provider` meta-argument. Which provider configuration will Terraform use for that resource?
options: Terraform picks whichever provider block was declared first
The aliased `west` provider, because aliases take precedence
The apply fails — every resource must declare an explicit provider
The unaliased (default) provider configuration, us-east-1
explain: Resources without an explicit provider meta-argument use the default (unaliased) configuration of that provider type. A is false — the default exists precisely so most resources need no declaration. C and D invent selection rules; the rule is simply default-vs-aliased.

q: An engineer tests an expression in terraform console: `split(",", "cache,web,api")`. What value does it produce?
options: ["cache", "web", "api"]
["cache,web,api"]
["cache", "web", "api", ""]
"cache,web,api"
explain: split() divides the string at each comma and returns a list of the three resulting names.

q: A teammate refers to the hosted HashiCorp platform as Terraform Cloud while reading 2023 documentation. What is its current name?
options: HashiCorp Cloud Runs, the replacement branding
HCP Terraform, the name HashiCorp adopted when it renamed Terraform Cloud in 2024
Terraform Enterprise Cloud, the new name for the hosted service
Waypoint Cloud, which absorbed the product
explain: HashiCorp renamed Terraform Cloud to HCP Terraform in 2024; older docs and questions may still say Terraform Cloud but they mean the same hosted platform. Terraform Enterprise remains the separate self-hosted offering and was not renamed.

q: A module outputs the value of `replace("prod-web-01", "prod", "dev")`. What value does it produce?
options: prod-dev-01
dev-web
dev-web-01
prod-web-01
explain: replace() substitutes every occurrence of the search substring, so only the leading prod segment changes to dev.

q: A workspace's working directory is set to /services/api in a large monorepo. A commit changes only files under /services/billing. Will this commit queue a run in the api workspace, and why?
options: No, because monorepos are not supported by the VCS workflow
No, directory-based triggering means changes outside the workspace's working directory do not queue a run for it
Yes, any commit anywhere in a connected repository queues runs in every workspace
Yes, but the run is automatically cancelled before planning starts
explain: Automatic runs are scoped by the workspace's working directory, so unrelated directory changes do not trigger that workspace. The repository connection alone does not broadcast every commit to all workspaces, runs are not queued-then-cancelled for this, and monorepos are a supported pattern.

Each provider defines the import ID format per resource type, and for Azure that is typically the full /subscriptions/.../resourceGroups/... path, so a short name cannot be resolved. Azure imports are fully supported, there is no same-day rule, and running state does not block an import lookup in this way.
options: Azure resources can only be imported on the day they were created
Import blocks do not support Azure providers at all
The virtual network must be stopped before any import can be attempted
The import ID format is wrong for that provider and resource type: Azure expects the full resource ID path, not a short name
q: An engineer tries to import an Azure virtual network using only its short display name as the id in an import block, and the import errors out before any state is written. What is the most likely reason?
A team applies changes to a workspace whose backend supports locking, and a stale lock from a crashed run blocks the new apply. What does this reveal about apply's locking design?
options: Apply depends on the lock to serialize state writes, so a leftover lock must be dealt with deliberately (such as force-unlock with the lock ID) rather than apply ignoring locks when they seem old
A blocked apply indicates the backend does not support locking at all
Apply ignores locks older than ten minutes automatically
Locks are advisory only and never block an apply
explain: The lock is a hard serialization mechanism for state writers; Terraform will not silently disregard it, which is why force-unlock exists as a deliberate, ID-specific operation. A backend that supports locking is exactly the kind that can leave a stale lock after a crash.

q: A junior engineer writes step-by-step instructions: create the bucket, wait, enable versioning, then attach a policy, checking each step manually. How should this approach be classified?
options: Imperative only if it is written in Bash rather than English
Declarative, because the final bucket properties are mentioned
Imperative, because it prescribes an ordered sequence of actions to perform
Declarative, because any written instruction counts as code
explain: Classification depends on style, not language: ordered steps that say how to do it are imperative, even in plain English. A declarative version would simply state the bucket with versioning and policy as desired properties and let the tool sequence the work.

q: Which two practices make sharing state between configurations safer? (Choose two.)
options: Give every consumer direct read access patterns that depend on internal resource attributes of the source state
Restrict access to the source backend to authorized teams and automation
Expose only the values other configurations need through the source configuration's outputs
Publish the source state file in a shared wiki for convenience
explain: Consuming published outputs limits coupling to a stable interface, and backend access control limits who can read the full state with its secrets. Depending on internal attributes is brittle, and publishing raw state exposes sensitive values broadly.

q: A configuration contains the expression `contains(["eu-central-1", "ap-south-1", "eu-west-1"], "sa-east-1")`. What does Terraform return?
options: error: value not found
true
false
null
explain: contains() returns true only when the exact value is an element of the list; "sa-east-1" is not in the list, and contains() returns false rather than erroring when it is absent.

q: A required_providers entry for a dashboard tool reads source = "grafana/grafana". What does this tell Terraform?
options: grafana before the slash is a hostname for a private registry
The provider type is grafana and it is published under the grafana namespace on the public registry
The entry declares a module, not a provider
The provider is an official HashiCorp provider named grafana
explain: In a two-part address, the first segment is the publisher namespace and the second is the provider type, so this is the grafana provider published by the grafana organization. Only hashicorp-namespace providers are HashiCorp's official ones, and a hostname would require a three-part address.

q: A team using the azurerm backend discovers the current state blob was overwritten with a truncated file during a failed maintenance script. The storage account has blob snapshots of the state container from earlier in the day. How do those snapshots help?
options: They automatically merge with the truncated blob on the next terraform init
They are point-in-time copies of the state blob that can be promoted or copied back to restore the last good state content
They store only blob metadata, so they cannot help recover state content
They act as the state lock, so deleting the lock lease restores the file
explain: Azure blob snapshots preserve the blob's content at a point in time, so an earlier snapshot of the state blob can be restored as the state file. They are not a locking mechanism and never merge automatically with a damaged blob; the operator deliberately restores the good copy.

q: A new engineer asks what terraform graph is for when reviewing a large configuration. Which description is correct?
options: It renders the state file as an interactive web dashboard
It emits a dependency graph of resources and modules that can be visualized to understand relationships and ordering
It draws a chart of monthly cloud spending per resource
It graphs CPU utilization of managed instances over time
explain: terraform graph outputs the dependency structure Terraform derives from references, typically in DOT format for visualization, which helps explain creation order. It has nothing to do with billing, instance metrics, or interactive state dashboards.

q: A team applies the same Terraform configuration to a brand-new account and gets an environment that matches production in structure. Which property made this possible?
options: Production was left untouched, which guarantees matching structure
The state file from production was copied and edited by hand
The configuration is reproducible because it declares the complete desired state rather than a history of manual actions
The cloud provider copied production automatically
explain: Reproducibility comes from a complete declarative definition that can be applied anywhere, not from copying state by hand, which is fragile and unsupported as a cloning method. The provider does not clone environments on its own.

q: A configuration sets an AWS region argument to the string us-easst-1, a typo. terraform validate reports the configuration is valid, but a later plan fails when the provider rejects the region. Why did validate let the typo through?
options: Validate ignores the provider block entirely, including its argument names
Validate only checks the first provider block in a file and the region sat in the second

The value is a perfectly valid string, and validate checks types and structure rather than verifying provider-side value validity against live service data; it never calls the APIs that would reject the region
Region names are checked only when the configuration also sets a second provider alias
explain: A misspelled region is type-correct: it is a string where a string belongs. Validate does not enumerate real regions or call AWS to test values, so semantic value errors surface later. Validate does examine provider blocks for unsupported arguments (A), aliases are irrelevant (B), and there is no first-block-only limitation (D).

q: Which scenario best shows configuration as documentation failing under a manual process but succeeding under IaC?
options: A cloud console displays the current firewall rule when opened
A wiki page says a firewall allows port 443, but nobody updated it after the rule changed to 8443, while the Terraform file shows the current rule because it enforces it
A Terraform file is stored without any comments or descriptions
An operator keeps private notes about servers on paper
explain: Manual documentation drifts because it is separate from the thing it describes; IaC documentation is the enforcing definition itself, so reading the code shows the intended current rule. The other choices do not compare a stale manual record with an enforcing configuration.

Aliased provider configurations are selected per resource with the provider meta-argument; provider = aws.prod routes that resource through the production account's assumed-role configuration, and omitting it uses the default. The naming distractor is wrong because Terraform never infers provider selection from resource names.
options: By naming the bucket with a prod- prefix, which Terraform matches to the alias automatically
By running apply with -var targeting the production account
By setting region = "prod" inside the resource block
By setting the meta-argument provider = aws.prod on the resource, while resources without a provider meta-argument fall back to the default unaliased configuration
q: One root module manages resources in three cloud accounts. It declares a default provider "aws" block plus two aliased blocks, aws.dev and aws.prod, each with its own region and an assume_role block for its account. A bucket must be created in the production account. How does its resource block select the right configuration?
An author prepares to publish a module to the public registry. Which repository setup does the registry require?
options: A public GitHub repository named terraform-<PROVIDER>-<NAME>, with releases tagged using semantic versioning
A private GitHub repository named <NAME>-terraform with manually numbered releases
A GitHub repository whose name matches the author's username
Any public GitHub repository, regardless of name, with a single combined .tf file
explain: Public registry publishing mandates the terraform-<PROVIDER>-<NAME> naming convention and semantic version tags like v1.2.0, which become the module's published versions. Arbitrary names (A) and reversed names (C) are rejected, the repository must be public (C), and the author's username is irrelevant (D).

q: Why does Terraform show a referenced attribute as '(known after apply)' in the first plan for a new resource?
options: Because references are only evaluated on Tuesdays in HCP Terraform
Because the attribute is computed during creation, so no value exists yet for the reference to return during planning
Because the configuration has a syntax error that apply will fix
Because the referencing resource is missing a provider block
explain: A reference can only return a value that exists; for a not-yet-created resource, computed attributes are unknown until apply produces them. This is normal graph behavior, not a syntax problem (A), not a scheduling quirk (C), and not a missing provider configuration (B).

q: A regulated team must prove who approved a database change before it reached production. Their Terraform changes go through pull requests. Which two practices together provide that evidence? (Choose two.)
options: A screenshot of the console taken after the change
Verbal approval given in a standup meeting
Pull request approvals recorded before the merge
Git commit history showing author, timestamp, and diff
explain: Commit history and pull request approvals are timestamped, attributable, and reviewable, which is what an audit needs. Verbal approval leaves no record, and an after-the-fact screenshot shows the result but not who approved the change beforehand.

q: While debugging a configuration, an engineer evaluates `merge({ Name = "web", Env = "dev" }, { Env = "dr", Team = "ops" })` in the console. What value does it produce?
options: { Env = "dev", Name = "web" }
{ Env = "dr", Team = "ops" }
{ Env = "dr", Name = "web", Team = "ops" }
{ Env = "dev", Name = "web", Team = "ops" }
explain: merge() combines maps left to right and later maps win key conflicts, so Env is overwritten with "dr" while Name survives and Team is added.

q: A corrupted state file was pushed over the healthy state in an S3 backend bucket that has versioning enabled. The current state object is unusable, but the run from an hour earlier was healthy. What is the sound recovery move?
options: Retrieve the previous version of the state object from the bucket's version history and restore that known-good snapshot as the current state
Delete the corrupted object; S3 versioning automatically promotes the oldest version and repairs the serial
Empty the bucket and re-import every resource from scratch
Run terraform force-unlock repeatedly until Terraform rebuilds the state from the corrupted object
explain: Versioning keeps prior versions of the state object, so the pre-corruption snapshot can be fetched and restored instead of rebuilding management from nothing. force-unlock only deals with locks, not content corruption, and versioning never repairs or promotes versions automatically.

q: A root module must pass two different AWS provider configurations into one child module call. Which two elements make this work? (Choose two.)
options: The caller defines two provider configurations, one default and one aliased, in the root module
The child module sets count = 2 on its own resources
The module block includes a providers map assigning configurations to the aliases the child expects
The child module declares two provider blocks with hardcoded credentials
explain: Passing multiple configurations requires the caller to define them and hand them over explicitly through the providers map, matched to the child's declared aliases. Provider blocks inside the child (A) are the opposite pattern, and resource count inside the child (D) does not route provider configurations.

q: During a code review, a teammate asks what `cidrsubnet("10.0.0.0/16", 8, 255)` evaluates to. What is the result?
explain: cidrsubnet() adds 8 bits and picks subnet number 255: starting from 10.0.0.0/16, subnet 255 of the /24 series is 10.0.255.0/24.

q: Before deploying to an offline environment, a team runs terraform providers lock while still online. What does this command accomplish?
options: It downloads providers into the state backend for offline applies
It freezes required_providers so the constraints can never be edited
It proactively creates or updates .terraform.lock.hcl with the selected versions and hashes so later init runs can verify installs
It locks the state file so no other user can apply
explain: terraform providers lock pre-generates the lock file entries, including hashes, while a registry is reachable, so a later init can verify packages without resolving fresh selections. It is unrelated to state locking, does not freeze configuration files, and does not stage binaries in a backend.

q: A junior engineer believes terraform apply -auto-approve also approves terraform destroy prompts later in the same script. Is that correct?
options: Yes; once any command uses -auto-approve the whole session is approved
No; destroy can never skip its prompt under any flag
No; -auto-approve is per-command, so destroy in the script needs its own -auto-approve flag to skip its prompt
Yes; apply and destroy share a single approval stored in state
explain: Approval flags do not carry between commands: each of apply and destroy prompts independently unless its own invocation passes -auto-approve (or applies a saved plan, in apply's case). Destroy absolutely supports -auto-approve, which is how automated teardowns run.

q: A governance team maintains its Sentinel policies in a dedicated Git repository, versions them like application code, and connects that repository so HCP Terraform applies the policies consistently to selected workspaces. What is this collection called?
options: A module bundle in the private registry
A run task bundle
A variable set
A policy set, which groups one or more Sentinel policies and is commonly sourced from a VCS repository
explain: Policies are grouped into policy sets, which are typically connected to a VCS repository and assigned to workspaces or the whole organization. Variable sets share variables, run tasks are stage integrations, and registry bundles concern modules and providers, not Sentinel policies.

q: What does the serial field inside a Terraform state file represent?
options: A counter that increments each time the state is written, helping detect conflicting or overwritten writes
The number of resources currently recorded in the state
The sequence number of the provider plugin that last ran
The serial number of the Terraform CLI license in use
explain: The serial is a monotonically increasing version counter for that state lineage, bumped on every write. A lower serial being pushed over a higher one signals a stale overwrite risk, unlike the resource count or a license number.

q: Before running a CLI import for an existing S3 bucket, what must an engineer look up in the AWS provider documentation for that resource type?
options: The bucket's provider-specific import ID format, such as the bucket name for aws_s3_bucket
The bucket's billing cost center code
The default region for the Terraform backend
The version of Terraform that created the bucket
explain: Import IDs are defined by each provider for each resource type, so the engineer must find the exact format expected, like a bucket name or an ARN. Billing codes, backend regions, and creator versions play no role in identifying the object to Terraform.

q: A large root configuration is reorganized: networking resources move into a child module, but their existing state entries use root-level addresses. After the refactor, plan wants to destroy and recreate everything. What should the team investigate?
options: Whether outputs were declared for the subnets
Whether the module needs a version argument
Whether moved blocks (or state mv) are needed to map the old resource addresses to their new module addresses so Terraform tracks the same objects
Whether prevent_destroy was set on the VPC
explain: Moving resources into a module changes their state addresses to module.<name>.<resource>; without moved blocks or terraform state mv, Terraform sees new resources and orphaned old ones. prevent_destroy (A) would only error, version arguments (C) concern sourcing, and outputs (B) do not affect state identity.

q: A backend block deliberately leaves the bucket and key unset because each environment supplies its own values when the pipeline initializes the working directory. Which init flag supplies those missing backend settings at initialization time?
options: -var-file, because backend settings are ordinary input variables
-target, because the backend must be targeted before use
-backend-config, passed as a file path or as key=value pairs to complete the partial backend configuration
-refresh=false, because the backend is only read at refresh time
explain: Partial backend configuration is completed with -backend-config, which accepts a configuration file or key=value pairs. Backend blocks cannot use variables, so -var-file (A) cannot fill them; -target (B) limits plan and apply actions, not backend setup; and -refresh=false (D) is a plan and apply flag unrelated to initialization.

q: Two CI jobs triggered by the same merge both run terraform apply against a locking remote backend. The second job exits with an error acquiring the state lock while the first completes successfully. What does this outcome show?
options: The second job's changes were silently merged into the first job's state
The lock error means the first job's apply was rolled back automatically
State locking worked as designed: the second writer was blocked instead of interleaving writes, and the pipeline should serialize applies or let the second job retry after the first finishes
The backend is misconfigured, because both jobs should have applied concurrently
explain: A lock error for the second concurrent writer is the protection working, not a failure: only one run may write state at a time. The fix is pipeline design, such as a concurrency group that serializes applies, not removing locking or expecting concurrent applies to merge.

The plugin cache is purely a download cache shared across working directories: it saves bandwidth but changes nothing about version selection, lock verification, or required_providers declarations. The distractors fail because a cache cannot pin versions (that is the lock file's job) and cannot substitute for declaring a provider requirement.
options: The cache stores provider packages only; Terraform still resolves which version to use from the registry or a mirror and still verifies selections against the lock file
A provider found in the cache no longer needs to be declared in required_providers
Setting the cache makes .terraform.lock.hcl unnecessary, because cached versions are automatically treated as pinned
Multiple working directories on the same machine can share the cache, so the same provider version is downloaded only once instead of once per project
q: A platform engineer enables a shared plugin cache directory for the team by setting TF_PLUGIN_CACHE_DIR. Which two statements about the cache are true? (Choose two.)
A team wants to test a fix in a shared module without publishing a new version. Their root configuration currently pulls the module from the registry. What is a workable local-development approach?
options: Edit the copy inside .terraform/modules and commit that
Set version = "local" on the registry source
Modules cannot be tested locally once published
Temporarily point the module block's source at a local path checkout of the module, test, then restore the registry source and re-run init before committing
explain: Swapping source to a local path during development is the standard loop; the .terraform/modules copy is a managed download that init overwrites, so editing it (A) is futile. There is no local version value (C), and published modules remain ordinary directories of code that can always be checked out and tested (D).

q: A compliance rule states: `Database credentials must never be persisted in the Terraform state file, even in encrypted form.` Which Terraform feature satisfies this?
options: Storing the state file in a private Git repository
Marking the variable `sensitive = true`
Using `ephemeral` resource blocks or write-only attributes — the values are used during apply but never written to state
Using `terraform state push` after every apply
explain: Ephemeral values (and write-only attributes) exist precisely for secrets that must not touch state — used at apply time, never persisted. A only hides CLI output. C is terrible practice (state in Git). D uploads state but does not remove secrets from it.

q: A team sources a module directly from GitHub and needs builds to always use the v2.1.0 tag, never floating to newer commits. How is this declared?
options: `source = "github.com/org/vpc"` with `version = "2.1.0"`
`source = "github.com/org/vpc?ref=v2.1.0"` — Git sources pin with the `ref` query parameter
`source = "github.com/org/vpc"` with `ref = "v2.1.0"` as a separate argument
GitHub sources always float; pinning is impossible
explain: Git-sourced modules pin via `?ref=` (tag, branch, or commit SHA) appended to the source URL. A uses version, which is registry-only and invalid here. C invents a separate ref argument. D is false — ref pinning is the standard mechanism.

q: terraform init fails for a registry module call with: no available releases match the given constraints. The module block reads version = ">= 5.0, < 5.0". Other teams use this module successfully. What is the correct resolution?
options: Delete .terraform.lock.hcl, because the lock file is blocking the module
Run terraform init -upgrade repeatedly until a matching release appears

Correct the version constraint, because the two bounds intersect at nothing: no release can be both at least 5.0 and below 5.0, so the constraint itself must be fixed to a satisfiable range before init can select a version
Switch the source to the module's Git repository, because registry constraints cannot combine two bounds
explain: The error is arithmetic, not a download problem: the constraint's lower bound meets its upper bound, leaving an empty set of candidate releases, and only editing the constraint fixes that. Re-running init (A) cannot change set logic, the lock file records providers rather than module selections (B), and combined bounds such as >= 4.0, < 5.0 are normal valid registry constraints (D).

q: A provider is constrained with version = "~> 5.1.0". Which of these versions satisfies the constraint?
explain: With three components, ~> 5.1.0 means >= 5.1.0 and < 5.2.0, so only patch releases within 5.1.x qualify and 5.1.9 fits. Version 5.2.0 increments the minor component and is excluded, while 5.0.9 is below the floor.

q: While debugging a configuration, an engineer evaluates `tostring(42)` in the console. What does Terraform return?
explain: tostring() converts the number to its string representation, so the result is the string "42", not the number 42.

q: A module author adds a new required input variable to a widely used child module. What is the impact on existing callers?
options: Every existing module block calling it will fail until each caller supplies the new argument, making it a breaking change that warrants a major version bump when published
Callers automatically receive a null and continue
None; new variables are always optional
Only callers using count are affected
explain: A new required input breaks every existing call site, which is why published modules treat it as a major-version change under semantic versioning. It is not silently optional (A) or null-filled (B), and the breakage applies to all callers regardless of count usage (D).

q: Which two statements about terraform init are true? (Choose two.)
options: Init only ever needs to run once per repository, no matter how the configuration evolves afterward
Init is safe to re-run repeatedly; it prepares the working directory without changing managed infrastructure
Init must be re-run after adding a provider or a module, or after changing the backend configuration
Init creates cloud resources so that plan has something to compare against
explain: Init is idempotent preparation (B): running it again simply re-installs and re-configures as needed, and it must be re-run whenever providers, modules, or the backend change (D), because those are resolved at initialization time. Init creates no infrastructure (A), and the once-ever claim (C) is the classic trap: new checkouts, new machines, and configuration changes all require fresh initialization.

q: Which two statements about state metadata are accurate? (Choose two.)
options: The state format has its own version number, separate from the Terraform CLI version that wrote it
The lineage changes every time a resource is updated in place
State metadata includes the live cloud password for the provider account
The serial increases when state is written, giving each saved snapshot an ordering within its lineage
explain: State carries a format version and a serial that increments on writes within a single lineage; lineage stays constant for that state history across ordinary updates. It does not store a provider account password as metadata.

q: A team raises apply parallelism to 50 for a workspace of mostly independent resources, but total time barely improves and the provider begins returning throttling errors. What is the best interpretation?
options: Raising parallelism corrupted the dependency graph and resources were created in the wrong order
Throttling errors mean the state lock was released too early
Terraform ignores -parallelism values above 10
Parallelism is bounded by provider API rate limits and the dependency graph, so raising -parallelism past what the provider tolerates causes throttling rather than speed
explain: -parallelism controls how many graph operations run at once, but provider quotas still apply and dependent resources still serialize; overshooting trades speed for API throttling. Terraform honors values above 10 and graph ordering is never corrupted by the setting.

q: Which two statements about Terraform state locking are accurate? (Choose two.)
options: The local backend locks state using the .terraform.lock.hcl provider dependency file
Most remote backends support locking natively, while the local backend does not provide it
Locking prevents concurrent state writes that could corrupt state or lose updates
Terraform automatically force-unlocks a held lock after 60 seconds so runs never block
explain: Locking is a backend feature that most remote backends implement to stop concurrent writers from corrupting state. The dependency lock file is unrelated to state locking, and Terraform never force-unlocks automatically; that is always a deliberate manual action.

q: A plan command fails and terraform plan -detailed-exitcode returns exit code 1. What does code 1 indicate in this mode?
options: The plan was saved successfully to a file
No changes are needed
Changes are present but were auto-approved
An error occurred while producing the plan, distinct from both the empty-plan and changes-present results
explain: In detailed-exitcode mode, 1 is reserved for errors, while 0 is an empty successful plan and 2 is a successful plan with changes. Treating 1 as success would let a broken configuration flow downstream, which is why pipelines branch on all three values.

q: An engineer needs the recorded tags of a database that lives inside a networking module. Which command retrieves them?
options: terraform state list -module=networking, which displays tags for module resources
terraform output module.networking, which prints all attributes in a module
terraform state show module.networking.aws_db_instance.main, using the full module-qualified address
terraform state show aws_db_instance.main, because state show ignores module paths
explain: State addresses for module resources include the full module path, and state show needs that exact address to find the recorded attributes including tags. The unqualified address does not resolve inside a module, output shows root outputs only, and state list prints addresses rather than attribute values.

q: Which file is created by default in the working directory when you apply a configuration with no backend block configured?
options: .terraform.lock.hcl
terraform.tfstate
backend.tfstate.json
terraform.tfplan
explain: The default local backend writes terraform.tfstate in the working directory. The lock file .terraform.lock.hcl records provider selections, not resource state, and a saved plan file only exists when you use plan -out.

q: An engineer tests an expression in terraform console: `element(["us-east-1", "us-west-2", "eu-central-1", "eu-west-1"], 7)`. What value does it produce?
options: eu-central-1
us-west-2
us-east-1
eu-west-1
explain: element() selects by index modulo the list length: index 7 mod 4 = 3, which is "eu-west-1". It never errors on an out-of-range index — it wraps around, unlike direct indexing.

q: During a remote run, a provider needs a proxy address supplied through an environment variable, and the configuration needs a replica count supplied as an input. A trainee sets both as Terraform variables and the provider still cannot see the proxy. What went wrong?
options: The replica count should have been an environment variable and the proxy a Terraform variable
Terraform variables are visible to providers automatically, so the run must have failed for an unrelated reason
Environment variables cannot be set in HCP Terraform workspaces at all
The proxy is an environment concern and must be set as a workspace environment variable; Terraform variables only feed declared configuration inputs and are not exported to the provider's environment
explain: Providers read settings like proxies from the run environment, which workspace environment variables populate; Terraform variables exist to fill variable declarations in configuration and are not exported as environment values. Environment variables are fully supported, and swapping the two assignments would break both purposes.

q: A failure could be inside Terraform core or inside the provider plugin, and the logs are too tangled to tell. Which logging setup best separates the two sources?
options: Set TF_LOG_CORE and TF_LOG_PROVIDER to different levels or paths so core and provider messages can be examined independently
Rename the provider binary so its logs sort first in the file
Run plan twice and compare which output lines change
Set TF_LOG=OFF for core resources and TF_LOG=TRACE for data sources
explain: TF_LOG_CORE and TF_LOG_PROVIDER exist to split logging by component, so an engineer can raise or isolate one side when localizing a fault. The other suggestions misuse unrelated variables, rename binaries pointlessly, or rely on diffing runs instead of component-scoped logs.

q: How does a root module read an attribute of a resource created inside a child module?
options: By using a data source with the same address
Child module resources are automatically merged into the root namespace
By referencing the resource address directly, e.g., aws_vpc.this.id
The child module must declare an output value, which the root reads as module.<name>.<output>
explain: Modules are scoped: data flows out only through declared outputs, read as module.vpc.vpc_id. B fails because the address lives in the child's namespace. C is for unmanaged infrastructure. D is false — no automatic merging.

q: A module author changes an existing input variable instance_names from type string to type list(string) and publishes it as a patch release, 1.4.1. Callers break immediately. Why was the patch bump wrong?
options: Type changes are always safe because Terraform converts strings to lists automatically
Patch releases are not allowed to touch variables.tf at all
Changing the type of an existing input breaks every caller passing the old shape, so it is a breaking interface change that required a major version bump, not a patch
The callers broke because patch releases force terraform init -upgrade on every machine
explain: Semantic versioning for modules is about the interface contract: altering an input's type invalidates existing module blocks, which is the definition of a breaking change and demands a major bump so callers can opt in deliberately. Patch releases may fix internals and documentation (B overstates the rule), nothing forces an upgrade on callers (C), and a scalar string does not auto-convert into a list of names (D).

q: A team applies a saved plan two weeks after creating it. No applies happened in between, but an engineer ran terraform plan -refresh-only followed by terraform apply -refresh-only yesterday, updating state. Why might the old saved plan now fail?
options: Refresh-only mode deletes all saved plan files in the directory
Saved plans expire automatically after seven days regardless of state
The refresh-only apply advanced the state, so the saved plan's expected prior state no longer matches and Terraform treats the plan as stale
The old plan fails because plan files can only be applied by the same user who created them
explain: Staleness is about state, not age: any state write, including a refresh-only apply, moves the serial and invalidates plans based on the older snapshot. There is no seven-day expiry, no plan-file deletion, and no per-user binding in Terraform.

q: A provider constraint is version = "<= 4.5.0" and the registry offers 4.5.0, 4.5.1, and 4.6.0. Which version is the newest init may select?
options: 4.5.1, because patch releases ignore the bound
4.6.0, because <= is only a recommendation
None; <= cannot be combined with version selection
4.5.0, because <= includes the named version and everything below it
explain: The <= operator sets an inclusive ceiling: 4.5.0 itself qualifies, while 4.5.1 and 4.6.0 exceed the bound and are rejected. Bounds are enforced strictly during version resolution, not treated as hints.

An orphaned object outside state and configuration is invisible to Terraform, so choosing to leave it unmanaged means accepting fully manual governance with no drift detection or lifecycle control. Terraform does not watch, back up, or convert unmanaged objects on its own; adoption would require an explicit import.
options: The bucket gains drift protection because Terraform watches unmanaged objects
No Terraform plan, apply, or destroy in that workspace will ever see, protect, or clean up the bucket, so its settings and lifecycle remain entirely manual
Terraform will still back up the bucket during every apply
Leaving it unmanaged automatically converts it to a data source
q: A cloud storage bucket exists in the account but appears in no Terraform state and no configuration. The team deliberately decides to leave it unmanaged for now. What is the direct trade-off of that decision?

The variable "region" receives values from several places: a value in terraform.tfvars sets it to "ca-central-1"; a value in terraform.tfvars.json sets it to "ap-south-1"; TF_VAR_ is set in the shell environment sets it to "eu-west-1". No other sources set it. Which value does Terraform use?
options: us-west-2
ca-central-1
ap-south-1
eu-west-1
explain: Variable precedence, lowest to highest: default < TF_VAR_ environment < terraform.tfvars < terraform.tfvars.json < *.auto.tfvars < -var-file < -var. The highest source present here is terraform.tfvars.json, so its value "ap-south-1" wins.

q: A child module finishes building a database and the caller needs its endpoint address. Which construct inside the child module exposes that value to the caller?
options: A variable block with a default
An output block whose value references the endpoint attribute
A locals block naming the endpoint
A provider block for the database engine
explain: Outputs are the only way a child module returns values to its caller. Variables (A) carry values into a module, not out of it, and locals (B) are private to the module that declares them, while provider blocks (C) configure APIs rather than export values.

q: A plan fails because a data source argument references a variable that has no value. What is the root cause chain?
options: The provider is not installed
The variable is required (no default) and was never assigned, so the data source's query cannot be built and the read cannot proceed
The data source needs a lifecycle block
Data sources cannot use variables at all
explain: Data source arguments are ordinary expressions and may use variables; the failure is that a required variable with no default and no assignment has no value to build the query from. The other options invent restrictions or causes that do not match this failure chain.

q: A monitoring script deleted a managed log bucket out-of-band last night, but the team still needs the bucket and its configuration block is untouched. What will the next apply do, and why is no import needed?
options: Apply recreates the bucket, because state no longer contains a live object while configuration still declares it, and recreation uses the existing block
Apply imports the bucket first, because recreation always requires an import step
Apply does nothing, because the state entry proves the bucket still exists
Apply fails permanently, because deleted objects can never be recreated from configuration
explain: Once refresh removes the vanished object from the working picture, the declared block drives a straightforward create, no adoption step involved. Import is for objects that exist outside state, not for recreating missing ones, and neither permanent failure nor silent inaction matches how reconciliation works.

q: A team wants fully reproducible builds: the same configuration must install the same module and provider versions on every machine, every time. Which two practices together achieve this?
options: Pinning module `version` constraints and committing the `.terraform.lock.hcl` file
Using only local-path modules and deleting `.terraform/` before each run
Running `terraform init -upgrade` before every apply
Storing modules in the same Git repo as the root configuration
explain: Reproducibility is version pins (constraints that bound what init may select) plus the committed lock file (the exact selections). B avoids the problem rather than solving it. C does the opposite — it actively re-resolves to newest. D helps availability but pins nothing.

q: A teammate asks: `What AMI is that web instance actually running according to Terraform's records?` Which command shows the full recorded attributes of one resource?
options: `terraform state show aws_instance.web`
`terraform console aws_instance.web`
`terraform get aws_instance.web`
`terraform state list aws_instance.web`
explain: `state show ` displays the recorded attributes of a single resource. B lists addresses (and takes no address argument). C and D are not the right tools — `terraform console` evaluates expressions interactively but is not the direct answer for inspecting recorded attributes.

q: An author first writes a naming formula inline in twelve resources, then refactors it into a local. What improves, and what stays the same?
options: The resources no longer need the naming formula
The deployed infrastructure changes because locals create new objects
Maintainability improves — one definition to fix — while the resulting values, and therefore the planned infrastructure, stay the same
The formula becomes overridable by callers after the refactor
explain: Refactoring a repeated expression into a local is a no-behavior-change cleanup: the same values flow to the same arguments. Locals create no objects (A), callers gain no override ability (C), and resources still consume the formula, now via the local reference (D).

q: While debugging a configuration, an engineer evaluates `["batch", "web"][5]` in the console. What does Terraform return?
options: batch
null
Error: index out of range
web
explain: Direct indexing does not wrap like element() does; index 5 on a two-element list is an error. element() is the function that wraps modulo the length.

q: A workspace defines two variables: instance_count as a Terraform variable and AWS_REGION as an environment variable. What is the difference in how each is used during a remote run?
options: Both are passed as inputs to the root module's variable declarations
The Terraform variable supplies a configuration input value, while the environment variable sets a value in the run environment, such as for provider configuration or shell-level settings
The environment variable overrides the configuration code itself
Environment variables in a workspace are ignored during remote runs
explain: Terraform variables feed declared configuration inputs, while workspace environment variables populate the run environment used by providers and Terraform itself. Environment variables do not override configuration code and are fully honored in remote runs.

q: A developer's cloud credentials expired overnight. The configuration itself is unchanged and correct. They run terraform validate in the morning and want to know the expected result.
options: Validate succeeds, because it checks syntax and internal consistency only and never authenticates to any provider or API
Validate fails, because it verifies credentials before checking the configuration
Validate fails, because expired credentials invalidate the provider schemas
Validate succeeds only if the state file is less than 24 hours old
explain: Validate is credential-free by design, which is why it fits pre-commit hooks and early CI stages: expired credentials are irrelevant to it. It performs no authentication (A), schemas remain valid regardless of credential state (B), and state age (D) plays no role in a check that does not even require state.

q: Which arguments belong in a data block for aws_ami to narrow the search to images owned by Canonical that match a name pattern?
options: A count argument that creates that many images
Arguments such as filter, owners, and most_recent that describe the query the provider should run
A provisioner block that runs after the image is found
Arguments such as instance_type and key_name that describe a server to launch
explain: Data source arguments are query criteria for the provider's read API, such as filters, owners, and most_recent for aws_ami. Instance arguments (B) belong to aws_instance resources, count on a data source does not create images (C), and data blocks do not run provisioners (A).

q: A configuration contains: ```hcl terraform { backend "s3" { bucket = var.state_bucket key = "prod/terraform.tfstate" } } ``` What is wrong with this backend block?
options: Nothing — variables are the recommended way to parameterize backends
The `key` argument is not valid for the S3 backend
S3 backends require the `region` to be hardcoded
Backend blocks cannot contain variables or references — backends initialize before configuration is evaluated; use partial configuration with `-backend-config` flags instead
explain: EXAM TRAP: the backend block is evaluated before variables exist, so no variables or references are allowed inside it. The workaround is partial backend configuration via -backend-config files or flags. A states the exact misconception. C is false — key is required. D is false; region can come from -backend-config or env.

q: A variable block includes both a default and, in terraform.tfvars, an assignment for the same variable. Which value is used, conceptually?
options: The run fails because a variable may only be set in one place
The tfvars assignment, because supplied values override the declared default, which only applies when nothing supplies a value
Both values are merged into a list
The default, because defaults are locked once declared
explain: A default is a fallback, not a lock: any actual assignment from a file, environment, or flag replaces it. Values are not merged (C), and setting a variable in more than one place is normal Terraform usage resolved by precedence, not an error (B).

q: An engineer needs a module from a Git repository over SSH rather than HTTPS. Which source form is valid?
options: ssh::https://example.com/module.git
git::ssh://git@example.com/org/module.git with the git:: prefix and SSH URL
The version argument set to the SSH URL
SSH is unsupported; Git sources are HTTPS only
explain: Forced git:: sources accept SSH URLs, letting Terraform clone using the operator's SSH credentials or agent. There is no ssh:: module source type (B), the version argument never carries addresses (C), and SSH cloning is a standard supported path (D).

q: A `terraform apply` was killed mid-run and now every command fails with `Error acquiring the state lock`. You have confirmed no Terraform process is running anywhere. What is the safe remediation?
options: Delete the state file and re-apply from scratch
Wait 24 hours for the lock to expire on its own
Run `terraform init -upgrade` to clear the lock
`terraform force-unlock ` — manually release the stuck lock, only because you verified no run is actually in progress
explain: force-unlock releases a stale lock — safe only when you are certain nothing is running, since unlocking under a live run invites corruption. A destroys your state record. C does not touch locks. D invents an expiry; stuck locks persist until released.
