q: A cloud architect wants one team to manage AWS accounts, Azure subscriptions, and an on-premises OpenStack deployment without three separate toolchains. Which Terraform capability addresses this directly?
options: Provider ecosystem with a single core workflow for cloud and on-premises platforms
A built-in converter that rewrites OpenStack templates into ARM
Guaranteed feature parity between every provider on day one
Automatic migration of workloads between platforms without configuration changes
explain: Terraform's provider ecosystem plus one HCL and CLI workflow is what unifies cloud and on-premises management. It does not convert template formats, guarantee day-one parity for every provider feature, or migrate workloads without configuration work.

q: A configuration uses backend "gcs". What does that backend store state in?
options: A PostgreSQL database table
An Azure storage container
A local file replicated to Google Drive
A Google Cloud Storage bucket, optionally under a prefix path
explain: The gcs backend stores the state object in a named Cloud Storage bucket, with a prefix to organize objects within it. It does not use Azure containers, Postgres tables, or Drive-synced local files.

q: A consultant reviews an estate where one project holds forty unrelated workspaces owned by five different teams, and access complaints are constant. Which redesign best matches the intended use of projects?
options: Rename the workspaces with team prefixes and leave the project structure unchanged
Create projects aligned to teams or products and grant team access at the project level, keeping workspace permissions for finer control
Move every workspace into a single organization-wide project to simplify the list view
Delete the project and manage all access purely with API tokens shared by email
explain: Projects are meant to group related workspaces under a team or product governance boundary, so realigning projects to ownership fixes access at the right level. Consolidating further worsens the problem, shared tokens are a security failure, and renaming changes nothing about access control.

q: An engineer writes a shell script that creates a VPC, then a subnet, then a security group, executing each AWS CLI call in order. A colleague proposes replacing it with Terraform. What is the fundamental difference between the two approaches?
options: The shell script describes ordered steps to execute, while Terraform describes the desired end state and determines the steps itself
The shell script is declarative and Terraform is imperative
There is no difference; both are Infrastructure as Code
Terraform runs shell scripts faster than bash does
explain: The shell script is imperative — it lists steps in order and knows nothing about the desired end state. Terraform is declarative — you declare what you want and it computes the how, including ordering from the dependency graph. A reverses the terms. C is nonsense. D is wrong: a hand-run script with no state, no plan, and no versioning of intent is not IaC practice.

q: Which two summaries of terraform fmt flag behavior are correct? (Choose two.)
options: -recursive extends formatting to subdirectories instead of only the current directory
-list=false adds JSON and state files to the set of files fmt will format
-check reports files that need formatting and exits non-zero, without rewriting anything
-write=false rewrites files in place but keeps a backup copy
explain: -recursive widens fmt beyond the current directory (A), and -check is the read-only CI gate whose exit code signals unformatted files (C). -write=false does the opposite of B: it prevents writing. -list=false (D) only controls whether file names are listed; it never changes which file types fmt handles.

q: Which two statements about provider installation are true? (Choose two.)
options: Each provider is a separate binary whose version is managed independently of Terraform Core
Terraform Core ships with every official provider compiled in, and init only activates them
Installing a provider once makes it available to every project on the machine without init
terraform init installs providers into the working directory's .terraform/providers area for that project
explain: Installation is per working directory: init places the selected provider binaries under .terraform/providers, and each provider versions independently of Core. Nothing is compiled into Core, and a provider present in one project does not excuse another project from running init.

q: What does terraform apply -refresh-only do that terraform plan -refresh-only does not?
options: There is no terraform apply -refresh-only; only the plan form exists
apply -refresh-only actually writes the refreshed state to the backend, while plan -refresh-only only previews the refresh
apply -refresh-only also applies pending configuration changes in the same run
plan -refresh-only writes state and apply -refresh-only only previews it
explain: Refresh-only has a preview and a commit form: plan shows what state would learn from reality, and apply -refresh-only persists that updated state without proposing configuration-driven changes. Neither form applies normal config changes.

q: A data source references an attribute of a resource that Terraform itself manages (e.g., the ID of an `aws_instance` created in the same configuration). When is that data source read?
options: Always during plan, before any resources are created
It is read once at init time and cached
Data sources can never reference managed resources — the configuration is invalid
Its read is deferred until apply, because the value it needs does not exist yet
explain: Data sources are read during plan when possible, but if they depend on a not-yet-created resource, the read must wait until apply when the value exists. A ignores the ordering problem. C is false — this pattern is legal and common. D invents init-time caching.

q: With the local backend, an engineer lists the working directory and finds both terraform.tfstate and a terraform.tfstate.d directory. Which statement is correct?
options: terraform.tfstate is a backup that Terraform restores automatically if terraform.tfstate.d is deleted
terraform.tfstate holds the default workspace's state, while terraform.tfstate.d holds state files for the non-default workspaces
terraform.tfstate.d stores saved plan files for all workspaces
Both locations hold identical copies of every workspace's state for redundancy
explain: The root terraform.tfstate is specifically the default workspace's state; each named workspace gets its own file under terraform.tfstate.d/<workspace>/. It is not an automatic backup of the workspace directory, and saved plans are separate files created only with plan -out.

q: A release manager wants merges to the main branch of a low-risk sandbox workspace to deploy without anyone opening the HCP Terraform UI, while keeping the same repository's production workspace fully manual. Which combination achieves this?
options: Connect both workspaces to the same branch and delete the production workspace
Enable auto-apply on the sandbox workspace only, leaving production requiring manual confirmation
Enable auto-apply at the organization level so every workspace deploys on merge
Set both workspaces to local execution mode and rely on developer laptops
explain: Auto-apply is a per-workspace setting, so the sandbox can apply automatically after successful plans while production still waits for confirmation. There is no organization-wide auto-apply switch that should be used this way, local execution defeats the goal, and deleting production is obviously wrong.

q: An architect describes replacing a server entirely with a freshly built image for every change instead of patching the running server. Which concept is this?
options: Immutable infrastructure, because servers are replaced rather than modified in place
State drift, because the new server differs from the old one
Imperative management, because replacement requires ordered steps
Mutable infrastructure, because the server changes over time
explain: Immutable infrastructure treats servers as disposable: changes ship as new instances and old ones are terminated, avoiding configuration drift from in-place patching. Mutable infrastructure is the opposite model of updating running servers over their lifetime.

q: How do locals differ from input variables in terms of who can change them?
options: There is no difference; both accept -var assignments
Local values are fixed by expressions in the configuration and cannot be overridden by callers, tfvars, or flags, while variable values are supplied from outside the configuration
Variables are computed, locals are typed in by the operator
Locals can be set from the command line, variables cannot
explain: This is the defining distinction: locals are internal constants/expressions owned by the author, whereas variables are the configuration's external interface. Callers, files, and flags change variables only, which rules out A and C, and neither type is typed in interactively as D describes.

q: A configuration pins a provider with version = "= 4.2.0" in required_providers. The registry also offers 4.2.1 and 4.3.0. What will init install?
options: Exactly 4.2.0, because the = operator admits one version only
4.2.1, because patch upgrades are always permitted
Whichever version the lock file prefers, ignoring the constraint
4.3.0, because init always prefers the newest release
explain: The = operator is an exact pin: only 4.2.0 satisfies it, so init must select that build or fail. Newer patch or minor releases never satisfy an exact constraint, and the lock file records selections rather than overriding constraints.

q: A new team member asks why the configuration bothers with an output for the load balancer DNS name when the team could find it in the cloud console. What is the strongest answer?
options: Outputs make the load balancer cheaper to run
The console cannot display DNS names
The output makes the value part of the configuration's contract: printed after apply, stored in state, queryable by scripts, and consumable by parent modules without console hunting
Outputs are required or Terraform will not apply
explain: Outputs turn important results into a stable, automatable interface to the deployment rather than tribal knowledge found by clicking around a console. Outputs are optional for apply to succeed (A), consoles do display DNS names (C), and outputs have no effect on cloud pricing (D).

q: An apply finishes with errors on a module's resources while the root resources succeeded. The team fixes the module code. What is the standard recovery path?
options: Delete the module resources from state with state rm so they can be recreated
Restore the pre-apply state backup before planning again
Run terraform plan to see the remaining diff against the partially updated state, then terraform apply again to converge; no rollback or state surgery is needed for a normal provider error
Run terraform destroy to empty the workspace, then apply from scratch
explain: Partial applies converge by re-planning against the state that records what succeeded; the remaining diff is just the unfinished work. Destroying everything or restoring backups is disproportionate, and state rm would orphan real resources that Terraform is correctly tracking.

q: A generated configuration file from plan -generate-config-out is moved into production configuration verbatim, and the next plan proposes changing dozens of attributes on the freshly imported resources and replacing two of them. What went wrong, and what is the correct practice?
options: Generated blocks record every attribute of the real objects verbatim, including computed and defaulted values that fight the provider when declared explicitly, so generated code must be reviewed, pruned to intended arguments, and reconciled until plan is clean
The generated file was corrupted in transit, and regenerating it always produces plan-clean code
Generated configuration only works when the state file is deleted before the first real plan
Import blocks were left in place, which forces generated blocks to propose changes forever
explain: Generated configuration is a faithful dump rather than idiomatic configuration: declaring every returned attribute can create conflicts and force replacements, which is why the documented workflow is to review, trim, and iterate until the verification plan shows no changes. Regeneration reproduces the same dump, leftover import blocks are harmless, and deleting state would orphan everything just adopted.

q: Reviewing a plan whose summary reads: Plan: 6 to add, 2 to change, 0 to destroy. A reviewer asks how many existing resources the apply will permanently delete. What is the number?
explain: The "to destroy" count is 0; those are the existing resources apply will delete. Additions create new resources and changes update existing ones in place.

q: Which of the following are valid module source types Terraform can install at init? (Choose two.)
options: An npm package name such as lodash@4.17.21
A generic Git source such as git::https://example.com/repo.git
A Terraform Registry address such as terraform-aws-modules/vpc/aws
A Docker image reference such as docker.io/library/nginx
explain: Registry addresses and forced git:: sources are both documented module source types installed during init. Terraform has no Docker-image (B) or npm (D) module sources; those ecosystems package unrelated artifacts.

q: A platform team is documenting the VCS-driven workflow for new hires. Which two statements about it are accurate? (Choose two.)
options: Developers must keep a terminal session open for the entire run or it is cancelled
Pushes to a workspace's connected branch automatically queue runs in that workspace
Pull requests produce speculative plans that reviewers can use to judge infrastructure impact before merging
Every speculative plan is automatically applied once all code reviewers approve the pull request
explain: VCS-driven workspaces queue runs from branch pushes and produce non-applying speculative plans on pull requests for review. Runs execute server-side with no terminal held open, and reviewer approval never applies a speculative plan; only a post-merge run can apply.

q: While debugging a configuration, an engineer evaluates `distinct(["b", "a", "b", "c", "a"])` in the console. What does Terraform return?
explain: distinct() removes duplicate elements while preserving the order of first occurrence, so b stays first even though a sorts earlier.

q: Which two version constraints both allow provider version 5.3.0 to be selected? (Choose two.)
options: version = "~> 5.3.1"
version = "= 5.3.1"
version = "~> 5.0"
explain: Both ~> 5.0 (>= 5.0.0, < 6.0.0) and the explicit range >= 5.0, < 6.0 admit 5.3.0. The three-component ~> 5.3.1 sets a floor of 5.3.1, so 5.3.0 falls below it and is excluded, and = 5.3.1 is an exact pin naming a different build, so neither distractor can select 5.3.0.

q: An engineer lists resources with terraform state list and sees module.app.aws_instance.web[0]. What does the [0] portion indicate?
options: That the module is at version zero in the registry
That instance is the zero-indexed instance of a resource created with count
That the resource failed zero times during the last apply
That the state serial is zero for that resource
explain: In a state address, [0] is the instance key produced by count, identifying a specific instance of the resource. It has nothing to do with failure counts, module versions, or the overall state serial.

The pipeline mirrors the safe workflow left to right: fmt -check catches style issues cheaply, validate catches static errors before any cloud calls, plan -out freezes the exact change set, the manual gate reviews that artifact, and apply executes only the reviewed file. Running apply before the gate or before plan -out, as in the main distractor, destroys the review guarantee because there is no fixed plan left to approve.
options: terraform validate, then terraform apply tfplan, then terraform fmt -check, then terraform plan -out=tfplan, then a manual approval gate
terraform apply tfplan, then terraform plan -out=tfplan, then terraform validate, then terraform fmt -check, then a manual approval gate
terraform plan -out=tfplan, then terraform fmt -check, then terraform apply tfplan, then terraform validate, then a manual approval gate
terraform fmt -check, then terraform validate, then terraform plan -out=tfplan, then a manual approval gate, then terraform apply tfplan
q: A CI/CD pipeline for a Terraform project is being assembled from individual stages: formatting check, syntax and schema validation, generating a saved plan, human approval, and executing that plan. Which ordering correctly reflects the end-to-end workflow the pipeline should enforce?

A lifecycle block on a queue references another resource so the queue is recreated whenever that resource changes. At an operational level, which feature is in play, without needing to author it here?
options: replace_triggered_by, which forces replacement of the queue when the referenced resource or attribute changes
prevent_destroy, which schedules recreation instead of destruction
create_before_destroy, which triggers replacement on every apply
ignore_changes, which recreates resources when listed attributes change
explain: replace_triggered_by ties one resource's replacement to changes in another resource, which matches the queue being recreated when its trigger changes. ignore_changes suppresses diffs, prevent_destroy blocks destruction, and create_before_destroy only reorders a replacement already happening.

q: Before computing its diff, `terraform plan` first reaches out to providers to read the current values of managed resources. What is this step called, and why does it matter?
options: Rebase — it rewrites the state file to match the configuration
Locking — it prevents other engineers from running plan concurrently
Reconciliation — it deletes resources that are no longer in the configuration
Refresh — it syncs state with real-world values so the plan is computed against reality, which is also how drift gets detected
explain: Plan's first phase is refresh: read live values into state, then diff. That is why plan detects drift — reality changed, so the diff shows corrections. A describes destroy behavior. C invents a term. D describes state locking, a separate backend feature.

q: A team writes a removed block with lifecycle destroy = true explicitly. What are they declaring?
options: That the object should be moved to another module automatically
That state should be encrypted for that resource only
That Terraform should remove the resource from state and destroy the real object
That Terraform should keep the object in state forever as a placeholder
explain: destroy = true inside a removed block is the explicit form of the default: forget and destroy. It is the opposite of destroy = false, which preserves the real object while dropping it from state.

q: A team is scoping what their validation stage can and cannot promise reviewers. Which two checks does terraform validate NOT perform? (Choose two.)
options: Confirming that the identity running Terraform holds the IAM permissions an apply would need
Confirming the internal consistency of references between resources
Verifying that block types used in the configuration exist
Looking up referenced data sources in the cloud account to confirm they return values
explain: Validate never evaluates permissions (A) and never calls cloud APIs to resolve data sources or any other live values (D); both belong to plan and apply. Block-type existence (B) and reference consistency (C) are squarely inside validate's static checking, which is why they are the distractors here.

q: A child database module declares variable "db_name" with a validation block requiring lowercase letters and a custom error_message. The root module passes db_name = "Prod_DB" and terraform plan fails, showing the child's error message. What does this demonstrate?
options: The plan failure means the root module needs its own copy of the same validation block before the child's can work
Variable validation declared inside a child module is enforced on values the caller passes in, so invalid inputs are rejected at plan time with the module author's own message
The child's validation was ignored and the failure must have come from the database provider
Validation blocks only run when the child module is applied as a standalone root
explain: Input variable validation travels with the module: when a caller supplies a value that violates the child's validation condition, Terraform reports the author's error_message during plan, before any resources are created. Validation is not root-only (B), the root needs no duplicate block (C), and the custom message in the error proves the child's check fired rather than a provider error (D).

q: A project pins its provider with version = "~> 5.1.0, != 5.1.2" and Core with required_version = ">= 1.10, < 2.0". The registry offers provider 5.1.2, 5.1.5, and 5.2.0, and the workstation runs Core 1.12. After init -upgrade, which pairing is installed and running?
options: Core 1.12 with provider 5.2.0, because -upgrade always takes the newest minor
Core auto-upgraded to 2.0 with provider 5.1.5, because < 2.0 permits the boundary
Core 1.12 with provider 5.1.2, because != is ignored once -upgrade runs
Core 1.12 with provider 5.1.5: Core satisfies its range, and 5.1.5 is the newest provider build inside >= 5.1.0, < 5.2.0 that is not excluded
explain: Core 1.12 sits inside >= 1.10 and < 2.0, and Core is never auto-upgraded by init. For the provider, the pessimistic ceiling excludes 5.2.0 and the != clause excludes 5.1.2 even under -upgrade, leaving 5.1.5 as the only newest valid selection.

q: An import fails with an error saying the given address does not exist in the configuration, even though the instance ID is correct. What is the most likely missing step in the CLI workflow?
options: The provider version constraint excludes imported resources
The backend was not migrated to a remote location first
The matching resource block was never written before running terraform import
terraform init was run more than once in the directory
explain: CLI import binds a real object to an address that configuration must already declare, so a correct ID with a missing block produces exactly this failure. Backend location, provider constraints, and repeated init runs do not create the address the import is looking for.

q: Bulk-importing thirty existing subnets, an engineer writes one import block with for_each over a map of subnet IDs paired with a for_each resource. After apply, plan still wants to replace two subnets. What is the most likely cause and fix?
options: The import blocks must be deleted before plan can ever report no changes
Bulk import only works for twenty-nine resources, so one subnet must stay unmanaged
Two map entries pair IDs with the wrong resource instances or their blocks declare attributes that force replacement, so correct the pairings and align those blocks with the real subnets
for_each import blocks always replace the first two resources as a confirmation step
explain: With bulk imports, a replacement proposal points at mismatched pairings or configuration values that cannot update in place for those specific instances, and fixing the map or the blocks resolves it. There is no twenty-nine resource limit, no sacrificial first-two behavior, and leftover import blocks do not cause replacement plans.

q: A private registry module is published as version 1.4.0, then a backward-compatible fix is released as 1.4.1 and a breaking change is planned. Why does the registry's versioning matter to consuming workspaces?
options: Only version 1.0.0 of any private module can ever be consumed
Versions are decorative labels that Terraform ignores when downloading modules
Consumers pin or constrain module versions in their configuration, so they adopt 1.4.1 deliberately and are not surprised by the breaking release
Versioning forces every workspace to upgrade to the newest release immediately
explain: Registry versioning lets each consumer select and pin the module version it has validated, making upgrades deliberate. Nothing forces instant upgrades, Terraform actively uses version constraints at init, and all published versions are consumable.

q: An SRE wants to preview exactly what terraform destroy would do tomorrow, including order and scope, without any risk of execution. Which command should the SRE run today?
options: terraform destroy -auto-approve
terraform apply -refresh-only
terraform plan -destroy
terraform plan -refresh=false
explain: terraform plan -destroy generates the destroy plan for review with zero execution, showing everything in state slated for removal. destroy -auto-approve would execute the teardown, and the other options neither preview nor perform a destroy.

q: An engineer runs `terraform import aws_instance.legacy i-0abcd1234` on the CLI and the import succeeds, but the next `terraform plan` proposes to change several attributes of the instance. Why?
options: CLI imports always recreate the resource on the next apply
The instance ID changed during import
The import failed silently
Import adopts the real object into state but does not generate configuration — the (possibly empty or mismatched) resource block differs from reality, so plan proposes reconciling the diff
explain: EXAM TRAP: import never writes configuration for you. It maps the real object into state; your resource block is your own declaration, and any mismatch shows up as a planned diff. That is why the workflow is import -> plan -> reconcile config -> apply. A is wrong (the import succeeded). C is false — import never recreates. D is nonsense.

q: A deployment must replace a single aws_instance whose user data changed in a way the provider cannot apply in place, but the plan currently shows only an in-place update for a different attribute. Which apply-time option forces replacement of that one instance?
options: terraform apply -replace=aws_instance.web
terraform apply -destroy=aws_instance.web
terraform apply -refresh-only
terraform apply -target=aws_instance.web
explain: -replace=ADDRESS on plan or apply forces Terraform to treat the named object as needing destroy-and-recreate even when the diff alone would not. -target only narrows scope, refresh-only changes no resources, and -destroy is not a per-resource apply flag.

q: A team is writing a required_providers entry for the AWS provider. Which two elements belong in that entry? (Choose two.)
options: A version constraint selecting which provider releases are acceptable
The AWS region the provider should operate in
An alias assigning the entry to one account
A source address such as hashicorp/aws identifying where the provider comes from
explain: A required_providers entry declares exactly where a provider comes from (source) and which releases are acceptable (version constraint). Region is provider configuration and lives in the provider block, and aliases are also declared in provider blocks, never in required_providers.

q: Plans have started showing an unexpected diff on a load balancer that nobody admits to changing, and the team needs evidence of what the provider is actually returning. Which step best supports the investigation?
options: Lower TF_LOG to ERROR so the diff output becomes clearer
Delete the load balancer from state so the next plan starts fresh
Run terraform fmt on the configuration to normalize the diff
Enable DEBUG or TRACE logging for a run to capture the provider's returned values and Terraform's diff reasoning
explain: Unexpected diffs are a classic reason to raise log verbosity: detailed logs show refreshed values and provider responses that explain where the difference originates. Formatting changes nothing semantically, removing state orphans the resource, and quieter logs hide the very evidence needed.

q: An operator runs terraform plan -destroy and sees 14 resources to destroy, but the real goal is deleting only the 2 resources from a retired module. What is the cleanest next step?
options: Approve the destroy plan and rebuild the other 12 resources afterward
Edit the state file by hand to delete the 2 entries
Remove the retired module's blocks (or the module call) from the configuration and run a normal plan and apply, which will propose destroying exactly those 2 resources
Run terraform destroy -auto-approve and stop it after 2 resources
explain: Scoping deletion through configuration is the routine, reviewable path: the normal plan then shows exactly the retired resources as destroys. Approving a 14-resource teardown to delete 2 is reckless, interrupting destroy mid-run is unreliable, and hand-editing state is never the clean answer.

q: While debugging a configuration, an engineer evaluates `join("-", ["qa", "prod"])` in the console. What is displayed?
options: qa-prod
qa/prod
qaprod
qa,prod
explain: join() concatenates the list elements with the given separator between them.

q: A locals block defines a value with the expression `values({ "b-team" = "ops", "a-team" = "dev", "c-team" = "sec" })`. What does Terraform return?
options: ["ops", "dev", "sec"]
["a-team", "b-team", "c-team"]
["dev", "ops", "sec"]
["sec", "ops", "dev"]
explain: values() returns values in the order of the sorted keys (a-team, b-team, c-team), so the values come out as dev, ops, sec.

q: A load balancer listener references a target group, and the target group references nothing back. During destroy, in what order does Terraform act, and why?
options: Both are destroyed simultaneously with no ordering
The target group is destroyed first because it was referenced
Alphabetical order by resource type
The listener is destroyed before the target group, because destroy reverses the dependency order implied by the reference
explain: Dependencies are created first and destroyed last: creation follows the reference graph forward, destruction runs it in reverse so dependents are removed before what they depend on. Alphabetical order (A) and simultaneity (B) ignore the graph, and D reverses the correct destroy order.

q: Inside a resource using for_each over a map of environments, which expression gives the current instance's map key?
options: var.key from the input map variable
self.key, referring to the resource itself
each.key, paired with each.value for the corresponding map value
count.index, which works for both count and for_each
explain: for_each exposes each.key and each.value for the instance being configured; count.index belongs only to count-based resources. Self references are invalid for a resource's own attributes (C), and the map variable itself does not provide a per-instance key expression (D).

q: A configuration sets required_version = ">= 1.9" but a developer runs it with Terraform 1.7.5. What happens?
options: Terraform automatically downloads Core 1.9 and restarts itself
The constraint is ignored because required_version only applies in HCP Terraform
Terraform warns once and then runs normally
Terraform stops with an error that the running Core version does not satisfy required_version, before planning or applying
explain: required_version is a hard gate: when the running Core binary falls outside the constraint, Terraform refuses to run the configuration. It never warns and continues, never self-upgrades, and the check applies to the plain CLI as well.

q: A variable set is applied at the project level rather than to individual workspaces. A workspace is later added to that project. What happens to the set's variables for the new workspace?
options: The workspace is blocked from joining the project until the set is removed
The new workspace inherits the project-level variable set, so its runs receive those values without anyone applying the set workspace by workspace
Nothing, because project-level sets only affect workspaces that existed when the set was applied
The values are converted into Terraform code defaults inside the workspace
explain: Project-level variable sets cascade to the project's workspaces, including ones added later, giving teams one attachment point per project. The set is not frozen to existing members, it does not block project membership, and values stay configuration data rather than becoming code defaults.

q: A local references a data source attribute: 'locals { vpc_cidr = data.aws_vpc.main.cidr_block }'. What does this illustrate?
options: Locals can only contain literal strings and numbers
The data source becomes managed once a local references it
Locals can be built from any expression available in the configuration, including data source and resource attributes, not just literals
Data sources are a kind of local value
explain: A local is a named expression, so it can wrap data reads, resource attributes, variables, and combinations of them. Restricting locals to literals (A) is false, data sources remain a separate read mechanism (C), and referencing an object never changes its managed status (D).

q: A team evaluates Pulumi-style imperative code habits against Terraform for an exam-style decision: they want the tool to decide creation order from dependencies automatically. Which Terraform behavior provides this?
options: Terraform asks the operator to confirm each resource's order at apply time
Terraform builds a dependency graph from references and orders operations from that graph
Engineers must number each resource block in sequence
Terraform runs resources in file order from top to bottom
explain: Declarative references let Terraform construct the dependency graph and sequence creation, update, and deletion automatically. File order and manual numbering are imperative habits, and no per-resource ordering prompt exists in the workflow.

q: A team debates `terraform import` (CLI) versus `import` blocks. What is the 004 exam's framing of the difference?
options: The CLI can import resources that import blocks cannot
Import blocks are deprecated; the CLI is the modern approach
They are identical in every way
The CLI command is a one-shot imperative action; the `import` block is declarative, version-controlled, peer-reviewable, and shows up in `terraform plan` before anything happens
explain: 004 prefers import blocks because they fit the IaC model: reviewed in PRs, stored in version control, and previewed in plans. The CLI still works but is imperative and invisible until run. A erases a real distinction. C reverses the deprecation direction. D is false — both import the same resource types.

q: Right after an import, plan unexpectedly proposes to destroy and recreate the imported server instead of reporting no changes. What does that signal?
options: The provider is asking for the import to be run a second time
The written configuration still mismatches reality on an attribute that forces replacement, such as an identifier or image that cannot be updated in place
Destroy proposals are the normal confirmation that an import succeeded
The import silently failed and the server was never added to state
explain: A replacement proposal after import means some declared value differs from the real object in a way the provider cannot change in place, so the fix is to align the block with the object's actual attributes. A failed import would error rather than plan a replacement, and a destroy proposal is a warning sign, never a success signal.

q: A module outputs the value of `cidrhost("10.1.2.0/24", 5)`. What does Terraform return?
explain: cidrhost() returns the address at host number 5 within the prefix, counting from the network address 10.1.2.0, which gives 10.1.2.5.

The gate is a human control point on a fixed artifact: reviewers inspect the precise plan that apply will execute and can reject it before anything changes. It does not download providers, encrypt the plan, or regenerate it with a second refresh, and the main distractor about provider downloads confuses the gate with init and -upgrade behavior that happens much earlier in the workflow.
options: It lets a human review the exact saved plan that will be executed and stop the deployment if it contains unexpected creates, updates, or destroys, before any real infrastructure changes
It allows Terraform to refresh state a second time so the saved plan is regenerated with fresher data
It gives the CI runner time to download newer provider versions before apply runs
It encrypts the saved plan file while the pipeline waits for the next stage
q: In a pipeline, the plan stage finishes and the job pauses at a manual approval gate before the apply stage is allowed to run terraform apply on the saved plan file. What is the primary purpose of inserting that gate between plan and apply?
Why does the exam group Terraform apart from Ansible, Chef, and Puppet even though playbooks and cookbooks are also code?
options: Because HashiCorp tools use HCL and the others use no language at all
Because Terraform's primary scope is provisioning infrastructure through provider APIs, while theirs is configuring and maintaining software on existing systems
Because configuration management tools never automate anything
Because those tools cannot be stored in version control
explain: Scope is the grouping principle: provisioning versus configuration management, even though all are code and all automate. The other tools are versionable, written in real languages and formats, and plainly do automate configuration tasks.

q: A provider returns a cryptic error during apply. You need maximum diagnostic detail written to a file for a bug report. Which environment setup does this?
options: `TF_DEBUG=1`
`TF_LOG=OFF` with `TF_LOG_PATH=./terraform.log`
`TF_LOG=TRACE` with `TF_LOG_PATH=./terraform.log` — TRACE is the most verbose level and TF_LOG_PATH redirects logs to a file
`terraform apply -verbose`
explain: TF_LOG controls verbosity (TRACE > DEBUG > INFO > WARN > ERROR) and TF_LOG_PATH redirects from stderr to a file. B and C are not real settings. D sets logging OFF — the opposite of diagnostics. Remember to disable verbose logging afterward: TRACE logs are huge and can contain secrets.

q: A reviewer reads: Plan: 4 to add, 0 to change, 0 to destroy. A stakeholder asks how many existing resources will be modified or removed by this apply. What is the answer?
options: The counts cannot be interpreted without the state file password
None; all four actions are creations of new resources and nothing existing is changed or destroyed
Two will be changed and two destroyed, splitting the total evenly
Four existing resources will be modified, one per add
explain: With 0 to change and 0 to destroy, the apply only creates 4 new objects and touches nothing that already exists. Adds are never modifications of existing resources, and the summary line is fully interpretable on its own.

q: Terraform must tear down a VPC, its subnets, and the instances inside them. In what order does terraform destroy remove these resources, and why?
options: In the same order they were created, VPC first, to mirror the apply log
In reverse dependency order — instances first, then subnets, then the VPC — so a resource is never destroyed while something depending on it still needs it
In alphabetical order by resource address
In random order, because teardown order does not matter to providers
explain: Destroy walks the dependency graph in reverse of creation: dependents go first, dependencies last, which is what providers require (an instance must be gone before its subnet and VPC can be removed). Creation order, alphabetical order, and random order would all strand dependencies.

q: A developer accidentally committed terraform.tfstate, containing a database password and an access key in plaintext, to the team's Git repository, and the commit was pushed and cloned by several teammates. Which two remediation steps are required? (Choose two.)
options: Rewrite the repository history to purge the state file and move state to a remote backend, adding the local state file to .gitignore
Base64-encode the state file in the repository so the secrets are no longer readable
Delete the file in a new commit and consider the incident closed, since the file no longer appears in the latest tree
Rotate or revoke the credentials and secrets that were in the state file, because they must be treated as exposed
explain: Secrets committed to Git must be rotated because clones and history retain them, and the file must be purged from history while state moves to a proper backend. Deleting the file in a later commit leaves the secret fully recoverable from history, and base64 is a reversible encoding, not protection.

q: During an incident review, an auditor finds a run that was queued at 02:00 with no associated commit, pull request, or terminal session in any log the team controls. Investigation shows a scheduler in their deployment platform created it. Which workflow produced this run?
options: Speculative planning, which queues full runs overnight by default
The VCS-driven workflow, triggered by a deleted branch
The API-driven workflow, invoked by the deployment platform's automation
The CLI-driven workflow, triggered by an unattended laptop waking from sleep
explain: Runs created programmatically by external automation come from the API-driven workflow. There was no commit or terminal session to support the VCS or CLI explanations, and speculative plans are previews tied to pull requests, never unattended full runs.

q: A module variable is declared as object({ name = string, size = number, tags = optional(map(string), {}) }). A caller passes only name and size. What happens?
options: The call fails because every object attribute must always be supplied
The tags attribute becomes a random map chosen by Terraform
Optional attributes are converted to required attributes at plan time
The call succeeds because optional() marks tags as omittable and supplies its default when absent
explain: The optional() modifier inside an object type constraint makes an attribute omittable and lets a default be supplied when the caller omits it. Without optional(), a missing attribute would fail type conversion; optional() exists precisely for evolving object schemas.

q: A platform team provides outputs vpc_id and private_subnet_ids from its state. A service team hardcodes those same IDs after copying them from the console. What does the service team lose compared with using terraform_remote_state?
options: The ability to ever change the IDs in their own configuration
Access to the VPC, because hardcoding blocks provider calls
A state file of their own for their service resources
Automatic updates when the platform team changes the network, because hardcoded copies do not track the source state's outputs
explain: Reading remote state outputs creates a live dependency on the published values, so platform changes flow into the consumer's next plan. Hardcoded copies silently go stale, which is the maintainability problem remote state is meant to solve.

q: An organization owner wants a junior platform group to administer one project's workspaces without giving them control over organization membership, billing, or other projects. Which assignment best follows least-privilege in HCP Terraform?
options: Share the owner team's API token with the group for convenience
Grant the group admin permission on that project's workspaces only, leaving organization-level management with the owners team
Give the group write permission on every workspace in the organization
Make the group organization owners so nothing blocks their work
explain: Workspace admin scoped to the relevant workspaces gives the group the control it needs without organization-wide powers. Organization ownership and org-wide write are excessive, and sharing API tokens destroys accountability and is never an acceptable access model.

q: A configuration uses backend "azurerm" for state. Which set of details would you expect that backend to need at a concept level?
options: A resource group, a storage account, a container, and a key naming the state blob
An HCP Terraform organization and workspace token only
A DynamoDB table and an S3 bucket name
A GCS bucket and a prefix only, with no storage account concept
explain: The azurerm backend stores state as a blob, so it identifies the resource group, storage account, container, and blob key. DynamoDB belongs to the classic S3 pattern and GCS or remote backends use their own distinct settings.

q: After running terraform state replace-provider, what should the team expect on the next plan if configuration provider requirements were also updated correctly?
options: All resources are recreated because a new provider always starts empty
No destroy and recreate solely because of the provider change; resources stay mapped under the new provider
The old provider continues to manage resources indefinitely in parallel
State is deleted and must be rebuilt with import for every resource
explain: When required_providers and state agree on the new provider address, the same real objects remain managed with no recreation caused by the switch itself. A mismatch, by contrast, would produce confusing plans until the addresses align.

Terraform evaluates required_version before doing real work, and 1.12.3 falls outside >= 1.10, < 1.12, so the run stops at startup by design. The distractor about providers is wrong because this gate is about the Core binary itself, not about any provider release.
options: required_version is checked against the running Core binary at the start of a run; the workstation must run a Core version inside the constraint, or the team must deliberately widen the constraint
Plan never checks required_version; the failure must be a corrupted terraform binary
The error comes from the backend; running init -reconfigure bypasses the Core version check
The provider versions are too new for Core 1.12; pinning older providers removes the error
q: A configuration declares required_version = ">= 1.10, < 1.12" in its terraform block. A workstation running Terraform 1.12.3 refuses to run even terraform plan, failing immediately with an unsupported Terraform Core version error. Why, and what is the fix?
How do Terraform Core and a provider plugin actually exchange requests while a plan or apply runs?
options: Core loads the provider's Go source code and compiles it into itself at init
Core launches the provider as a separate process and communicates with it over a plugin protocol (RPC)
Providers communicate through the registry, which relays each API call
The provider polls the state file every few seconds for work
explain: The plugin model is process-based: Core starts the provider binary and talks to it through a versioned plugin protocol over RPC. Source code is never compiled into Core at runtime, providers do not poll state, and the registry only distributes plugins, never relays run traffic.

Cattle are interchangeable and disposable: a failed unit is terminated and replaced from the same code-defined build. Pets are the opposite model of named, uniquely tended servers that engineers try to heal in place, which does not scale and cannot be reproduced reliably.
options: Each server gets a name, hand-tuned settings, and individual nursing back to health when it fails
Only one physical server is used so it can be closely watched
Servers are identical, interchangeable, and replaced from code instead of being individually repaired
Servers are kept running forever because replacing them is forbidden
q: A gaming company treats its game servers as cattle rather than pets. What does that mean in practice?
Which two capabilities are provided by HCP Terraform for teams using the hosted platform? (Choose two.)
options: Workspace-based remote state management with access controls for teams
Remote runs, where plans and applies execute in HashiCorp's hosted environment
Offline applies with no network connection to any system
A modified terraform binary that embeds every provider
explain: HCP Terraform's hosted value is remote execution of runs and centrally managed, workspace-scoped state with team access controls. Providers remain separate plugins used by the standard CLI workflow, and a hosted platform inherently requires connectivity rather than enabling offline applies.

q: During a code review, a teammate asks what `sort([9, 28, 25])` evaluates to. What is displayed?
explain: sort() orders the elements ascending: 9, 25, 28. The original written order is not preserved.

q: A module outputs the value of `distinct(["b", "a", "b", "c", "a"])`. What is the result?
explain: distinct() removes duplicate elements while preserving the order of first occurrence, so b stays first even though a sorts earlier.

q: Which variable types are valid in a Terraform variable declaration? (Choose two.)
options: provider, for passing provider configurations as values
number, for numeric values such as a replica count
template, for files rendered at apply time
string, for text values such as a region name
explain: string and number (along with bool) are Terraform's primitive variable types. There is no template type or provider type for variable values; providers are configured in provider blocks, not passed as ordinary variable values.

q: A company has a manually created database (ID `db-0abc123`) that must come under Terraform management without any downtime or recreation. What is the modern, exam-preferred approach?
options: Import is impossible for databases; only new resources can be managed
Write an `import` block (`to` + `id`) plus a matching resource block, then plan and apply — the import is configuration-driven, reviewable, and visible in the plan
Run `terraform destroy` first, then let Terraform recreate the database
Copy the database's configuration into a data source
explain: The 004-era pattern is the configuration-driven import block: write it with a matching resource block, review the import in the plan, apply to adopt. B destroys production data. C only reads; it never manages. D is false — import works for any importable resource type.

q: A script needs just the plain string value of the output named bucket_name, with no quotes or formatting, for use in a shell variable. Which command fits?
options: terraform output -json bucket_name
terraform plan -raw bucket_name
terraform show bucket_name
terraform output -raw bucket_name
explain: The -raw flag prints a primitive output value as a plain string without JSON quoting, which is exactly what shell capture needs. -json would include quotes and structure (B), plan does not print stored outputs this way (C), and terraform show displays state or plans, not a single raw output (D).

q: A team keeps environment-specific values in a file named staging.tfvars that is not auto-loaded. Which command uses it?
options: terraform output -var-file="staging.tfvars"
terraform plan, because all .tfvars files load automatically
terraform init -var-file="staging.tfvars"
terraform plan -var-file="staging.tfvars", passing the file explicitly
explain: Only terraform.tfvars and *.auto.tfvars load automatically; any other values file must be named with -var-file at plan or apply time. A plain plan would not read staging.tfvars (B), and init and output do not consume variable files for this purpose (C and D).

q: In a `terraform plan` output, a resource is marked with `~` (tilde). What will Terraform do to this resource?
options: Destroy it and then recreate it
Create it from scratch
Update it in place, without destroying and recreating it
Remove it from state but leave the real object running
explain: `~` means in-place update: the change can be applied without replacement (e.g., changing tags). `+` is create, `-/+` is destroy-then-recreate, and removal from state without destruction is `terraform state rm` — none of which is `~`.

q: A release manager asks why the pipeline saves plans instead of running terraform apply -auto-approve directly. Which answer is most accurate?
options: Saved plans are required because apply cannot generate its own plan

The saved plan is the exact reviewed artifact that apply will execute, creating an auditable gap between proposing changes and executing them, while a direct apply plans and executes in one unreviewed step
Saved plans encrypt all sensitive values so they can be committed to Git
Saved plans run faster because they skip provider downloads
explain: The value of -out plus apply of the file is separation of duties: humans review the precise plan that will run. Apply can generate its own plan (that is the default interactive flow), plan files are not an encryption tool, and speed is not the motivation.

q: In 'resource "aws_eip" "web" { instance = aws_instance.web.id }', what does the expression aws_instance.web.id evaluate to?
options: The value of the id attribute of the managed resource of type aws_instance named web
A variable named web in the aws_instance namespace
The literal string 'aws_instance.web.id'
The IP address of the person running Terraform
explain: A reference of the form type.name.attribute reads that attribute from the named managed object once it is known. It is an expression, not a literal string (A), and it has nothing to do with the operator (B) or with variables (D).

q: Which command downloads or updates only the child modules, without doing the rest of init's backend and provider setup?
options: terraform modules sync
terraform plan -get
terraform get
terraform fetch
explain: terraform get exists specifically to download and update modules into .terraform/modules, and init runs it as one of its steps. The other commands are invented; plan assumes modules are already installed rather than fetching them (D).

q: One configuration must manage a default AWS account plus aliased accounts for prod and dev, and a child module builds the shared network in whichever account it is handed. Which arrangement is correct?
options: Resources inside the child module pick accounts from their names at apply time
The child module declares all three provider blocks itself so the root stays empty
The root declares one unaliased default plus aliased prod and dev configurations, and each module call passes the intended one through its providers argument such as providers = { aws = aws.prod }
The module is called three times with -target to switch accounts between calls
explain: Provider configurations are declared in the root, where credentials and regions belong, and are handed down per module call through the providers mapping, which is what lets one module serve different accounts. Child modules should not embed provider blocks, resource names route nothing, and targeting does not switch configurations.

q: A configuration declares two backend blocks: `backend "s3"` for production state and `backend "gcs"` as a backup. What happens at init?
options: Terraform writes state to both backends for redundancy
Terraform merges both into a combined backend
The first backend is used and the second is silently ignored
Init fails — a configuration may have only one backend; state has a single home
explain: One configuration, one backend — state has exactly one home. A, C, and D invent multi-backend behaviors Terraform does not have. Redundancy comes from the backend's own durability (e.g., S3 versioning), not from two backends.

q: A platform team wants a data-loss-prevention check to run immediately before infrastructure changes are executed, after the plan and policy checks have already passed. Which run task stage fits?
options: Pre-plan, because it runs first in the sequence
Post-plan, because it runs before policies are evaluated
Pre-apply, because it executes after planning and policy evaluation but before the apply itself
There is no such stage; run tasks can only run after apply
explain: Pre-apply tasks run late in the lifecycle, after plan and policy stages, but before changes execute, which matches the requirement exactly. Pre-plan is the earliest stage, post-plan precedes policy outcomes, and post-apply-only is false because pre-plan, post-plan, and pre-apply stages all exist.

q: When a provider source address omits the hostname entirely, which registry does Terraform use by default?
options: releases.hashicorp.com, the binary download site
github.com, the default provider source host
registry.terraform.io, the public Terraform Registry
A local registry running on the workstation
explain: A two-part source such as hashicorp/aws implies the public registry hostname registry.terraform.io. GitHub hosts provider source code and releases.hashicorp.com hosts Core downloads, but neither is the default provider registry.

q: An engineer argues that a perfectly written bash script using cloud CLI commands IS declarative because it creates the right resources when run on an empty account. Why is this argument flawed?
options: The script encodes steps, not desired state, so on a non-empty or partially built account it has no model of what should exist versus what does
Any use of a CLI automatically makes a tool declarative
Terraform configurations cannot run on empty accounts
Bash cannot create cloud resources at all
explain: The flaw is the missing state model: an imperative script works from a blank slate but cannot reconcile an existing, drifted environment against a declared target. Bash can create resources, CLI use does not define declarativeness, and Terraform works fine on empty accounts.

q: A variable declares 'type = list(string)' and the team assigns a single plain string to it in tfvars. What does Terraform do?
options: It converts the variable declaration to type string
It accepts the string as a one-element list automatically in all cases
It reports a type error, because the assigned value does not match the declared list(string) type
It ignores the assignment and uses null
explain: Declared types are enforced: a value that cannot be converted to list(string) fails with a type error rather than being silently reshaped. Terraform does not rewrite declarations to fit bad input (C) and does not discard the assignment for null (B).

q: Before forcing a replacement in production, a lead wants to review exactly what recreation will look like without executing it. Which command supports that review?
options: terraform state show -replace aws_instance.web, which renders a hypothetical plan
terraform plan -replace=aws_instance.web, which previews the forced destroy-and-recreate plan for approval
terraform apply -replace=aws_instance.web -dry-run, which simulates the replacement
terraform taint -plan aws_instance.web, which shows replacement without applying
explain: The -replace flag works on plan as well as apply, so the team can inspect the exact replacement diff, including dependent effects, before anyone approves an apply. There is no apply dry-run flag, taint takes no plan mode, and state show displays recorded attributes rather than hypothetical plans.

q: A configuration passes terraform validate cleanly, yet the first apply fails because the referenced AMI ID, while correctly formatted as a string, does not exist in the account. Why is this outcome consistent with what validate promises?
options: Validate checks static correctness such as syntax, types, and references, but it does not reach cloud APIs to confirm that real-world values like an AMI actually exist, so existence errors only surface at plan or apply
Validate silently skips every tenth check unless -json is used
The AMI would have been caught if the provider block had included a region
Validate was run in the wrong directory, so it checked a different configuration
explain: Validate's boundary is the exam's favorite validate trap: it proves the configuration is well-formed and internally consistent, not that the world matches it. Existence of AMIs, quotas, and permissions are runtime facts checked when providers call APIs during plan and apply. Directory mistakes (A) would have produced different errors, and neither -json (B) nor a region argument (C) extends validate to live lookups.

q: A local value needs to combine a project variable and a fixed suffix to form a naming standard. Which definition is valid?
options: variable { bucket_name = "${var.project}-logs" }, declaring it as a variable with a computed default
locals { bucket_name = "${var.project}-logs" }, computing the local from a variable and literal text
locals { bucket_name = var.project } named with a dash in the local's own name
output { bucket_name = "${var.project}-logs" } with no value argument
explain: Locals are expressions, so interpolating a variable into a string is a normal local definition. A variable's default cannot reference another variable (B), an output requires a value argument and serves a different purpose (C), and the distractor in D misstates how the local itself is written.

q: An operator wants a local copy of the current remote state for inspection before a risky refactor. Which command retrieves it?
options: terraform state pull
terraform state fetch
terraform get -state
terraform plan -download-state
explain: terraform state pull downloads the current state from the configured backend and writes it to stdout, where it can be redirected to a file. Fetch and the other forms are not real state retrieval commands.

q: A new analyst joins a team and is granted the read permission level on a production workspace. What can the analyst do there?
options: Manage team membership for the workspace
Apply runs and change workspace settings
View the workspace, its runs, variables metadata, and state information, without queueing plans or applies
Queue speculative plans but not view state
explain: Read is the view-only workspace permission level: the analyst can inspect the workspace and its history but cannot queue runs or change anything. Applying and settings changes require higher levels, and team membership is an administrative function.

q: An automation script must migrate state to a new backend without an interactive prompt. Which init flag is designed for that migration path?
options: terraform init -migrate-state
terraform state migrate
terraform apply -migrate-state
terraform init -auto-migrate
explain: The -migrate-state flag on init forces the state migration path and handles the copy prompt in automation. Apply has no such flag, and there is no terraform state migrate subcommand.

q: Two state files were created independently for the same environment after a copy was restored incorrectly. Even though their resources look similar, Terraform treats them as unrelated histories. Which field explains this?
options: The lineage value, a unique identifier assigned when state is first created that distinguishes one state history from another
The outputs field, which embeds the backend address
The check_results field, which stores the workspace name
The terraform_version field, which must match exactly
explain: Lineage identifies a distinct state history and is set at initial creation; a copied or independently created state with a different lineage is not the same line of state. Version and outputs describe other things and do not establish state identity.

q: A provider is returning cryptic errors and HashiCorp support asks for detailed logs. Which setup produces them?
options: Setting log_level = "debug" inside the provider block
TF_LOG=DEBUG terraform apply, optionally with TF_LOG_PATH to write to a file
terraform validate -verbose
terraform plan -out=debug.log
explain: TF_LOG controls log verbosity (TRACE/DEBUG/INFO/WARN/ERROR); TF_LOG_PATH redirects to a file. B is not a real flag. C writes a plan file, not logs. D is not valid configuration.

q: You need to inspect outputs recorded in a remotely stored state without opening the backend console. Which approach uses a Terraform state command appropriately?
options: Outputs can never be read from state, only from configuration files
Pull the state with terraform state pull and read the outputs recorded in the downloaded snapshot
Use terraform force-unlock to print outputs after unlocking
Use terraform state rm to extract outputs into a file
explain: state pull retrieves the current backend snapshot, which includes recorded root outputs alongside resource attributes. The other commands either remove state entries or deal with locks, not with reading a state snapshot.

q: While debugging a configuration, an engineer evaluates `format("%s-%s", "web", "dr")` in the console. What does Terraform return?
options: web-dr
webdr
%s-%s
dr-web
explain: format() substitutes the arguments into the format string in order, so the first %s takes the first argument.

q: You run terraform state rm aws_instance.legacy but forget to remove its resource block from configuration. What happens on the next plan?
options: Terraform proposes creating the resource again, because it is still in configuration but no longer in state
Terraform permanently bans that address from being managed again
The real instance is destroyed during the next plan automatically
Nothing, because state rm also deletes the configuration block automatically
explain: state rm only forgets the resource in state; if the block remains in configuration, Terraform sees a desired resource with no tracked object and plans to create it. It never edits your .tf files for you.

q: An engineer opens a folder containing only main.tf, variables.tf, and outputs.tf that creates a complete load balancer setup. Even though nothing calls it yet, what is this folder?
options: A workspace, because it groups related resources
A module — any directory of .tf files defining resources is a module, whether or not something calls it yet
A child module only after a registry publishes it
A provider, because it contains variables.tf
explain: Every directory of Terraform configuration is a module by definition; being called by another configuration is what makes it a child module, but it is already a module. A registry listing (A) is optional, providers (B) are plugins, and workspaces (D) share one configuration rather than packaging one.

q: A constraint reads version = "~> 3.0" and the registry lists 2.9.0, 3.0.0, 3.7.2, and 4.0.0. A teammate argues init will pick 4.0.0 because it is newest. Who is right?
options: Init fails; ~> requires three version components
Init picks 3.0.0; pessimistic constraints always pick the floor
The teammate; init ignores upper bounds when a newer major exists
Init picks 3.7.2; ~> 3.0 means >= 3.0.0 and < 4.0.0, so the newest registry release is out of range
explain: Pessimistic constraints cap selection below the next major when two components are given, so 3.7.2 is the newest valid pick and 4.0.0 is excluded despite being newest overall. Init enforces upper bounds strictly and never defaults to the floor when newer allowed builds exist.

q: Someone edited a production security group directly in the AWS console. You suspect drift but want to see exactly what changed in the real world before deciding whether to revert it or update the configuration. Which command shows you the drift without proposing any configuration changes?
options: terraform state push
terraform destroy -target=aws_security_group.web
terraform plan -refresh-only — syncs state to reality and reports drift, proposing no changes
terraform apply -auto-approve
explain: Refresh-only mode updates state to match reality and shows what drifted, without proposing config changes — the safe first step in a drift investigation. B would blindly apply. C destroys the resource. D uploads a state file, which is dangerous and unrelated.

q: Inside which block does a configuration declare the providers it requires, together with their sources and version constraints?
options: The terraform block, in its required_providers sub-block
A standalone providers.tfvars file
The backend block, alongside the state settings
Each resource block, in a providers argument
explain: Provider requirements live in required_providers inside the terraform settings block, where each entry names a source and a version constraint. Resource blocks consume providers, backends configure state storage, and tfvars files only assign variable values.

q: The variable "image_id" receives values from several places: a value in terraform.tfvars sets it to "ami-0aaa111"; a value in settings.auto.tfvars sets it to "ami-0ddd444"; a value in terraform.tfvars.json sets it to "ami-0fff666". No other sources set it. Which value does Terraform use?
options: ami-0ddd444
ami-0aaa111
ami-0fff666
explain: Variable precedence, lowest to highest: default < TF_VAR_ environment < terraform.tfvars < terraform.tfvars.json < *.auto.tfvars < -var-file < -var. The highest source present here is an .auto.tfvars file, so its value "ami-0ddd444" wins.

q: The networking workspace manages the VPC; the application workspace needs to plan automatically whenever networking successfully applies. Which feature chains them?
options: Remote state sharing
Run triggers — one workspace's successful apply automatically queues a run in downstream workspaces
The `depends_on` meta-argument across workspaces
Workspace variables
explain: Run triggers chain workspaces: upstream apply -> downstream plan/apply. A lets workspaces read each other's outputs but triggers nothing. C shares values, not runs. D works within a configuration, not across HCP workspaces.

q: A team wants a child module to be reusable across accounts. Which two design choices support that goal? (Choose two.)
options: The module contains a provider block with the production account's credentials
The module hardcodes the production account ID in a local value
The module takes account-specific values, such as CIDR blocks and names, as input variables
The module exposes the attributes callers need through outputs instead of expecting callers to reach into its resources
explain: Parameterizing environment specifics as inputs and publishing a clean output interface are what make a module portable across accounts. Hardcoding an account ID (B) or embedding credentialed provider configurations (C) welds the module to one account.

q: Which scenario is the legitimate primary use case for terraform state push?
options: Routinely syncing a laptop's local state to the team backend after every apply
Sharing configuration files with a teammate who lacks Git access
Overwriting a teammate's newer state because your local copy is more convenient
Recovering from a disaster by deliberately restoring a known-good state file to the backend when no better recovery path exists
explain: Push is a recovery and manual state-management tool, appropriate when an operator intentionally restores a verified state snapshot. As a routine sync habit it invites stale overwrites and serial or lineage conflicts with the team's real state.

q: A team uses the classic S3 backend for state and wants native state locking without HCP Terraform. In the traditional S3 setup, what provided the locking?
options: The S3 bucket versioning setting alone
A separate EC2 instance running a lock server
An S3 object lock retention policy on the state object
A DynamoDB table configured for the backend, used to manage the lock record
explain: In the classic S3 backend pattern, a DynamoDB table is configured alongside the bucket to handle state locking and consistency. Bucket versioning helps with recovery history but by itself is not the lock mechanism described in this setup.

q: A configuration sets required_version = ">= 1.9, < 1.13" and pins its provider with ~> 5.0. A workstation has Core 1.12.5 and provider 5.9.0 available. A second workstation has Core 1.13.0 and the same provider. What differs between them?
options: The second runs; provider compatibility overrides the Core constraint
The first workstation runs the configuration; the second is rejected at startup because Core 1.13.0 violates < 1.13, even though its provider is fine
Both fail; provider 5.9.0 requires Core below 1.12
Both run; required_version is checked only once per project
explain: The two gates are independent and both must pass: provider 5.9.0 satisfies ~> 5.0 on both machines, but Core 1.13.0 breaches the < 1.13 ceiling in required_version, so that workstation is stopped before any provider work begins. Passing one gate never excuses failing the other.

q: A platform team wants one specific security group replaced during an otherwise normal apply, leaving every other planned action untouched. Which command achieves exactly that?
options: terraform apply -refresh-only -replace=aws_security_group.app
terraform destroy -target=aws_security_group.app followed by terraform plan
terraform apply -target=aws_security_group.app
terraform apply -replace=aws_security_group.app
explain: -replace scoped to the one address forces just that object's recreation inside the normal apply, preserving all other actions. -target would shrink the whole run to one resource, the destroy-then-plan route is two disruptive steps, and refresh-only performs no replacements at all.

q: A configuration provisions an Amazon EC2 instance and a Kubernetes cluster in one run, using the AWS and Kubernetes providers together. What makes this combination work?
options: Core converts Kubernetes resources into AWS resources at plan time
Each resource type prefix routes the resource to its provider, and both providers are declared in required_providers and installed by init
Only the first provider in required_providers is used, for all resources
The Kubernetes provider is a submodule of the AWS provider
explain: Resource type prefixes such as aws_instance and kubernetes_ identify the owning provider, and a configuration can declare any number of providers side by side. Providers are independent plugins, Core performs no cross-cloud conversion, and every declared provider can manage resources.

q: A workspace is configured for dynamic provider credentials with AWS. Instead of storing an access key in the workspace, what happens at run time?
options: HCP Terraform presents an OIDC identity token for the run, which AWS exchanges for short-lived credentials scoped to that run through a trust relationship
The run borrows credentials from the last developer who ran terraform login
AWS disables authentication entirely for HCP Terraform workspaces
HCP Terraform emails a long-lived key to the run environment at the start of each run
explain: Dynamic credentials use workload identity: the run presents an OIDC token that the cloud provider's trust configuration exchanges for temporary, short-lived credentials. No long-lived key is emailed or stored, developer login tokens are unrelated, and authentication is strengthened rather than disabled.

q: Three months after an incident, investigators ask who queued a controversial production run, who confirmed its apply, and what the plan proposed. Where does HCP Terraform provide this evidence?
options: Only in the cloud provider's billing console
In the Git repository's commit messages, which HCP Terraform writes automatically
Nowhere, because run records are deleted after each successful apply
In the workspace's run history and audit trail, which record each run, its plan, and the users who queued and confirmed it
explain: Run history is the audit trail: every run records its plan, status transitions, and the actors who queued, confirmed, or discarded it. Billing consoles show costs not run actors, records persist after applies, and HCP Terraform does not write commit messages.

q: A configuration must create resources in two Azure subscriptions. The engineer writes two azurerm provider blocks. What must be true for this to be valid?
options: Both blocks may omit aliases if their subscription IDs differ
The blocks must live in separate files within the configuration
Exactly one block has no alias (the default) and the other declares a distinct alias and its own subscription settings
Both blocks must declare different aliases and no default may exist
explain: Multiple configurations of one provider type require aliases to distinguish them, with at most one unaliased default. Two unaliased blocks are a duplicate-configuration error even if their arguments differ, file placement is irrelevant, and a default configuration is allowed to coexist with aliased ones.

q: A team enables auto-apply on a development workspace but leaves it off for production. A queued production run finishes planning successfully. What happens next?
options: The production run waits in a pending confirmation state until a user with apply permission confirms it
The production run is discarded because auto-apply is off
The production run applies only the resources that did not change tags
The production run applies automatically after a five-minute timer expires
explain: Without auto-apply, a successful plan pauses for manual confirmation by an authorized user before applying. There is no timer-based apply, the run is not discarded, and applies never execute a partial subset based on tag changes.

q: A team uses Terraform to manage DNS records in a SaaS provider, user groups in an identity platform, and VMs in AWS from one repository. What exam concept does this best demonstrate?
options: A service-agnostic workflow where providers expose many API-backed platforms through the same process
Terraform requires a separate language for each SaaS platform
Terraform is a configuration management tool for DNS only
SaaS resources cannot be version controlled like cloud resources
explain: Managing cloud and SaaS resources with one workflow demonstrates service-agnosticism: providers abstract many APIs behind the same HCL and lifecycle. Each platform does not need its own language, and SaaS definitions are versioned exactly like cloud definitions.

q: A security review finds production state in an S3 bucket with no encryption and access granted to the whole engineering organization. Which remediation set is most complete?
options: Mark all outputs sensitive and leave bucket settings unchanged
Enable encryption at rest for the bucket, narrow backend access to those who operate the infrastructure, and treat any exposed values in state as compromised secrets to rotate
Move the state file into the application repository with branch protection
Rename the state key to something obscure and keep the same access list
explain: State confidentiality rests on encrypted storage plus least-privilege backend access, and values already exposed to a broad audience should be rotated. Obscure names, repo storage, and display redaction do not undo broad read access to plaintext state.

q: The variable "instance_type" receives values from several places: a value in terraform.tfvars sets it to "m5.large"; a value in terraform.tfvars.json sets it to "t3.medium"; a value passed with -var on the command line sets it to "t3.small". No other sources set it. Which value does Terraform use?
options: t3.medium
t3.small
t3.large
m5.large
explain: Variable precedence, lowest to highest: default < TF_VAR_ environment < terraform.tfvars < terraform.tfvars.json < *.auto.tfvars < -var-file < -var. The highest source present here is a -var flag, so its value "t3.small" wins.

q: During an incident, an operator enlarges a managed instance in the cloud console and tells nobody. Assuming configuration is unchanged, what will the next terraform plan propose?
options: An update that reverts the instance toward the size declared in configuration, because refresh exposes the drift
Destruction of the entire configuration, because any drift invalidates state
Creation of a second instance matching the console size alongside the original
