No changes, because console edits are adopted automatically into configuration
explain: Plan refreshes state from reality, sees the instance no longer matches configuration, and proposes changing it back to the declared size. Terraform never edits configuration to match the console, drift does not invalidate the whole state, and no duplicate instance is proposed.

q: A soft-mandatory Sentinel policy fails on a production run at 18:00. The on-call lead, who holds override permission, reviews the exception and decides the change must proceed tonight. What does soft-mandatory enforcement allow?
options: The policy failure is ignored silently with no record kept
Nothing; the run must wait until the policy itself is edited in the morning
An authorized user can override the policy failure and let the run continue, with the override recorded
Any anonymous viewer of the workspace can override the failure
explain: Soft-mandatory means the failure blocks the run by default but users with the required permission can override it, and that override is part of the run record. It does not require editing the policy, is never silent, and is never available to anonymous viewers.

q: While debugging a configuration, an engineer evaluates `try(element([], 0), "fallback")` in the console. What value does it produce?
options: error: index out of range
null
fallback
explain: try() evaluates its arguments in order and returns the first that succeeds; element() on an empty list errors, so try() falls through to "fallback".

q: A team renames a resource block from aws_instance.web to aws_instance.app but updates no references. What happens on the next plan?
options: Nothing; resource names are cosmetic
Terraform silently updates all references automatically
Terraform creates both resources and merges them
Validation or planning fails because other blocks still reference the old address aws_instance.web, which no longer exists
explain: References are by exact address, so renaming a block breaks every expression that still points at the old name until they are updated. Terraform does not rewrite references on rename (A), does not merge objects (C), and addresses are functional, not cosmetic (B).

q: A company suffers a regional outage and needs its stack running in another region quickly. Because the whole stack is Terraform code, what becomes feasible?
options: Guaranteeing zero data loss regardless of database design
Recreating the environment from code in the new region with adjusted variables
Recovering servers that were never defined anywhere
Avoiding any need to test backups or runbooks ever again
explain: Disaster recovery is faster when the environment is reproducible code: apply the same configuration in another region with new inputs. IaC cannot recreate what was never defined, and it does not by itself guarantee data protection, which depends on backup and database design.

q: A locals block defines a value with the expression `concat(["cache"], ["queue", "cache-2"])`. What is the result?
options: ["cache", "queue"]
["cache", "queue", "cache-2"]
["cache-2", "queue", "cache"]
["queue", "cache-2"]
explain: concat() appends the elements of each later list to the earlier ones in order, producing a single combined list.

q: A provider block for Google Cloud sets project and region, and no alias is written. A second block for a different project adds alias = "analytics". Which block is the default configuration?
options: The block declared last in the file becomes the default
The aliased block becomes the default because aliases take priority
Neither is a default; every resource must name a provider explicitly
The block without an alias is the default; the aliased block is used only when explicitly selected
explain: For each provider type, the single configuration without an alias is the default used by resources that do not specify otherwise. Aliased configurations are opt-in only, file order is irrelevant, and most resources rely on the default without naming it.

q: One Terraform configuration manages an AWS S3 bucket and also generates a random password with the `random` provider. How does Terraform handle the two providers?
options: The random provider must be wrapped in a module; the root module may only use one provider
Terraform merges both providers into a single plugin at init Domain 3: Core Terraform Workflow — 19 questions
Each resource block is handled by the provider matching its resource type prefix (`aws_*` vs `random_*`); both providers are declared in `required_providers`
It cannot — a configuration may only use one provider type
explain: A configuration routinely uses many providers (objective 2c): each resource's type prefix selects its provider, and all are declared in required_providers and downloaded at init. A is false — multi-provider configs are normal. C invents a module restriction. D misunderstands the plugin architecture.

q: Immediately after a successful first apply of a new VPC, what has Terraform written into state about that VPC?
options: A promise to create the VPC on the next run
The VPC's real cloud ID bound to its configuration address, along with its recorded attributes
Only the HCL text of the resource block, with no cloud identifiers
Nothing; state is only written when resources change
explain: Apply records the created object's real-world identifier against its configuration address, plus observed attributes, so later plans can find and diff the same object. Without that binding Terraform could not know the VPC in the account is the one it manages.

q: A platform lead is listing reasons to replace manual provisioning with Terraform. Which two reasons are valid IaC advantages? (Choose two.)
options: New environments can be created in minutes through automation instead of days of tickets
Cloud providers stop charging for resources built by code
Provisioning becomes repeatable because the same code runs every time
Engineers no longer need to understand networking or cloud concepts
explain: Repeatability and automated speed are foundational IaC advantages. IaC does not remove the need for engineering knowledge, and providers charge for resources regardless of how they were created.

q: Two engineers debug the same failing run: one insists the bug is in Terraform core's graph handling, the other blames the provider's API responses. Which evidence best settles the dispute?
options: The size of the state file before and after the run
Separate TF_LOG_CORE and TF_LOG_PROVIDER output for the same run, showing whether errors originate in core processing or provider calls
The order in which resources appear in terraform state list output
A screenshot of the plan summary counts from both laptops
explain: Component-split logging was designed for this attribution problem: core logs reveal graph and workflow behavior while provider logs show API requests and responses, so the failing layer identifies itself. State size, list ordering, and plan counts carry no diagnostic detail about where the error originates.

q: Which source string points at a module in an S3 bucket?
options: s3::https://s3-eu-west-1.amazonaws.com/example-bucket/network.zip
./modules/network
git::https://example.com/network.git
terraform-aws-modules/network/aws
explain: Remote module packages in buckets use the forced source prefix form, here s3:: followed by the bucket object URL; GCS uses gcs:: similarly. The git:: form (B) clones a repository, the ./ path (C) is local, and the bare three-part address (D) is a registry source.

q: In Terraform's architecture, which component reads the configuration, builds the dependency graph, and produces the execution plan?
options: The Terraform Registry, which generates plans remotely
The state backend, which computes the plan before providers load
The AWS provider, which plans resources for every cloud
Terraform Core, the main terraform binary that plans and coordinates the run
explain: Terraform Core is the engine: it loads configuration, builds the graph, and creates the plan, then asks providers to act. Providers only translate their own resources to API calls; the backend stores state and the registry distributes plugins, so neither plans the run.

q: A team wants a provider constraint that permits patch fixes for the 2.3 line but never a 2.4 feature release. Which constraint expresses this?
options: version = "~> 2.3.0"
version = "~> 2.3"
version = ">= 2.3.0"
version = "= 2.3"
explain: The three-component pessimistic constraint ~> 2.3.0 allows >= 2.3.0 and < 2.4.0, admitting patches like 2.3.7 while excluding 2.4.0. The two-component ~> 2.3 would allow 2.4, >= 2.3.0 is unbounded, and = 2.3 is not a complete exact version.

q: A regulated bank cannot use a SaaS control plane and must run the HCP Terraform platform inside its own infrastructure, with the same workspaces, runs, and policy model. Which offering fits, and how does it relate to HCP Terraform?
options: A local Terraform install with the cloud block pointed at an internal file share
The public Terraform Registry, which can be mirrored to act as a control plane
Terraform Enterprise, the self-hosted distribution of the same platform, deployed and operated by the customer
HCP Terraform with a special offline mode that disables the hosted service
explain: Terraform Enterprise is the self-hosted counterpart to HCP Terraform: same workspace, run, and governance model, but installed in the customer's own environment. A file share is not a control plane, the registry distributes modules and providers only, and HCP Terraform has no offline self-hosted mode.

q: When should a moved block typically be removed from configuration after a successful refactor?
options: Only after destroying and recreating the resource once
Never; moved blocks must remain forever or state corrupts
After the refactor has been applied and all collaborators and branches have moved past the old address, so it does not linger as stale mapping
Immediately before the first plan that uses it, to keep files clean
explain: Moved blocks are transitional: once everyone’s state reflects the new address, the mapping is no longer needed and can be removed. Removing it before the migration applies would lose the instruction Terraform needs to avoid recreation.

q: A resource address in state is aws_instance.web["blue"] rather than aws_instance.web[0]. What created that form of address?
options: count with a starting offset named blue
for_each with a map or set key 'blue', giving the instance a stable keyed address instead of a positional index
The remote backend, which converts all indexes to strings
A moved block that renamed the index to a color
explain: for_each instances are addressed by their key, shown in quotes in the address, which keeps identity stable when other elements change. Count uses numeric indexes, and neither moved blocks nor backends rewrite that addressing scheme.

q: Why can a data source result sometimes show as 'known after apply' in a plan?
options: Because the data source's arguments depend on attribute values of resources that do not exist yet, so the read must wait until apply creates them
Because the data block is missing a lifecycle section
Because the provider forgot to implement the read function
Because data sources are always read only after all resources are destroyed
explain: When a data source's query arguments reference not-yet-created resource attributes, the read cannot complete during plan and is deferred until apply. Data reads are not tied to destruction (A), a missing provider function would be an error rather than a deferral (B), and lifecycle sections do not control data reads (D).

q: Why does scheduled drift detection add value even for a team that runs terraform plan from CI several times a day?
options: It makes CI plans run faster by caching their results
CI plans already detect drift, so scheduled detection is purely a duplicate feature with no added value
It prevents cloud consoles from accepting any manual changes
It catches drift in workspaces that are rarely planned, covers periods when CI is down, and surfaces divergence as a health signal and notification rather than burying it in pipeline logs
explain: Scheduled detection is platform-level and continuous: it watches quiet workspaces, runs even when pipelines are broken, and presents drift as a first-class health status with notifications. It does not cache CI plans, cannot block console changes, and is not redundant for estates with uneven run activity.

q: Which two statements about terraform destroy are true? (Choose two.)
options: Destroy edits the configuration files to comment out every resource block
Destroy first builds a destroy plan showing everything that will be removed and asks for confirmation unless -auto-approve is given
Destruction proceeds in reverse dependency order relative to creation
Destroy can remove infrastructure that Terraform has never tracked in state if it is in the same cloud account
explain: Destroy is plan-then-execute with a confirmation gate, and it unwinds the graph in reverse so dependents are removed before their dependencies. It can only act on state-tracked resources and it never rewrites configuration files.

q: A caller passes a value for a variable that the root module never declared. What is the practical lesson about variable declarations?
options: Undeclared variables passed with -var produce a warning and are not usable, because only declared variable blocks create inputs the configuration can reference as var.<name>
Undeclared variables crash the provider plugins
Undeclared variables are automatically created with type any
Undeclared variables are stored as outputs
explain: Only a variable block creates a referenceable input; an assignment to an undeclared name is not accessible as var.<name> and at the root only draws a warning. Terraform does not auto-declare it (B), affect providers (C), or convert it into an output (D).

q: The plan output ends with: Plan: 0 to add, 2 to change, 0 to destroy. What will apply do?
options: Fail, because a valid plan must contain at least one add
Read two data sources and change nothing
Update two existing resources in place, creating and destroying nothing
Create two resources and destroy two resources as replacements
explain: Two changes with zero adds and zero destroys means two in-place updates (~) and nothing else. Replacements would appear as both an add and a destroy in the counts, and a changes-only plan is perfectly valid.

q: A runbook written for Terraform 0.12 tells operators to run terraform taint to recreate a broken server. How should the team treat that instruction on Terraform 1.12?
options: Treat taint as deprecated since Terraform 0.15 and plan to replace the instruction with the -replace flag
Ignore it, because broken servers can never be recreated by Terraform
Follow it unchanged, because taint is the preferred modern method
Run taint twice so the deprecation warning is cleared
explain: terraform taint was deprecated in Terraform 0.15 in favor of -replace on plan and apply, so old runbooks should be updated rather than followed literally. Taint still being recognized does not make it preferred, and running it twice does not clear any deprecation.

Replacing a backend with a cloud block and re-running init triggers state migration: the existing state is copied into the named workspace, and HCP Terraform manages it from then on. The state is not deleted or ignored, which would orphan or duplicate real resources, and HCP Terraform does not split state storage back to S3 while only hosting logs.
options: It offers to copy the existing state from the S3 backend into the HCP Terraform workspace, which then becomes the authoritative state source for future runs
It deletes the S3 state immediately and starts the workspace with an empty state
It keeps using S3 for state permanently while only borrowing HCP Terraform for run logs
It ignores the S3 state, so the first remote plan proposes creating every resource again from scratch
q: A team has used an S3 backend with CLI-driven runs for two years. To migrate, they replace the backend block with a cloud block naming their HCP Terraform organization and workspace, then run terraform init in the working directory. What should they expect init to do about the state that currently lives in S3?

A module published for reuse declares its own required_providers with a minimum provider version but no upper bound, while the root module pins tighter. Why do module authors write minimum-only constraints?
options: Minimum-only constraints force every consumer to the newest provider release
Root module constraints are ignored whenever a child module declares any constraint
So the module stays composable: it states the oldest provider it works with and lets each root module choose the actual version within its own constraints
Providers ignore child module constraints during init
explain: Child modules declare the range they are compatible with, conventionally a floor, and version selection is resolved once for the whole configuration under all constraints together. A floor does not force the newest release, and root constraints are never discarded; init intersects every module's requirements.

q: A run finishes its plan successfully. Before any infrastructure changes begin, HCP Terraform evaluates the plan against the organization's Sentinel policies. At which point in the run lifecycle does this evaluation happen?
options: After the plan and before the apply, so a failing mandatory policy can stop changes before they happen
During terraform init, before providers are downloaded
After the apply completes, as a final report
Only when a user manually requests a policy review from the CLI
explain: Sentinel policies evaluate the completed plan before apply, which is what allows them to gate real changes. Post-apply evaluation could not prevent anything, init is far too early to judge a plan, and evaluation is automatic for runs in policy-covered workspaces.

q: A plan marks an existing aws_db_instance with a single minus sign (-). No replacement is shown. What happens to that instance on apply?
options: It is removed from state but the database keeps running
It is updated in place to the newest engine version
It is created fresh alongside the old instance
It is destroyed and not recreated, because it was removed from the configuration or targeted for removal
explain: A lone - means destroy with no recreation, typically because the block left the configuration. Removing from state while leaving the object running is state rm, not a plan destroy; an update in place would be ~ and a replacement would be -/+.

q: A new hire clones a project and gets exactly the provider builds the rest of the team uses, even though newer releases exist. Which mechanism is responsible?
options: The committed .terraform.lock.hcl, which pins the exact versions and hashes init must reproduce
The state file, which embeds the provider versions from the last apply
The required_providers block, which always resolves to the oldest allowed version
The plugin cache, which freezes versions after first use
explain: The lock file is the pinning mechanism: init reproduces its recorded versions and verifies hashes instead of resolving fresh ones. Constraints alone would let each machine drift to the newest allowed release, and neither the cache nor state pins provider builds.

terraform graph emits the configuration dependency graph in DOT format, a text graph description that visualization tools render as nodes and edges, making implicit and explicit dependencies visible for review. It produces no timing metrics, variable tables, or apply replay, and the metrics-chart distractor confuses a static dependency model with runtime telemetry Terraform does not collect.
options: A dependency graph of the configuration in DOT format that can be rendered with a tool such as Graphviz to visualize which resources depend on which
A live metrics chart of resource creation times from the last apply
A formatted table of every variable value ordered by dependency depth
An animated replay of the last apply showing resources lighting up in creation order
q: A reviewer cannot tell from the configuration files alone why an application instance is always created after a particular database subnet group. The team wants a visual picture of how all resources in the configuration depend on each other. What does terraform graph provide for this review?

A legacy team provisions with a 400-line imperative script that must run in perfect order and fails if a resource already exists. What will Terraform do differently when a resource already exists and matches the configuration?
options: Delete the existing resource and recreate it to be safe
Fail with a duplicate resource error like the script
Ignore all existing resources and build duplicates
Detect the match through state and refresh and propose no action for that resource
explain: Terraform reconciles: state and refresh tell it what exists, so matching resources need no action, unlike a naive imperative script that assumes a blank slate. It does not fail on duplicates it manages, recreate unnecessarily, or build unmanaged duplicates.

q: A team manages one module call per environment using for_each over a map of environment names to CIDR blocks. Inside the module block, how do they pass the CIDR for the current instance?
options: cidr_block = module.cidr
cidr_block = each.value
cidr_block = var.cidr[each]
cidr_block = each.key.cidr
explain: Module blocks with for_each expose each.key and each.value in their arguments, so each.value carries the CIDR from the current map entry. each.key here is the environment name string, which has no cidr attribute (B), var.cidr is not the iteration source (C), and D references a module output that does not exist.

q: A module in the public registry is published by the hashicorp organization itself, such as a Consul module. How is that provenance typically presented in its source address and page?
options: Its address omits the provider segment
Its address starts with the prefix private/
Its namespace is hashicorp, and official modules are maintained and supported directly by HashiCorp
Its page hides the publisher identity
explain: Official modules live in the hashicorp namespace and are maintained by HashiCorp itself, a stronger provenance than community or partner modules. Addresses keep all three segments including provider (B is false), there is no private/ prefix in public addresses (A), and publisher identity is prominently shown (D).

q: A reviewer asks what -parallelism actually limits during apply. Which answer is correct?
options: The number of providers that can be downloaded during init
The number of concurrent operations Terraform performs while walking the resource dependency graph
The number of variables that can be passed with -var in one command
The number of saved plan files retained in the working directory
explain: Parallelism caps concurrent graph operations (creates, updates, destroys) during plan, apply, and destroy walks. It has nothing to do with provider downloads, variable counts, or plan file retention.

q: An operations lead says Terraform is declarative. What does that mean in one sentence?
options: You describe the desired end state and Terraform decides how to reach it
You list every API call in the exact order it must run
You write procedures that operators must follow manually
You run commands interactively and adjust based on each result
explain: Declarative means stating the target state; Terraform builds the dependency graph and ordering itself. Listing ordered API calls or manual procedures is imperative, and interactive trial-and-error is not a declarative model at all.

q: An engineer combines flags: terraform plan -refresh-only -out=drift.plan . A reviewer objects that the saved file will change infrastructure when applied. Who is right?
options: The engineer is wrong because refresh-only mode cannot be used after drift occurs
The reviewer is wrong because -out is ignored in refresh-only mode and no file is written
The reviewer is wrong; applying a refresh-only plan only updates state to match reality and proposes no resource creates, updates, or destroys
The reviewer is right; any saved plan applied later executes the full configuration
explain: A refresh-only plan captures only state-refresh actions, so applying it syncs state without touching real resources. -out still works in this mode, and refresh-only exists precisely for drift situations, so the last two distractors invert its purpose.

terraform console is the interactive debugging tool for this job: you type expressions such as a resource attribute or a function call and it resolves them using the loaded configuration and state, with no plan or apply involved. fmt only restyles text, graph only draws dependencies, and providers only reports provider requirements, so none of the distractors evaluates expressions at all.
options: terraform console, which opens an interactive prompt that evaluates HCL expressions and references against the current state and configuration
terraform graph, which evaluates the expression and prints the resulting string as a node label
terraform providers, which evaluates expressions that reference provider attributes
terraform fmt, which evaluates each expression while it reformats the files that contain it
q: An engineer suspects an output expression that combines a VPC ID and a subnet list is producing the wrong string, and wants to test the expression interactively against the real values already recorded for the deployed infrastructure, without creating a plan or changing anything. Which workflow tool fits this debugging task, and how does it work?

A repository's backend block declares only backend "s3" with no arguments. Each CI pipeline job runs terraform init -backend-config=backend.hcl, where a per-environment backend.hcl supplies bucket, key, and dynamodb_table. What is this pattern and why is it used?
options: Variable interpolation for backends, which lets one tfvars file serve every environment
Remote state sharing, because backend.hcl is read by terraform_remote_state data sources
Partial backend configuration: the code stays environment-neutral while each pipeline supplies its own state location at init time
A backend migration, because supplying a config file copies state between buckets automatically
explain: Leaving backend arguments out of code and completing them at init with -backend-config files is partial configuration, ideal for CI where the same code deploys to several environments with different state buckets and keys. Backend blocks cannot use variables, and the file does not migrate state or feed remote state data sources.

q: A provider constraint is version = "~> 5.1.0". The registry offers 5.1.0, 5.1.4, 5.2.0, and a prerelease 5.3.0-beta.1. A release notes page claims running init -upgrade will land the team on 5.2.0. Evaluate the claim.
options: The claim is true only if the lock file is deleted first
The claim is true: -upgrade ignores pessimistic ceilings when newer minors exist
The claim is false: ~> 5.1.0 caps selection below 5.2.0, prereleases are not selected by default, so init -upgrade lands on 5.1.4
The claim is false because init -upgrade lands on the prerelease 5.3.0-beta.1
explain: Two rules decide this: the three-component pessimistic ceiling excludes everything from 5.2.0 upward, and Terraform does not select prerelease builds unless a constraint explicitly names one. That leaves 5.1.4 as the newest selectable release, and neither -upgrade nor lock deletion changes constraint semantics.

q: A provisioner on an `aws_instance` needs a DNS record to exist first, but nothing in the configuration references the DNS record from the instance. How do you guarantee the ordering?
options: Ordering cannot be controlled; provisioners always run first
Add a `lifecycle { create_before_destroy = true }` block
Add an explicit `depends_on = [aws_route53_record.web]` to the instance — depends_on covers orderings that references cannot express
Rename the resources so alphabetical order works out
explain: depends_on is the explicit dependency mechanism for orderings invisible to the reference graph (provisioners, external side effects). A is nonsense. C controls replacement behavior, not ordering. D is false — depends_on exists exactly for this.

q: A team runs one module call with for_each keyed by team name, and a second team is removed from the map. During plan, Terraform proposes destroying exactly that team's infrastructure and leaving the other instances untouched. Why does for_each make this safe where count would be risky?
options: for_each instances are keyed by stable map keys, so removing one key targets only that instance; count instances are addressed by numeric position, so removing an element can shift indexes and reassign identities
for_each modules are never destroyed, only archived
for_each disables state tracking for removed instances
count cannot be used on module blocks at all
explain: Stable keys are the core advantage: each for_each instance keeps its identity regardless of its siblings, while count's positional addressing renumbers survivors when an element disappears. for_each instances are destroyed normally when removed (B), count works fine on modules (C), and state tracking applies equally to both (A).

q: During a refactor, a resource block is renamed from web to frontend in one file, but an output in another file still references the old address. The team wants the earliest, fastest command that will surface this dangling reference. Which command is it?
options: terraform state list, which validates outputs against state
terraform fmt, which rewrites stale references when it reformats the file
terraform validate, which checks that references point at objects that actually exist in the configuration
terraform init -upgrade, which rebuilds the reference index
explain: Reference integrity is part of validate's internal-consistency checking: a reference to an undeclared object fails validation immediately and locally. fmt (B) never repairs references, init -upgrade (C) only re-resolves versions, and state list (D) merely prints addresses already in state without checking configuration references.

q: After a successful terraform init in a new working directory, where on disk do the installed provider plugins live?
options: Inside the .terraform.lock.hcl file as embedded binaries
In a global system folder shared by every Terraform project
In the same folder as the terraform binary itself
In the .terraform/providers subdirectory of the working directory
explain: Init installs providers under .terraform/providers inside the working directory, scoped to that project. The lock file only records versions and hashes, it embeds no binaries, and provider installation is per working directory rather than global.

q: During a code review, a teammate asks what `max(9, 15, 24)` evaluates to. What is the result?
explain: max() returns the largest argument, 24. The distractor values come from applying the wrong operation or rounding the wrong way.

q: A platform team pins a registry module with version = ">= 4.0, < 5.0" instead of an exact version. Six months later a fresh clone behaves slightly differently from the original deployment. What most likely explains it?
options: A newer 4.x module release was published in the meantime and a fresh init selected it, since the constraint allows any 4.x
Registry modules mutate in place after publication
The lock file rewrote the module constraint
Local path modules were mixed into the build
explain: Range constraints float within their bounds: a fresh init installs the newest allowed module release, which may differ from what the original deployment used. Published registry versions are immutable (A), the lock file pins providers rather than rewriting module constraints (C), and nothing here involves local modules (B).

q: A finance lead asks why ephemeral test environments should be built with Terraform instead of being left running permanently. What is the best response?
options: Leaving resources running is required for version control to work
Test environments cannot be destroyed if they were built with IaC
Terraform makes the cloud provider waive charges for test resources
Environments defined as code can be destroyed when not in use and recreated identically when needed, so the team stops paying for idle resources
explain: Safe teardown and faithful recreation is the cost argument: destroy saves money because apply can rebuild the same environment later. Terraform does not waive charges, and version control has nothing to do with leaving resources running.

q: A private provider is referenced with the full address terraform.example.com/acme/platform. Which part of the address is the provider type?
options: platform, the final segment after hostname and namespace
acme, the middle segment
terraform.example.com, the first segment
The type is not encoded; it comes from the provider block name
explain: A full provider address is hostname/namespace/type, so platform in the final position is the provider type, acme is the publishing namespace, and terraform.example.com is the registry hostname. The block name in configuration is just a local name and does not define the type.

q: Why prefer a removed block with destroy = false over simply deleting the resource block and running terraform state rm afterward?
options: There is no difference; both sequences produce a destroy plan first

The removed block declares the intent in configuration for review and applies the forget operation as part of a planned run, instead of relying on an unreviewed manual state edit after a destroy plan appears
Removed blocks are the only way to delete a resource block from a file
The state rm approach destroys the object before it can be removed from state
explain: Deleting a block alone proposes destruction, so pairing it with a later state rm is fragile and outside the reviewed plan. A removed block puts the preserve decision in code, reviewed like any other change, and the plan shows forgetting without destroying.

q: A plan fails with a lock error whose Lock Info shows ID, Path, Operation: OperationTypeApply, Who: ci-runner@build-agent-04, and a Created timestamp from two minutes ago. A teammate urges an immediate force-unlock. What is the best diagnosis?
options: The lock information shows a CI runner acquired it moments ago for an apply, so a run is very likely still active and force-unlocking now risks concurrent writes and state corruption
The Who field names the engineer who must personally delete the state file
The lock is stale because any lock older than one minute can be safely forced
The Created field proves the lock belongs to a plan, and plans never write state, so forcing is harmless
explain: The lock metadata is diagnostic evidence: a recent Created time, an apply operation, and a CI runner as holder indicate a live run, not a stale lock. Force-unlock is only justified after confirming no run is active; the one-minute staleness rule the teammate cites does not exist.

q: In a terraform plan, the resource aws_vpc.core is shown with the symbol -/+ next to it (# aws_vpc.core -/+ be created / will be updated style notation). What does the symbol tell the reviewer?
options: the resource is a data source being read
the resource will be removed from state but left running
the resource will be destroyed and then recreated (replacement)
the resource will be updated in place
explain: In plan output, + means create, ~ means update in place, -/+ means destroy and recreate (replacement), and <= means a data source read. The symbol -/+ indicates: the resource will be destroyed and then recreated (replacement).

terraform providers is the workflow command for inspecting the provider dependency tree across the root and child modules before an upgrade, so the engineer can see selections and constraints together. Workspace list, output, and state list report workspaces, output values, and resource addresses respectively, and none of them reports provider versions, which is why the state list distractor fails.
options: terraform providers, which displays the provider requirement tree for the configuration and its modules, including the selected versions and constraints in effect
terraform output, which lists provider versions alongside the configuration outputs
terraform workspace list, which annotates each workspace with its provider versions
terraform state list, which prefixes every resource address with its provider version
q: Before scheduling a provider upgrade, a platform engineer wants to confirm exactly which provider versions the current working directory is using and which version constraints each module in the tree imposes. Which command gives the engineer that provider-focused view?
A child module reads a data source for the caller's AWS account ID instead of receiving it as an input. A reviewer flags this. What is the underlying design concern?
options: The data source will run before init completes
The module becomes coupled to the caller's environment and harder to reuse elsewhere; passing account-specific values in as inputs keeps the module portable and explicit
Data sources are forbidden inside child modules
The account ID will leak into the registry listing
explain: Modules may use data sources, but reaching out to environment-specific data makes the module less reusable and hides a dependency its interface should declare as an input. Data sources are legal in child modules (A), they run at plan time rather than during init (B), and registry listings show code structure, not runtime account values (D).

q: After a state file was committed to Git by mistake, a developer deletes it, commits the deletion, and announces the leak is fixed. A security reviewer disagrees. Why?
options: The deletion commit encrypts the file, making future reviews impossible
The deleted file is automatically emailed to all repository watchers by Git
Terraform refuses to run in any directory that was ever a Git repository with state committed
Git retains the state file's contents in prior commits, so anyone with the repository can still check out the old commit and read the plaintext secrets
explain: Git history is append-only in normal use: the deletion removes the file from the current tree but the earlier commit still contains the full state with its plaintext secrets. That is why remediation requires history purging and credential rotation, not just a delete commit.

q: A provider is constrained with version = "~> 5.0". The registry offers 5.0.0, 5.9.3, and 6.0.0. Which is the newest version init may select?
options: None; two-part constraints like ~> 5.0 are invalid
5.0.0, because ~> pins the exact version written
5.9.3, because ~> 5.0 allows anything at or above 5.0.0 and below 6.0.0
6.0.0, because ~> always allows the next major release
explain: With two components, ~> 5.0 means >= 5.0.0 and < 6.0.0, so 5.9.3 is the newest allowed and 6.0.0 is excluded. It is not an exact pin like the = operator, and two-part pessimistic constraints are valid and common.

q: Which command-line form correctly supplies a backend configuration file during initialization?
options: terraform apply -backend-config=backend.hcl
terraform plan -backend=backend.hcl
terraform backend config backend.hcl
terraform init -backend-config=backend.hcl
explain: The -backend-config flag belongs to terraform init, because the backend must be configured before plan or apply can use remote state. There is no terraform backend subcommand, and apply does not accept backend configuration at that stage.

q: An engineer sets TF_LOG=OFF before running terraform apply in a shared terminal. What effect does this have?
options: It forces Terraform to run offline without providers
It deletes any existing log files in the working directory
It prevents Terraform from writing to the state file
It disables Terraform logging output for that run
explain: OFF is the TF_LOG level that silences logging entirely, which is useful when even error-level diagnostic noise is unwanted. It does not change provider connectivity, delete files, or block state writes, which continue normally during apply.

q: A child module declares variable "environment" with no default. The root passes environment = var.env in the module block, and var.env defaults to dev in the root. Reviewing a plan for production, the module still uses dev. Why?
options: The value flowing into the child is whatever the root variable resolves to at runtime; production required overriding the root variable itself (for example with -var or tfvars), which nobody did
Child modules ignore root arguments when the root variable has a default
Defaults inside child modules always beat caller arguments
The child module cached dev during init
explain: The child faithfully received the root variable's resolved value — dev — because nothing overrode the root input for production. Caller arguments are not ignored (B), init does not cache variable values (C), and a child with no default simply takes what the caller passes (D describes the opposite precedence).

q: An engineer tests an expression in terraform console: `pow(2, 9)`. What does Terraform return?
explain: pow() raises the first number to the power of the second: 2^9 = 512. The distractor values come from applying the wrong operation or rounding the wrong way.

q: A locals block defines a value with the expression `cidrhost("10.1.2.0/24", 254)`. What value does it produce?
explain: cidrhost() returns the address at host number 254 within the prefix, counting from the network address 10.1.2.0, which gives 10.1.2.254.

q: A firm runs hundreds of workspaces and wants CLI-driven configurations to select workspaces dynamically rather than hard-coding one workspace name per directory. Which cloud block feature supports this pattern?
options: A wildcard organization name that spans several organizations
A backend-config file listing every workspace password
Workspace tags in the cloud block, which can match multiple workspaces that share the tags
The terraform workspace command creating matching cloud accounts automatically
explain: The cloud block supports selecting workspaces by tags as an alternative to a single named workspace, which suits large estates managed from shared configurations. There are no workspace passwords, CLI workspaces do not create HCP workspaces, and organization names cannot be wildcarded.

q: What does 'terraform output web_ip' (naming one output) do differently from running 'terraform output' with no arguments?
options: It deletes all outputs except web_ip
It works without state, unlike the bare command
It applies the configuration first, then prints the output
It prints only the web_ip output's value from state instead of listing all outputs
explain: Naming an output selects just that one value from state for display; the bare command lists every output. Neither form applies anything (A) or deletes outputs (C), and both read from the same state, so the named form needs state too (D).

q: A variable declares type = number and a tfvars file supplies the value as the string "8080". What does Terraform do?
options: It stores the value as a string and lets the provider sort it out at apply
It automatically converts the string to the number 8080 because the conversion is unambiguous
It rejects the value because a quoted string can never become a number
It requires the author to wrap the value in tonumber() inside the tfvars file
explain: Terraform automatically converts primitive values when the target type requires it and the conversion is unambiguous, so "8080" becomes the number 8080. Explicit conversion functions exist for manual work, but they are not required for standard primitive conversions in variable assignment.

q: After running terraform login and accepting the prompt to create a token in the browser, where does the CLI use that token?
options: It replaces the need for any workspace variables in remote runs
It is embedded in the state file so teammates can reuse the same identity
It is sent to the cloud provider as the provider credential for every resource call
It authenticates CLI-driven runs and API calls from this machine to HCP Terraform
explain: The token from terraform login authenticates the local CLI to HCP Terraform for CLI-driven runs and API access. Provider credentials are a separate layer handled by workspace variables or dynamic credentials, and tokens are never embedded in state for sharing.

q: A variable is declared sensitive and set through -var-file. In the saved terminal transcript of terraform plan, where does its value appear?
options: In clear text, because -var-file values are exempt from redaction
In a separate secrets section at the end of the plan
In the plan summary line, appended after the counts
Nowhere in clear text; attributes using it render as (sensitive value) in the plan output
explain: Sensitivity follows the value regardless of how it was supplied: CLI output shows (sensitive value) instead of the secret. There is no secrets section or summary leak, and the source of the value (flag, file, or environment) does not change the redaction.

q: A company wants auditors to review infrastructure changes BEFORE they happen, not after. Which IaC workflow feature best supports this?
options: Reviewing server logs after deployment completes
Reviewing screenshots of the console after changes go live
Reviewing the proposed change as a pull request and plan output before merge and apply
Reviewing cloud billing reports at the end of the month
explain: Code review plus plan preview moves scrutiny before execution, which is a core governance advantage of IaC. Billing reports, logs, and screenshots are all after-the-fact evidence and cannot prevent an unapproved change.

q: An engineer tweaked an instance type directly in the cloud console. The next `terraform plan` shows `~` update to revert the instance type to the configured value. What is this phenomenon called, and what caused Terraform to notice?
options: Taint — the resource was marked for recreation
Drift — the real infrastructure diverged from state/config, detected when plan refreshed live values
State locking — caused by concurrent applies
Import — the console change was imported automatically
explain: Drift is out-of-band change; plan's refresh phase reads live values and the diff proposes reverting to config. A is about concurrency. C requires explicit tainting. D is backwards — import brings things under management deliberately, never automatically.

q: A moved block is written in configuration. A new hire expects to run it like a command after saving the file. How does a moved block actually take effect?
options: It only takes effect after the state file is deleted and recreated
It must be executed with terraform moved apply after editing
It is declarative configuration evaluated during plan and apply; Terraform uses it to update state addresses when the plan runs
It runs automatically the moment the file is saved in the editor
explain: Moved blocks are part of configuration, not a CLI subcommand. When plan runs, Terraform follows the from/to mapping, updates the recorded address, and avoids destroy/recreate for that object; the rename is applied as part of the normal run.

q: An architect wants a module fetched from a plain HTTPS URL that serves a zip archive of the configuration. Which source form does that?
options: Modules can never be fetched over HTTP; only Git and the registry are supported
The URL goes in the version argument while source stays empty
The URL must be wrapped so Terraform treats it as a generic package download rather than a registry address
source = "https://example.com/module.zip" used directly, because Terraform auto-detects archives
explain: Arbitrary HTTP(S) archive URLs are supported as module sources and Terraform downloads and unpacks the archive at init. Option A is wrong in its reasoning because a bare URL is still interpreted through source detection rules, and pinning such sources is weaker than Git refs. C is false, and D misplaces the address entirely.

q: A custom CI system builds and tests configurations, then needs to start HCP Terraform runs, upload configurations, and poll run status programmatically as part of a larger pipeline. Which HCP Terraform workflow model fits this design?
options: The API-driven workflow, where the pipeline uses the HCP Terraform API to create workspaces runs and manage run lifecycle
The CLI-driven workflow, because only humans at terminals can start runs
There is no supported model; external CI cannot interact with HCP Terraform runs
The VCS-driven workflow, because all runs must come from Git pushes
explain: The API-driven workflow exists precisely for custom pipelines that create runs, upload configuration versions, and monitor status through the API. VCS-driven and CLI-driven models describe Git-triggered and terminal-triggered runs, and claiming no integration exists ignores the documented API.

q: In a composed root, the compute module block sets subnet_id = module.network.private_subnet_id and the database module block sets vpc_id = module.network.vpc_id. A reviewer asks where the depends_on arguments are that force network to be created first. What is the correct answer?
options: The modules run in alphabetical order by block name, which happens to put network first here only by luck

Terraform infers the ordering from the output references themselves: passing module.network outputs as arguments tells Terraform the compute and database modules depend on the network module, so no explicit depends_on is needed for that ordering
Every module block in a composition is required to list depends_on for correctness
The ordering only works because all three modules share one state file
explain: References are dependencies: when a module block argument reads another module's output, Terraform's graph orders the consumer after the producer automatically, and explicit depends_on is reserved for dependencies no reference can express. Execution order is graph-driven, never alphabetical (C), sharing a state file does not order anything (D), and A turns a fallback tool into a false requirement.

q: A workspace's state tracks 30 resources. Without removing any configuration blocks, an operator runs terraform destroy and approves it. What is the end state of the workspace?
options: The configuration files are deleted along with the resources
Only resources whose blocks were deleted beforehand are destroyed
All 30 tracked resources are destroyed in reverse dependency order, and their entries are removed from state, while the configuration files remain on disk for a future apply to recreate everything
The 30 resources keep running but are removed from state
explain: Destroy acts on state regardless of the blocks still present, tears down everything tracked in reverse order, and leaves the configuration intact — which is why a later apply can rebuild the same environment. It never deletes .tf files and never merely untracks running resources.

q: A company creates a variable set containing the standard logging endpoint and compliance contact used by sixty workspaces. A new workspace is created for a new product. How does it receive those standard values?
options: The variable set only works for workspaces created in the same project on the same day
Someone must retype the values into the workspace, because variable sets cannot be reused
The values are copied into the configuration code during workspace creation
The variable set is applied to the workspace, and its values become available to that workspace's runs alongside any workspace-specific variables
explain: Applying a variable set to a workspace makes its variables available to that workspace's runs without duplicating definitions. Retyping defeats the feature, values are not written into code, and sets have no same-day or same-project restriction on application.

q: A company runs production on AWS, analytics on GCP, and DNS with Cloudflare. They want one tool, one language, and one workflow to manage all three instead of learning each cloud's native tooling. Which Terraform characteristic makes this possible?
options: Terraform is faster than cloud-native tools at provisioning
Terraform's provider-agnostic, multi-cloud workflow with a single CLI and language
Terraform automatically translates CloudFormation templates to HCL
Terraform includes free cloud credits for multi-cloud use
explain: Provider-agnosticism — one HCL language and one workflow across providers — is Terraform's core differentiator versus cloud-native tools like CloudFormation or ARM templates. A is unprovable marketing. C is false. D is false; Terraform does not translate CloudFormation.

q: An engineer tests an expression in terraform console: `cidrsubnets("10.0.0.0/16", 8, 8)`. What is displayed?
explain: cidrsubnets() allocates consecutive subnets of the requested sizes in order: the first /24 is 10.0.0.0/24 and the second is 10.0.1.0/24.

q: Which statement about whether Terraform can operate without any state is correct?
options: State can be disabled with a flag for stateless applies in production
State is only required for the local backend, not for remote backends
State is optional and only needed when using modules
State is required for Terraform to track managed resources across runs; without it Terraform cannot know what it already manages
explain: Terraform requires state to map configuration to real infrastructure, track metadata, and compute diffs between runs. Remote backends still store state, just remotely, and there is no supported stateless mode for normal managed resources.

q: A team writes: { for name, cfg in var.services : name => cfg.port if cfg.enabled }. What does this expression produce?
options: The original map unchanged, because for expressions cannot filter
A list of ports for every service, including disabled ones
A new map keeping each enabled service's key mapped to its port, with disabled services filtered out by the if clause
A set of service names with no values attached
explain: A for expression over a map iterates key/value pairs, the => form builds a result map, and the trailing if clause filters which elements are included. Disabled services are excluded entirely; the result is a transformed map, not a list or a set.

q: A module outputs the value of `formatdate("DD MMM YYYY", "2026-10-23T12:00:00Z")`. What is displayed?
options: 23 Oct 26
explain: formatdate() renders the timestamp with the given specifiers: DD is the day, MMM the abbreviated month name, and YYYY the four-digit year.

q: A pipeline runs terraform init -backend-config=base.hcl -backend-config="key=prod/app.tfstate" so shared settings come from a file and the state key is overridden per environment. How do multiple -backend-config values behave?
options: Each value initializes a separate backend and Terraform load-balances state between them
Only the first value is used and the rest are silently ignored
They are combined, with later values taking precedence for any key set more than once, completing the partial backend configuration together
Terraform errors out because the flag may only appear once
explain: -backend-config may be specified multiple times; the values merge into one effective backend configuration, and a later occurrence wins when the same key is set twice, which is exactly how the pipeline overrides just the key. Terraform supports a single backend per configuration (D), never errors merely because the flag repeats (C), and does not ignore trailing values (A).

q: A managed file server's underlying volume is corrupted at the block level, yet its configuration attributes have not changed, so normal plans show no diff. What is the appropriate operational response?
options: Run terraform refresh, which repairs corrupted volumes in place
Wait for the next plan, because Terraform automatically detects block-level corruption
Edit an unrelated tag back and forth until apply rebuilds the volume
Force replacement with -replace so Terraform destroys and recreates the object even though configuration is unchanged
explain: Replacement flags exist for exactly this gap: the object is broken in reality while configuration shows no change, so an operator explicitly forces recreation. Terraform cannot detect low-level corruption on its own, tag churn does not rebuild anything, and refresh only reads state without repairing infrastructure.

Parity comes from sharing one definition: topology and dependencies match across environments, and legitimate differences are explicit variable values. Costs and data are not made identical, and variables are the mechanism that makes the controlled differences possible.
options: Prod data is automatically copied into dev for testing
Dev and prod become byte-for-byte identical in cost
Variables are eliminated so environments can never differ
Environment parity, because structure and wiring stay the same while only declared inputs differ
q: A retailer builds dev and prod from the exact same Terraform module, passing a small instance size and one replica for dev and larger sizes with three replicas for prod. What benefit does this pattern deliver?
A subnet resource sets 'vpc_id = aws_vpc.main.id'. Beyond passing a value, what else does this reference do?
options: It merges the two resources into a single object
It copies the VPC's tags into the subnet
Nothing else; ordering must still be declared separately in every case
It records an implicit dependency so Terraform creates the VPC before the subnet and destroys them in reverse order
explain: Attribute references are how Terraform builds its dependency graph: the referencing resource depends on the referenced one automatically. No separate ordering declaration is needed for this case (A), the resources remain distinct objects (B), and tags are not copied by a reference (D).

q: During a code review, a teammate asks what `substr("terraform", 0, 5)` evaluates to. What does Terraform return?
options: terr
terraform
terra
form
explain: substr() takes characters starting at offset 0 for a length of 5, giving "terra".

q: A platform monorepo holds three environment roots (environments/prod, environments/staging, environments/dev) that all reuse the same in-house modules. Which layout follows the common convention for the shared module code?
options: A top-level modules/ folder at the repository root holds the shared child modules, and each environment root calls them with a relative source such as ../../modules/vpc
Shared modules live inside the environments/prod folder and the other environments import from prod
Shared modules are stored in a folder named after the first engineer who wrote them
Each environment folder keeps its own private copy of every module it uses
explain: Keeping reusable child modules in a single top-level modules/ directory, referenced by relative local paths from each environment root, is the standard monorepo pattern: one maintained copy, many callers. Copying modules per environment (A) guarantees drift, sourcing from another environment (C) couples staging and dev to prod, and D describes no convention at all.

q: A team writes a second provider block for the same provider type and gives it alias = "eu". What does the alias accomplish?
options: It publishes the provider to a second registry namespace
It pins the provider to an older version for one region
It creates an additional, separately configured instance of that provider that resources can select
It renames the provider so the original block is deleted
explain: An alias defines an extra configuration of the same provider type, for example a different region or account, that resources opt into explicitly. It does not rename or remove the default block, publish anything, or change version selection.

q: A plan takes nine minutes because refresh reads thousands of resources. For a quick syntax-adjacent preview of a tagging change, the engineer adds -refresh=false. Which statement best describes the result?
options: The plan automatically falls back to a full refresh if any drift exists
The diff is computed from the last recorded state, so a resource deleted in the console an hour ago will still appear unchanged in this plan
The plan will fail because -refresh=false is incompatible with tag changes
The state file is deleted and rebuilt from the configuration
explain: Skipping refresh means planning against stale recorded state: the console deletion is invisible until a refreshing plan runs. The flag is valid for any change type, never triggers a hidden refresh, and does not rebuild or delete state.

q: A for expression iterates over a map variable without an if clause and without grouping. In what order does Terraform process the map's keys during iteration?
options: Lexical (sorted) order of the keys, because maps iterate in key order
Random order that changes on every run
The order the provider returns the keys in
Insertion order from the tfvars file
explain: For expressions over maps iterate keys in lexical order, which makes map-derived results deterministic across runs. Lists iterate in their element order instead; insertion order from a file is not a map property once values are loaded.

q: Does Terraform automatically retry later or automatically force-unlock when it encounters a state lock held by another run?
options: Yes, after 60 seconds Terraform force-unlocks automatically
Yes, terraform apply includes an automatic unlock retry loop by default
No, Terraform reports the lock error and stops; unlocking a stuck lock is a deliberate manual action
Only in HCP Terraform, where locks expire after one minute
explain: Terraform never force-unlocks on its own; it surfaces the error with the lock ID and exits. Automatic unlocking would defeat locking, because a slow legitimate run looks identical to a stale lock from the outside.

q: After converting a single module call to for_each, other code that read module.app.endpoint now fails. How must the reference change for the prod instance?
options: module.app.endpoint.prod
module.app["prod"].endpoint — for_each module instances are addressed by their map key
data.module.app["prod"].endpoint
module.app.*.endpoint with a splat, which is the only valid form
explain: for_each turns the module into a map of instances, so outputs are read per instance as module.app["prod"].endpoint. The old bare reference (and B's reordering) no longer resolves, modules are not data sources (A), and while splats can collect all instances, they are not the way to read one named instance (D).

q: Two resources have no references between them and no depends_on. During apply, what ordering guarantee exists between them?
options: Terraform refuses to apply configurations with unrelated resources
No ordering is guaranteed; Terraform may create them in any order or in parallel because the graph has no edge between them
They are guaranteed to be created in file order
The resource with the longer name is created first
explain: Ordering comes only from graph edges — references or explicit depends_on. Unrelated resources are independent nodes that Terraform can process concurrently. File order (A) and name length (C) play no role, and unrelated resources in one configuration are completely normal (D).

q: An engineer says: 'Our Terraform code is our documentation, so a new hire can read the repository to learn the architecture.' When is this claim strongest?
options: When the repository is private and never updated
When the code is complete, current, and is the actual source used to build the environments
When documentation means screenshots stored outside the repository
When the team also maintains a separate secret wiki as the real source
explain: Configuration-as-documentation only holds when the code is the real, current source of truth for what gets built. Stale, private, or bypassed code documents nothing reliably, and screenshots outside the repo are the manual pattern IaC replaces.

q: A variable has a default in its declaration and is also set in terraform.tfvars. Which two statements about precedence are true? (Choose two.)
options: A value in terraform.tfvars overrides the declared default
TF_VAR_ environment variables override -var flag values
The declared default overrides terraform.tfvars
A -var flag value overrides both the tfvars value and the default
explain: Precedence rises from the default (lowest) through TF_VAR_ environment variables, tfvars files, auto.tfvars, -var-file, and finally -var flags (highest). So tfvars beats the default, and -var beats everything — including environment variables.

q: A workspace was initialized months ago. A colleague adds a brand-new provider to required_providers and runs terraform validate, which reports that the provider's schema is unavailable. What is the root cause?
options: Validate never works with more than one provider in a configuration
Init has not been re-run since the requirement was added, so the new provider was never downloaded and its schema cannot be loaded
The new provider must be added to the backend block first
The lock file must be deleted before validate can see new providers
explain: Validate reasons over provider schemas, and schemas only exist locally after init installs the provider into .terraform/providers. The sequence is always: declare the requirement, run init, then validate. Backends and lock deletion have nothing to do with schema availability.

q: A team configures the AWS provider with hardcoded `access_key` and `secret_key` arguments in `provider "aws"`. What is the exam-correct best practice, and why?
options: Pass credentials via environment variables or shared config files instead — never commit secrets to version-controlled configuration
Credentials must always be passed with `-var` on the command line
The AWS provider does not accept credentials; it uses IAM roles only
Hardcoding is fine as long as the file is committed to a private repository
explain: Provider credentials belong in environment variables, shared credentials files, or workload identity — never in committed configuration. A is the classic exam trap: private repos still leak, get cloned, and get breached. C is too narrow (one of several valid methods). D is false; the provider accepts multiple auth methods.

q: A module block specifies both count = 2 and a providers map passing aws = aws.west. A reviewer worries the two instances might split across regions. What actually happens?
options: Both instances receive the same passed provider configuration from the providers map; per-instance provider variation requires separate module blocks or for_each-driven calls with different arguments
Each count instance gets a different provider automatically
The combination of count and providers is invalid and init fails
count automatically load-balances providers
explain: The providers map applies uniformly to every instance a single block creates; varying providers per instance means restructuring the calls. Terraform never rotates providers across count instances (A, C), and count with providers is valid syntax that plans fine (D).

q: A team pipes 'terraform output -json' into a deployment script. Why is the JSON form preferred over scraping the human-readable apply output?
options: Because JSON gives a stable, structured name-to-value mapping that scripts can parse reliably, while console formatting is meant for people and can change
Because JSON output bypasses the need for state
Because terraform output without -json deletes the values after printing
Because the human-readable output is encrypted
explain: Automation needs a parseable contract, and -json provides output names, values, and types in one structured document. Console output is not encrypted (A), plain terraform output does not consume or delete values (C), and both forms read from the same state (D).

q: A root module calls module "net" with for_each over a map, and module "app" needs, for each environment, the subnet output of the matching net instance plus a guarantee app is planned after net completes even where no direct reference exists for one legacy environment. Which combination correctly expresses this?
options: depends_on inside the net child module pointing at module.app
Outputs from for_each modules can only be consumed with count.index

The app module block takes subnet_id = module.net[each.key].subnet_id for keyed access, and an explicit depends_on = [module.net] on the app module block covers the environment lacking a data reference
module.app reads module.net.subnet_id directly and relies on alphabetical ordering
explain: Keyed instance access module.net[each.key] pairs matching instances, and module blocks support depends_on on whole modules for ordering that references cannot express. Direct unkeyed access fails for for_each modules (B), depends_on belongs in the dependent block rather than the dependency (C), and count.index is irrelevant under for_each (D).

q: Documentation for a migration states that operators must stop using terraform taint and start using the modern replacement mechanism. Which mechanism is meant?
options: Running terraform state mv with the -taint option
Passing -replace with the resource address to terraform plan or terraform apply
Adding a tainted = true argument inside the resource block
Setting TF_LOG=DEBUG so apply recreates unhealthy resources
explain: Since taint was deprecated, the supported way to force recreation is the -replace flag on plan or apply, scoped to a specific address. There is no tainted argument in resource blocks or -taint option on state mv, and logging verbosity never changes lifecycle behavior.

q: A published module's registry page shows an Inputs table, but the Description column is blank for every row even though the README explains each input at length. What is the author missing?
options: Descriptions must be repeated in the module's source argument at every call site
The README must be renamed to INPUTS.md for the registry to parse it
A docs.tf file listing the descriptions separately
A description argument inside each variable and output block, because the Inputs and Outputs tables are generated from the variable and output declarations themselves, not from the README prose
explain: Registry and generated module documentation build the Inputs and Outputs tables from the actual variable and output blocks, and the Description column comes from each block's description argument. README text (and D's invented filename) never feeds those tables, no docs.tf file exists in the convention (A), and call sites play no part in documenting the module (B).

q: A plan summary reads: `Plan: 2 to add, 1 to change, 0 to destroy.` What does this tell the reviewer?
options: Two resources will be created, one will be updated in place, and nothing will be deleted
Two resources will be destroyed and one created
The plan failed — these numbers should always be zero
Two data sources will be read and one state file rewritten
explain: The summary is literal: 2 creates (+), 1 in-place update (~), 0 deletions. B inverts the meaning. C is wrong — non-zero plans are the normal reason you run plan. D confuses the summary with data-source reads (<=).

q: After cloning a Terraform repository, which file tells you the exact provider versions and checksums the team last used, so your run matches theirs?
options: .terraform.lock.hcl
main.tf
versions.tf
terraform.tfstate
explain: The dependency lock file records exact provider versions and hashes selected at init. Commit it so every run is reproducible. A holds configuration, not versions. B is state, not provider pins. D is a conventional filename for version constraints, not the recorded selections.

q: Provider logs are essential for a support case, but core Terraform messages are drowning them out in a single combined log. Which setting isolates core logging instead?
options: TF_LOG_OUTPUT, which routes core messages to a second terminal
TF_CORE_LOG_PATH, which names a dedicated core log file
TF_LOG_CORE, which controls the log level for Terraform core separately from provider plugins
A provider block argument named core_logging set to false
explain: TF_LOG_CORE is the component-specific counterpart to TF_LOG_PROVIDER, letting engineers tune or quiet core messages while keeping provider detail. The other variable names and provider arguments are invented, and TF_LOG_PATH alone changes destination, not which component is logged.

q: Which two locations or mechanisms does Terraform use when installing modules during terraform init? (Choose two.)
options: Modules are installed into the state file as compressed archives
A modules.json manifest is recorded under .terraform/modules tracking each installed module's source and directory
Modules from remote sources are stored under .terraform/modules in the working directory
Modules are installed into the Terraform CLI binary itself
explain: Init places downloaded modules in .terraform/modules and records them in its modules.json manifest, which is how Terraform maps module calls to installed code. State stores resource data, not module archives (A), and the CLI binary is never modified by init (D).

q: A junior engineer writes 'instance_id = aws_instance.web' hoping to get the instance ID. What is missing?
options: Nothing; a bare resource address returns its ID by default
An attribute selection such as .id, because a reference must name the specific attribute of the resource to use
Brackets with an index, in all cases
A data. prefix in front of the address
explain: A usable reference names type, name, and the attribute being read, such as aws_instance.web.id; a bare two-part address does not select a value. The data. prefix is for data sources (C), and index brackets are only needed for counted or for_each instances, not in all cases (B).

q: An engineer runs `terraform destroy` in a directory whose state tracks 12 resources. The AWS account also contains 5 manually created EC2 instances. What will be destroyed?
options: Nothing — destroy requires a `-target` for each resource
Only resources whose configuration files still exist in the directory
All 17 instances — destroy removes everything in the account
Only the 12 state-tracked resources; the 5 manually created instances are untouched because destroy only acts on what Terraform manages
explain: EXAM TRAP: destroy acts on state, not on the account. Anything Terraform does not track in state is invisible to it — manually created infrastructure survives. (Bringing such resources under management is what import is for.) A overstates destroy's reach. C invents a requirement. D confuses config presence with state tracking.

q: A developer changes a Terraform file, opens a pull request, and two teammates comment on the plan output before merging. Which IaC benefit is the team exercising most directly?
options: Immutable infrastructure through image replacement
Cost optimization through automatic instance rightsizing
Disaster recovery through regional failover
Collaboration through code review, just like application changes
explain: Pull request review of infrastructure code is collaboration and peer review borrowed from software development. No resizing, image replacement, or failover is described in the scenario, so those advantages are not the ones being exercised.

q: A variable uses type = tuple([string, number, bool]). Which assignment is valid for this variable?
options: ["web", 2, true] — exactly three positional values whose types match the declared sequence
["web", 2] — a tuple may omit trailing elements
["web", 2, true, "extra"] — a tuple accepts extra elements at the end
[2, "web", true] — order does not matter as long as all three types are present
explain: A tuple is a fixed-length, positional type: the value must supply exactly the declared number of elements, in order, with matching types at each position. Shorter or longer sequences fail conversion, and reordering breaks the positional type match.

q: A configuration manages twelve workers with count. Only worker index 4 has a corrupted disk and must be recreated, leaving the other eleven untouched. Which command achieves exactly that?
options: terraform taint aws_instance.worker, which recreates every index in one run
terraform apply -replace=aws_instance.worker, which replaces only the most recently changed index
terraform apply -replace=aws_instance.worker[4], scoped to the single indexed instance that is broken
terraform destroy -target=aws_instance.worker[4] followed by removing its block
explain: -replace honors full instance addresses, so the bracketed index targets worker 4 alone and the plan confirms no other index is recreated. The unindexed address does not single out the newest change, taint is deprecated and unscoped here, and destroying plus deleting the block would remove the worker permanently.

q: During a code review, a teammate asks what `element(["eu-west-1", "ap-northeast-1", "us-west-2", "ap-south-1"], 2)` evaluates to. What does Terraform return?
options: ap-south-1
us-west-2
ap-northeast-1
eu-west-1
explain: element() selects by index modulo the list length: index 2 mod 4 = 2, which is "us-west-2". It never errors on an out-of-range index — it wraps around, unlike direct indexing.

q: A project with existing local state adds a remote backend block pointing at a new HCP Terraform workspace and the engineer runs terraform init for the first time. What should they expect?
options: Init silently deletes the local state file and starts the workspace empty
Init detects the existing local state and asks whether to migrate it into the remote workspace; answering yes copies it so the same resources stay managed under the remote backend
Init immediately applies the configuration to create fresh resources in the new workspace
Init refuses to run until the engineer manually uploads terraform.tfstate through the HCP Terraform web UI
explain: First initialization against a new backend triggers Terraform's migration flow: it notices the existing local state and offers to copy it into the remote workspace, preserving management continuity. It does not delete local state silently, require a manual UI upload, or apply anything.

q: A company runs `terraform apply` twice in a row with no configuration changes. The second run reports `0 to add, 0 to change, 0 to destroy`. Which IaC advantage does this demonstrate?
options: High availability
Idempotency — the same configuration applied repeatedly converges on the same result
Immutable infrastructure
Elasticity
explain: Idempotency is exactly this: repeated applies of the same configuration produce no changes after the first converges. Elasticity (A) is about scaling capacity; high availability (C) is about uptime design; immutability (D) is about replacing rather than modifying — related, but the observed behavior is idempotency.

q: Plan output is noisy with core workflow messages, but the engineer only cares about what the AWS provider plugin is doing. Which variable narrows logging to the provider side?
options: TF_VAR_provider, which enables provider-only debug mode
TF_LOG_PATH, which filters core messages out of the log file
TF_LOG_PROVIDER, which sets the log level for provider plugins separately from core
TF_LOG, which can be set to the literal value PROVIDER
