explain: TF_LOG_PROVIDER controls verbosity for provider plugins independently, letting an engineer raise provider detail without core noise. TF_LOG_PATH only chooses the destination file, TF_VAR_ sets input variables, and TF_LOG takes level names like DEBUG, not the word PROVIDER.

A provider address is hostname/namespace/type: registry.terraform.io is the registry hostname, hashicorp is the publisher namespace, and aws is the provider type. The other options scramble the same three tokens; order matters because Terraform resolves each segment in exactly this sequence.
options: Hostname hashicorp, namespace aws, type registry.terraform.io
Hostname aws, namespace registry.terraform.io, type hashicorp
Hostname registry.terraform.io, namespace aws, type hashicorp
Hostname registry.terraform.io, namespace hashicorp, type aws
q: A provider address is written in full as registry.terraform.io/hashicorp/aws. How should the three parts of that address be read?

A teammate applied a console change to a managed cluster, then removed the cluster's resource block from configuration and ran terraform state rm for its address before anyone noticed. Leadership asks for the safest path back to full management of the unchanged real cluster. Which sequence is correct?
options: Run terraform apply immediately so Terraform rediscovers the cluster on its own
Restore management by running terraform destroy, which re-registers orphaned objects

Re-add a resource block matching the cluster's current real attributes, import the cluster with its provider-specific ID using an import block or CLI import, then verify with a plan that shows no changes
Edit the backend configuration so the cluster's old state entry is recreated automatically
explain: The cluster is now an orphan: unmanaged and invisible, so recovery means declaring it again accurately and explicitly importing it, with the clean-plan check proving the block matches reality. Apply cannot rediscover unknown objects, destroy cannot register anything, and backend settings have no power to resurrect removed state entries.

q: Nobody has touched the `prod` workspace in weeks, but the dashboard flags it as `drifted`. What produced this flag?
options: An expired workspace token
The workspace was automatically destroyed
A failed speculative plan
Drift detection — HCP Terraform's scheduled health checks compare real infrastructure against state and flag divergence
explain: HCP Terraform runs scheduled drift detection: refresh the real world, compare to state, flag drifted workspaces in the UI. B is PR-related. C is auth. D is false — detection flags, never destroys.

q: A variable of type list(string) is explicitly assigned null by a caller module. How should resource code that consumes this variable treat that case?
options: Null is converted to a list containing one empty string
Terraform replaces null with the variable's type zero value automatically
A null collection usually means no value was given, so expressions should guard for it, for example with coalesce(var.list, []) or a conditional
Null assignments to typed variables are always rejected at parse time
explain: Terraform allows null as a value for any type, conventionally meaning the argument is omitted, and unguarded length() or indexing against null fails. Guarding with coalesce() to an empty list or a conditional is the standard defensive pattern; null is not auto-expanded into elements.

q: A team stores state remotely but leaves backend credentials in a world-readable CI artifact. An auditor flags this. What is the auditor's core concern?
options: The lock file, not the state, contains all the secrets in this setup
Backend access is the control point for state, so exposed backend credentials expose the plaintext secrets inside state
World-readable credentials force Terraform to use the local backend
CI artifacts automatically corrupt state serial numbers
explain: Whoever can authenticate to the backend can pull state and read its sensitive values, so backend credentials deserve secret-level handling. The exposure does not change which backend is used or corrupt serials by itself.

q: A provider's documentation says releases 7.x require Terraform Core 1.10 or later because they use a newer plugin protocol. The team runs Core 1.9. What is the correct course of action?
options: Force the 7.x provider with init -upgrade; protocol requirements are advisory
Upgrade Terraform Core to a supported release, or stay on a 6.x provider release compatible with Core 1.9
Edit the provider binary to report the older protocol
Set required_version lower so Core accepts the provider
explain: Core and provider compatibility is a real pairing constraint: a provider built on a newer plugin protocol cannot run on an older Core, so one side of the pairing must move. Flags cannot waive protocol checks, binaries are never edited, and required_version describes Core itself rather than unlocking providers.

q: A configuration pins a provider with version = "~> 5.0". Which of these versions would terraform init REJECT as not satisfying the constraint?
explain: The constraint ~> 5.0 allows 5.0.0, 5.31.0 but excludes 4.67.0: it falls outside the permitted range (with ~>, only the rightmost specified version component may increase).

q: A platform team wants one module call to create a complete environment in each of two AWS regions. Which module block feature, combined with provider aliases, supports this cleanly?
options: Modules cannot span regions; separate root configurations are mandatory
count = 2 on one module block with no provider configuration
A single module block with region listed twice in source
Two module blocks with different names, each given a different aliased provider configuration in its providers argument
explain: Calling the module once per region, passing a different aliased provider configuration to each call, is the standard pattern. B source address is a single location (A), count with no provider mapping (C) would build both copies in the default region, and D is false because aliased providers exist for this case.

q: Why do teams commonly keep secrets out of terraform.tfvars files committed to version control?
options: Because tfvars files are published to the Terraform Registry automatically
Because committed files expose the secret values to everyone with repository access; secrets belong in environment variables, secret managers, or uncommitted files instead
Because Terraform refuses to read tfvars files that contain the word password
Because tfvars files cannot contain strings
explain: A tfvars file is plain text, so committing one with credentials leaks them to the whole repository audience. The format handles strings fine (A), Terraform applies no keyword censorship (C), and tfvars files are not published anywhere automatically (B).

q: The plan output ends with: Plan: 3 to add, 1 to change, 2 to destroy. An engineer claims this guarantees exactly 3 new objects will exist after apply. Is the claim fully supported by the summary line alone?
options: No; the summary actually guarantees 6 new objects, one for every counted action

Not entirely: 3 creates are guaranteed, but whether either destroy also produces a successor object depends on the per-resource detail — a destroy shown as -/+ is a replacement that creates a new object, while a plain - destroy does not
Yes; the summary proves both destroys are standalone removals with no recreation
Yes; destroys never create successors under any circumstances in Terraform
explain: The summary counts actions, not object outcomes: the 3 adds are certain creates and the 1 change is an in-place update, but a destroy paired with a create in a -/+ replacement yields a successor object, and only the detail lines reveal that. The distractors that read certainty into the totals, in either direction, are the trap.

q: A pipeline was terminated mid-apply yesterday and today every run reports that state is locked, yet no process is running. What kind of lock is this describing?
options: A permanent lock that can only be cleared by the cloud provider
A stale lock left behind because the run that held it never released it cleanly
A lock created by terraform validate running in the pipeline
A read lock that blocks only data source reads
explain: A killed run can leave a stale lock because it never reached the normal unlock step. Validate does not take a write lock, and stale locks are cleared by the operator with force-unlock using the lock ID, not by waiting for a provider to clear them.

q: A security architect is explaining Sentinel policy sets to auditors. Which two statements are accurate? (Choose two.)
options: A policy set can be scoped to specific workspaces or applied across the organization
Sentinel policies run inside the cloud provider after resources are created and delete violators
Policies in a set all share one enforcement level that can never differ between policies
Sentinel policies evaluate plan output, so they can judge proposed resources before anything is created
explain: Policy sets are assignable to chosen workspaces or globally, and Sentinel judges the plan before creation, which is the point of policy as code gating. Policies do not act as post-creation cleanup inside providers, and enforcement levels are set per policy, so a set can mix advisory, soft-mandatory, and hard-mandatory rules.

q: A team needs the most recent Ubuntu AMI ID at deploy time rather than a hardcoded ID from six months ago. Which approach fits?
options: A variable with the old AMI ID copied into every module
An output block that prints an AMI ID after apply
A resource block for aws_ami that creates a new image each run
A data block for aws_ami with filters such as most_recent and owners, referenced where an AMI ID is needed
explain: A data source query returns current information about existing images at plan time, keeping the configuration current without managing any image. A resource cannot create an AMI lookup (A), a copied variable goes stale (B), and outputs expose values after apply rather than fetching inputs (D).

q: A locals block defines a value with the expression `element(["eu-central-1", "us-west-2", "eu-west-1", "ap-south-1"], 2)`. What does Terraform return?
options: eu-central-1
eu-west-1
ap-south-1
us-west-2
explain: element() selects by index modulo the list length: index 2 mod 4 = 2, which is "eu-west-1". It never errors on an out-of-range index — it wraps around, unlike direct indexing.

Project-level grants apply across the project's workspaces, so separating prod into its own project is what makes the access boundary real: the application team's grant no longer reaches prod at all. Renaming only hides a name, sensitive variables protect values rather than workspace access, and project membership is precisely the mechanism that scopes team access.
options: Rename app-prod so the application team cannot find it in the workspace list
Leave the structure unchanged, because project membership has no effect on what a team can access
Move app-prod into its own project, grant the release team access there, and leave the application team's project-level grant covering only the dev and stage project
Mark the prod workspace variables sensitive so the application team is blocked from the workspace
q: A platform group first placed app-dev, app-stage, and app-prod in one project and granted the application team access at the project level. Auditors now require that the application team must not be able to view or queue anything in prod, while a smaller release team controls prod alone. Which redesign best satisfies the auditors using project boundaries?
Where would you look first to obtain the lock ID needed for a force-unlock decision?
options: In terraform.tfvars, where lock IDs are stored per environment
In the resource's tags in the cloud console
In the .terraform.lock.hcl provider lock file
In the error output of the Terraform command that failed to acquire the lock, which reports the lock details
explain: The lock error message itself prints the lock info including its ID, holder, and time, specifically so an operator can make an informed force-unlock decision. That ID is unrelated to the provider dependency lock file or tfvars.

q: A sensitive variable's value is used to build a non-sensitive output. What risk should the reviewer flag?
options: The sensitive value can leak through the output's display, because sensitivity must be tracked deliberately — the output should also be marked sensitive if it carries the secret
No risk; outputs strip sensitivity automatically in a safe way
The configuration will fail because sensitive and non-sensitive values can never mix
The variable becomes non-sensitive permanently
explain: Sensitivity propagates through expressions, and Terraform will actually require outputs derived from sensitive values to be marked sensitive to avoid accidental exposure; ignoring that leaks secrets in CLI output. The values can mix when handled correctly (C), and the variable's marking is not erased (D).

q: A team renames a module from module.network to module.vpc in code and wants the contained resources to keep running with no recreation, using only declarative configuration. What should they add?
options: A new backend block pointing at the same state file
A lifecycle ignore_changes block on every resource in the module
A removed block for module.network with destroy = false
A moved block from module.network to module.vpc so state addresses follow the module rename
explain: A module-level moved block maps all addresses under the old module path to the new one in state during plan. Removed would drop management, and neither a backend change nor ignore_changes renames state addresses.

q: A database is being handed from the network team's state to the application team's state. The operator pulls both states to local files and runs terraform state mv with -state and -state-out pointing at the two files to move the resource entry. What must happen next for the handover to be complete and safe?
options: Only the destination state needs pushing; the source backend detects the removal on its next refresh

Both modified state files must be deliberately pushed back to their respective backends, and the move must be verified, because an interruption between the two pushes can leave the resource recorded in both states or in neither
The configuration must be destroyed and re-imported in the destination workspace before any push
Nothing further; state mv updates both remote backends automatically when -state-out is used
explain: The -state/-state-out form of state mv edits local state files only; the backends change only when each file is pushed. That two-step, non-atomic process is exactly the risk of cross-state moves: pushing one side but not the other leaves duplicate or missing management records.

q: Two teams share one Git repository holding a platform module. Team A needs the commit on the main branch from March, Team B needs tag v3.0.0. How do their source arguments differ?
options: Both use version arguments with different values
Team A uses a local path and Team B uses the registry
Team A uses ?ref= with the branch name or commit SHA, Team B uses ?ref=v3.0.0; both pin through the ref query parameter on the Git source
Only Team B can pin; branch references are not supported in refs
explain: Git sources pin any Git reference — branch, tag, or commit SHA — through ?ref=, so both teams express their pin the same way with different ref values. Git sources reject version arguments (A), local paths and registry addresses describe different storage entirely (C), and branches are valid refs (D).

q: Which statements about Terraform sets are true? (Choose two.)
options: Sets have no guaranteed iteration order, so code must not depend on element sequence
Set elements must be unique; assigning a duplicate value does not create a second element
Set elements can be retrieved reliably by numeric index, such as element zero
Sets accept mixed element types in a single collection
explain: Sets enforce uniqueness and are unordered, so neither indexing nor sequence-dependent logic is safe with them. Elements of a set all share the collection's element type, so mixing strings and numbers in one set(string) is not permitted.

q: A disaster recovery drill deletes an entire development VPC. The team recreates it exactly from the repository in under an hour. Which combination of IaC properties did the drill prove?
options: Immutability of the cloud provider's control plane
Elasticity and billing consolidation
Reproducibility and safe teardown, because the environment was code-defined and rebuildable
Manual documentation quality
explain: The drill proves the environment existed as reproducible code, making destruction safe and recreation faithful. Elasticity and billing are unrelated, the provider control plane is not the team's infrastructure model, and manual documentation played no role.

Creating networks and managed services from nothing is provisioning, which is Terraform's primary role via provider APIs. Configuration management assumes hosts already exist to configure, and checklists and monitoring do not create the infrastructure at all.
options: A provisioning tool such as Terraform that creates infrastructure through provider APIs
A configuration management tool that tunes packages on servers that already exist
A spreadsheet checklist an engineer follows in the console
A monitoring tool that alerts when servers go down
q: A logistics startup has no cloud footprint yet and needs to create a VPC, subnets, and a managed database from scratch. Which tool category fits this job first?
Two workspaces connect to the same repository: one tracks the release branch, the other tracks the main branch. A push lands on main only. Which workspace queues a run?
options: The release workspace, because release branches always take priority
Only the workspace connected to main, because branch-based triggering queues runs for pushes to each workspace's connected branch
Neither, because a repository can only drive one workspace at a time
Both, because branch settings are advisory in HCP Terraform
explain: Each workspace's VCS settings name its branch, and pushes queue runs only in workspaces connected to that branch. Branch settings are enforced, one repository can drive many workspaces, and no branch has automatic priority over another.

q: What is the purpose of the description argument inside a variable block?
options: It is printed as the resource's name in the cloud console
It sets the variable's value for documentation builds only
It makes the variable sensitive
It documents what the variable is for, shown in generated documentation and module documentation, without affecting the value used
explain: description is human-facing documentation for the variable; it does not supply, change, or hide the value. It is not a value source (A), does not name cloud resources (C), and sensitivity is controlled by the separate sensitive argument (B).

q: A module outputs the value of `element(["eu-west-1", "us-west-2", "eu-central-1", "ap-south-1"], 7)`. What does Terraform return?
options: eu-west-1
eu-central-1
ap-south-1
us-west-2
explain: element() selects by index modulo the list length: index 7 mod 4 = 3, which is "ap-south-1". It never errors on an out-of-range index — it wraps around, unlike direct indexing.

q: A workspace is connected to a Git repository and uses the version control workflow. A developer merges a feature branch change into the connected branch. What does HCP Terraform do without anyone running a CLI command?
options: It opens a new pull request proposing the plan output as code changes
Nothing, until a developer runs terraform apply from a laptop
It immediately deletes the previous state so the new code starts clean
It queues a run for the workspace that plans the merged code, then awaits confirmation or auto-applies according to workspace settings
explain: In the VCS-driven workflow, pushes to the connected branch automatically queue runs in the workspace. No laptop command is needed, state is never wiped on a push, and plan output is shown as run results, not as a new pull request.

q: A caller writes: module "app" { source = "./modules/app"; instance_count = 3 }. The child module has no variable named instance_count. What happens?
options: The child module auto-creates a variable with that name
The value is stored as a root-level variable instead
Terraform ignores unknown arguments in module blocks
Init or plan fails, because arguments in a module block must match variables the child module actually declares (apart from reserved meta-arguments)
explain: Module block arguments correspond to the child's declared input variables; undeclared names are an error, which catches typos early. Terraform does not silently ignore them (A), reroute them to the root (C), or synthesize variables inside the child (B).

q: A company has dev, staging, and prod environments that must never share state, with separate variables and run history for each. In HCP Terraform, how should this be structured?
options: One workspace with three backend blocks, one per environment
Three separate workspaces — one workspace maps to one state file
One workspace and three terraform.tfvars files switched with -var-file
Three organizations, one per environment
explain: The 1:1 rule: one workspace = one state file + one variable set + one run history. A is invalid (one backend per config). B shares one state file — environments would collide. C is massive overkill.

q: A team wants init to forget the previous backend entirely and NOT copy state from it, starting with whatever state the new backend already has. Which flag fits that intent?
options: terraform init -force-copy
terraform init -reconfigure
terraform init -migrate-state
terraform plan -reconfigure
explain: -reconfigure makes init disregard the previous backend configuration and configure the new one without migrating state. That is the opposite choice from -migrate-state and -force-copy, which do copy state forward.

q: The variable "image_id" receives values from several places: TF_VAR_ is set in the shell environment sets it to "ami-0ccc333"; the variable block declares default = "ami-0aaa111"; a value in a file passed with -var-file sets it to "ami-0fff666". No other sources set it. Which value does Terraform use?
options: ami-0fff666
ami-0ccc333
ami-0bbb222
ami-0aaa111
explain: Variable precedence, lowest to highest: default < TF_VAR_ environment < terraform.tfvars < terraform.tfvars.json < *.auto.tfvars < -var-file < -var. The highest source present here is a -var-file flag, so its value "ami-0fff666" wins.

q: A team uses CLI workspaces heavily and migrates to HCP Terraform. A consultant warns that a one-to-one rename is not enough. What is the most important behavioral difference the team must plan around?
options: In HCP Terraform each workspace can have its own VCS connection, Terraform version, execution mode, and team permissions, unlike CLI workspaces that share one configuration and backend setup
HCP Terraform workspaces cannot run terraform plan at all
HCP Terraform workspaces delete their state whenever a run is discarded
CLI workspaces support Sentinel policies but HCP Terraform workspaces do not
explain: HCP workspaces are full environments with independent settings, VCS links, versions, and permissions per workspace. CLI workspaces share the same configuration and backend behavior. HCP workspaces obviously run plans, support policies, and retain state across discarded runs.

q: Why does Terraform need to store the ID of an aws_instance it created, rather than looking it up by name tag at every run?
options: Providers charge extra for lookup queries, so state avoids that cost
Terraform looks up resources by tag by default and only uses IDs for databases
State stores IDs only as a backup in case the provider API goes offline
State maps each resource address to its real-world object using provider IDs, because names and tags are not reliable unique identifiers
explain: State is the mapping from configuration addresses like aws_instance.web to real objects, recorded by their provider-assigned IDs and attributes. Tags can be duplicated or changed, so relying on them would be unreliable; the ID mapping is what lets plan diff config against reality.

q: A team runs terraform plan -out=release.plan on Friday, gets approval, and runs terraform apply release.plan on Monday with no configuration edits in between. What happens at apply time?
options: Terraform applies exactly the saved plan without prompting for confirmation and without re-planning
Terraform discards the saved plan and generates a brand-new plan for approval
Terraform requires -auto-approve to be added or the apply fails
Terraform prompts for variable values because the plan file stores no values
explain: Applying an explicit plan file executes that artifact as-is: no confirmation prompt and no fresh plan, which is the point of the review-then-apply pattern. Variables are already baked into the saved plan, and -auto-approve is unnecessary and not accepted as a substitute.

q: A caller's plan fails with an error that a value for a module variable does not conform to the child's declared type object({ size = number }). The caller passed a map built from mixed CLI variables. What is the most precise diagnosis?
options: The caller must wrap the value in tostring()
The child module needs a provider block to coerce types

Module input values are type-checked against the child variable's type constraint just like root variables, and a map whose values cannot convert to the declared object shape fails before resources are planned
Module inputs skip type checking, so the error must come from a resource
explain: Input variables enforce their type constraints at the module boundary, including complex object conversions; a mismatched structure errors during planning. Module inputs are not exempt from checking (A), provider blocks play no role in coercion (B), and tostring cannot turn a map into an object (D).

q: A child module declares variable "cidr" but the root module never passes it, and the variable has no default. What happens at plan time?
options: The plan fails — required input variables with no default and no passed value are an error
Terraform inherits the value from the root module's variables automatically
The variable silently defaults to an empty string
Terraform prompts interactively for the value
explain: A variable with no default that receives no value is an error — modules are strictly scoped and inherit nothing. A only happens in interactive CLI for root variables in some flows, not module inputs. B and D misunderstand module scoping.

q: A state lock is held by a CI job that is legitimately still applying, but it is taking a long time. A teammate proposes force-unlock to 'speed things up'. What is the risk?
options: Force-unlock only affects plans, never applies that write state
Removing a live lock allows a second write to run concurrently, risking interleaved writes and state corruption
Force-unlock will pause the CI job until it finishes normally
The CI job will automatically reacquire the lock with no risk to state
explain: Force-unlock against a live run defeats the locking guarantee: two writers can then update state at once and corrupt it or lose updates. It does not pause or safely coordinate the running job.

q: Why does `terraform plan` need the state file even when the configuration alone describes everything to be built?
options: The state file caches provider binaries so plan runs faster
Plan diffs the desired configuration against the state (the record of what already exists) to decide what to create, update, or destroy
The state file stores the plan output for later approval
It doesn't — plan works identically with no state file present
explain: State is Terraform's memory of reality: plan compares desired config against recorded state to compute the diff. With no state (first run), everything is new — hence all `+` creates. B confuses state with .terraform/. D confuses state with saved plan files (-out).

q: A project plan lists the artifacts each workflow stage produces. Which artifact belongs to the Write stage of the core workflow?
options: The terraform.tfstate file recording deployed resource IDs
The .tf configuration files that declare resources, variables, and modules
A saved binary plan file ready for execution
The .terraform.lock.hcl file recording selected provider versions
explain: Writing produces configuration: the .tf files are the human-authored declaration of desired infrastructure. A plan file (A) comes from the plan stage, state (B) is written by apply, and the lock file (D) is produced by init, so each distractor belongs to a different stage than Write.

q: How do removing a resource block from the configuration and running terraform destroy differ in scope?
options: Both do exactly the same thing and the choice is purely stylistic
terraform destroy only deletes resources whose blocks were already removed
Removing a block deletes only that resource on the next apply, while terraform destroy plans the destruction of every resource tracked in the workspace state
Removing a block deletes the resource immediately without a plan or apply
explain: Block removal is surgical — one resource leaves through the normal plan and apply — whereas destroy is total for the workspace's state. Neither acts instantly without an apply step, and destroy does not require blocks to be removed first.

q: A consultant notes a team uses Terraform for AWS and also for creating projects in a SaaS CI system and teams in a SaaS chat tool. She calls this evidence against which misconception?
options: That Terraform providers must be written by HashiCorp
That Terraform is only a cloud provisioning tool rather than a general API-driven workflow
That SaaS tools expose no APIs for automation
That version control cannot store SaaS configuration
explain: Using providers for SaaS platforms disproves the cloud-only misconception: Terraform manages any API-backed resource. Providers are written by many vendors and the community, SaaS APIs clearly exist here, and the configurations are versioned like any other.

q: Immediately after fixing every attribute mismatch on an imported resource, an engineer runs terraform plan one more time before calling the import finished. What result confirms success?
options: The plan reports no changes for the imported resource, showing configuration, state, and reality now agree
The plan offers to destroy the imported resource, which proves it is managed
The plan fails validation, which proves the resource block was removed correctly
Any result is acceptable, because plans are not involved after import
explain: A clean plan with no proposed changes for the imported resource is the verification step of every import workflow: it proves the written configuration describes the real object accurately. A proposed destroy signals a serious mismatch, not success, and skipping this check leaves drift hidden.

q: A bank's policy requires every production infrastructure change to be reviewed as a plan before anything is applied, with a guarantee that apply executes exactly what was reviewed. Which workflow satisfies this?
options: `terraform plan -out=tfplan`, review the file, then `terraform apply tfplan`
`terraform plan -refresh-only`, then `terraform destroy`
`terraform validate`, then `terraform apply` immediately
`terraform apply -auto-approve`, then review the logs afterward
explain: A saved plan file decouples review from execution: `apply tfplan` runs the identical artifact that was reviewed, skipping the prompt. B skips review entirely — the opposite of the policy. C never previews changes. D is incoherent: refresh-only proposes nothing, and destroy tears everything down.

q: A platform team wants a constraint that accepts new minor releases of a provider but never a new major release, starting from 4.0. Which constraint expresses this?
options: version = "< 5.0"
version = "~> 4.0.0"
version = "~> 4.0"
explain: The two-component pessimistic constraint ~> 4.0 allows >= 4.0.0 and < 5.0.0, so minor and patch releases arrive but a major release never does. The three-component form would block minor releases too, and the other options either miss the 4.0 floor or only exclude one version.

q: A variable named instance_type is set in four places: TF_VAR_instance_type=large, terraform.tfvars sets medium, an auto.tfvars file sets small, and the command line passes -var="instance_type=xlarge". Which value wins?
options: medium (terraform.tfvars)
xlarge (command-line -var)
large (environment variable)
small (auto.tfvars)
explain: Precedence, lowest to highest: environment variables < terraform.tfvars < *.auto.tfvars < -var-file < -var. Command-line -var always wins.

q: An operator needs a one-off preview with a different instance count without editing any files. Which invocation is correct?
options: terraform plan -var="instance_count=5"
terraform plan -env instance_count=5
terraform plan -var-file=instance_count=5
terraform plan --set instance_count=5
explain: Single values are overridden with -var="name=value" on the command line. -var-file expects a filename containing assignments, not a name=value pair, and --set and -env are not Terraform plan flags.

q: While debugging a configuration, an engineer evaluates `parseint("ff", 16)` in the console. What is displayed?
explain: parseint() interprets the string in the given base: ff in hexadecimal is 15×16 + 15 = 255.

q: A team reads an existing KMS key with a data source and uses its ARN in several resources. Months later the key is rotated externally to a new key selected by the same tags. What happens on the next plan?
options: The plan fails because data source results may never change
The data read runs again and returns the new key's ARN, so the referencing resources show planned updates to use it
Nothing can change, because data source results are frozen at first read
Terraform destroys the old key because it is no longer referenced
explain: Because data sources are re-read during refresh and plan, a lookup by tags follows external changes, and dependents plan updates accordingly. Results are not frozen (A), Terraform does not manage or destroy the external key (C), and changing read results are expected behavior, not an error (D).

q: A team keeps per-environment values in files named dev.tfvars and prod.tfvars. How does the team plan the production environment explicitly?
options: terraform plan -var=prod.tfvars
terraform plan -var-file=prod.tfvars
terraform plan prod.tfvars
terraform plan -env=prod.tfvars
explain: -var-file loads variable values from the named file, so -var-file=prod.tfvars selects the production set. Passing the filename positionally or with -var is wrong because -var sets a single named variable, and -env is not a plan flag.

q: A parent module needs the subnet ID that a child networking module creates. How is that value designed to travel?
options: The parent reaches into the child and references the subnet resource directly
The child writes it to a shared local file the parent reads
The child declares an output for the subnet ID, and the parent references it as module.<name>.<output_name>
The child declares a variable that the parent reads after apply
explain: Outputs are the only sanctioned channel for a child module to return values to its caller. Parents cannot address resources inside a child directly (C), file handoffs bypass Terraform's graph (A), and variables carry values into a module, not back out (D).

q: A change freeze requires proof that no objects will be deleted this week. An engineer runs terraform plan -destroy. What does this command produce?
options: A refreshed state file with all resources removed
A plan that shows the destruction of every resource Terraform manages, without destroying anything yet
An immediate destruction of all managed resources with no prompt
A plan containing only creates and in-place updates
explain: plan -destroy previews a full teardown: it is still just a plan, so nothing is destroyed until an apply or destroy executes it. Confusing it with terraform destroy is the main trap; destroy is the command that actually removes the resources after approval.

q: A resource using count exposes instances aws_subnet.app[0], [1], and [2]. An output needs a list of all three subnet IDs. Which expression is the idiomatic way to build it?
options: aws_subnet.app.id, referenced once for the whole resource
aws_subnet.app[*].id — a splat expression that projects the id attribute across every instance into a list
aws_subnet.app.all_ids, a built-in summary attribute
for_each = aws_subnet.app inside the output block
explain: The full splat expression resource[*].attribute applies the attribute access to every instance of a multi-instance resource and collects the results into a list. A bare resource reference with no index or splat is invalid for a counted resource, and outputs have no for_each argument.

q: An EIP resource references `aws_instance.web.id`. Why does Terraform create the instance before the EIP, even though nothing in the configuration states an order?
options: The EIP resource has an invisible `depends_on` added by the provider
The reference creates an implicit dependency — Terraform builds a dependency graph from references and orders operations automatically
It is coincidence; Terraform creates resources in random order
Resources are always created in alphabetical order by type
explain: Cross-resource references create implicit dependencies; Terraform topologically sorts the resource graph so dependencies are created first. A invents alphabetical ordering. C is wrong — depends_on is explicit and written by you. D denies the deterministic graph ordering.

q: Which two statements about the dependency lock file are true? (Choose two.)
options: Deleting it and re-running init guarantees the same versions will be chosen again
It must be listed in .gitignore because it contains cloud credentials
It records cryptographic hashes so later installs can verify they received the identical provider packages
It is created and updated by terraform init and records the exact provider versions selected
explain: The lock file is init's record of the exact provider selections and their hashes, and committing it is what makes installs reproducible and verifiable. It contains no credentials, and deleting it removes the pinning guarantee because a fresh resolution may pick newer allowed versions.

q: A team uses Terraform to create a Kubernetes cluster, then uses it to manage a SaaS monitoring account and its alert rules through an API provider. What does the second use show?
options: Terraform can only manage resources that run inside a cloud account
Terraform replaces the monitoring vendor's own alert engine
Terraform is service-agnostic and can manage any resource exposed through an API provider
Terraform is limited to infrastructure owned by HashiCorp
explain: Providers exist for SaaS platforms, so Terraform can manage API-backed resources far beyond VMs and networks. It does not replace the vendor's engine; it configures the vendor's service through its API, and ownership by HashiCorp is irrelevant.

q: An engineer renames `aws_instance.web` to `aws_instance.frontend` in the configuration. Without any other change, `terraform plan` proposes to destroy the instance and create a new one. How do you rename it without recreation or downtime?
options: Add a `moved` block mapping `from = aws_instance.web` to `to = aws_instance.frontend` — Terraform updates the state address in place, keeping the same real object
Renames are impossible without recreation
Run `terraform state rm` on the old address first
Add `lifecycle { create_before_destroy = true }`
explain: A moved block tells Terraform the address changed but the object is identical — state is rewritten, zero destruction. B would make Terraform plan to create a brand-new instance. C changes replacement ordering, not addressing. D denies the exact feature built for refactoring.

q: Like apply, `terraform destroy` prompts for confirmation. An engineer wants to script nightly teardown of a dev environment. Which is the correct automation approach?
options: Run `terraform plan -destroy` and exit — the plan alone tears down the environment
`-auto-approve` is not supported on destroy; nightly teardown must be manual
Pipe `yes` into the command with `yes | terraform destroy`
Use `terraform destroy -auto-approve` in the scheduled job, after the pipeline has already reviewed what will be destroyed
explain: -auto-approve is the designed automation path for both apply and destroy, used inside pipelines where review happened earlier. A is a hack the exam would not bless. C is wrong — plan -destroy only previews destruction. D is false; the flag works on destroy.

q: A variable declares type = bool but a legacy tfvars file supplies the string "true". What is the outcome?
options: The value is treated as the non-empty string and always evaluates as false
The variable silently becomes type string for the whole run
The plan fails because bool never converts from string
Terraform converts the string "true" to the boolean true automatically
explain: Automatic primitive conversion covers string-to-bool for the unambiguous values "true" and "false", just as it covers string-to-number. The declared bool type stays in force; the input representation is converted, not the constraint.

q: A variable needs to hold a structured server spec: a name (string), a CPU count (number), and a list of tags. Which type fits, and how does it differ from a tuple?
options: `tuple([string])` — the only complex type allowed for variables
`map(string)` — identical to an object in every way
`object({ name = string, cpus = number, tags = list(string) })` — an object types each attribute by name, while a tuple is a fixed-length sequence of positional types
`list(string)` — it holds mixed attribute types
explain: object() gives each named attribute its own type — the workhorse for structured variables. A tuple is positional ([string, number]) with fixed length. A is wrong (list(string) holds only strings). C is wrong (maps have uniform value types). D is false.

q: A module is called with source = "github.com/org/network" and version = "1.2.0". What happens at terraform init?
options: Init converts the Git URL to a registry address automatically
Init downloads the module and pins version 1.2.0
Init ignores the version and uses the repository's default branch
Init fails — the version argument is only valid for registry sources, not Git
explain: version is only valid for registry module sources. Git sources are pinned with ?ref= (e.g., source = "github.com/org/network?ref=v1.2.0"). A describes registry behavior. C and D are false.

q: An organization compares two integrations: a Sentinel policy that checks tags in the plan, and a run task that sends plan data to an external image-scanning service. What is the fundamental difference between the two mechanisms?
options: Sentinel runs only on developer laptops, while run tasks run in the cloud
There is no difference; run tasks are simply Sentinel policies with a different name
Run tasks replace Sentinel entirely and make policies impossible to use
Sentinel evaluates rules inside HCP Terraform's run lifecycle, while a run task calls out to an external integration at a run stage and reports a pass or fail result back
explain: Sentinel is HCP Terraform's built-in policy-as-code engine judging plans, whereas run tasks integrate external tools at run stages and return results that can be advisory or mandatory. They coexist rather than replacing each other, Sentinel runs server-side in the run lifecycle, and the mechanisms are genuinely distinct.

q: An organization is tightening governance across fifty workspaces. Which two actions use HCP Terraform collaboration and governance features as designed? (Choose two.)
options: Sharing one personal API token among all operators so actions appear to come from a single account
Recording run history so every plan, apply, and confirmation is attributable to a user
Assigning teams different workspace permission levels so auditors can read production while operators hold write access
Disabling run records in production to keep the workspace list tidy
explain: Team-based permission levels enforce who can view, plan, apply, or administer each workspace, and run history provides the attributable audit trail governance requires. Sharing tokens destroys attribution, and run records cannot and should not be disabled for tidiness.

terraform state list is purely read-only: it prints the addresses Terraform already tracks, giving an inventory with zero mutation risk. Apply reconciles and can change infrastructure, import writes a new state entry, and state mv rewrites state addresses, so none of those are safe first inventory steps.
options: terraform import, which lists resources by adopting them
terraform state mv, which inventories resources by renaming them
terraform state list, which enumerates every resource address currently recorded in state without modifying anything
terraform apply, which inventories resources by reconciling them
q: You inherit a production workspace you have never seen before and must build an inventory without changing any infrastructure or state. Which single command is the safest first step?
A module author wants callers to be able to omit the tags input entirely. How should the child's variables.tf define it?
options: Declare variable "tags" with no type and no default
Callers can always omit any input, so nothing special is needed
Declare variable "tags" with a default value, such as an empty map, making the argument optional for callers
Declare variable "tags" as sensitive = true
explain: An input variable with a default is optional; without a default it is required and omitting it errors. Option A leaves the variable required despite having no type, sensitive (B) only hides values in output, and D is false for required variables.

q: A root configuration calls an external module published on a registry. After init succeeds, where does Terraform keep its local copy of that downloaded module?
options: In the provider binary's installation folder under .terraform/providers
Under .terraform/modules in the working directory
Inside terraform.tfstate, so the module travels with the state
Appended to the end of the root module's main.tf file
explain: Downloaded modules are installed under .terraform/modules, separate from provider binaries, which live under .terraform/providers (B). Modules are never embedded in state (A) or merged into your source files (C); your .tf files keep only the module call, and init fetches the implementation.

q: Which file layout will the public registry expect when it ingests a published module?
options: Only a README; the registry generates the .tf files from it
Standard module structure: main.tf, variables.tf, and outputs.tf at the repository root, plus a README describing the module
A single file named module.tf containing everything
Files nested under a src/ directory with no root-level .tf files
explain: The registry expects the standard module structure at the root — main.tf for resources, variables.tf for inputs, outputs.tf for outputs — and renders the README as the module's documentation. A lone module.tf (B) breaks the convention, the registry never generates configuration (C), and burying files under src/ (D) leaves no root module to publish.

The lock file's hashes exist to guarantee the exact provider build the team selected; a mismatch means what arrived is not what was locked, and the safe path is to investigate and either fix the supply or intentionally re-lock. Hand-editing hashes (the main distractor) defeats the entire integrity check while looking like a fix.
options: Re-run init with -get-plugins=false; that disables checksum checking for mirrored providers
Edit .terraform.lock.hcl by hand and paste in the new checksum so init proceeds

Treat it as an integrity failure: the delivered package is not the locked selection (corrupt, wrong build, or wrong platform), so verify the source, restore the correct package, or deliberately regenerate the lock with terraform providers lock if the change is legitimate
Delete the lock file permanently; checksum verification is optional and safe to skip
q: terraform init downloads a provider from the team mirror and then fails, reporting that the package's checksum does not match the hashes recorded in .terraform.lock.hcl. What is the exam-correct response?
A healthcare company must show regulators a complete trail of infrastructure changes for the past year. They manage everything with Terraform in Git with protected branches. Which statement is true?
options: They still have no record because Terraform deletes change history after apply
They can reconstruct who changed what, when, and through which reviewed merge for the entire year
Regulators require console change logs instead of code history
Git history only records file names, not content changes
explain: A year of commits and merges in Git is exactly the change trail regulators want: content diffs, authors, timestamps, and approvals. Terraform does not erase Git history, and Git records full content changes, not just filenames.

q: Beyond mapping configuration resources to real-world IDs, which foundational metadata does Terraform state record to make future plans correct?
options: Resource dependencies and attribute values captured when resources were created or last refreshed
The source code of every provider plugin in use
User credentials for each provider, rotated automatically
A rolling backup of the configuration files from each apply
explain: State stores each managed object's attributes and its dependency relationships, which Core uses to order operations and compute diffs. Plugin code lives in .terraform, configurations live in version control, and state does not rotate anyone's credentials.

q: An engineer runs `terraform state rm aws_instance.old` and a colleague runs `terraform destroy -target=aws_instance.old` in a different, identical setup. What is the difference in outcome?
options: state rm removes the resource from state but leaves the real instance running; destroy deletes the real instance
There is no difference — the commands are aliases
state rm deletes the instance and destroy only removes it from state
Both destroy the EC2 instance
explain: EXAM TRAP, tested constantly: `state rm` = forget (object lives on, unmanaged); `destroy` = delete the real infrastructure. A and C swap or merge the meanings. D is false — they are opposites in effect on the real world.

q: A resource was created with count and only instance [1] needs to move to a new address. How should the state mv source be written?
options: With only the module name, because individual instances cannot be moved
By deleting the whole resource from state and reimporting instance 1
With its full instance address, for example 'aws_instance.web[1]' as the source argument
Individual count instances can never be addressed in state commands
explain: Count and for_each instances have distinct addresses including their index or key, and state commands can target that exact instance. Moving just [1] does not require removing the entire resource from state.

q: A variable `ami_id` must reject any value that does not start with `ami-`. Where does this rule belong?
options: In the `terraform` block under `required_version`
In a `precondition` on each resource using the variable
In a `check` block at the root
In a `validation` block inside the variable declaration, with a `condition` and an `error_message`
explain: Variable validation blocks reject bad input at the earliest moment — before plan even evaluates resources. B works but is the wrong layer (preconditions guard resource actions, not input). C constrains Terraform CLI versions. D warns post-apply instead of rejecting early.

q: An S3 backend block is placed in main.tf alongside resources. A reviewer says backend configuration does not belong in a resource block. Where does it belong?
options: Inside the terraform block, as a nested backend block
In terraform.tfvars as a backend variable map
Inside a provider block for the cloud being used
In a separate data block named backend
explain: Backend configuration lives in the terraform settings block as backend "<type>" with its arguments. Provider blocks configure providers, tfvars supply variable values, and there is no backend data block.

q: A pipeline stage runs terraform plan -out=app.plan , and the next stage runs terraform apply -auto-approve with no file argument, assuming it will pick up app.plan. What actually happens in the apply stage?
options: Apply finds app.plan automatically because it is the only .plan file present
Apply ignores the saved file, generates a fresh plan from the current configuration and state, and auto-approves that new plan, so the reviewed artifact is not what runs
Apply applies app.plan and also re-plans to verify they match
Apply fails because a saved plan exists and must be consumed first
explain: Apply only uses a saved plan when the file is passed as an explicit argument; otherwise it plans fresh, and -auto-approve then removes the human check on that unreviewed plan. Terraform never auto-discovers plan files, which is why the pipeline must pass the filename.

q: A configuration contains the expression `replace("prod-web-01", "prod", "dev")`. What value does it produce?
options: dev-web-01
prod-dev-01
prod-web-01
dev-web
explain: replace() substitutes every occurrence of the search substring, so only the leading prod segment changes to dev.

q: An engineer runs `terraform apply -auto-approve` from their laptop during a production incident `to go faster`. What is the exam-correct view of this?
options: `-auto-approve` only works with `terraform destroy`, not apply
Acceptable only in automation (CI/CD) where the plan was already reviewed; by hand it skips the last safety check and is treated as a red flag
Best practice — incidents justify skipping confirmations
Required — apply will not run in production without it
explain: -auto-approve is for automation pipelines where review happened earlier (e.g., on the saved plan). Interactively it removes the final human confirmation — the exam treats that as dangerous. A glorifies skipping safety. C is false. D is false; the flag works on both apply and destroy.

q: After a moved block has done its job in a shared repository, one teammate still has an old branch that never applied it. What risk does deleting the moved block immediately create for that teammate?
options: No risk exists, because moved blocks apply globally to all branches at once
Their next plan from the old branch may propose destroying and recreating the renamed resources, because their state has not yet recorded the new address through the moved mapping
The moved block deletion recreates the resources for everyone immediately
Their local state file will be deleted automatically by Git
explain: Moved mappings only help runs that actually execute a plan containing them while state still uses the old address. Premature cleanup strands anyone whose state has not migrated, which is why teams keep moved blocks until all state copies have moved past the rename.

q: Which two kinds of problems is terraform validate designed to catch? (Choose two.)
options: Real-world resources that were deleted in the console outside Terraform
Argument names and value types that do not match the provider's schema, and references to objects the configuration does not declare
Expired or missing cloud provider credentials
HCL syntax errors and malformed block structure in the configuration
explain: Validate covers static correctness: the HCL must parse and be structurally sound (A), and arguments, types, and references must agree with provider schemas and the configuration itself (C). Credentials (B) are never consulted, and out-of-band deletions (D) are drift, which only refresh during plan can observe by calling real APIs.

Once apply has performed an import, the resource is managed normally and the block has no further effect, so keeping it is harmless but adds noise to configuration reviews. It does not block updates, trigger recreation, or protect the resource from destruction if the block is later removed.
options: They are harmless but noisy: the import already happened, so they add clutter to reviews and should be removed for hygiene
They must stay forever or Terraform will destroy the imported resources
They will force the resources to be re-imported and briefly recreated on the next apply
They prevent any future updates to the imported resources until they are deleted
q: Three months after a successful migration, the import blocks used for the adoption are still in the configuration and every plan is clean. What is the accurate assessment of leaving them there?

A team uses the same registry module in a dev root and a production root. They want early warning of upstream changes in dev but zero surprise upgrades in production. Which pinning strategy matches that intent?
options: Give dev a loose constraint such as version = ">= 2.0" so fresh inits surface new releases there first, and give production a tight constraint such as version = "~> 2.4.0" or an exact version so it only moves when the team deliberately edits it
Use version = "latest" in dev and no version argument in production
Leave both roots unpinned so they always match each other
Pin both roots to the newest release number manually every Monday
explain: Different environments legitimately want different exposure to upstream releases: a floating dev constraint acts as an early-warning canary, while a tight production constraint makes upgrades an explicit, reviewable edit. There is no "latest" keyword (C), leaving production unpinned (B) creates exactly the surprise upgrades the team wants to avoid, and A couples both environments to a manual chore instead of encoding intent in the constraints.

q: A second pipeline job runs terraform plan -detailed-exitcode and exits with code 0. A teammate wants to run apply anyway to be safe. What is the correct interpretation?
options: Exit code 0 means changes are pending approval
The plan succeeded and there are no changes, so an apply would do nothing
The plan failed silently and apply is required to surface the error
The state file is corrupted and must be rebuilt
explain: Exit code 0 under -detailed-exitcode means a successful, empty plan: configuration and state already agree. It is 2 that signals pending changes and 1 that signals an error, so running apply here is a harmless no-op, not a fix.

q: A company keeps terraform.tfstate on a shared laptop drive with no access controls. A database password set in configuration appears in a security review of that file. Why?
options: The laptop drive automatically decrypts all provider secrets
The password appears because the variable was not marked required
Terraform writes passwords to state only when debug logging is enabled
State stores attribute values, including sensitive values, in plaintext in the state snapshot
explain: Terraform must record the actual attribute values it manages, so secrets that are resource attributes end up in state in plaintext form. Marking a variable required affects input handling, not whether values are persisted in state.

q: Which two statements distinguish state pull from state show? (Choose two.)
options: state show displays the recorded attributes of one addressed resource instance from state
state show uploads a modified snapshot back to the backend
state pull deletes the resource it displays from state
state pull retrieves the entire current state snapshot from the backend
explain: Pull is about obtaining the whole snapshot as stored remotely, while show is a focused view of a single resource instance's attributes. Neither command deletes or uploads state as part of its normal purpose.

q: A team builds a standard tag set once as 'locals { common_tags = { Team = "platform"; Env = var.environment } }' and applies it to twenty resources. What problem does this solve?
options: It defines the tag set in one place so every resource stays consistent and a change is made once, not twenty times
It encrypts the tags in state
It creates the tags as separate managed resources
It lets each resource team override the tags from the command line
explain: Centralizing a repeated expression in a local is a reuse and consistency pattern: edit once, apply everywhere. Locals cannot be overridden from the command line (A), provide no encryption (C), and are values, not managed resources (D).

q: A developer edits required_providers to add the TLS provider and immediately runs terraform plan, which fails saying the provider is not installed. What is the correct next step?
options: Add a provider block for TLS; blocks install providers automatically
Run terraform apply, which installs missing providers as it goes
Restart the terminal so Core rescans for providers
Run terraform init so the new provider is downloaded, its schema loaded, and the lock file updated
explain: Adding a provider requirement always requires re-running init: init downloads the plugin into .terraform/providers, records it in the lock file, and makes its schema available. Apply and provider blocks never install plugins, and a new shell changes nothing.

q: An engineer proposes solving state secret exposure by base64-encoding terraform.tfstate before storing it locally. Why is this not a real control?
options: Terraform state already uses base64 for all sensitive values natively
Encoding is not encryption; anyone who obtains the file can decode it and read the plaintext values
Encoding changes the state lineage and breaks all resource mappings
Base64 makes the state file unreadable to Terraform as well
explain: Base64 is a reversible encoding with no key, so it provides no confidentiality for secrets in state. Real controls are encrypted remote storage and restricted access; encoding also does not alter lineage or mappings when decoded.

q: An engineer tests an expression in terraform console: `lookup({ dev = "t3.micro", staging = "t3.small", prod = "m5.large", qa = "t3.medium" }, "qa")`. What is displayed?
options: t3.micro
t3.medium
m5.large
t3.small
explain: lookup() returns the value stored under the key "qa", which is "t3.medium". Without a third argument, lookup() would error if the key were absent.

q: A growing team of six engineers shares one local terraform.tfstate through a synced folder, and applies begin overwriting each other's work. Which two changes address the root causes? (Choose two.)
options: Move state to a remote backend that supports locking for the team
Require every engineer to rename their local tfstate file before applying
Use the remote backend as the single shared source of truth instead of synced file copies
Disable state locking so synced copies stop conflicting
explain: A shared remote backend gives one authoritative, lockable state location, removing both the divergent-copy problem and concurrent-write races. Renaming local files multiplies divergence, and disabling locking removes protection rather than adding it.

q: A module outputs the value of `index(["eu-central-1", "ap-northeast-1", "us-east-1"], "us-east-1")`. What is the result?
explain: index() returns the zero-based position of the value: "us-east-1" is the third element, index 2.

q: Files named dev.auto.tfvars and prod.auto.tfvars both sit in the same working directory. What should the team understand about them?
options: Only one of them will ever be read, chosen at random
Terraform merges them into a new file named combined.tfvars
Both are auto-loaded because they match the *.auto.tfvars pattern, so keeping conflicting environment files together like this is a mistake
Neither loads; auto.tfvars files must be passed with -var-file
explain: Every *.auto.tfvars file in the working directory loads automatically in lexical order, so two environment files in one directory will both apply, with later files winning conflicts. Selection is deterministic, not random (A); no -var-file flag is needed (C); and no combined file is produced (B).

q: During a design review, a manager proposes saving time by letting engineers apply changes first and produce a plan afterward for the records. Why does the core workflow insist that plan comes before apply?
options: Plan is the only step that downloads the providers apply needs
Plan converts HCL into JSON that the cloud APIs can read
Plan encrypts the state file so that apply can use it safely

Plan previews the creates, updates, and destroys computed from configuration and state, so mistakes are caught before any real resource is changed; a plan produced after apply shows little or nothing and the risky changes have already happened
explain: Plan exists as a pre-execution preview: it diffs desired configuration against state so reviewers can catch an unintended destroy before it happens. Once apply has run, that preview value is gone. Plan does not encrypt state (A), download providers (B, that is init), or translate HCL for cloud APIs (D).

q: A reviewer wants a formatting preview that is guaranteed to leave every file byte-for-byte untouched while still showing what would change. Which combination achieves that?
options: terraform fmt -recursive, because recursion is read-only
terraform fmt -check -diff, because check mode prevents any rewriting while diff displays the changes that would be made
terraform fmt -upgrade, because previewing is part of upgrading
terraform fmt -list=false, because hidden file names cannot be modified
explain: -check turns fmt into a pure gate: it writes nothing, exits non-zero when files are unformatted, and with -diff it also shows the pending changes, giving a safe preview. -recursive (A) happily rewrites subdirectories, -list=false (C) only quiets the file listing, and -upgrade (B) is an init flag, not an fmt mode.

q: You clone a Terraform repository, skip init, and run `terraform plan`. What happens?
options: Plan succeeds but skips the refresh phase
Plan automatically runs init for you and continues
Plan runs using providers cached from a previous project
Plan fails — providers and modules are not installed and the backend is not configured until init runs
explain: Without init there are no provider plugins, no modules, and no backend — plan cannot run and errors out. A is wrong; providers are per-working-directory in .terraform/. C is wrong; there is no degraded plan mode. D is wrong — Terraform never auto-inits (that would hide backend and version decisions).

q: A workspace is pinned to an older Terraform version while the organization standard has moved on. After a version upgrade in workspace settings, the next run fails with state compatibility warnings the team did not expect. What lesson does this illustrate?
options: Terraform version is a per-workspace setting, and changing it can affect how runs interpret state, so upgrades should be planned and tested like configuration changes
State files automatically downgrade themselves after any version change
Workspace settings cannot change the Terraform version once a workspace exists
Terraform version is set globally and cannot differ between workspaces
explain: Each workspace carries its own Terraform version setting, and bumping it is a real change that should be tested because run behavior and state handling can shift. Versions are not global, state never downgrades itself, and the setting is editable after creation.

q: A child module needs the value of the root module's `environment` variable. The child declares no input variable for it. What happens?
options: The child automatically inherits all root variables
The child reads it from the state file
Terraform copies root variables into every child module at init
The reference fails — variables are scoped to their module; the root must pass the value explicitly via a module block argument into a declared input variable
explain: EXAM TRAP: module variable scope is strict. A child sees only its own declared inputs, its locals, and its data sources. Data flows in through module block arguments and out through outputs — there is no inheritance (A), no auto-copying (C), and state is not a variable channel (D).

q: An engineer runs terraform plan -refresh=false against a large workspace to get a fast preview. What tradeoff has the engineer accepted?
options: The plan becomes read-only and cannot be saved with -out
Variable values are ignored for this run
Terraform skips building the dependency graph entirely
The plan is computed against the existing state as-is without reading live resources, so it may miss drift that happened since the last refresh
explain: -refresh=false skips the provider reads that sync state to reality, making plan faster but blind to out-of-band drift until a later refresh. It does not disable -out, the graph, or variables; those all still work normally.

q: A variable declaration includes 'default = null' behavior aside — an author instead simply omits the default and marks the variable in documentation as required. How will CI (non-interactive) runs behave when the value is not supplied?
options: CI runs skip validation of that variable
CI runs generate a value from the variable's description
CI runs proceed with an empty string
CI runs fail with an error that the required variable has no value, because there is no terminal to prompt at
explain: Non-interactive runs cannot answer prompts, so a required variable with no supplied value is a hard error — which is why pipelines pass values via files, environment, or flags. Terraform never substitutes empty strings (A), skips the check (C), or mines the description for a value (D).

q: A constraint reads version = ">= 3.0, < 4.0". Which offered version will init select as the newest match?
explain: Comma-separated constraints are combined with AND logic, so a version must be at least 3.0 and strictly below 4.0; 3.9.0 is the newest match. Version 4.0.0 fails the < 4.0 bound and 2.9.9 fails the >= 3.0 floor.

q: A configuration contains the expression `upper("staging")`. What value does it produce?
options: Staging
STAGING
gnigats
staging
explain: upper() converts every cased character in the string to uppercase.
